Sneha understood that the room told how fair, fixed measures slowly came to be trusted by all.
payload.title: Fixed weights made trade fair for all
decoys: The room held old balance scales and rods
Markets have existed for a very long time
Sneha tried to lift one of the weights

payload.passage: A garden sprinkler spins and sprays water all round. Water rushes in through a hose and out of slanted holes in the arms. As the water shoots out sideways, its push spins the arms round. The turning arms then fling water over a wide circle of lawn. So a sprinkler waters a lawn by spinning as water jets from its arms.
payload.title: How jets of water spin a garden sprinkler
decoys: Water shoots out of slanted holes

payload.passage: A bucket lift uses two buckets and a wheel over a well. The two buckets hang from the ends of one rope over a top wheel. As you lower the empty bucket, the full one rises on the other side. The weight of the falling bucket helps lift the rising one. So a two-bucket lift uses one falling bucket to raise the other.
payload.title: How one falling bucket lifts another at a well
decoys: Both buckets hang from one rope
The empty bucket is lowered down

payload.passage: A beam balance weighs a parcel against a set of known weights. The parcel sits in one hanging pan and small known weights in the other. You add or take away weights until the beam hangs perfectly level. The total of the weights then equals the weight of the parcel. So a beam balance finds a parcel's weight by matching it with known weights.
payload.title: How a beam balance matches a parcel's weight
decoys: The parcel sits in one pan
You add weights until it is level

payload.passage: The guide led Dhruv past a row of grand old statues carved from single blocks of stone. She explained that long ago, sculptors had no glue or joints, so each figure had to be chipped from one piece without a single mistake. One wrong blow could ruin months of work. Dhruv understood that the statues showed the great skill and care of the carvers.
payload.title: Stone statues show the carvers' great skill
decoys: Each statue was carved from one block
Statues can be seen in many places
Dhruv tried to copy a statue's pose

payload.passage: A bookseller runs a shop full of books for the whole neighbourhood. He arranges the books neatly by subject on his shelves. When a customer asks for a story or a textbook, he helps them find it. He keeps new books coming in so there is always something to read. So a bookseller's work is to bring good books to readers.
payload.title: How a bookseller brings books to readers
decoys: He arranges books neatly by subject

payload.passage: The Bird Helpers club fills clay bowls with water and hangs them around the school in summer. They keep the bowls clean and topped up so thirsty birds and squirrels can drink during the hot months. Soon many birds visit the school garden. The club learned that a little water can help small creatures through the summer heat.
payload.title: Water bowls help creatures through summer
decoys: The club hangs clay bowls of water

payload.passage: Aarav rolled a toy car down a ramp onto a smooth tile floor and marked where it stopped. Then he laid a soft towel on the floor and ran the car again from the same spot. On the towel the car stopped much sooner than on the tile. His teacher said the rough towel drags more. Aarav learned that a car rolls less far on a rough surface.
payload.title: A car rolls less far on a rough surface
decoys: Aarav marked where the car stopped
Toy cars are fun to roll
He used a ramp for the car

payload.passage: The Nature Club at school collects empty bottles, jars and boxes that families would throw away. The children wash them carefully and turn them into pen stands, planters and pretty lamps. They sell these at a stall during the school fair. The money they earn buys new saplings for the school garden. The club learned that old things can be made useful and beautiful again.
payload.title: Old things can be made useful again
decoys: The club sells crafts at the fair

payload.passage: A crossing keeper guards the place where a road meets the railway line. When a train is coming, a bell rings to warn him. He quickly lowers the gates so that no car drives onto the track. Once the train has safely passed, he lifts the gates again. So a crossing keeper's job is to keep people safe at the rail crossing.
payload.title: How a crossing keeper guards the rail line
decoys: He lowers the gates when a train is coming
Many helpers keep us safe each day
Trains move very fast on open tracks

payload.passage: A dentist takes care of our teeth and keeps them strong. When we visit, the dentist looks closely at each tooth for any holes. If a tooth has a cavity, the dentist cleans and fills it. The dentist also shows us how to brush and floss the right way. So a dentist's main work is to keep our teeth healthy.
payload.title: How a dentist keeps our teeth healthy
decoys: The dentist fills a tooth with a cavity
Many helpers look after our health
Eating too many sweets can harm teeth

payload.passage: Lata wanted to grow vegetables in pots on her balcony. Her first seeds never sprouted because she poured too much water on them. She read a small gardening book and learned to water only when the soil felt dry. The next batch of seeds pushed up tiny green shoots within a week. Soon her balcony was full of leafy plants and a few shiny tomatoes.
payload.title: Right watering helped Lata grow balcony plants
decoys: Lata's first seeds never sprouted at all
Gardening can feed a whole family forever
Lata kept her vegetable pots on the balcony

payload.passage: A news reporter tells people what is happening around them. She goes to where something important is taking place. She watches carefully and asks questions to learn the facts. Then she writes or speaks the story so others can hear the news. So a reporter's main work is to share true news with people.
payload.title: How a reporter shares the news
decoys: She asks questions to learn the facts
Many people help us in daily life
Newspapers arrive early in the morning

payload.passage: Mihir wanted to learn how to make lemon juice that tasted just right. His first glass was too sour and his second one was too sweet. He learned to taste and add a little sugar or water at a time. The juice slowly came out perfectly balanced and refreshing. Mihir served cool glasses of his lemon juice to thirsty guests.
payload.title: Tasting as he mixed taught Mihir to make lemon juice
decoys: Mihir's first glass was far too sour
Cool drinks are loved by everyone in summer
Mihir served the juice to thirsty guests

payload.passage: Harsh wondered why fields sometimes flood even when the rain falls far up in the hills. His teacher explained that heavy rain on the high hills runs downhill into the rivers, which then carry all that water down to the low plains days later. By the time it arrives, the river is swollen and spills over. Harsh learned that rain in the hills can flood the plains far below.
payload.title: Hill rain can flood the plains far below
decoys: Heavy rain fell on the high hills

payload.passage: A oil-lamp wick can be turned up or down to change the flame. A little wheel on the side moves the cloth wick higher or lower. Raising the wick lets more oil reach the flame, so it burns bigger and brighter. Lowering it makes the flame small and dim. So turning the wick wheel sets how big the lamp's flame burns.
payload.title: How a wick wheel sets a lamp flame's size
decoys: A wheel moves the wick up or down
Raising the wick lets up more oil

payload.passage: Mansi wanted to learn how to make her bed neatly every morning. Her sheets always stayed wrinkled and the pillow ended up crooked. Her mother showed her to smooth the sheet from the centre outwards. With a few minutes of care, her bed began to look tidy and flat. Soon Mansi made her bed neatly without being reminded at all.
payload.title: Smoothing from the centre taught Mansi to make her bed
decoys: A tidy room makes a person feel calm and happy
Mansi's mother showed her a simple trick

payload.passage: At home, the kitchen got smoky whenever Mother cooked with the window shut. The smoke stung everyone's eyes and filled the room. Father fitted a small exhaust fan above the cooking stove. The fan pulled the smoke straight out of the kitchen. Cooking became pleasant and the smoky eyes were a thing of the past.
payload.title: An exhaust fan solved the smoky kitchen
decoys: A good kitchen makes cooking a joy
Father fitted a fan above the stove

payload.passage: An onion is a special bud that grows under the ground. It is made of many soft layers wrapped tightly around each other. The plant fills these layers with food to use later for growing. We dig up this swollen bud and use it in our cooking. So an onion is really a food store packed in layers.
payload.title: An onion is a layered food store
decoys: An onion is made of many soft layers
Plants store food in clever ways
Onions can make our eyes water

payload.passage: The school steps grew slippery with moss during the rainy weeks. A couple of children skidded and the teachers grew worried. A worker scrubbed off the green moss and the steps turned safe again. He added rough strips to give shoes a better grip. The children climbed the steps without slipping after that.
payload.title: Scrubbing the moss solved the slippery steps
decoys: A couple of children skidded on the steps
Rain causes many slips and falls each year
A worker scrubbed off the green moss

payload.passage: At the railway museum, Vivek climbed beside a huge old steam engine. The guide explained that the engine burned coal to boil water, and the rushing steam pushed the wheels along the track. These engines, she said, once carried people and goods across the whole country for the first time. Vivek understood that the old engine showed how steam trains first connected far-off places.
payload.title: Steam trains first connected faraway places
decoys: The engine burned coal to boil water
Trains are a popular way to travel
Vivek thought the engine looked enormous

payload.passage: A magnifying glass makes small things look big with a curved lens. The glass is thicker in the middle and thinner at the edges. When light from a tiny object passes through, the lens bends the rays outward. Your eye then sees the object as much larger than it really is. So a magnifying glass works by bending light through a curved lens.
payload.title: How a magnifying glass makes things look bigger
decoys: The lens is thicker in the middle
Reading small print can be hard

payload.passage: The Green Guards noticed people picking flowers and breaking branches in the school garden. The plants were left bare and damaged. So the guards put up gentle signs and took turns reminding others to look but not to pluck. After that the plants stayed whole and bloomed for much longer. The guards learned that leaving plants untouched lets a garden flourish.
payload.title: Leaving plants untouched lets a garden flourish

payload.passage: Rudra grew two trays of grass from the same packet of seed. He trimmed one tray short every few days but left the other tray to grow tall and untouched. After a month the trimmed tray was thick and bushy, while the tall one had turned thin and sparse. His teacher said cutting often makes grass grow fuller from the base. Rudra learned that trimming grass often makes it grow thicker.
payload.title: Trimming grass often makes it grow thicker
decoys: The tall tray grew thin and sparse
Rudra grew two trays of grass

payload.passage: Pari's class turned the strip of bare land along the school boundary into a tiny forest. They planted many kinds of native trees close together in the small space. In just a few years the trees grew thick and tall. The little forest cooled the air, drew many birds, and soaked up the rain. The class learned that a tiny dense forest can green a small space fast.
payload.title: A tiny dense forest greens a space fast
decoys: The trees were planted close together
Forests are home to many animals

payload.passage: Tara filled two balloons with the same amount of air and tied them. She left one in the cold fridge and kept the other in the warm room. After an hour the fridge balloon looked smaller and limp, while the warm one stayed full. Her teacher said cold makes air shrink. Tara learned that air takes up less room when it gets cold.
payload.title: Air takes up less room when it gets cold
decoys: Tara tied both balloons the same

payload.passage: Nivaan held a sheet of card with a small hole in the middle up to the sun. On the ground below, the sun made a tiny round spot of light through the hole. When a cloud crossed the sun, the bright spot faded too. His teacher said the small hole lets through an image of the sun. Nivaan learned that a tiny hole can throw an image of the sun on the ground.
payload.title: A tiny hole throws an image of the sun
decoys: A cloud made the bright spot fade
Nivaan used a sheet of card

payload.passage: Asma watched fat snowflakes drift down on a trip to the cold hills, the first snow she had ever seen. Her father explained that high clouds can be colder than freezing inside. There the tiny water drops do not stay liquid at all. Instead they turn straight into delicate six-sided ice crystals that float gently down. Asma learned that snow forms when cloud drops freeze into ice.
payload.title: Snow forms when cloud drops freeze
decoys: The hills can be very cold
Asma saw snow for the first time

payload.passage: A torch made from a clear bottle and a small bulb shows a circuit plainly. A wire runs from one end of a cell to the bulb. A second wire runs from the bulb back to the other end of the cell. When both wires touch the cell, the loop is complete and the bulb glows. So this homemade torch shines only when the wires form a full loop.
payload.title: How a full wire loop makes a bulb glow
decoys: A wire runs from the cell to the bulb
Two wires connect to the cell

payload.passage: A school music teacher helps children learn songs and instruments. She teaches them how to sing in tune together. She shows some children how to play the harmonium or tabla. She leads the choir when the school holds a function. So a music teacher's work is to bring music into the children's lives.
payload.title: How a music teacher shares music with children
decoys: She leads the choir at school functions
Many helpers teach children new skills

payload.passage: Anvi found her bicycle too heavy to push up the slope to school. She arrived tired and sweaty long before her first class. Her father checked the bicycle and pumped air into the soft tyres. The firm tyres rolled easily and the bicycle felt light. Anvi reached school fresh and on time after that simple fix.
payload.title: Pumping the tyres solved Anvi's heavy bicycle
decoys: A bicycle is a handy way to get to school
Her father pumped air into the tyres

payload.passage: Kabir expected the palace tour to be only about gold and jewels. Instead, the guide showed how the rooms were planned for cool air: high ceilings, shady courtyards and screens that let the breeze pass through. Even without fans, the palace stayed pleasant in the hot months. Kabir left thinking that the old builders were as clever about comfort as they were about beauty.
payload.title: An old palace was built to stay cool
decoys: Carved screens let the breeze pass into the rooms
Kings of the past lived in grand palaces
Kabir had hoped to see gold and jewels

payload.passage: Devansh wanted to test if salt water floats an egg. He dropped a fresh egg into plain water and it sank to the bottom. Then he stirred in spoon after spoon of salt, and slowly the egg rose and floated. His teacher said salty water is heavier and holds things up better. Devansh learned that an egg floats in salty water but sinks in plain.
payload.title: An egg floats in salty water, sinks in plain
decoys: The egg sank in plain water
Devansh stirred in spoons of salt

payload.passage: Bhumi wanted to learn how to make rotating paper windmills that spin. Her early windmills were too tight and never turned in the breeze. She learned to pin the blades loosely so they could move freely. Soon her windmills spun fast and bright in the slightest wind. Bhumi planted a row of spinning windmills along her garden fence.
payload.title: Pinning blades loosely taught Bhumi to make windmills
decoys: A breezy day is the best day for outdoor play
Bhumi lined windmills along the garden fence

payload.passage: A frog must change completely to leave the water for land. The young tadpole breathes through gills, just as a fish does. As it grows, it slowly grows lungs to breathe the open air. At the same time it grows legs and loses its swimming tail. So a frog rebuilds its body to live on land.
payload.title: How a frog's body changes for land
decoys: A tadpole breathes through gills like a fish
Animals change in many surprising ways
Frogs hide near ponds during the day

payload.passage: A windmill-style egg whisk beats eggs fast with turning blades. When you turn the handle, a set of gears spins the loops at the bottom much faster. The fast loops slice through the egg again and again. This whips lots of air into the egg and makes it frothy. So a whisk beats eggs by spinning loops quickly through them.
payload.title: How a whisk beats eggs with spinning loops
decoys: Turning the handle drives the whisk

payload.passage: Palak wondered whether all soils soak up water the same way. She poured equal cups of water into a jar of sandy soil and a jar of clay soil. The water rushed straight through the sandy soil but sat on top of the clay for a long time. Her teacher said sandy soil has big gaps while clay packs tight. Palak learned that water drains faster through sandy soil than clay.
payload.title: Water drains faster through sandy soil than clay
decoys: Water rushed straight through the sand
Palak poured equal cups of water

payload.passage: Naina rubbed a steel needle along one end of a magnet many times in the same direction. Then she floated the needle on a leaf in a still bowl of water. The needle slowly swung round and pointed the same way each time it settled. Her brother said the needle had become a tiny magnet that lines up north and south. Naina learned that a magnetised needle can act like a simple compass.
payload.title: A magnetised needle acts like a simple compass
decoys: Naina floated the needle on a leaf
Magnets are useful in everyday life
A bowl of water can be very still

payload.passage: Tara's little brother kept changing the channel during her favourite show. The fights over the remote upset the whole family. Their parents gave each child a fixed half hour to choose the channel. Both children watched their shows in turn without any quarrel. The remote fights ended and evenings turned peaceful again.
payload.title: Fixed viewing turns ended the remote fights
decoys: The fights over the remote upset the family
Children must learn to take turns at home
Their parents gave each child half an hour

payload.passage: A spinning-disc thaumatrope blends two pictures into one. A small card has a bird on one side and a cage on the other. When you twirl it fast on two threads, your eyes cannot keep up. The bird and cage seem to join, so the bird looks inside the cage. So a fast-spun card tricks the eye into blending two pictures.
payload.title: How a spinning card blends two pictures
decoys: A bird is on one side
You twirl it on two threads

payload.passage: Summer in many Indian cities can be very hot and dry. The sun beats down from a clear sky and the ground feels burning to touch. People stay indoors at noon and drink cool water and juice to feel better. Fans and coolers run all day, and everyone waits for the evening breeze. So summer brings strong heat that changes how people spend their day.
payload.title: Hot summer days change daily life
decoys: People drink cool water and juice in summer
The weather is different in every season
Mangoes ripen and taste sweet in summer

payload.passage: The colony children noticed stray cows and goats eating plastic from open rubbish heaps. They were worried the animals would fall sick. So they told the grown-ups, and together they set up covered bins and a daily pickup. With the rubbish shut safely away, the animals stopped eating plastic. The children learned that covered bins keep animals from eating harmful waste.
payload.title: Covered bins keep animals from eating waste
decoys: Animals were eating plastic from heaps
Many animals live in the colony

payload.passage: Anvi wanted to learn how to make a smoothie without spilling everywhere. Her first try splashed fruit all over the kitchen counter. She learned to fill the jar only halfway and close the lid tightly. The smoothie then blended smoothly with no mess at all. Anvi made cool fruit smoothies for the family every Sunday after that.
payload.title: Filling halfway taught Anvi to blend without spills
decoys: Anvi splashed fruit over the counter
Fruit is full of goodness for growing children

payload.passage: Rohan's society dug a pit to catch the rain that ran off their roofs and let it sink into the ground. His grandfather explained that this slowly refills the wells below, so there is more water in the dry months. After two monsoons, the colony well stayed full longer. They learned that catching rooftop rain refills the wells below.
payload.title: Catching rooftop rain refills the wells
decoys: The pit catches rain from the roofs

payload.passage: The Garden Club found a heap of broken pots and old tyres lying behind the school. Instead of throwing them out, the children painted the tyres in bright colours. They filled them with soil and grew flowers and herbs inside. What had been ugly junk became a cheerful corner everyone loved. The club learned that old junk can be turned into a beautiful garden.
payload.title: Old junk can be turned into a garden
decoys: The club painted the old tyres
The yard had broken pots lying around

payload.passage: Aisha's class collected old newspapers from every home in their lane and gave them to a recycling man instead of throwing them out. He told them that recycled paper saves trees and the energy used to make new paper. In a month they filled his cart twice. The class learned that collecting old paper for recycling saves trees.
payload.title: Collecting old paper for recycling saves trees
decoys: Paper is used in many ways

payload.passage: A drop of rain helps shape the land long after it falls. As rain runs over a slope, it carries away tiny bits of soil. Many drops together cut small grooves into the bare ground. Over the years these grooves can grow into deep gullies and even valleys. So gentle rain slowly carves the shape of the land.
payload.title: How rain slowly shapes the land
decoys: Running water cuts grooves into the soil
Nature changes the land in many ways
Plants help hold the soil in place

payload.passage: Many trees change with the four seasons of the year. In spring they grow fresh green leaves and soft buds. In summer the leaves spread wide to catch the warm sunlight. When autumn comes the leaves turn brown and float to the ground, and in winter the bare tree rests. So a tree shows us each season by the way it looks.
payload.title: A tree changes through the four seasons
decoys: In autumn the leaves turn brown and fall
Nature is full of beautiful changing things
Birds build their nests in tall trees

payload.passage: At home, Jay's school uniform was never ironed in time for the morning. He left in a wrinkled shirt and felt shabby all day. He started ironing and laying out his uniform the night before. Each morning he simply slipped into the neat, ready clothes. Jay looked smart and was never rushed before school again.
payload.title: Ironing the night before solved Jay's wrinkled uniform
decoys: Jay left in a wrinkled shirt
A neat uniform shows respect for the school
Jay laid out his uniform the night before

payload.passage: A road repair worker mends the holes and cracks in our streets. When rain and traffic break the road, his team comes to fix it. They clear the loose pieces and pour fresh tar into the holes. Then they press it flat and smooth so cars can pass easily. So a road worker's job is to keep the streets smooth and safe.
payload.title: How a road worker repairs the streets
decoys: They pour fresh tar into the holes
Many helpers keep the town in order
Smooth roads make for a safe drive

payload.passage: Mahi saw that after the monsoon, the brown hillside burst into green grass and flowers. Her teacher explained that seeds had lain asleep in the dry soil all summer. They waited quietly for water, doing nothing for months. The first rain woke them all at once, so the whole slope turned green in days. Mahi learned that the first rains wake sleeping seeds across the land.
payload.title: The first rains wake sleeping seeds
decoys: The hillside burst into green grass
Mahi saw the change after the monsoon

payload.passage: A community health worker helps keep a whole locality healthy. She walks from house to house to check on families. She reminds parents to take their babies for vaccines on time. She shares simple tips on clean water, good food, and washing hands. So a health worker's job is to keep the neighbourhood healthy.
payload.title: How a health worker keeps the locality healthy
decoys: She reminds parents about baby vaccines
Many helpers work to keep us well
Washing hands stops the spread of germs

payload.passage: At home, the family kept burning the morning toast while busy with other tasks. The smell of burnt bread filled the kitchen each day. Mother set a small timer whenever she put bread on to toast. The timer beeped in time, and the toast came out golden. Burnt toast became a thing of the past in their home.
payload.title: A kitchen timer solved the burnt-toast problem
decoys: Burnt bread smell filled the kitchen
A calm morning helps a family start the day
Mother set a small timer for the toast

payload.passage: At the museum, Anjali found a wall of old maps drawn long before satellites. The guide explained that sailors and travellers drew them by hand from what they saw, so the shapes were a little wrong and some places were just guesses. Yet the maps slowly grew more correct as people explored more. Anjali learned that the maps showed how our picture of the world slowly grew clearer.
payload.title: Old maps show our world slowly growing clearer
decoys: Some places on the maps were just guesses
Maps help us find our way around
Anjali looked for her own city on a map

payload.passage: The colony children noticed water standing in old tyres and broken pots after every rain. They learned at school that mosquitoes breed in such still water. So they went around the lane tipping it out and clearing the junk that held it. With no standing water left anywhere, far fewer mosquitoes buzzed about. The children learned that clearing standing water keeps mosquitoes away.
payload.title: Clearing standing water keeps mosquitoes away

payload.passage: A sunflower seems to follow the sun across the sky each day. In the morning the young flower faces east where the sun comes up. As the sun moves across the sky, the flower slowly turns to keep facing it. By evening the flower is pointing west towards the setting sun. This slow turning helps the sunflower soak up as much sunlight as it can.
payload.title: A sunflower turns to follow the sun
decoys: In the morning the flower faces east
Plants do many clever things to live
Sunflower seeds are tasty and good to eat

payload.passage: A librarian keeps a library tidy and helps people find books. She arranges thousands of books neatly so each one is easy to find. When someone asks for a book, she knows just where to look. She notes which books are borrowed and welcomes them back later. So a librarian's job is to care for books and help readers.
payload.title: How a librarian helps people find books
decoys: She notes which books have been borrowed
Many quiet helpers serve our town
Reading books helps us learn new words

payload.passage: Myra wanted to learn how to make her own bookmark with a tassel. Her first tassels fell apart and the thread came loose. She learned to wind the thread many times and tie it firmly. The tassels then hung neat and full at the end of the bookmark. Myra made a different bookmark for each of her favourite books.
payload.title: Winding the thread firmly taught Myra to make tassels
decoys: Bookmarks help readers keep their place easily
Myra made bookmarks for her favourite books

payload.passage: A street light worker keeps the lamps along our roads glowing. By day he checks which lamps have stopped working. He climbs up to each dead lamp on his tall ladder. He changes the broken bulb so the street is bright again at night. So a street light worker's job is to keep our roads lit after dark.
payload.title: How a street light worker lights the road
decoys: He climbs up to change the broken bulb
Lit streets feel safer at night

payload.passage: The roots of a plant do quiet but vital work underground. They grip the soil so the plant does not fall over in the wind. They also drink up water and food from the earth around them. This water travels up the stem to feed the leaves and flowers. So a plant depends on its hidden roots to live and grow.
payload.title: Hidden roots keep a plant alive
decoys: Roots grip the soil against the wind
Green leaves make food using sunlight

payload.passage: Winter mornings in the north of India can be very cold and foggy. Thick white mist hangs in the air so you can hardly see the road ahead. People wrap themselves in warm shawls and sit close to small fires. The sun rises late and gives only weak, soft light during the short days. So winter brings cold, fog, and shorter days to the north.
payload.title: Cold foggy winter days in the north
decoys: People wrap themselves in warm shawls
The seasons change all over the world
Hot tea tastes wonderful on a cold day

payload.passage: The Craft Club gathered worn-out jeans and shirts that were too old to wear. Instead of throwing them away, the children cut and stitched them. They turned the old cloth into bags, pouches and pencil cases. They sold these at the school fair and used the money for tree planting. The club learned that worn-out clothes can be remade into useful new things.
payload.title: Worn-out clothes can be remade into new things
decoys: The club made bags from old jeans
The money went to tree planting

payload.passage: The class visited a fort built high on a steep rocky hill. The guide explained that the builders chose the hill on purpose, because enemies climbing up would be tired and easy to spot, while the guards above stayed fresh and safe. The steep path itself was part of the defence. Pankaj learned that the fort's high spot was chosen to keep it safe.
payload.title: A hill fort was placed high to stay safe
decoys: The path up the hill was very steep
Hills offer lovely views of the land
Pankaj was out of breath after the climb

payload.passage: A solar lamp in the garden lights itself using the sun. A small panel on top soaks up sunlight during the day. The panel turns the light into power and fills a tiny cell inside. When evening falls, the stored power runs a little bulb until morning. So a solar lamp gathers sun by day to glow at night.
payload.title: How a solar lamp gathers sun to glow
decoys: A panel soaks up the sunlight

payload.passage: Bhumi wondered why the big river never dried up, even in the hottest weeks with no rain. Her teacher explained that high in the mountains, snow melts slowly all summer and trickles down to feed the river, keeping it flowing long after the rains have stopped. The mountains act like a slow water store. Bhumi learned that melting mountain snow keeps a river flowing.
payload.title: Melting mountain snow keeps a river flowing
decoys: The river did not dry up in summer
Bhumi lives near a big river

payload.passage: A vet, or animal doctor, looks after the health of animals. When a pet falls ill, its owner brings it to the vet's clinic. The vet checks the animal gently to find out what is wrong. Then she gives medicine or other care to help it get better. So a vet's main work is to keep animals healthy.
payload.title: How a vet keeps animals healthy
decoys: The vet checks the animal gently
Many helpers care for living things
Pets need fresh water every day

payload.passage: A coral animal looks like a tiny flower but it is not a plant. The coral polyp has a soft tube body topped with little arms. At night it spreads its arms to catch tiny food drifting in the water. By day it may pull back into its hard stony cup. So a coral polyp is a tiny hungry animal, not a plant.
payload.title: A coral polyp is a tiny animal
decoys: The polyp catches food with little arms
The sea hides many odd living things
Coral reefs grow in warm shallow seas

payload.passage: In the museum's textile room, Nidhi saw cloth woven in patterns hundreds of years old. The guide explained how the colours all came from plants and roots, since there were no factory dyes back then. Each region had its own pattern that families passed down for generations. Nidhi learned that the room showed how weaving skills and patterns were handed from parents to children.
payload.title: Weaving patterns passed from parents to children
decoys: The old cloth colours came from plants
Nidhi liked the bright stripes on one piece

Many helpers come to our aid
Hospitals have doctors ready all day

decoys: Summer heats the land more than the sea
The weather changes through the year

payload.passage: A wheelbarrow lets one person carry a heavy load with ease. It has a single wheel at the front and two long handles at the back. When you lift the handles, the load sits mostly over the wheel, not in your arms. The wheel rolls the weight along while you only steer and balance it. So a wheelbarrow moves a heavy load by resting it over one rolling wheel.
payload.title: How a wheelbarrow carries a heavy load
decoys: Two long handles stick out at the back
Gardens need tools for heavy work
The wheel sits at the front

payload.passage: A pinwheel spins merrily whenever the wind blows or you puff at it. Its little paper sails are bent at an angle round a central pin. When air strikes the slanted sails, it pushes each one sideways. Because all the sails are turned the same way, the whole wheel spins round. So a pinwheel turns because slanted sails catch and follow the wind.
payload.title: How slanted sails make a pinwheel spin
decoys: The sails are bent round a central pin

payload.passage: A spring tide is an extra high tide that comes a few times a month. Tides rise and fall because the moon's pull tugs the sea. When the sun and moon line up, their pulls add together. This stronger pull lifts the sea higher than usual at high tide. So a spring tide happens when the sun and moon pull as one.
payload.title: Why the sun and moon make spring tides
decoys: The moon's pull tugs the sea up and down
The sea and sky work together in many ways
Fishermen watch the tides before sailing

payload.passage: Tisha set two thermometers in the playground at noon, one on bare concrete and one on the grassy field. She came back and read both after fifteen minutes. The thermometer on the concrete showed a much higher number than the one on the grass. Her teacher said hard, dark concrete soaks up far more heat than green grass. Tisha learned that concrete grows hotter than grass in the sun.
payload.title: Concrete grows hotter than grass in sunshine
decoys: Tisha used two thermometers in the playground
The sun heats up the ground daily
Grass is soft and green underfoot

payload.passage: The students kept slipping on the wet bathroom floor at school. A few children fell and hurt themselves during the rush. The school put down rough rubber mats outside the bathroom doors. The mats wiped wet feet and stopped the slipping at once. Now the children walk safely even when the floor is damp.
payload.title: Rubber mats solved the slippery bathroom floor
decoys: A few children fell and hurt themselves
Wet floors are a danger in every building
The school put rough mats outside the doors

payload.passage: Saira wondered why a swing slows down on its own if no one pushes. She gave the swing a single big push and counted as it swung. Each swing was a little shorter than the one before, until it stopped. Her uncle said the air and the chains slowly steal its motion. Saira learned that a swing slowly loses its motion without a push.
payload.title: A swing slowly loses motion without a push
decoys: Saira gave the swing one big push
Swings are fun in the park
Each swing was a little shorter

payload.passage: A seed drill helps a farmer sow seeds in a neat row. Seeds are poured into a box that rolls along on a wheel. As the wheel turns, it lets seeds drop one by one down a thin pipe. The pipe drops each seed into the open furrow at an even spacing. So a seed drill sows seeds evenly as its wheel turns along the row.
payload.title: How a seed drill sows seeds in even rows
decoys: Seeds drop down a thin pipe
Seeds are poured into a box

payload.passage: A lemon battery can light a tiny bulb. A strip of copper and a strip of zinc are pushed into a juicy lemon. The sour juice lets a small flow of power run between the two metals. Joined to a tiny bulb, this flow makes it give the faintest glow. So a lemon and two metals can make a little power.
payload.title: How a lemon and two metals make power
decoys: The sour juice lets power flow
Copper and zinc go into the lemon

payload.passage: A municipal worker keeps the town's drains clear of blockage. When leaves and waste clog a drain, the water cannot flow. He opens the drain cover and clears out all the rubbish. The water then flows freely so the street does not flood. So a municipal worker's job is to keep the drains flowing well.
payload.title: How a municipal worker keeps drains clear
decoys: He clears the rubbish from the drain
Many helpers keep the town in order
Blocked drains can flood the road in rain

payload.passage: Tanvi struggled to spell long words during the weekly spelling test. The letters always seemed to jump around inside her head. She started clapping out the syllables of each tricky word at home. Breaking the words into small beats made them far easier to remember. By the next test Tanvi spelled every long word correctly and beamed with joy.
payload.title: Clapping out syllables improved Tanvi's spelling
decoys: The letters jumped around in Tanvi's head
Spelling well makes a person sound very clever
Tanvi had a spelling test every single week

payload.passage: The students kept mixing up their identical water bottles in class. Bottles got swapped and arguments broke out over them. The teacher asked everyone to stick a name label on their bottle. Each child could now spot their own bottle at a glance. The mix-ups and arguments stopped from that day onward.
payload.title: Name labels solved the mixed-up water bottles
decoys: Arguments broke out over swapped bottles
Drinking water keeps every child healthy
The teacher asked for name labels

payload.passage: The guide showed Simran's class a museum room about old roads. A long model traced a route lined with rest houses, wells and shady trees, built so traders and travellers could cross the land safely. Such roads, she said, joined far cities and helped goods and news travel. Simran learned that old roads were built to link distant places together.
payload.title: Old roads were built to link distant places
decoys: Shady trees were planted along the road
Simran followed the model road with her eyes

payload.passage: Pranav left a bowl of cooked rice in the warm kitchen and another bowl in the fridge. After two days he sniffed each one carefully. The kitchen rice smelt sour and had a slimy look, but the fridge rice still smelt fresh. His mother said warmth lets tiny germs spoil food fast. Pranav learned that food spoils faster in warmth than in the cold.
payload.title: Food spoils faster in warmth than cold
decoys: Cooked food should be stored well

payload.passage: Saira watched a snail glide across a smooth glass jar from the inside. She could see a wave ripple along the bottom of its foot as it moved. A shiny wet trail was left behind everywhere it went. Her teacher said the snail makes slime to slide on. Saira learned that a snail moves on a ripple of slime under its foot.
payload.title: A snail glides on a ripple of slime
decoys: A wet trail was left behind it
Saira watched through a glass jar

payload.passage: The shopkeepers of Market Road agreed to stop giving out plastic bags. They now keep cloth bags and paper bags ready at every counter. Many customers have also begun to bring their own bags from home. After a few months, far less plastic litter blew about the street. The shopkeepers showed that a whole market can cut its plastic waste by working together.
payload.title: A market cuts plastic waste by working together
decoys: The shops now keep cloth bags ready

payload.passage: Arjun could not concentrate on homework because the television was loud. His scores in tests began slipping due to the constant noise. He asked his parents if he could study in the quiet back room. There he finished his work without any disturbance at all. Arjun's test scores soon climbed back up to where they had been.
payload.title: A quiet room solved Arjun's homework trouble
decoys: Television noise is harmful for every child
Arjun moved to the quiet back room

payload.passage: A sliding drawer opens and shuts on smooth runners. Each side of the drawer sits on a narrow rail fixed to the cupboard. When you pull the handle, the drawer rolls out along these rails with little effort. A small stop at the end keeps it from falling right out. So a drawer glides in and out on rails fixed to the cupboard.
payload.title: How a drawer glides on its runners
decoys: A small stop keeps the drawer in
Each side sits on a narrow rail

payload.passage: A power line repair team restores electricity after a storm. When strong winds snap the wires, whole streets go dark. The team drives out to find where the line has broken. They climb the poles and join the wires to bring back the power. So a repair team's job is to restore power to the homes after a storm.
payload.title: How a repair team restores power after a storm
decoys: They climb the poles to join the wires
Many helpers come to our aid
Storms can knock down many trees

payload.passage: Vedant set two saucers of water out to watch evaporation: one wide and shallow, one narrow and deep, with equal water. He left both in the same sunny spot for a day. The wide shallow saucer lost far more water than the deep narrow one. His teacher said a bigger surface dries faster. Vedant learned that water evaporates faster from a wider surface.
payload.title: Water evaporates faster from a wider surface
decoys: Vedant used a wide and a deep saucer

payload.passage: Faizan's class visited a museum room about old writing. The guide showed how people first scratched marks on wet clay, then wrote on dried leaves, then on paper made from cloth. Each new way let people keep words longer and carry them farther. Faizan saw that the room was really about a long search for a better way to save our words.
payload.title: People kept finding better ways to write
decoys: Early people scratched marks onto wet clay
Museums are full of fascinating old things
Faizan thought the clay tablets looked heavy

payload.passage: Sumit noticed that a single heavy shower could flood the city streets in minutes, though the same rain on a field caused no trouble. His teacher explained that roads and concrete cannot soak up water, so it has nowhere to go but the drains, which quickly overflow. Open soil drinks the rain instead. Sumit learned that hard city ground floods because it cannot soak up rain.
payload.title: Hard city ground floods because it cannot soak rain
decoys: The shower flooded the streets in minutes

payload.passage: The museum had a whole room of old musical instruments behind glass. The guide showed how a simple gourd with strings slowly grew into fancy instruments with many keys and pipes. Each one, he said, was made better than the last so it could play more notes more clearly. Nakul understood that the room told the story of how people kept improving the way they made music.
payload.title: Old instruments show how music tools improved
decoys: One early instrument was a gourd with strings
Music has been loved by people for ages
Nakul wished he could play the instruments

payload.passage: Anvita stood a jam jar upside down over a small lit candle on a plate of water. The flame burned for a while, then went out, and water rose up a little into the jar. Her teacher said the flame used up part of the air, leaving room for water. Anvita learned that a flame uses up some air as it burns.
payload.title: A flame uses up some of the air
decoys: Water rose up into the jar
Anvita used a jam jar and plate

payload.passage: Yusuf wanted to learn how to spin a basketball on one finger. The ball kept sliding off before it even started to turn. He learned to give the ball a strong, level spin first. Slowly the ball balanced on his fingertip for a second or two. After much practice Yusuf spun the ball for a long, steady time.
payload.title: Learning the level spin taught Yusuf the ball trick
decoys: The ball kept sliding off Yusuf's finger
Basketball tricks always impress a watching crowd
Yusuf gave the ball a strong, level spin

payload.passage: Tanvi could not concentrate because her desk wobbled on its uneven legs. Every time she wrote, the shaky desk made her lines crooked. She slipped a folded piece of card under the short leg. The desk stood firm and steady on the floor after that. Tanvi's writing turned neat once her desk stopped wobbling.
payload.title: A card under the leg solved Tanvi's wobbly desk
decoys: The shaky desk made her lines crooked
A steady desk helps any student work well
Tanvi slipped a card under the short leg

payload.passage: The Young Farmers club grows vegetables in the school plot every season. Instead of buying chemical fertiliser, they make compost from kitchen waste. The dark compost feeds the soil and keeps it soft and crumbly. The vegetables grow well without harming the ground or the water nearby. The club learned that compost grows healthy plants without harmful chemicals.
payload.title: Compost grows plants without harmful chemicals
decoys: The club makes compost from kitchen waste
The school has a farming plot

payload.passage: The guide took Pooja's class to a temple pond with wide stone steps on all four sides. She explained that the pond stored rainwater for the temple and gave pilgrims a place to wash before prayers. Its steps let people reach the water even when it was low. Pooja learned that the temple pond both stored water and served the worshippers.
payload.title: A temple pond stored water and served worshippers
decoys: The pond had stone steps on four sides
Temples are visited by many people
Pooja saw lotus flowers on the water

payload.passage: Avni kept arriving at class without her sharpened pencils. She wasted time borrowing and the teacher grew annoyed. She started sharpening a few pencils every night and packing them. Each morning her pencil box was ready with sharp points. Avni was never caught without a working pencil again.
payload.title: Sharpening at night solved Avni's blunt-pencil problem
decoys: Being ready helps a student do their best

payload.passage: Reva set up a tray of dry sand and gently blew across it with a straw. Little ripples formed in the sand and slowly crept along in the direction she blew. The harder she blew, the faster the ripples moved. Her teacher said wind shapes sand into ripples. Reva learned that blowing air shapes sand into moving ripples.
payload.title: Blowing air shapes sand into moving ripples
decoys: Harder blowing moved the ripples faster
Reva blew across the tray with a straw

payload.passage: A weather forecaster tells people what the sky will do next. He studies clouds, winds, and special charts each day. From these he works out whether it will rain or stay dry. Then he shares the forecast so people can plan their day. So a weather forecaster's job is to warn us about coming weather.
payload.title: How a forecaster predicts the weather
decoys: He studies clouds, winds, and charts
Many helpers give us useful news
Heavy rain can flood low streets

payload.passage: Sara's group planted a thick ring of grass and reeds around the school pond. The plants trap the mud and dirty water that used to run straight in. Because of this, the pond water now stays much cleaner. Tadpoles and dragonflies have slowly come back to live there. The group learned that a border of plants keeps pond water clean.
payload.title: A border of plants keeps pond water clean
decoys: The plants trap mud before the pond
Ponds are home to many creatures

payload.passage: The colony fitted small mesh covers over every open drain. Before this, plastic and leaves kept slipping in and blocking them, which caused floods. Now the mesh catches the rubbish before it can go inside. A worker comes and clears the mesh each day. So the drains run freely in the rain, and the colony learned that covering drains with mesh stops them blocking.
payload.title: Covering drains with mesh stops them blocking
decoys: The mesh catches plastic and leaves
A worker clears the mesh daily

payload.passage: Nisha's group looked at how the school canteen served its food. They saw it used paper plates that were thrown away after one meal. So they asked the canteen to use steel plates that are washed and reused instead. Soon the canteen produced far less waste each day. The group learned that washable plates cut down the canteen's daily waste.
payload.title: Washable plates cut the canteen's daily waste
decoys: The canteen now uses steel plates

payload.passage: Ravi wanted to ride his new bicycle without help. On the first day he fell down four times and scraped his knee. Ravi learned that hard practice slowly turns a scary thing into an easy one.
payload.title: Steady practice helped Ravi learn cycling
decoys: Ravi scraped his knee on the first day
Practice can teach a child anything in the world
Ravi got a brand new bicycle to ride

payload.passage: The guide led Arjun's class to a tall stone tower built hundreds of years ago. She explained that it once worked as a watchtower: guards climbed it to spot trouble far away and lit a fire on top to warn the town. From so high, they could see roads and fields for miles. Arjun understood that the tower was really an old way of sending warnings across a long distance.
payload.title: An old tower warned a town of danger
decoys: Guards lit a fire on the top of the tower
Towers from the past were very tall
Arjun was tired after climbing all the stairs

payload.passage: Zoya wanted to make her own paper from old scraps. She tore up waste paper, soaked it in water and mashed it into a grey pulp. She spread the pulp thin on a mesh and pressed out the water, then let it dry in the sun. By evening she peeled off a fresh, rough sheet of paper. Zoya learned that old paper can be made into new paper at home.
payload.title: Old paper can be made into new paper
decoys: Zoya pressed the water out of the pulp
We should not waste useful things
Paper is used for writing and drawing

payload.passage: A spinning salad drier flings water off wet leaves. Washed leaves go into a basket inside a bowl with a lid. When you turn the handle, the basket spins round very fast. The spin throws the water drops out through the holes to the bowl below. So a salad spinner dries leaves by flinging off water as it spins.
payload.title: How spinning flings water off salad leaves
decoys: Water is thrown to the bowl

payload.passage: A strawberry plant spreads itself in a clever creeping way. Besides making fruit, it sends out long thin stems called runners along the ground. Where a runner touches the soil, it puts down roots and grows a new plant. Soon one strawberry plant has spread into a whole patch. So a strawberry plant fills a patch by sending out runners.
payload.title: How a strawberry plant spreads itself
decoys: A runner roots where it touches the soil
Plants spread in many different ways
Strawberries are sweet and bright red

payload.passage: A spinning fan above your head moves a lot of air with tilted blades. A motor in the middle turns the blades round and round. Because each blade is set at a slant, it scoops air and pushes it downward. The breeze it makes sweeps away the warm air clinging to you. So a ceiling fan cools a room by pushing the air down with slanted blades.
payload.title: How a ceiling fan pushes air downward
decoys: Each blade is set at a slant
Fans help on hot summer days
A motor turns the blades round

payload.passage: A see-saw style escalator carries people up on a moving stair. A loop of linked steps runs round and round, driven by a motor below. As you step on, the flat step rises up with you to the next floor. At the top each step flattens out and slides back under to return. So an escalator lifts people on a never-ending loop of steps.
payload.title: How a moving loop of steps lifts people
decoys: Each step flattens out at the top
A motor drives the steps below

payload.passage: A school sports coach trains children to play games well. He teaches them the rules of cricket, football, and other games. He shows them how to run, throw, and catch the right way. He cheers their efforts and helps them play fair and as a team. So a sports coach's work is to help children learn and enjoy games.
payload.title: How a sports coach trains children
decoys: He teaches the rules of each game
Exercise keeps the body fit and strong

payload.passage: A signal operator keeps trains moving safely along the tracks. He sits in a cabin filled with levers and bright lights. He watches where each train is and sets the signals to green or red. This tells the drivers when to go and when to wait. So a signal operator's job is to guide trains safely on the railway.
payload.title: How a signal operator guides the trains
decoys: He sets the signals to green or red
Many helpers keep us moving safely

payload.passage: Zoya wanted to learn how to make a simple paper boat that floats. Her first boats sank or fell apart in the water bucket. She watched the steps slowly and pressed each fold sharp and tight. Her new boats held their shape and bobbed proudly on the water. Zoya raced her paper boats in the rain puddles with great delight.
payload.title: Sharp folds taught Zoya to make floating boats
decoys: Zoya's first boats sank in the bucket
Rainy days are always full of fun and games
Zoya raced her boats in the rain puddles

payload.passage: A train ticket clerk helps people travel by railway. He sits behind a window at the busy station counter. When travellers tell him where they wish to go, he prints their tickets. He takes their money and gives back the right change. So a ticket clerk's job is to sell tickets so people can travel.
payload.title: How a ticket clerk sells train tickets
decoys: He prints the tickets travellers ask for
Many helpers serve at the station
Trains carry people to faraway cities

payload.passage: The youth group set up a small market once every month. People bring along things they no longer need, such as books, clothes, toys and tools. They give these away or swap them with one another for free. So useful things change hands instead of being thrown out. The group learned that a free swap market keeps good things in use.
payload.title: A free swap market keeps good things in use
decoys: People bring books and toys to swap
Markets are held in many places
The youth group runs it monthly

payload.passage: Vihaan's group set up a station to collect used pens and markers from every class. They added broken plastic toys to it too. payload.title: Small plastic items can be collected and recycled
decoys: Plastic is found in many toys

payload.passage: Aman noticed cool air rushing toward the sea every afternoon. His uncle, a fisherman, explained that the land heats up faster than the sea on a sunny day, and the warm air over the land rises, pulling cooler air in from the water. This steady breeze is called a sea breeze. Aman learned that uneven heating of land and sea makes a sea breeze.
payload.title: Uneven heating makes a sea breeze
decoys: The breeze blew in every afternoon
The sea is a busy place for fishing

payload.passage: When you push a bicycle pedal, you are not driving the wheel straight away. Your foot turns a large toothed wheel joined to the pedals. So a bicycle uses a chain and gears to turn slow pedalling into quick rolling.
payload.title: How a bicycle turns pedalling into rolling
decoys: The chain loops to a small rear wheel
Cycling is a healthy way to travel
A bicycle has two rubber tyres

payload.passage: A goldsmith makes pretty ornaments out of gold and silver. He heats the metal until it grows soft enough to shape. With small tools he beats and bends it into rings and chains. He polishes each piece until it shines brightly. So a goldsmith's work is to shape metal into beautiful jewellery.
payload.title: How a goldsmith makes jewellery
decoys: He polishes each piece until it shines
Many skilled helpers serve our town
Gold ornaments are worn at weddings

payload.passage: Lakshya hung a small bar magnet from a thread and let it settle. It slowly swung round and came to rest pointing the same way every time. When he nudged it, it always returned to that same line. His teacher said a free magnet lines up north and south. Lakshya learned that a freely hung magnet always settles the same way.
payload.title: A freely hung magnet settles the same way
decoys: He nudged it but it returned
Lakshya hung the magnet from a thread

payload.passage: A bucket-and-rope well lifts water by hand. The rope is tied to a bucket and slung over a smooth log at the top. You lower the bucket until it fills with water below. Then you pull the rope hand over hand to raise the heavy bucket up. So a rope over a log lets you draw a bucket of water up a well.
payload.title: How a rope and bucket draw well water
decoys: The rope slings over a smooth log
You pull the rope hand over hand

payload.passage: Pari struggled to do a handstand against the wall in gym class. Her arms wobbled and she came crashing down within seconds. She built her wrist strength with simple exercises every morning. Slowly she held the handstand longer, counting the seconds in her head. By the end of the term Pari balanced upside down for a whole ten seconds.
payload.title: Building wrist strength helped Pari hold a handstand
decoys: Pari came crashing down within seconds
Gym class is the most fun period of the day
Pari practised handstands against the wall

payload.passage: An umbrella stays open over your head with a clever set of folding ribs. When you slide a small ring up the central pole, it pushes the thin ribs outward. The ribs stretch the cloth tight into a wide dome shape. A little catch then clicks to hold the ring in place. So sliding one ring up the pole opens and locks the whole umbrella.
payload.title: How an umbrella opens with sliding ribs
decoys: A catch clicks to hold the ring
Umbrellas keep us dry in the rain
The cloth is stretched into a dome

payload.passage: A simple wall clock keeps time with a swinging part hidden inside it. A coiled spring or a battery slowly feeds power to a set of tiny toothed wheels. These wheels turn each other in order, some fast and some slow. The fast wheel drives the second hand and the slow ones move the minute and hour hands. In this way the clock splits one steady beat into hours, minutes and seconds.
payload.title: How a clock turns one beat into the time
decoys: The second hand is driven by the fast wheel
Clocks are found in almost every home
A coiled spring can store some power

payload.passage: The guide showed Kiaan's class a museum model of an old town's water system. Clay pipes carried fresh water from a spring to homes, while separate drains took dirty water away. Keeping the two apart, she said, kept people healthy long before anyone knew about germs. Kiaan understood that the model showed how clever old water pipes kept a town clean.
payload.title: Old water pipes kept a town clean
decoys: Clay pipes carried water from a spring
Water is needed by every town
Kiaan traced the pipes with his finger

payload.passage: A spider builds its web with great care and patience. It spins fine silk threads from its own body and joins them together. First it makes a strong frame, then it adds lines that cross like the spokes of a wheel. Finally it lays a sticky spiral to catch passing insects. So a spider weaves a clever trap out of its own silk.
payload.title: A spider weaves a clever silk web
decoys: The spider adds lines like spokes of a wheel
Small creatures can do amazing things
Spiders eat the insects they catch in webs

payload.passage: Ira watched water drip steadily from the roof of a cave on a school trip. The guide explained that rainwater seeps through the rock above and carries tiny bits of stone with it. As each drop hangs and dries, it leaves a little speck behind. Over thousands of years these specks build up into long stone shapes. payload.title: Dripping water slowly builds cave stones
decoys: Water dripped from the cave roof
Ira went on a school trip

payload.passage: Naina wanted to learn how to make her own greeting cards by hand. Her first cards looked plain and the glue left ugly marks. Soon Naina was making birthday cards for the whole family herself.
payload.title: Practice taught Naina to make tidy greeting cards

Handmade gifts always mean more than bought ones
Naina made birthday cards for the family

payload.passage: A seismograph-style shake detector uses a hanging weight and a pen. A heavy weight hangs still on a spring above a moving strip of paper. payload.title: How a hanging pen records a shake
decoys: The heavy weight tends to stay put
The pen traces onto moving paper

payload.passage: Divya was sure that warm air rises, so she made a simple test with her father. payload.title: Warm air rises and spins a paper spiral
decoys: The paper spiral hung from a thin thread
Air can make many objects move around
A table lamp gives out a gentle warmth

payload.passage: A spider's egg sac is a soft silk bag full of tiny eggs. The mother spider spins it carefully and guards it from harm. payload.title: Many baby spiders hatch from one sac
decoys: The mother spider guards her egg sac
Baby animals begin life in many ways
Spiders use silk to catch their food

payload.passage: A laundry shop worker washes and presses clothes for many people. People drop off shirts, sarees, and suits at the counter. The worker cleans each piece carefully and dries it well. payload.title: How a laundry worker cleans our clothes
decoys: He presses out the creases neatly
Neat clothes make a good impression

payload.passage: At the natural history museum, Madhu stood before a huge dinosaur skeleton. payload.title: Old bones teach us about long-gone animals
decoys: Workers cleaned the bones very gently
Madhu thought the dinosaur looked huge

payload.passage: A bicycle bell makes a bright ring with a hidden spring and hammer. When you flick the small lever with your thumb, it sets a tiny hammer moving fast. payload.title: How a flicked hammer rings a bicycle bell
decoys: A tiny hammer strikes the metal dome
Bells warn people on the road
You flick the lever with your thumb

payload.passage: Lavanya watched a line of black clouds gather before a storm. The sky grew dark, a cool wind sprang up and the birds went quiet. payload.title: The sky gives warning signs before rain
decoys: A cool wind sprang up suddenly

payload.passage: A toll-free helpline worker answers calls from people in need. She sits at a desk wearing a headset all day. When the phone rings, she listens carefully to the caller's problem. She gives clear advice or sends the right help to them. So a helpline worker's job is to guide and help people who call.
payload.title: How a helpline worker assists callers
decoys: She listens carefully to each caller
Many helpers serve people in need
A phone can reach help from far away

payload.passage: Roshni noticed it felt cooler and rained more on the green hillside than on the bare one nearby. Her teacher explained that thick trees give off water vapour from their leaves. They also throw shade that keeps the ground cool. Together this cools the air above and helps clouds form there. Roshni learned that forests help cool the air and bring rain.
payload.title: Forests help cool the air and bring rain
decoys: Trees are good for the earth

payload.passage: A see-through hourglass measures time with falling sand. It has two glass bulbs joined by a thin neck in the middle. When you turn it over, the sand in the top bulb trickles down through the narrow neck, which lets only a little fall each second. When the top bulb is empty, a set amount of time has passed. So an hourglass marks time by sand falling through a narrow neck.
payload.title: How an hourglass measures time with sand
decoys: The neck lets only a little sand fall
Time can be measured in many ways
Two glass bulbs hold the sand

payload.passage: A radio jockey keeps listeners company on the airwaves. She sits in a small studio with a microphone in front of her. She plays songs and talks cheerfully between them. She shares news, jokes, and messages from people who tune in. So a radio jockey's work is to entertain and inform her listeners.
payload.title: How a radio jockey entertains listeners
decoys: She plays songs between her talk
Many helpers bring us news and fun
Many people listen to the radio while driving

payload.passage: Tia wanted to learn how to fold a paper plane that flew far. Her first planes nose-dived or spun in tiny circles. She made the folds sharp and kept both wings exactly even. The plane then sailed long and straight across the room. Tia's paper plane flew the farthest in the class flying contest.
payload.title: Even wings taught Tia to fold a far-flying plane
decoys: Tia's first planes spun in tiny circles
Paper planes never fail to amuse children
Tia won the class flying contest

payload.passage: A ward boy helps look after patients in a hospital. He moves patients gently from one bed or room to another. He fetches things the nurses and doctors need quickly. He keeps the ward neat and helps the patients feel at ease. So a ward boy's work is to support the care of patients in hospital.
payload.title: How a ward boy supports hospital patients
decoys: He fetches things the nurses need
Many helpers care for the sick
Hospitals need to be kept very clean

payload.passage: The students planted shady trees and grass around the bare school playground. The dusty ground used to bake in the hot summer sun. As the green spread, the ground stayed cooler and the dust no longer blew about. Children could then play outside happily even at noon. The students learned that greening a playground keeps it cool and dust-free.
payload.title: Greening a playground keeps it cool and dust-free
decoys: The playground used to bake in heat

payload.passage: At home, the family kept tripping on the rolled-up edge of the doormat. The curled corner caught everyone's feet at the door. Mother stuck the corners down flat with strong tape. The mat lay smooth and no one tripped over it again. The doorway became safe to walk over for everyone.
payload.title: Taping the mat down solved the tripping corner
decoys: The curled corner caught their feet
A small fix can prevent a nasty fall
Mother taped the corners down flat

payload.passage: A screw-jack lifts a heavy load with little effort. A handle turns a thick screw that runs up through a block. Each turn raises the block a tiny bit and the load on top with it. Because the screw thread is gentle, a small turn does big lifting. So a screw-jack raises a heavy load by winding it slowly up a thread.
payload.title: How a screw-jack lifts a heavy load slowly
decoys: A handle turns the thick screw
Heavy loads are hard to lift
Each turn raises the block a bit

payload.passage: Akash wanted to learn how to skip a flat stone across the pond. His stones kept sinking the moment they hit the water with a plop. He learned to throw the stone low and flat with a quick spin. After many tries a stone finally skipped three times before it sank. Akash whooped with joy and kept practising till the sun went down.
payload.title: Learning the flat throw taught Akash to skip stones
decoys: Akash's stones kept sinking with a plop
Ponds are wonderful places to spend the evening
Akash practised until the sun went down

payload.passage: Ishita wanted to know if leaves are really green all the way through. She crushed a few green leaves and soaked them in a little warm liquid for an hour. The liquid slowly turned a soft green as the colour leaked out of the leaves. Her teacher said the green is a stuff that helps plants catch sunlight. Ishita learned that the green colour can be drawn out of a leaf.
payload.title: The green colour can be drawn from a leaf
decoys: The soaking liquid turned a soft green
Ishita crushed a few green leaves

payload.passage: A revolving door turns to let people in and out. Several glass panels are joined to a central pole like spokes. As you push a panel, the whole set spins slowly round the pole. One person can enter as another leaves in a different gap. So a revolving door lets people pass by turning panels round a centre.
payload.title: How a revolving door turns panels round a centre
decoys: Glass panels join to a central pole
Pushing a panel spins the set

payload.passage: Mishti set out shallow dishes of plain water, salty water and vinegar and floated a tiny paper boat in each. She blew gently and timed how the boats moved. The boats slid much the same in plain and salty water but the vinegar smelt sharp. Her teacher said the smell does not change the floating. Mishti learned that a smell does not change how a boat floats.
payload.title: A smell does not change how a boat floats

payload.passage: Aaisha hung a thin chain from two nails so it sagged in a curve. She turned it upside down and traced the same curve onto card to make an arch. The card arch stood up firmly and held a small weight on top. Her teacher said this curve is a strong shape for arches. Aaisha learned that a hanging chain's curve makes a strong arch.
payload.title: A hanging chain's curve makes a strong arch
decoys: The card arch held a small weight
Aaisha hung the chain from nails

payload.passage: Veer wanted to touch his toes but his body felt as stiff as a board. Every morning he stretched a little, though at first he could barely reach his knees. He never forced himself and stopped the moment it hurt too much. Slowly, week after week, his fingers crept closer to the floor. After two months he touched his toes easily and felt light and strong.
payload.title: Gentle daily stretching made Veer more flexible
decoys: At first Veer could only reach his knees
Exercise can fix every problem in the body
Veer wanted to be able to touch his toes

payload.passage: A hand-crank torch needs no batteries at all to give light. You squeeze and release a lever again and again with your hand. Each squeeze spins a tiny generator inside that makes a little power, and that power runs straight to the bulb to keep it glowing. The faster you squeeze, the brighter the little bulb shines. So a hand-crank torch lights up from the power your squeezing makes.
payload.title: How squeezing a lever lights a crank torch
decoys: Each squeeze spins a small generator
Torches help in a power cut
You squeeze and release the lever

payload.passage: Dhruv's family began carrying their own steel straws everywhere. They started refusing the plastic ones that come with drinks. They learned that thrown-away straws often reach the sea. There they can harm fish and turtles that mistake them for food. Soon their friends copied the habit too, and the family learned that skipping plastic straws helps sea creatures.
payload.title: Skipping plastic straws helps sea creatures
decoys: Drinks are often served with straws

payload.passage: Inaya wanted to test how clean rainwater really is. She set out a clean funnel and jar in the open to catch the next shower. After the rain she poured the water through a coffee filter into a second jar. The filter caught little specks of grey dust. Inaya learned that even rainwater carries tiny bits of dust from the air.
payload.title: Rainwater carries tiny bits of dust from the air
decoys: The filter caught little grey specks
Rain is part of nature's cycle
Inaya set out a clean funnel and jar

payload.passage: Nisha saw water vapour rise from a boiling pot, then turn back into drops on the cold lid. Her mother explained that this is just like the sky above us. The sun lifts water from rivers and seas as invisible vapour. High up, the cool air turns it back into drops that gather into clouds and fall as rain. Nisha learned that water keeps moving between the earth and sky.
payload.title: Water keeps moving between earth and sky
decoys: Vapour turned to drops on the cold lid
Water is used in every kitchen

payload.passage: At home, the family's cupboard door kept swinging open on its own. Clothes tumbled out and the open door blocked the room. Father fitted a small magnet to keep the door shut tight. The door now stayed closed and nothing fell out. The bedroom looked tidy and the swinging door was no trouble at all.
payload.title: A magnet solved the swinging cupboard door
decoys: Clothes tumbled out of the cupboard
A tidy bedroom is a calm place to rest
Father fitted a small magnet on the door

payload.passage: Nisha kept losing marks because her answers were too messy to read. The teacher often could not make out her crowded writing. Nisha began leaving a blank line between every answer in her book. Her work suddenly looked clear and easy to mark. Her marks improved simply because the teacher could read everything now.
payload.title: Spacing out answers solved Nisha's lost marks
decoys: The teacher could not read Nisha's writing
Neatness is the path to top marks in school
Nisha left a blank line between answers

payload.passage: At home, Karan's family kept tripping over shoes left near the door. Someone almost fell down badly one busy morning. Karan suggested keeping a simple shoe rack by the entrance. Everyone began placing their shoes neatly on the rack. The doorway became safe and tidy, and the tripping stopped at once.
payload.title: A shoe rack solved the messy doorway problem
decoys: Someone almost fell down one morning
A tidy home keeps every family safe and happy
Karan suggested a rack by the entrance

payload.passage: A spider can travel through the air without any wings. A tiny spider climbs to a high spot and lifts its body up. It then lets out a long thread of silk into the breeze. The wind catches the silk like a sail and lifts the spider away. So a spider can float to a new home on a thread of silk.
payload.title: How a spider floats away on silk
decoys: The wind catches the silk like a sail
Small creatures travel in clever ways
Spiders spin silk to catch their food

payload.passage: The students often dropped their pens through the gaps in the old desks. The pens rolled away and were lost under the heavy furniture. The carpenter fitted thin strips to close the gaps in the desk tops. Pens no longer slipped through and rolled away. The children stopped losing their pens during every lesson.
payload.title: Closing the desk gaps solved the lost pens
decoys: Pens rolled away under the furniture
Old furniture causes many small problems
The carpenter fitted strips on the desks

payload.passage: A push-button torch turns on with a single click. Pressing the button pushes a small spring contact onto the battery, joining it to the bulb in a closed loop. The bulb then lights while the button stays pressed in and clicked. Pressing it again pops the button out and breaks the loop. So a push-button torch lights up when a click closes its loop.
payload.title: How a click closes a push-button torch loop
decoys: A spring contact touches the battery
Torches help us see in the dark

payload.passage: Trisha wanted to learn how to read a clock with hands, not numbers. The two hands confused her and she often guessed the wrong time. Her father drew a big clock and let her move the hands herself. By moving the hands she finally understood the hours and minutes. Soon Trisha read the wall clock quickly and even taught her younger sister.
payload.title: A practice clock helped Trisha tell the time
decoys: The two clock hands confused Trisha
Knowing the time keeps everyone neat and punctual
Trisha taught her younger sister too

payload.passage: At home, the family kept burning their hands on the hot kettle handle. The metal handle grew too hot to hold after boiling. Mother slipped a thick cloth cover over the kettle handle. Everyone could lift the kettle safely without getting burnt. The painful little burns stopped happening in the kitchen.
payload.title: A cloth cover solved the hot-kettle burns
decoys: The metal handle grew too hot to hold
Kitchen safety matters for the whole family
Mother slipped a cloth over the handle

payload.passage: Dev planted four marigold seeds and gave each pot a different place: full sun, half shade, deep shade and a dark cupboard. He watered them all the same. The full-sun plant grew strongest and the cupboard plant died, with the others in between. His teacher said more light usually means stronger growth. Dev learned that plants grow stronger with more light.
payload.title: Plants grow stronger with more light
decoys: Dev watered all the pots the same

payload.passage: A river does not stay the same along its whole path. High in the hills it starts as a thin, fast stream rushing over stones. As it flows down it grows wider and slower, picking up water from smaller streams. By the time it nears the sea it is broad and calm. So a single river keeps changing as it travels to the sea.
payload.title: How a river changes on its journey
decoys: A river starts as a thin stream in the hills
Water moves around the Earth in many ways
Boats and fish live along big rivers

payload.passage: The class toured a grand old library kept as a museum. The guide showed shelves of books copied entirely by hand, each taking months to finish. Because so few existed, the books were chained to the shelves so none would be lost. Krish was amazed at how precious books once were. He saw that the library showed how rare and valued books used to be.
payload.title: An old library shows how rare books once were
decoys: Some books were chained to the shelves
Libraries are quiet places to read
Krish liked the smell of the old paper

payload.passage: Rohan struggled to remember the multiplication tables for his test. The numbers all jumbled together and he kept mixing up sevens and eights. His grandmother taught him to sing the tables like a song. He hummed the tunes on the way to school and while brushing his teeth. By the day of the test the tables came out of his mouth without any effort.
payload.title: Singing the tables helped Rohan remember them
decoys: Rohan kept mixing up his sevens and eights
Songs can teach a child every single subject
