Rohan's grandmother taught him many useful things

payload.passage: At the museum, Kunal's class entered a room of old armour and shields. The guide showed how the metal was bent and joined so a soldier could move and still be protected. Heavier armour gave more safety but slowed a fighter down, so makers always had to find a balance. Kunal understood that the room showed how armour was designed to guard a body without trapping it.
payload.title: Old armour balanced safety and movement
decoys: Heavier armour slowed a soldier down
Soldiers have fought in wars for ages
Kunal wanted to try on the shiny helmet

payload.passage: The guide led Nandini's class to a grand baoli, a step-pond with many levels of carved arches going down to the water. She explained that the deeper levels stayed cool even in peak summer. People gathered there to escape the heat as much as to fetch water. Some even sat and chatted on the shaded steps for hours. Nandini learned that the step-pond was both a water store and a cool summer retreat.
payload.title: A step pond was a cool summer retreat
decoys: The lower levels stayed cool in summer
Old buildings are interesting to visit
Nandini walked down to the lowest level

payload.passage: The classroom got terribly hot in the afternoon sun every day. The children sweated and found it hard to pay attention. The teacher hung thick curtains on the sunny side of the windows. The curtains blocked the harsh heat and cooled the whole room. The class felt fresh again and lessons became easy to follow.
payload.title: Thick curtains solved the hot afternoon classroom
decoys: The children sweated in the afternoon heat
The teacher hung curtains on the windows

payload.passage: A bus driver carries many people safely across the busy city. Early in the morning he checks his bus before the first trip. Then he drives along his route, stopping at each bus stop on time. He watches the road carefully so that every passenger reaches home safely. So a bus driver's job is to take people safely from place to place.
payload.title: How a bus driver keeps passengers safe
decoys: The driver stops at each bus stop on time
Many workers keep the city moving
Buses can get very crowded at rush hour

payload.passage: Vihaan held a long ruler half over the edge of the desk and gave it a flick. It made a low, slow twang as its free end waved up and down. He slid the ruler in so less stuck out and flicked again, and the note rose higher. His teacher said a shorter free end shakes faster. Vihaan learned that a shorter shaking ruler makes a higher sound.
payload.title: A shorter shaking ruler makes a higher sound
decoys: Vihaan flicked the ruler on the desk
Sounds can be high or low
The free end waved up and down

payload.passage: Anushka set out two saucers of water, one wide and flat and one in a narrow tall glass, with equal water in each. She left both in the shade this time, not the sun. Even in the shade the wide saucer lost more water than the narrow glass. Her teacher said a wider top always dries faster. Anushka learned that a wider water surface dries faster even in the shade.
payload.title: A wider water surface dries faster in shade
decoys: The narrow glass kept more water
Anushka kept both in the shade

payload.passage: Simran wanted to learn how to do a backbend for her dance class. Her back felt tight and she was scared of falling over. She did gentle stretches and bent only a little each day. Her spine grew softer and her fear slowly melted away. After a month Simran did a smooth backbend that amazed her dance teacher.
payload.title: Gentle stretching helped Simran do a backbend
decoys: Simran was scared of falling over
Dancers must always have very flexible bodies
Simran's dance teacher was amazed by her

payload.passage: A rope-and-pulley flagpole raises a flag to the top. A loop of rope runs over a small wheel fixed at the top of the pole. The flag is tied to one side of the loop down at the bottom. When you pull the other side down, the flag side rises smoothly up. So a flagpole pulley lets you raise a flag by pulling the rope down.
payload.title: How a pulley raises a flag up a pole
decoys: A loop of rope runs over a wheel
The flag is tied to one side

payload.passage: At the museum, Manav's class entered a hall of old weapons and tools placed side by side. The guide pointed out that the very same skill of working metal made both a sharp sword and a useful plough. The metalworkers, she said, served the kingdom in war and in peace. Manav learned that old metalwork helped people in both fighting and farming.
payload.title: Old metalwork served both war and farming
decoys: The same skill made a sword and a plough
Metal is useful in countless ways
Manav liked the gleam of the old blade

payload.passage: Mehul left out a saucer of plain water, a saucer of soapy water and a saucer of sugar water to see which dried first. He kept all three in the same sunny spot. By evening the plain water had shrunk most, while the sugary one held back the longest. His teacher said dissolved stuff slows drying. Mehul learned that plain water dries faster than sugary water.
payload.title: Plain water dries faster than sugary water
decoys: The sugary saucer held back longest
Water dries up in the sun

payload.passage: A tomato plant grows from a small flat seed inside a juicy tomato. Planted in warm soil, the seed sprouts into a leafy green plant. Yellow flowers appear, and after bees visit them, tiny green tomatoes form. These slowly swell and ripen from green to a bright red. So one tiny seed can grow a plant full of red tomatoes.
payload.title: How a tomato grows from a seed
decoys: The tomatoes ripen from green to bright red
Many tasty foods grow on plants
Tomatoes are used in many Indian dishes

payload.passage: A coral reef is bright and busy during the day but quiet at night. By day, colourful fish dart among the coral looking for food. Some sea creatures only come out after dark to feed safely. The reef changes who is awake as day turns into night. So a coral reef has a busy day shift and a different night shift.
payload.title: A coral reef changes from day to night
decoys: Colourful fish dart among the coral by day
The ocean is full of busy life
Coral reefs grow only in warm seas

payload.passage: Karan noticed that the colony drains overflowed every monsoon because of plastic stuck inside them. His youth group spent a whole Sunday clearing out the choked drains. They also asked people to bin their waste instead of throwing it on the road. That year, for the first time, the lanes did not flood. The group learned that keeping drains clear stops the streets from flooding.
payload.title: Keeping drains clear stops streets flooding
decoys: Plastic was stuck inside the drains
Karan belongs to a youth group

payload.passage: A bicycle pump pushes air into a flat tyre. When you pull the handle up, air rushes into the long barrel. Pushing the handle down squeezes that air through a tube into the tyre. A small one-way flap keeps the air from sliding back out. So a bicycle pump fills a tyre by squeezing trapped air into it.
payload.title: How a bicycle pump pushes air into a tyre
decoys: A one-way flap stops air sliding back
Tyres need air to roll well

payload.passage: Avni left a shiny tin and a black tin of equal water side by side in the sun. After an hour she dipped a finger into each to feel the warmth. The water in the black tin was clearly warmer than in the shiny one. Her teacher said dark colours soak up more sunlight than bright ones. Avni learned that dark surfaces absorb more heat from the sun.
payload.title: Dark surfaces absorb more heat from the sun
decoys: Avni dipped a finger into each tin
The sun shines down on everything
Tins can be shiny or dull

payload.passage: A barnacle leads two very different lives. As a baby it swims freely about in the sea like tiny dust. When it finds a good rock or ship, it sticks down head first and never moves again. There it grows a hard shell and waves its feet to catch food from the water. So a wandering baby barnacle settles down to a still life.
payload.title: A swimming barnacle settles on a rock
decoys: A barnacle sticks itself down head first
Sea creatures live in many odd ways
Barnacles often cling to the sides of ships

payload.passage: Charvi planted radish seeds in a sunny bed and watered them every day. She marked the date and watched the tiny shoots push up through the soil. Within a few weeks the leaves were broad and the roots had swelled into round radishes. Her grandmother said radishes are one of the quickest crops to grow. Charvi learned that radishes grow from seed to food very quickly.
payload.title: Radishes grow from seed to food quickly
decoys: Charvi watered the seeds every day
Vegetables are good for our health
The radish leaves grew broad and green

payload.passage: Vivek rubbed an inflated balloon on his hair and held it near a thin trickle of water from the tap. Then he held a plain, unrubbed balloon near the same trickle. The rubbed balloon bent the water towards it, but the plain one did nothing. His teacher said only the charged balloon pulls the water. Vivek learned that only a rubbed balloon can bend a water stream.
payload.title: Only a rubbed balloon can bend water
decoys: Balloons can be filled with air
Vivek rubbed a balloon on his hair

payload.passage: The guide led Sana to a fort with a clever winding entrance that bent sharply several times. She explained that this was no mistake: the turns slowed down any attacking army and stopped them from charging straight in. Guards above could strike them at each bend. Sana learned that even the twisting path was planned to defend the fort.
payload.title: A fort's winding path slowed attackers
decoys: The entrance bent sharply several times
Forts were built to be very strong
Sana enjoyed walking through the bends

payload.passage: A dragonfly spends most of its early life under water. It hatches from an egg into a creature called a nymph that lives in a pond. The hungry nymph hunts tiny water animals for months or even years. At last it climbs up a reed, splits its skin, and unfolds bright wings. So the water nymph finally changes into a flying dragonfly.
payload.title: A water nymph becomes a dragonfly
decoys: The nymph hunts tiny animals under water
Pond life is full of surprises
Dragonflies dart quickly over the water

payload.passage: Nidhi tried to learn embroidery to decorate a small handkerchief. The thread kept knotting and her flowers looked like tangled blobs. Her grandmother taught her to take short, even stitches without rushing. Slowly Nidhi's flowers grew neat petals and curling green leaves. The finished handkerchief was so pretty that her grandmother kept it for herself.
payload.title: Patient stitching taught Nidhi to embroider
decoys: Nidhi's thread kept knotting at the start
Sewing is a useful skill that lasts forever
Nidhi decorated a small white handkerchief

payload.passage: A school watchman keeps the children safe inside the school gate. He opens the gate in the morning and shuts it once classes begin. He checks anyone who comes during school hours. He makes sure no child wanders out onto the busy road. So a watchman's work is to guard the school and its children.
payload.title: How a watchman guards the school gate
decoys: He shuts the gate once classes begin
The road outside school is busy

payload.passage: Geeta found knitting very hard when she first held the needles. Her stitches were loose and the wool kept slipping off the points. Her aunt showed her one stitch and asked her to repeat it slowly. Geeta practised the same row again and again until her hands stopped shaking. By winter she had knitted a small scarf for her little brother.
payload.title: Repeating one stitch taught Geeta to knit
decoys: Geeta's wool kept slipping off the needles
Knitting is a hobby that keeps people warm
Geeta made a scarf for her little brother

payload.passage: Drishti soaked a handful of dry beans overnight in a bowl of water and left an equal number out dry. In the morning the soaked beans were fat, soft and free of wrinkles. The dry beans beside them were still small, hard and shrivelled. Her teacher said the soaked beans had drunk up the water and swelled. Drishti learned that dry beans swell up when they soak in water.
payload.title: Dry beans swell up when they soak in water
decoys: The dry beans stayed small and hard

payload.passage: A bulb is a clever way for some flowers to survive a harsh season. The plant stores food in a fat underground bulb before the cold or dry time. Above ground the leaves may wither away completely. When good weather returns, the bulb sends up fresh shoots and flowers. So a hidden bulb lets a plant rest and then grow again.
payload.title: How a bulb helps a plant survive
decoys: The plant stores food in a fat bulb
Plants have many ways to stay alive
Tulips and onions grow from bulbs

payload.passage: Hriday floated a cork in the middle of a bowl of water and tried to keep it there. Each time it drifted to the edge and stayed by the side. He filled the bowl right to the brim and tried again, and now the cork sat in the middle. His teacher said a cork goes to the highest point of the water. Hriday learned that a cork floats to the highest part of the water.
payload.title: A cork floats to the highest part of water
decoys: The cork kept drifting to the edge
Hriday filled the bowl to the brim

payload.passage: A sundial on a windowsill marks the hours with a shadow. A small upright pin stands on a card ringed with hour marks. As the sun moves across the sky, the pin's shadow swings round the card. You read the hour where the shadow points. So a pin and card tell the hour by the swing of a shadow.
payload.title: How a pin and card tell hours by shadow
decoys: An upright pin stands on the card

payload.passage: At the museum, Avni found old jewellery laid out in glass cases. The guide explained that more than mere decoration, the jewellery once showed who a person was: which family they came from, whether they were married, and even their work. Each piece carried a meaning everyone could read. Avni learned that old jewellery once told people's stories without a single word.
payload.title: Old jewellery told people's stories
decoys: Some jewellery showed if a person was married
Jewellery is worn all over the world
Avni thought the gold pieces sparkled

payload.passage: Shaan placed a wide tray of muddy water in the sun and left it for two days. Slowly the water rose as vapour, leaving the mud behind on the tray. He collected the vapour on a cool lid and found the drops were clear and clean. His teacher said only the water rises, not the dirt. Shaan learned that the sun can clean dirty water by evaporating it.
payload.title: The sun cleans dirty water by evaporating it
decoys: The mud was left behind on the tray
Clean water is precious for everyone
Shaan used a wide tray of water

payload.passage: A chameleon is a lizard that can change the colour of its skin. When it sits on a green leaf, it can turn green to match. On a brown branch it can turn brown and almost disappear. This change helps it hide from enemies and sneak up on insects. So a chameleon shifts colour to blend in with its world.
payload.title: A chameleon changes colour to hide
decoys: A chameleon turns green on a green leaf
Animals protect themselves in clever ways
Chameleons catch insects with long tongues

payload.passage: The football kept rolling into the busy road beside the school field. The children ran after it and gave their teachers a fright. The teachers asked for a tall net fence around the playing area. The new fence stopped the ball from leaving the field. Now the children play freely without anyone running into the road.
payload.title: A net fence kept the football off the road
decoys: The children gave their teachers a fright
Roads near schools are always very dangerous
The teachers asked for a tall net fence

payload.passage: Yashvi shone a torch through a glass of clear water at a sheet of white paper. The light went straight through and made a plain bright patch. Then she stirred in a spoon of milk and shone again, and the beam scattered into a soft glow. Her teacher said the milk bits bounced the light around. Yashvi learned that tiny bits in water scatter a beam of light.
payload.title: Tiny bits in water scatter a light beam
decoys: The beam scattered after adding milk
Yashvi shone a torch through water

payload.passage: A catapult toy flings a soft ball across the room. A springy arm is pulled down and held against a stretchy band. A small ball is set in the cup at the end of the arm. When you release the arm, the band snaps it up and the ball flies off. So a catapult throws a ball as a stretched band snaps the arm up.
payload.title: How a stretched band flings a catapult ball
decoys: A ball sits in the cup
The springy arm is pulled down

payload.passage: Veer's group set up a small library of toys and games at school. Families can borrow a toy for a week and then return it. This way children play with many toys without buying new ones they soon grow bored of. So fewer toys are bought and wasted. The group learned that a toy library means less is bought and thrown away.
payload.title: A toy library means less is bought and wasted
decoys: Families borrow toys for a week
Veer's group set up the library

payload.passage: Lakshya wanted to know if heavier balls bounce higher. He dropped a light rubber ball and a heavier one from the same height onto the floor. To his surprise, the bouncy light ball sprang back higher than the heavy one. His teacher said how high a ball bounces depends on what it is made of, not just its weight. Lakshya learned that a ball's material, not its weight, decides its bounce.
payload.title: A ball's material decides its bounce, not weight
decoys: Lakshya dropped both balls from the same height
Balls are used in many games

payload.passage: A school nurse looks after children who feel unwell during the day. She has a small room with a bed and a box of medicines. When a child has a headache or a scraped knee, she helps right away. She cleans cuts, gives rest, and calls home if a child is very sick. So a school nurse's job is to care for unwell children at school.
payload.title: How a school nurse cares for children
decoys: She cleans cuts and gives rest

payload.passage: Ria's class started a paper-saving plan after seeing how many sheets they threw away. Now they write on both sides, reuse one-side paper for rough work, and collect old sheets for recycling. In one month they used half as much paper as before. The class learned that small habits can save a lot of paper, and a lot of trees.
payload.title: Small habits can save paper and trees
decoys: The class writes on both sides of paper
Schools use a great deal of paper
Ria's class made a new plan

payload.passage: An apple does not appear on a tree all at once. First the tree grows soft pink and white flowers in spring. After the flowers are visited by bees, their petals fall away. A tiny green fruit then begins to swell where each flower used to be. Through the summer it grows bigger and turns red, until it is a ripe apple.
payload.title: How an apple grows from a flower
decoys: The apple tree grows pink and white flowers
Fruit trees are a lovely part of nature
Apples are crunchy and full of good juice

payload.passage: Sia wanted to learn how to fold her clothes into neat little squares. Her early folds left the clothes lumpy and falling open. She watched a video and practised pressing each fold flat with her palm. Her clothes soon stacked up tidy and even in the cupboard. Soon Sia could fold a whole pile of laundry by herself in minutes.
payload.title: Pressing folds flat taught Sia to fold clothes neatly
decoys: Sia's early folds left the clothes lumpy
A neat cupboard makes finding clothes very easy
Sia folded a whole pile of laundry

payload.passage: Dev noticed the river water looked thick and brown after three days of rain. His teacher explained that fast-moving water scrapes loose soil from the banks and fields and carries it along, so a swollen river is full of mud. When it slows, the mud settles again. Dev learned that a fast river carries away soil and mud.
payload.title: A fast river carries away soil and mud
decoys: Dev saw the river after the rain

payload.passage: Yug pressed his ear flat against the long metal railing while a friend tapped the far end softly with a spoon. He heard the taps clearly and quickly through the railing. When he listened through the air alone, the sound was much fainter. His teacher said sound moves well through solid metal. Yug learned that sound travels better through metal than through air.
payload.title: Sound travels better through metal than air
decoys: Yug pressed his ear to the railing
A friend tapped the far end

payload.passage: At the museum, Rakesh found a room about old trade by sea. The guide showed jars, beads and cloth that ships once carried between distant lands. Because of this trade, she said, new foods, ideas and stories spread from country to country. Rakesh understood that the room showed how sea trade carried goods and ideas around the world.
payload.title: Sea trade carried goods and ideas worldwide
decoys: Ships once carried jars and beads
The sea is important for many countries
Rakesh liked the shiny old beads

payload.passage: The students planted shady trees and leafy creepers along the school's hot brick wall. As the plants grew taller, they shaded both the wall and the windows from the sun. Because of this, the classrooms stayed cooler in summer without any extra fans. Birds came to nest among the leaves as well. The students learned that shady plants cool a building and save electricity.
payload.title: Shady plants cool a building and save power
decoys: Creepers grew along the brick wall
Summers are hot in the city

payload.passage: A cyclone is a giant storm that spins over warm seas. Warm wet air rises quickly and begins to swirl in a huge circle. As more warm air feeds it, the storm grows wider and stronger. It carries fierce winds and heavy rain towards the coast. So a cyclone is a powerful spinning storm born over the sea.
payload.title: How a cyclone forms over the sea
decoys: Warm wet air rises and starts to swirl
The weather can become very wild
People near the coast prepare for cyclones

payload.passage: A torch-bulb dimmer shows how a longer wire dims a light. In the loop with the battery and bulb sits a length of thin coiled wire. When the loop is short, the bulb glows brightly. When more of the coiled wire is used, the bulb glows dimmer. So adding more thin wire into a loop makes a bulb glow dimmer.
payload.title: How more wire dims a bulb in a loop
decoys: A short loop made the bulb bright
Thin coiled wire sits in the loop

payload.passage: Shaurya wondered why his shadow grew long in the evening. He stood in the same spot in the morning, at noon and just before sunset and asked a friend to draw round his shadow each time. The shadow was short at noon but stretched far at sunset. His teacher said a low sun throws a long shadow and a high sun a short one. Shaurya learned that the sun's height decides his shadow's length.
payload.title: The sun's height decides a shadow's length
decoys: The shadow was shortest at noon
The sun travels across the sky daily
A friend drew round Shaurya's shadow

payload.passage: At home, the family kept losing the house keys somewhere every day. Mornings began with a frantic search before leaving for work. Father nailed a small hook by the door for hanging the keys. Everyone hung the keys there the moment they came in. The morning searches ended and no one was ever late again.
payload.title: A key hook solved the lost-keys mornings
decoys: Mornings began with a frantic search
A small change can fix a big daily trouble
Father nailed a hook by the front door

payload.passage: Spiders, snakes, and crabs all share one odd habit, they shed their skin. As a young creature grows, its old outer skin becomes too tight. So the animal wriggles out of the old skin, leaving it behind. Underneath is a fresh, roomier skin ready for the bigger body. So shedding skin lets these animals keep growing larger.
payload.title: Shedding skin lets animals keep growing
decoys: A snake wriggles out of its old skin
Animals change in many surprising ways
Some snakes can swim in rivers and ponds

payload.passage: A bicycle dynamo lights the lamp as you ride. A little wheel on the dynamo rests against the moving tyre. As the tyre turns, it spins this wheel and a magnet inside. The spinning magnet makes power that flows up the wire to the lamp. So a dynamo lights a bicycle lamp by turning wheel motion into power.
payload.title: How a dynamo lights a lamp as you ride
decoys: A little wheel rests on the tyre
Lights keep riders safe at night
A magnet spins inside the dynamo

payload.passage: Kavya was puzzled that the wet clothes on the line dried even on a cool day with no sun. Her mother explained that drying does not need heat alone. As long as the air around the cloth is dry and moving, it keeps pulling water away. The water leaves the cloth as invisible vapour. Kavya learned that moving air dries clothes by carrying water away.
payload.title: Moving air dries clothes by carrying water away
decoys: The clothes dried on a cool day
Washing clothes is a daily chore

payload.passage: A see-saw in the park lets two children lift each other with ease. A long plank rests across a bar in the middle, which works as a pivot. When one child pushes down on one end, that end sinks and the far end rises. By shifting nearer or further from the middle, even a lighter child can lift a heavier friend. So a see-saw uses a pivot to balance and swap weight.
payload.title: How a see-saw uses a pivot to lift
decoys: The plank rests across a middle bar
Parks are fun places to play
One end rises as the other sinks

payload.passage: A vegetable weigher helps the seller serve customers at the stall. As people pick their vegetables, he places them on the scale. He reads the weight and works out the price to charge. He packs the vegetables into bags and takes the money. So a weigher's work is to weigh and bill the goods for buyers.
payload.title: How a weigher serves customers at the stall
decoys: He places the vegetables on the scale
Fresh vegetables are sold by weight

payload.passage: Meera's little brother kept scribbling on her school notes at home. Her neat pages were ruined and she had to copy them again. She found a high shelf where her brother could not reach. Every day after homework she kept her books safely up there. After that her notes stayed clean and she stopped redoing her work.
payload.title: A high shelf saved Meera's notes from her brother
decoys: Meera's neat pages were ruined by scribbles
Younger children always trouble their elder ones
Meera had to copy her notes again

payload.passage: A weather balloon climbs high to sniff the sky. It is filled with a gas lighter than air and let go from the ground. Being lighter, the balloon rises higher and higher into the cool air. A small box hanging below sends back readings as it goes. So a weather balloon rises high because it is filled with a light gas.
payload.title: How a light gas lifts a weather balloon high
decoys: A small box hangs below it
The balloon is let go from the ground

payload.passage: In the museum's farming room, Anaya saw old wooden ploughs, sickles and grinding stones. The guide explained that every tool was shaped for one job and used the strength of animals or hands, not engines. Together they showed how families grew and made their food before tractors and mills. Anaya understood that the room told the story of farming in the days before machines.
payload.title: Old tools show farming before machines
decoys: A grinding stone was used to make flour
Farmers work very hard to grow our food
Anaya liked the smell of the old wood

payload.passage: The students kept knocking over the open paint pots during art class. Spilled paint stained the desks and the floor badly. The teacher gave each child a wide, heavy tray to hold the pots. The steady trays stopped the pots from tipping over. Art class became neat and free of messy spills after that.
payload.title: Heavy trays solved the spilling paint pots
decoys: Art lets every child show their creativity
The teacher gave each child a heavy tray

payload.passage: Tara wanted to skip rope a hundred times without stopping. In the beginning the rope kept catching on her feet after just five jumps. She counted her best score each day and tried to beat it by a few jumps. The numbers slowly climbed from ten to fifty and then towards a hundred. On a bright Sunday morning Tara finally skipped past a hundred and cheered out loud.
payload.title: Beating her own score helped Tara skip longer
decoys: The rope kept catching on Tara's feet
Sports teach children to never give up at all
Tara skipped rope on a bright Sunday morning

payload.passage: At home, the study table was always too cluttered to work on. Old papers and odd things piled up and left no space. Geeta cleared the table each evening before starting her homework. With a clean, open space, she could spread out her books. Her homework grew faster and far less frustrating after that.
payload.title: Clearing the table eased Geeta's homework
decoys: Old papers piled up on the table
A clean space makes any work easier to do
Geeta cleared the table every evening

payload.passage: The school's gate often stayed locked because the watchman lost the key. Children waited outside until a spare was hunted down. A duplicate key was made and kept safely in the office. Whenever the key went missing, the spare opened the gate at once. The morning waits at the locked gate ended for good.
payload.title: A duplicate key solved the locked-gate waits
decoys: Children waited outside the locked gate
A watchman keeps every school safe and secure
A duplicate key was kept in the office

payload.passage: A counterweight lift raises a heavy gate with a hanging weight. A rope runs from the gate over a wheel to a heavy block on the other side. The block's weight pulls down and helps lift the gate up. With the block doing much of the work, a small tug raises the gate. So a counterweight helps lift a heavy gate with little effort.
payload.title: How a counterweight helps lift a heavy gate
decoys: A rope runs over a wheel
The block pulls down on its side

payload.passage: A flush tank refills itself after you press the lever, which lets the stored water rush down to clean the bowl. As the tank empties, a hollow float inside drops down with the falling water. The sinking float opens a valve that lets fresh water flow back in. When the water rises again, the float lifts and shuts the valve. So a floating ball controls when the tank fills and stops.
payload.title: How a float refills a flush tank
decoys: Pressing the lever empties the tank
Bathrooms need a clean water supply
A hollow float sits inside the tank

payload.passage: Maya could never wake up in time because her curtains kept the room dark. She slept past the alarm in the gloomy room each morning. She started leaving the curtains a little open at night. The morning light streamed in and woke her gently and naturally. Maya now rose on time and felt fresh for school.
payload.title: Open curtains solved Maya's oversleeping
decoys: Maya slept past the alarm each morning
Morning sunlight is healthy for everyone
Maya left her curtains a little open

payload.passage: A coral polyp is a tiny animal, but it does not live alone inside its cup. Even tinier living things make their home inside the polyp's body. These tiny helpers use sunlight to make food and share some with the coral. In return the polyp gives them a safe place to stay. So coral and its tiny guests help each other live.
payload.title: Coral and tiny helpers live together
decoys: Tiny helpers make food using sunlight
The sea hides many tiny living things
Coral reefs grow in warm clear water

payload.passage: An electrician fixes the wiring that brings power to our homes. When the lights go out or a fan stops, people call him for help. He checks the wires and switches carefully to find the fault. Then he repairs or replaces the broken part to set things right. So an electrician's work is to keep our power running safely.
payload.title: How an electrician keeps power running
decoys: He checks the wires to find the fault
Many skilled helpers serve our homes
We should never touch a live wire

payload.passage: Nivaan stood a flowerpot of soil in a tray and tipped a jug of water onto the bare soil all at once. Muddy water ran straight off and carried soil into the tray. Then he covered the soil with dry leaves and poured again, and far less soil washed away. His teacher said the cover shields the soil. Nivaan learned that a leaf cover stops soil from washing away.
payload.title: A leaf cover stops soil washing away
decoys: Muddy water ran off the bare soil
Nivaan poured water from a jug

payload.passage: After a downpour, Tanvi saw a bright rainbow arch across the sky. Her mother explained that sunlight is really a mix of many colours, and when it shines through tiny raindrops still in the air, each drop bends and splits the light into its colours. That is why a rainbow needs both sun and rain. Tanvi learned that a rainbow forms when sunlight passes through raindrops.
payload.title: A rainbow forms when sunlight meets raindrops
decoys: The rainbow arched across the sky
Tanvi watched the sky after the rain

payload.passage: Kunal balanced a ruler on a pencil and put a coin on one end. He slid the pencil along until the ruler lay level again. He found that the heavier the coin, the closer the pencil had to sit to it. His teacher said the balance point shifts towards the heavier side. Kunal learned that the balance point moves towards the heavier weight.
payload.title: The balance point moves towards heavier weight
decoys: Kunal slid the pencil along the ruler
He put a coin on one end

payload.passage: A carpenter makes and mends things out of wood. He measures and cuts planks to just the right size. He then joins them with nails, glue, or screws into useful shapes. From his hands come tables, chairs, doors, and shelves. So a carpenter's work is to build helpful things from wood.
payload.title: How a carpenter builds things from wood
decoys: He joins the planks with nails and glue
Many skilled helpers serve our homes
Wood comes from trees that grow tall

payload.passage: Kiara stood two plants of the same kind side by side on a sunny windowsill. She turned one pot a quarter-turn every single day but left the other one as it was. After two weeks the turned plant had grown straight and even, while the still plant leaned over to one side. Her teacher said turning shares the light all round. Kiara learned that turning a plant keeps it growing straight.
payload.title: Turning a plant keeps it growing straight
decoys: The still plant leaned to one side

payload.passage: Yuvraj watched a line of geese fly over the lake in a neat V shape. The lead bird flew at the front point, and the others trailed behind on each side. After a while a different goose moved up to take the lead. His uncle said the V shape helps them save their strength. Yuvraj learned that geese fly in a V to make the long trip easier.
payload.title: Geese fly in a V to save strength
decoys: A new goose took the lead
The lead bird was at the front

payload.passage: Veena set out a saucer of plain water and a saucer of sugar water in the garden to see which bees liked best. She watched quietly from a bench for half an hour. Bee after bee came to the sweet saucer, while the plain water was almost ignored. Her teacher said bees seek out sweet food for energy. Veena learned that bees are drawn to sweet water more than plain water.
payload.title: Bees prefer sweet water over plain water
decoys: Veena watched quietly from a bench
Insects visit gardens for many reasons

payload.passage: Aaradhya scattered the same number of seeds into a crowded pot and a roomy one. She watered both the same and watched them grow. The roomy pot grew a few strong plants, but the crowded pot grew many weak, thin ones. Her teacher said crowded plants must share food and light. Aaradhya learned that crowded plants grow weaker than spaced ones.
payload.title: Crowded plants grow weaker than spaced ones
decoys: The crowded pot grew thin plants

payload.passage: Tara left a slice of bread on a plate near the window and another slice in the dry, cool fridge. She checked both slices every day for a week with a magnifying glass. The window slice grew fuzzy green and grey patches, but the fridge slice stayed fresh. Her teacher said warmth and damp air help mould grow on food. Tara learned that bread goes mouldy faster in a warm, damp place.
payload.title: Warmth and damp make bread grow mould faster
decoys: Tara checked the slices with a magnifying glass
Food must be looked after with care
A fridge keeps many foods cool inside

payload.passage: Tanish placed a thin slice of bread in a closed box with a saucer of water and another slice in a dry closed box. He kept both warm and checked daily. The slice with water nearby grew mould first, while the dry one stayed clean far longer. His teacher said extra damp speeds up mould. Tanish learned that nearby water helps mould grow faster on bread.
payload.title: Nearby water helps mould grow faster on bread
decoys: The dry slice stayed clean longer

payload.passage: Tisha laid a sheet of dark paper and a sheet of foil under the noon sun with an ice cube on each. She watched to see which cube melted first. The cube on the dark paper melted quickly, while the foil one lasted much longer. Her teacher said shiny foil throws back the heat. Tisha learned that shiny foil keeps ice from melting fast.
payload.title: Shiny foil keeps ice from melting fast
decoys: The dark paper cube melted quickly

payload.passage: A bicycle freewheel lets you stop pedalling and still roll. The rear wheel has a clever ring of little catches inside it. When you pedal, the catches grip and drive the wheel forward. When you stop, the catches let go and the wheel spins freely on. So a freewheel lets a bicycle coast along even when the pedals are still.
payload.title: How a freewheel lets a bicycle coast
decoys: Little catches sit inside the wheel
The catches grip when you pedal

payload.passage: A mechanic repairs cars, scooters, and bikes when they break down. When a vehicle stops working, its owner brings it to his garage. He listens to the engine and checks the parts to find the trouble. Then he tightens, cleans, or changes the faulty part. So a mechanic's work is to mend vehicles and get them moving again.
payload.title: How a mechanic mends our vehicles
decoys: He checks the parts to find the trouble
Many skilled helpers serve our town

payload.passage: Aanya's family looked at how their old fridge used power. They set it to a steadier, sensible setting. They dusted the warm coils at the back. They also stopped leaving the door open while deciding what to eat. These small steps cut the electricity it used, and the family learned that simple care for a fridge saves electricity.
payload.title: Simple care for a fridge saves electricity

payload.passage: Diya filled a glass right up to the brim with water and slid coins in one at a time. She expected the water to spill at once, but it rose into a little dome above the rim first. Many coins went in before a single drop ran over. Her father said the water's skin held it together until the dome grew too heavy. Diya learned that water has a stretchy surface that holds it in a dome.
payload.title: Water has a stretchy skin holding a dome
decoys: Many coins went in before water spilled
Diya slid the coins in one by one

payload.passage: Naira watched a butterfly visit flower after flower in the garden. Each time it landed, it unrolled a long thin tube and dipped it into the bloom. After feeding, the tube curled back up neatly under its head. Her teacher said the butterfly sips sweet nectar through that tube. Naira learned that a butterfly drinks nectar through a long curling tube.
payload.title: A butterfly drinks nectar through a curling tube
decoys: The tube curled back under its head

payload.passage: A snowflake forms high in a freezing cloud as a tiny ice crystal. As it floats and falls, more water freezes onto its sides. The water always freezes in a six-sided pattern, building delicate arms. No two snowflakes grow in exactly the same way. So each falling snowflake becomes its own six-armed shape.
payload.title: How a six-armed snowflake forms
decoys: Water freezes onto the crystal's six sides
Winter weather can be very beautiful
Children build snowmen out of fresh snow

payload.passage: Advait blew gently across the mouth of an empty bottle and heard a low hooting note. He poured some water in and blew again, and the note became higher. The more water he added, the higher it sang. His teacher said less air in the bottle makes a higher note. Advait learned that the air left in a bottle decides its note.
payload.title: The air left in a bottle decides its note
decoys: More water gave a higher note
Advait blew across the bottle mouth

payload.passage: A sand dune is a hill of sand that slowly moves across a desert. The wind picks up loose grains and carries them up one side. The grains tumble down the far side and pile up there. Bit by bit, the whole dune creeps along in the direction of the wind. So a sand dune is a hill that the wind slowly walks across the land.
payload.title: How the wind moves a sand dune
decoys: Grains tumble down the far side of the dune
Camels can walk easily over soft sand

payload.passage: A craft teacher shows children how to make things with their hands. She brings paper, clay, and colours to the class. She guides the children to fold, cut, and shape these into crafts. She praises each child's work and helps fix any mistakes. So a craft teacher's work is to teach children to make things by hand.
payload.title: How a craft teacher guides young hands
decoys: She brings paper, clay, and colours
Many helpers teach children new skills
Making things by hand is good fun

payload.passage: A spinning fan of cards makes a breeze on the desk. Stiff cards are fixed at a slant around a spool on a stick. When you spin the stick fast between your hands, the slanted cards push the air. A small gust drifts towards your face. So a card fan makes a breeze as its slanted cards push air while spinning.
payload.title: How spinning slanted cards make a breeze
decoys: Cards are fixed around a spool
You spin the stick between your hands

payload.passage: A sandpaper block smooths a rough piece of wood with ease. The wooden block is wrapped in gritty paper covered in tiny hard specks. When you rub it firmly back and forth over the wood, the specks scrape off the rough bumps. Tiny shavings of wood come away from the surface as fine dust. So a sandpaper block smooths wood by scraping off its rough bumps.
payload.title: How sandpaper scrapes rough wood smooth
decoys: Tiny shavings come away as dust
Wood can be rough at first
The block is wrapped in gritty paper

payload.passage: A see-through syringe draws up liquid by pulling a tight plunger. When you pull the plunger back, it leaves an empty space inside the barrel. Liquid is pushed up through the thin tip to fill that space. Pressing the plunger in again squeezes the liquid back out. So a syringe pulls in and pushes out liquid by moving its plunger.
payload.title: How a plunger makes a syringe draw liquid
decoys: Pulling back leaves an empty space
Liquid enters through the thin tip

payload.passage: The children of Green Lane formed a club to save their dirty park. Every Saturday they pick up plastic, paper and tins, then sort them into three bins so the waste can be recycled instead of burned. They also plant a sapling each month. Slowly the park has grown clean and green. Their work shows how a small club can bring a park back to life.
payload.title: A children's club brings a park back to life
decoys: The children plant a sapling each month
Parks are nice places to play

payload.passage: Vanya laid a sheet of black paper on the sunny ground and a sheet of white paper beside it, then placed a thermometer on each. After a while the thermometer on the black paper read much higher. She swapped them and got the same result. Her teacher said dark soaks up more sun. Vanya learned that black paper grows warmer than white in the sun.
payload.title: Black paper grows warmer than white in sun
decoys: Vanya swapped the papers to be sure
She placed a thermometer on each

payload.passage: The classroom's spare books were stacked in a wobbly, falling pile. Books slid off and got their pages crumpled and bent. The teacher fitted a simple shelf to hold the books upright. The books stood neatly side by side and stopped falling. Children could pick out a book easily without toppling the rest.
payload.title: A shelf solved the wobbly book pile
decoys: Books slid off and got crumpled
Books are a treasure in any classroom
The teacher fitted a simple shelf

payload.passage: Hardik wanted to learn how to make a paper fortune teller for his friends. His first ones folded crooked and would not open and close. He followed the steps slowly and creased each fold neatly. The fortune teller then snapped open and shut in a fun way. Hardik amused his whole class with the paper toy at lunch break.
payload.title: Neat creasing taught Hardik to make a fortune teller
decoys: Hardik's first ones would not open
Simple toys can entertain a whole classroom
Hardik used the toy at lunch break

payload.passage: Reyaan rubbed a plastic ruler hard on his sleeve and held it over a thin stream of dry salt poured from a spoon. The falling salt swerved towards the charged ruler as it fell. When he set the ruler down, the salt fell straight again. His teacher said the charge pulled the light salt grains. Reyaan learned that a charged ruler can pull tiny salt grains as they fall.
payload.title: A charged ruler pulls falling salt grains
decoys: Reyaan rubbed the ruler on his sleeve
Salt is poured from a spoon

payload.passage: Priya's family swapped throwaway plastic bottles for steel ones they fill at home and carry everywhere. They also keep a cloth bag ready for shopping. For snacks, they pack steel boxes instead of plastic packets. Over a year, the family bought almost no single-use plastic at all. They learned that choosing reusable things sharply cuts a family's plastic waste.
payload.title: Choosing reusable things cuts plastic waste
decoys: The family uses steel water bottles
Plastic is used in many products

payload.passage: At home, Aarav's toys were scattered all over the living room floor. Guests had no place to sit and someone often stepped on a toy. He got a big basket to drop all his toys into after playing. The floor cleared up in minutes whenever someone came over. Aarav's tidy habit made the living room welcoming again.
payload.title: A toy basket solved the messy living room
decoys: Someone often stepped on a scattered toy
Children should always keep their homes neat
Aarav dropped his toys into a big basket

payload.passage: Trisha set up a row of marbles touching in a line and rolled one more marble hard into one end. The marble at the far end shot off, while the middle ones barely stirred. She tried with two marbles and two flew off the other end. Her teacher said the push passes through the line. Trisha learned that a push can pass through a row of touching marbles.
payload.title: A push passes through a row of marbles
decoys: The far marble shot off the end
Trisha rolled one marble in hard

payload.passage: A water wheel by a stream turns just from the flowing water. The wheel has many flat paddles set around its rim. As the stream pushes against the lower paddles, it forces the wheel to turn. The turning wheel can spin a shaft to grind grain or lift water. So a water wheel uses a flowing stream to make a steady turning.
payload.title: How a stream turns a water wheel
decoys: Flat paddles ring the wheel's rim
The wheel can spin a shaft

payload.passage: Pooja tried to learn a few card tricks to amaze her cousins. The cards kept slipping and her tricks were easy to spot at first. She practised in front of the mirror until her hands moved smoothly. Each failed trick taught her exactly which move to hide better. At the family dinner her cousins gasped, sure that real magic had happened.
payload.title: Mirror practice made Pooja's card tricks smooth
decoys: Pooja's cards kept slipping at first
Magic tricks can fool absolutely everyone around
Pooja wanted to amaze her many cousins

payload.passage: At home, Kunal's parents kept arguing about who would drop him at school. The morning rush often left him waiting and worried. They drew up a clear plan, taking turns on different days of the week. Each parent now knew exactly when it was their turn. The smooth mornings made Kunal calm and never late again.
payload.title: A turn plan solved Kunal's school-drop worry
decoys: Kunal was left waiting and worried
Planning ahead keeps every family stress-free
His parents took turns on different days

payload.passage: A drinking-bird toy dips and rises again and again. Its head is covered in felt that you wet at the start. As the water dries off the head, the toy slowly tips forward to drink. Dipping wets the head again, and it swings back up. So a drinking bird bobs because its wet head keeps drying and tipping.
payload.title: How a wet head makes a toy bird bob
decoys: Its head is covered in felt

payload.passage: At the seaside, Pari saw the water creep up the beach in the morning and pull back by evening. Her father explained that the moon's pull tugs gently on the ocean, making it bulge and rise on one side of the earth, then fall again as the earth turns. This rise and fall is called the tide. Pari learned that the moon's pull causes the daily tides.
payload.title: The moon's pull causes the daily tides
decoys: The water crept up the beach in the morning
The sea is large and full of water
Pari spent the day at the seaside

payload.passage: The school visited a stepwell, a deep stone well reached by many stairs. The guide said that long ago, before taps and pipes, towns dug these wells so people could walk down to the water even when it dropped low in summer. The cool shaded steps also gave travellers a place to rest. Riya saw that the stepwell was a clever old answer to the problem of finding water all year.
payload.title: A stepwell was a clever way to reach water
decoys: The shaded steps gave tired travellers a rest
People in the past built many useful things
The stepwell had a great many stone stairs

payload.passage: A lifeguard watches over swimmers at the beach or pool. He sits in a high seat where he can see the whole water. He keeps a sharp eye out for anyone who is in trouble. If a swimmer struggles, he jumps in at once to pull them out. So a lifeguard's main job is to keep swimmers safe.
payload.title: How a lifeguard keeps swimmers safe
decoys: He sits in a high seat to watch the water
Swimming is good exercise for the body

payload.passage: A gardener keeps the parks and gardens green and pretty. He waters the plants and pulls out the weeds that crowd them. He trims the hedges and plants fresh flowers in the beds. With his care the dull patch turns into a colourful garden. So a gardener's work is to make our green spaces beautiful.
payload.title: How a gardener keeps gardens beautiful
decoys: He pulls out the weeds that crowd the plants
Parks are a nice place to play

payload.passage: At the heritage house, Tara walked through rooms kept just as they were a hundred years ago. The guide said that nothing was modern: the lamps burned oil, the fans were pulled by hand, and water came from a well in the yard. Seeing it all together, Tara could almost picture a family living there long before electricity. She learned that the old house showed how people lived before machines made life easy.
payload.title: An old house shows life before machines
decoys: The lamps in the old house burned oil
Many homes look different from one another
Tara liked walking through the quiet rooms

payload.passage: A door hinge lets a door swing open and shut. The hinge has two flat plates joined by a pin down the middle. One plate is fixed to the door and the other to the frame. As you push the door, the plates turn around the pin and the door swings. So a hinge lets a door swing by turning two plates around a pin.
payload.title: How a hinge lets a door swing open
decoys: Two flat plates join at a pin
Doors are part of every room
One plate is fixed to the frame

payload.passage: Trisha could not study because her younger cousins played noisily nearby. The shouting and games broke her concentration every evening. She asked to use the quiet store room as her study spot. Away from the noise, she finished her work quickly and well. Trisha's evenings became peaceful and her marks improved.
payload.title: A quiet store room solved Trisha's noisy study time
decoys: Quiet surroundings help every learner focus
Trisha used the store room as her spot

payload.passage: Kavya noticed that the well in her courtyard rose and fell with the seasons. Her grandmother explained that rain soaks into the ground and is stored deep below as groundwater, which fills the well. In the rainy months the water rises; in the dry months it sinks as people draw it out. Kavya learned that wells are fed by rainwater stored under the ground.
payload.title: Wells are fed by water stored underground
decoys: The well water rose during the rains
Wells supply water to many homes
Kavya's well is in the courtyard

payload.passage: Kunal wanted to learn how to read a road map for the family trip. The tangled lines and tiny words made his head spin at first. His uncle showed him to find the main roads and follow them slowly. The map suddenly made sense, like a giant picture puzzle. On the trip Kunal proudly guided his family along the right route.
payload.title: Finding the main roads taught Kunal to read maps
decoys: The tangled lines made Kunal's head spin
Family trips create memories that last forever
Kunal's uncle helped him understand the map

payload.passage: A waterfall slowly moves backwards over hundreds of years. As the water crashes down, it wears away the soft rock at the bottom. This leaves the harder rock above sticking out with nothing beneath it. In time the edge breaks off and the fall shifts a little upstream. So a waterfall slowly eats its way back along the river.
payload.title: How a waterfall slowly moves upstream
decoys: The falling water wears away soft rock
Rivers shape the land in many ways
Tourists love to watch a roaring waterfall

payload.passage: The classroom plants on the windowsill kept getting knocked over. Children brushed past and the pots crashed to the floor often. The teacher moved the pots onto a sturdy shelf high on the wall. Safe up there, the plants were never bumped again. The room stayed clean and the plants grew tall and leafy.
payload.title: Moving the pots up saved the classroom plants
decoys: The pots crashed to the floor often
Greenery makes any room feel fresh and alive
The teacher used a sturdy high shelf

payload.passage: A torch makes light from a small battery tucked inside it. When you slide the switch, you join the two ends of the battery through a thin wire and the bulb. Power then flows in a full loop from the battery, through the bulb, and back again. The bulb glows because the power heats its tiny wire until it shines. So a torch lights up only when the switch closes the loop.
payload.title: How a torch lights up when you switch it
decoys: The bulb's tiny wire glows when heated
Torches are handy when the power fails
A torch holds a small battery inside

payload.passage: A new island can rise from the sea over a very long time. Under the water, a volcano erupts again and again, piling up lava. Layer upon layer of cooled rock slowly builds up higher. In time the pile breaks above the waves as a brand new island. So patient volcanoes can build land in the middle of the sea.
payload.title: How a volcano builds an island in the sea
decoys: Layers of cooled lava build up higher
The Earth changes slowly over time
New islands soon fill with plants and birds

payload.passage: A glacier is a huge, slow river made of ice. It forms high in the mountains where snow piles up year after year. The weight of the snow presses the bottom layers into thick, hard ice. Pulled by its own great weight, the glacier creeps downhill very slowly. So a glacier is really a mass of moving mountain ice.
payload.title: A glacier is slow moving mountain ice
decoys: Piled snow presses the bottom into hard ice
Mountains hold many wonders of nature
Melting glaciers feed many large rivers

payload.passage: Garv floated a small candle stub on a lid of water inside a wide dish and lit it. He covered it with a tall glass and watched. The flame burned, then dimmed and died, and the water climbed up into the glass. His teacher said the flame ate part of the air. Garv learned that a covered flame uses air and draws water up.
payload.title: A covered flame uses air and draws water up
decoys: The water climbed into the glass
Garv floated the candle on water

payload.passage: Karan filled a saucer with water and set it out in the hot afternoon sun. He marked the water level with a black pen and went off to play. When he came back in the evening the water level had dropped well below his mark. His grandmother told him the sun had turned some water into vapour that floated away. Karan learned that heat makes water slowly disappear into the air.
payload.title: Sun heat makes water evaporate into the air
decoys: Karan marked the starting level with a pen
The sun gives us heat and light each day
Water can be stored in a flat saucer

payload.passage: Pari placed a celery stalk with leaves into a glass of water coloured deep blue with food dye. She left it on the table and looked at it again the next morning. Thin blue lines had crept all the way up the stalk and into the tiny leaves. Her mother said the plant had drunk the coloured water through hidden tubes. Pari learned that plants pull water up through tubes inside their stems.
payload.title: Plants draw water up through tubes in their stems
decoys: Blue lines crept up the celery stalk
Plants do many things we cannot see
Food dye can colour water brightly

payload.passage: A school bus driver and helper work together to keep the trip safe. The driver watches the road and drives at a steady speed. The helper looks after the children inside the bus. Together they make sure each child gets on and off at the right stop. So the driver and helper team up to keep the children safe.
payload.title: How a driver and helper keep the bus trip safe
decoys: The helper looks after the children inside
A school bus stops at many points

payload.passage: A florist sells fresh flowers and makes pretty bunches. Early each day she buys flowers while they are still fresh. She trims their stems and arranges them by colour and kind. When people want flowers for a gift or function, she ties them into bouquets. So a florist's work is to prepare and sell fresh flowers.
payload.title: How a florist prepares fresh flowers
decoys: She arranges flowers by colour and kind
Flowers are given on happy days

payload.passage: A cobbler mends our shoes and chappals when they break. He sits at a small stall on the corner of the street with his tools. When a strap snaps or a sole comes loose, people bring them to him. With needle, thread, and glue he makes the old footwear like new. So a cobbler's work is to repair the shoes we wear.
payload.title: How a cobbler repairs our shoes
decoys: He sits at a small stall on the corner
Many handy helpers serve the street
New shoes can be costly to buy

payload.passage: A siphon tube moves water from a high bowl to a low one with no pump. You fill the bent tube and dip one end in the high bowl, the other hanging lower. Once started, the water keeps flowing up and over the bend to the low bowl. It runs until the high bowl is empty. So a siphon lets water flow over a bend to a lower place.
payload.title: How a siphon moves water to a lower bowl
decoys: The tube is bent in the middle
One end hangs lower than the other

payload.passage: Lokesh wanted to do a perfect somersault on the soft mats. He kept landing on his back and felt dizzy after each roll. His coach taught him to tuck his chin and curl into a tight ball. With this small change his rolls became smooth and dizziness faded. By practice day Lokesh did three neat somersaults in a row.
payload.title: Tucking his chin taught Lokesh to somersault
decoys: Lokesh kept landing on his back
Coaches can teach a child any sport at all
Lokesh practised somersaults on soft mats

payload.passage: A clothes iron presses out creases using both heat and weight. Power flows into a flat metal plate at the base and warms it up. You push the heavy warm plate slowly across the crumpled cloth. The heat softens the cloth while the weight flattens the folds out. So an iron smooths cloth by pressing it with a heavy hot plate.
payload.title: How a hot heavy plate irons out creases
decoys: Power warms the flat metal plate
The plate is heavy and warm

payload.passage: Laksh wanted to grow mould on purpose for a project. He put a damp piece of bread in a sealed box in a warm cupboard and a dry piece in the same box. He checked them every day with a torch. The damp bread soon grew thick green fuzz, but the dry piece stayed clean. Laksh learned that mould needs damp food to grow well.
payload.title: Mould needs damp food to grow well
decoys: Laksh checked the bread with a torch
Food can change over many days
A cupboard is a warm, dark place

payload.passage: A wind chime sings a soft tune whenever a breeze passes. Several metal tubes hang at different lengths from a top ring. A small clapper dangles in the middle among the tubes. When the wind swings the clapper, it taps the tubes and each rings its own note. So a wind chime makes music as the breeze swings a clapper onto its tubes.
payload.title: How a breeze makes a wind chime sing
decoys: A clapper hangs in the middle
The tubes hang at different lengths

payload.passage: A jellyfish has no bones, no heart, and no brain, yet it lives well in the sea. Its soft body is shaped like an open umbrella and is mostly water. It swims by squeezing this bell to push water out behind it. Long thin arms hang down to sting and catch tiny food. So a jellyfish is a simple but successful sea creature.
payload.title: How a simple jellyfish lives in the sea
decoys: A jellyfish swims by squeezing its bell
The sea holds many strange animals
Some jellyfish can give a painful sting

payload.passage: Anaya was puzzled why a kettle whistles, so she watched one heat up with her mother nearby. As the water grew hotter, tiny bubbles rose faster and faster from the bottom. Soon thick steam pushed out through the spout and made the lid rattle. Her mother said the boiling water was turning into steam that needs more room. Anaya learned that boiling turns water into steam that takes up much more space.
payload.title: Boiling turns water into space-hungry steam
decoys: Tiny bubbles rose faster as the water heated
Cooking needs heat from a stove or fire
Steam pushed out through the kettle spout

payload.passage: Yuvraj set a black tin and a silver tin of water on the terrace in the evening cold instead of the sun. He felt them after an hour. This time the black tin had cooled more than the shiny one. His teacher said dark things both soak up and give off heat well. Yuvraj learned that a dark tin loses heat faster in the cold.
payload.title: A dark tin loses heat faster in the cold
decoys: The shiny tin stayed a bit warmer
Yuvraj used a black and silver tin

payload.passage: Aarush wanted to learn how to do a proper cricket bowling action. His arm bent at the elbow and the ball went all wrong. His coach taught him to keep his arm straight and swing it over the top. Slowly his action smoothened and the ball landed on the right spot. Soon Aarush could bowl a full over without a single wide ball.
payload.title: Keeping his arm straight improved Aarush's bowling
decoys: Aarush's arm bent at the elbow
Bowlers are the heroes of every cricket match
Aarush bowled a full over at last

payload.passage: A spider plant makes copies of itself in an unusual way. Besides its leaves, it sends out long thin stems into the air. At the end of each stem a tiny new baby plant grows. If a baby touches soil, it grows roots and becomes a plant of its own. So one spider plant can quietly create many new plants.
payload.title: How a spider plant makes new plants
decoys: A baby plant grows at the end of each stem
Plants spread themselves in many ways
Spider plants are easy to keep at home

payload.passage: Vikram noticed the sky glow deep red as the sun set after a dusty day. His teacher explained that sunlight is really a mix of many colours. When it travels low through thick, dusty air, the blue light scatters away in all directions. Mostly the red light reaches our eyes, so the sky looks red. Vikram learned that scattered sunlight gives us a red sunset.
payload.title: Scattered sunlight gives us a red sunset
decoys: The sky glowed red at sunset
The sun rises and sets each day

payload.passage: The guide took Om's class to a grand old hall where the king once met his people. She explained that the room was built so that even a soft voice from the throne could be heard at the back, thanks to its shape and high roof. This let the ruler speak to a large crowd without shouting. Om learned that the hall was cleverly shaped so speech carried far.
payload.title: A royal hall was shaped to carry speech far
decoys: The hall had a very high roof
Kings met their people in grand halls
Om tested the echo with a whisper

payload.passage: Gaurav saw thick fog cover the road one cold winter morning so he could barely see the gate. His father explained that on still, cold nights the air near the ground cools down, and the moisture in it turns into a low cloud of tiny drops resting on the land. That low cloud is fog. Gaurav learned that fog is a cloud that forms close to the ground.
payload.title: Fog is a cloud that forms near the ground
decoys: The fog covered the road that morning
Gaurav could barely see his gate

payload.passage: Seasons in the high mountains change far more sharply than on the plains. In summer the slopes turn green and bright wildflowers bloom. In autumn the cold sets in early and the grass turns brown. By winter deep snow covers everything and most animals leave or hide. So mountain seasons swing quickly from green summer to snowy winter.
payload.title: How seasons change in the high mountains
decoys: Wildflowers bloom on the slopes in summer
Seasons change all over the world
Mountain air is cool and very clean

payload.passage: Nakul wanted to learn how to balance on one foot for a yoga pose. He kept toppling sideways after barely a few seconds. He learned to fix his gaze on a still spot ahead of him. With steady eyes his balance held longer and longer. By the end of the week Nakul stood on one foot for a full minute calmly.
payload.title: A steady gaze helped Nakul balance on one foot
decoys: Nakul toppled sideways after a few seconds
Yoga makes the body calm and very healthy
Nakul fixed his gaze on a still spot

payload.passage: A teacher guides children to learn new things every day. She plans lessons that make hard ideas easy to understand. She answers questions, explains mistakes, and cheers on every effort. Bit by bit she helps each child grow more confident and clever. So a teacher's main work is to help children learn and grow.
payload.title: How a teacher helps children learn
decoys: The teacher plans lessons for the class
Many people help children every day
Schools have a long holiday in summer

payload.passage: Saanvi pegged a thin wet handkerchief flat on the line and bunched a second one up in a ball. Both started equally wet in the same breeze. The flat one dried quickly while the bunched one stayed damp for hours. Her mother said spread-out cloth meets more air. Saanvi learned that spread-out cloth dries faster than bunched-up cloth.
payload.title: Spread-out cloth dries faster than bunched cloth

payload.passage: Mohit wanted to dribble a basketball without losing control of it. The ball kept bouncing away and rolling down the court. He practised dribbling slowly in one spot before trying to move. Once his hand learned the rhythm, he began walking and then jogging with the ball. Soon Mohit could weave around cones while keeping the ball close.
payload.title: Slow practice taught Mohit to dribble the ball
decoys: The ball kept rolling down the court
Basketball makes children taller and quicker
Mohit weaved the ball around some cones

payload.passage: A torch-style spinning fan toy runs on a button cell. A press joins the small cell to a tiny motor inside the handle. The motor's shaft spins fast and turns a soft foam blade on top. The whirling blade pushes a little breeze towards your face. So a handheld toy fan blows air by a small motor spinning a foam blade.
payload.title: How a tiny motor spins a handheld toy fan
decoys: A foam blade sits on the shaft
Small fans help on warm days
A press joins the cell to the motor

payload.passage: Nakul dropped a steel ball and a plastic ball of the same size into a tall jar of thick honey at the same moment. The heavy steel ball sank slowly while the plastic one barely sank at all. His teacher said heavier things push down harder through the honey. Nakul learned that a heavier ball sinks faster through thick honey.
payload.title: A heavier ball sinks faster through honey
decoys: Nakul used a tall jar of honey

payload.passage: A spring-loaded tape measure pulls out and snaps back. A long marked strip is coiled tight inside the round case. When you pull the end out, the strip uncoils and stretches along what you measure. Let it go and a spring inside winds it quickly back in. So a tape measure works by a coiled strip that springs back when freed.
payload.title: How a coiled strip springs a tape measure back
decoys: A marked strip coils inside the case

payload.passage: Desert plants have clever ways to live where almost no rain falls. A cactus stores water deep inside its thick, juicy stem. Instead of broad leaves, it grows sharp spines that lose very little water. Its roots spread wide and shallow to drink quickly when rare rain comes. So a cactus is well built to survive in a dry desert.
payload.title: How a cactus survives in the desert
decoys: A cactus stores water inside its thick stem
Plants live in many different places on Earth
Deserts can be very hot during the day

payload.passage: A hand-operated borewell pump brings up water with a piston and valves. As the handle is worked, a tight-fitting piston slides up and down a pipe. On the up-stroke a lower valve opens and lets water rise into the pipe. On the down-stroke that valve shuts and an upper valve lets the water pass. So a piston and two valves lift water up step by step.
payload.title: How a piston and valves lift water up
decoys: A tight piston slides up and down
Water is precious in dry areas
The lower valve opens on the up-stroke

payload.passage: Sameer wished to learn a few words of sign language for a deaf classmate. The hand shapes felt strange and he often mixed up the signs. He practised one new sign every day in front of the mirror. His hands grew confident and his classmate smiled at each correct sign. Soon Sameer could chat in simple signs and the two became close friends.
payload.title: Daily practice taught Sameer to sign with a friend
decoys: Sameer often mixed up the hand signs
Friendship can grow between any two children
Sameer had a classmate who could not hear

payload.passage: The classroom window would not stay open and kept slamming shut. The sudden slams startled the children and broke their focus. The teacher fixed a small wooden wedge to hold the window in place. The window now stayed open and let in fresh air all day. The class stayed calm and breathed easy after that.
payload.title: A wedge solved the slamming-window problem
decoys: Fresh air helps students think more clearly
The teacher used a small wooden wedge

payload.passage: A road builder helps lay the new roads that link our towns. His team clears the ground and flattens it with heavy machines. They spread layers of stone and tar to make a firm base. Then they roll it smooth so cars and buses can drive on it. So a road builder's work is to make new roads for everyone to use.
payload.title: How a road builder lays new roads
decoys: They roll the road smooth and flat
Many workers help build our country
Good roads link villages to cities

payload.passage: Aryan's class made simple ovens that cook using only the sun's heat. Each one is a shiny box with a clear glass lid. On sunny days they put food inside and let the trapped heat cook it. This uses no gas or wood and makes no smoke at all. The class learned that the sun's heat alone can cook food and save fuel.
payload.title: The sun's heat can cook food and save fuel
decoys: The oven uses a shiny box and glass lid
Sunny days are good for drying

payload.passage: Dhruv kept forgetting to bring his sports shoes on game days. He had to sit out and watch his friends play. He pinned a small note inside his bag listing the days he needed shoes. Each game-day morning the note reminded him to pack them. Dhruv never missed a single game for want of shoes again.
payload.title: A reminder note solved Dhruv's forgotten shoes
decoys: Dhruv had to sit out and watch
Sports give every child energy and joy
Dhruv pinned a note inside his bag

payload.passage: At home, Priya and her brother always argued over the one study lamp. Both wanted it at the same time, and the fights grew loud. Their father drew up a simple turn-by-turn timetable for the lamp. Each child now used the lamp at a fixed hour without any quarrel. The peaceful evenings made their study time much more useful.
payload.title: A lamp timetable ended the siblings' quarrels
decoys: Priya and her brother argued loudly
Sharing things is the answer to every fight
Their father drew up a turn-by-turn plan

payload.passage: Karan dreamed of becoming a fast runner for the inter-school race. At first he gasped for breath after only one round of the field. He started jogging a tiny bit more each morning, never pushing too hard. His legs grew tougher and his breathing stayed calm for longer runs. On race day Karan crossed the finish line second and grinned from ear to ear.
payload.title: Daily jogging built Karan's running stamina
decoys: Karan gasped for breath after one round
Running is the best exercise for every child
Karan took part in an inter-school race

payload.passage: Krish kept losing marks because he wrote answers in the wrong order. He jumped between questions and confused the examiner. His teacher told him to answer the questions in proper number order. His neat, ordered paper became easy to follow and mark. Krish stopped losing marks for muddled answers after that.
payload.title: Answering in order solved Krish's lost marks
decoys: Order and method help a student score well
His teacher told him to follow the numbers

payload.passage: Aditi wanted to learn how to make pancakes that did not stick to the pan. Her first pancakes tore apart whenever she tried to flip them. She learned to brush a little oil and wait for tiny bubbles to form. The pancakes then slid and flipped easily without breaking. Aditi stacked warm, round pancakes high on a plate for her family.
payload.title: Waiting for bubbles taught Aditi to flip pancakes
decoys: Aditi's first pancakes tore while flipping
Breakfast is the most important meal of the day
Aditi stacked the pancakes high on a plate

payload.passage: A paddle boat toy swims with a wound rubber band. A small paddle at the back is fixed between two arms with a band. You wind the paddle round to twist the band tight. When you set the boat on water and let go, the band unwinds and turns the paddle. So a wound band spins the paddle and pushes the toy boat along.
payload.title: How a wound band paddles a toy boat
decoys: The paddle sits between two arms
You wind the paddle to twist the band

payload.passage: A snake catcher keeps the neighbourhood safe from wandering snakes. When a snake slips into a house or garden, people call him at once. He arrives with a stick and a strong bag to do his work. He carefully catches the snake and carries it far away to safety. So a snake catcher's job is to remove snakes without harming anyone.
payload.title: How a snake catcher removes snakes safely
decoys: He carries the snake far away in a bag
Many brave helpers keep us safe
Some snakes hide during the rains

payload.passage: Nisha's class visited an old water tank built of stone in the middle of a village. The guide explained that for hundreds of years it stored the monsoon rain so people had water through the dry months. Steps led down to it, and everyone shared its water. Nisha learned that the old tank was a shared store of rain that kept the whole village going.
payload.title: An old village tank stored rain for everyone
decoys: Stone steps led down into the tank
Nisha saw small fish in the still water

payload.passage: The club gathered old cardboard boxes from the shops nearby. Instead of letting them be thrown away, the children put them to work. They made storage trays, file holders and toy boxes for the school. The cardboard found a useful second job, and the rooms grew tidier. The club learned that old cardboard can be reused for handy storage.
payload.title: Old cardboard can be reused for storage
decoys: The boxes came from local shops

payload.passage: The Walk-to-School group asked families living nearby to leave the car at home. They suggested walking or cycling to school instead of driving. Fewer cars meant less smoke and a quieter, safer road outside the gate. The children felt fitter and more awake too. The group learned that walking instead of driving keeps the air around the school cleaner.
payload.title: Walking instead of driving keeps air cleaner
decoys: Fewer cars made the road quieter

payload.passage: A hand water pump lifts water from deep underground without any motor. When you push the handle down, a part inside rises and leaves an empty space below it. Water from the well rushes up to fill that empty space through a one-way flap. The next push lifts this water higher and a second flap stops it sliding back. Step by step the pump raises water up to the spout and out.
payload.title: How a hand pump raises water from a well
decoys: A one-way flap stops water sliding back
Water is needed for many daily tasks
A hand pump works without a motor

payload.passage: Sara's family used to dry every wash in the electric dryer. They began hanging their wet clothes outside in the sun on most days instead. The sun and the wind dry the clothes for free and use no power at all. Their electricity use dropped steadily over the year. The family learned that drying clothes in the sun saves electricity.
payload.title: Drying clothes in the sun saves electricity
decoys: The sun and wind dry the clothes
Washing clothes is a daily task
Sara's family stopped using the dryer
