payload.passage: Vihaan's homework often got wet because his water bottle leaked in his bag. The soggy books were hard to write in and read. He began keeping his bottle in a separate side pocket of the bag. His books stayed bone dry, away from the leaky bottle. Vihaan never opened a wet homework book again after that.
payload.title: A separate pocket solved Vihaan's wet books
decoys: The soggy books were hard to read
A tidy school bag helps every student
Vihaan used a separate side pocket

payload.passage: Atharv noticed dew on the grass on cool mornings but not on warm ones. To check why, he left a metal cup out overnight on a cold night and on a mild night. The cup on the cold night had tiny water drops on its outside by dawn. His grandfather said cold air cannot hold its water, so drops settle on cool things. Atharv learned that dew forms when cool air drops its hidden water.
payload.title: Dew forms when cool air drops its water
decoys: The cup had water drops on a cold night
Mornings can be cool or warm
Grass feels wet on dewy days

payload.passage: Aarush filled a tray with flour and dropped a marble into it from low down, then from up high. The low drop made a small dent, but the high drop made a deep crater with little splashes around it. His teacher said a thing falling from higher up hits harder. Aarush learned that a marble dropped from higher makes a bigger crater.
payload.title: A marble dropped higher makes a bigger crater
decoys: The low drop made only a small dent
Aarush filled a tray with flour

payload.passage: Om hung a heavy bag on a rubber band and measured how far it stretched. Then he added a second bag and the band stretched even further down. He found the band grew longer each time he added weight. His teacher said a stretchy band pulls back harder the more you load it. Om learned that a rubber band stretches more as the weight grows.
payload.title: A rubber band stretches more as weight grows
decoys: The band stretched further with two bags
Bags can be heavy or light
Om hung a bag on the band

payload.passage: A street tap with a press-button shuts itself off to save water. When you press the button, it opens a path and water flows out. Inside, a spring is pushed back and slowly begins to return. As the spring pushes back, it closes the path again after a few seconds. So a press-tap gives water for a short while and then shuts on its own.
payload.title: How a press-tap shuts itself to save water
decoys: A spring slowly pushes back inside
Saving water is good for everyone
Pressing the button starts the flow

payload.passage: Aryan kept losing points because he forgot to write his name on tests. The teacher could not tell whose paper was whose. Aryan made it a rule to write his name first, before anything else. From then on every paper carried his name clearly. He never lost a single mark for a missing name again.
payload.title: Writing his name first solved Aryan's lost marks
decoys: The teacher could not tell whose paper it was
Following small rules helps every student
Aryan wrote his name before anything else

payload.passage: Rahul wanted to learn how to ride a unicycle from a video he loved. He fell off within a second and the wheel rolled away each time. He held a wall and practised balancing for just a few seconds daily. His balance slowly grew until he could pedal a short distance alone. By the holidays Rahul rode the unicycle across the whole verandah.
payload.title: Daily balancing practice taught Rahul the unicycle
decoys: Rahul fell off within a second at first
Videos can teach children any tricky skill
Rahul rode the unicycle across the verandah

payload.passage: A baker bakes the fresh bread and buns we enjoy each morning. Very early he mixes flour, water, and yeast into soft dough. He lets the dough rise, shapes it, and slides it into a hot oven. Out comes warm, golden bread filling the shop with a lovely smell. So a baker's work is to bake fresh bread for the neighbourhood.
payload.title: How a baker makes fresh bread daily
decoys: He mixes flour, water, and yeast
Many helpers work early to serve us
Warm bread smells wonderful in the morning

payload.passage: A vegetable cart vendor sells greens right in our lane. He fills his cart each morning with leafy greens and bright vegetables. He pushes it slowly through the streets calling out his goods. Neighbours come out and pick what they need without going far. So a cart vendor brings fresh vegetables straight to our lane.
payload.title: How a cart vendor brings vegetables to our lane
decoys: He pushes his cart slowly through the streets

payload.passage: A see-through ballpoint pen writes with a tiny rolling ball. At the very tip sits a small metal ball held in a socket. As you drag the pen across paper, the ball rolls and turns. Ink from the tube above coats the ball and is laid down on the page as it rolls. So a ballpoint pen writes by rolling ink onto the paper through a tiny ball.
payload.title: How a ballpoint pen rolls ink onto paper
decoys: A small metal ball sits at the tip
Pens are used to write notes
Ink is held in a tube

payload.passage: Lightning and thunder always happen during the same storm. Lightning is a sudden flash of electricity that jumps through the sky. It heats the air so fast that the air bursts apart with a loud bang. That loud bang is the thunder we hear after the flash. So lightning makes the light and thunder makes the sound.
payload.title: How lightning and thunder happen together
decoys: Lightning heats the air very quickly
Storms can be loud and exciting
Heavy rain often falls during a storm

payload.passage: A frog has special skin that helps it live both in and out of water. Its skin is thin, smooth, and always a little damp. The frog can breathe through this moist skin as well as through its lungs. The dampness must stay, so a frog keeps near water and shade. So a frog's moist skin lets it breathe and stay healthy.
payload.title: How a frog breathes through its skin
decoys: A frog's skin is thin and always damp
Animals breathe in many different ways
Frogs catch insects with sticky tongues

payload.passage: A pharmacist gives out the medicines that a doctor prescribes. When you bring a doctor's note, he reads it with great care. He finds the right medicines and packs them for you. He also tells you how and when to take each one. So a pharmacist's main work is to give the correct medicines safely.
payload.title: How a pharmacist gives the right medicine
decoys: He reads the doctor's note with care
Many helpers look after our health
Medicines must be kept away from children

payload.passage: The students learned that food grown nearby travels only a short way to the market. Food brought from far away uses much more fuel on the journey. So they asked their families to buy local, in-season fruits and vegetables. This food turned out to be fresher and cheaper too. The students learned that eating local food saves fuel and helps the earth.
payload.title: Eating local food saves fuel and helps the earth
decoys: Local food travels a shorter way

payload.passage: Vivek put one plant on the windowsill and turned its pot so the leaves faced away from the glass. He watered it and left it for a few days. When he came back, the stems had bent round to face the sunlight again. His teacher said plants lean towards light to feed themselves. Vivek learned that plant stems bend to grow towards the light.
payload.title: Plant stems bend to grow towards light
decoys: Vivek turned the pot away from the glass
Plants are full of clever tricks

payload.passage: Termites are tiny insects that build towering mud homes. Working together, they carry small bits of soil and spit to stick them. Slowly they raise tall, hard mounds that can stand higher than a person. Inside are cool tunnels and rooms where the whole colony lives. So tiny termites build huge strong homes out of mud.
payload.title: Tiny termites build tall mud homes
decoys: Termites stick soil together with their spit
Insects build homes in many ways

payload.passage: A moving-coil doorbell buzzer hums loudly whenever it is pressed. Pressing the button sends power to a small coil of wire inside. The coil becomes a magnet and tugs a thin metal strip towards it. The strip then snaps back and forth very fast and makes a buzzing sound. So a buzzer hums as a coil rapidly tugs a strip back and forth.
payload.title: How a tugged strip makes a buzzer hum
decoys: Pressing sends power to the coil

payload.passage: A pop-up book makes its flat pictures suddenly stand up. Folded paper shapes are glued across the crease of each printed page. When the page is shut, the shapes fold down flat and hide inside. When you open the page, the folds spring the picture up into the air. So a pop-up book lifts pictures up as the page is opened.
payload.title: How a pop-up book lifts pictures off the page
decoys: The shapes fold flat when shut
Paper shapes are glued to the crease

payload.passage: A postman makes sure that letters and parcels reach the right homes. Early each morning he sorts the post for his own area. He then sets off on his round, reading each address with care. He drops the right letter into each house's box, street after street. So a postman's work is to carry our post safely to its owner.
payload.title: How a postman delivers our letters
decoys: The postman sorts the post each morning
People love to receive letters from friends

payload.passage: The students kept getting wet because the school gate had no shelter. On rainy days they waited in the downpour for their vans. The principal had a small tin roof built over the waiting area. Now the children stand dry under the shelter until their ride comes. Parents were thankful that no child caught a cold from the rain.
payload.title: A shelter at the gate solved the rainy-day soaking
decoys: Children waited in the downpour for vans
Rain always makes school days difficult
The principal built a small tin roof

payload.passage: A park keeper looks after the public park where children play. Each morning he checks that the swings and slides are safe. He clears litter, waters the lawns, and tends the flower beds. He keeps the paths clean so families can stroll in comfort. So a park keeper's work is to keep the park safe and pleasant.
payload.title: How a park keeper looks after the park
decoys: He checks that the swings are safe
Parks give children a place to run

payload.passage: A field nurse visits villages to bring health care to the people. She travels to places far from any hospital. She gives the children their vaccines to keep them safe from disease. She also teaches families simple ways to stay healthy and clean. So a field nurse's work is to bring health care to faraway homes.
payload.title: How a field nurse brings care to villages
decoys: She gives the children their vaccines
Many helpers work to keep us well
Clean water helps prevent many illnesses

payload.passage: Avantika filled one glass with tap water and one with the same water that she had boiled and cooled. She added a drop of soap to each and shook them well. The boiled water made far more bubbles than the plain tap water. Her teacher said boiling removes the hardness that fights soap. Avantika learned that boiled water makes more soap bubbles than hard tap water.
payload.title: Boiled water makes more soap bubbles than hard water
decoys: She boiled and cooled one sample

payload.passage: Ishaan's group swapped the school's old bulbs for new ones that use far less electricity. The new bulbs give the same bright light for less power. They also put up reminders to switch off lights and fans in empty rooms. Soon the electricity bill dropped sharply. The group learned that saving electricity is good for the school and for the earth.
payload.title: Saving electricity helps the school and earth
decoys: The group switched the old bulbs
Schools use a lot of power

payload.passage: Bees do a special dance to tell each other where flowers are. When a worker bee finds good flowers, it flies back to the hive. There it dances in a pattern on the honeycomb wall. The way it moves shows the others which direction to fly and how far. So bees share the news of food through a clever dance.
payload.title: How bees dance to share food news
decoys: A worker bee dances on the honeycomb
Insects talk to each other in many ways
Bees gather sweet nectar from flowers

payload.passage: A windmill turns wind into useful turning. Its big sails are set at a slant on a central shaft high up. When the wind blows against the slanted sails, it pushes them round in a circle. The turning sails spin the shaft, which can grind grain or pump water below. So a windmill catches the wind to drive a turning shaft.
payload.title: How a windmill turns wind into work
decoys: The sails are set at a slant
A central shaft runs through it

payload.passage: At the museum's space room, Mahi looked at old tools once used to watch the sky. The guide explained that long before telescopes, people used careful charts and the naked eye to track the moon and stars, and used them to plan planting and festivals. Their patient watching, she said, built the first calendars. Mahi learned that early sky-watching helped people plan the year.
payload.title: Early sky watching helped people plan the year
decoys: People once watched the stars with their eyes
Space is a vast and exciting place
Mahi liked the painted star chart

payload.passage: A nurse cares for sick people gently both in hospitals and at home. She gives medicine at the right time and helps the doctor in many ways. She checks how each patient is feeling and writes it down. She also offers kind words to comfort those who are worried. So a nurse's main work is to care for the sick and help them heal.
payload.title: How a nurse cares for the sick
decoys: A nurse gives medicine at the right time
Many people work to keep us healthy
Hospitals can feel busy and noisy

payload.passage: Aryan placed a tray of soaked chickpeas on a warm sunny ledge and another tray in the cold fridge. He kept both damp and checked them daily. The warm tray sprouted tiny shoots within two days, while the cold tray barely changed. His teacher said warmth helps seeds wake up. Aryan learned that warmth helps seeds sprout faster.
payload.title: Warmth helps seeds sprout faster
decoys: The warm tray sprouted within two days

payload.passage: Dev held two identical sheets of paper at the same height. He left one flat and crumpled the other into a tight ball, then dropped them together. The crumpled ball thudded down first while the flat sheet drifted and floated slowly. His teacher said the flat sheet pushed against more air on the way down. Dev learned that air resistance slows a flat sheet more than a ball.
payload.title: Air slows a flat sheet more than a ball
decoys: The crumpled ball thudded down first
Dev used two identical sheets of paper

payload.passage: The school's chalkboard duster raised clouds of dust that made children sneeze. The chalky air filled the front rows during every lesson. The teacher switched to a damp sponge to wipe the board instead. The board cleaned without any dust rising into the air. The sneezing stopped and the front rows breathed easy again.
payload.title: A damp sponge solved the chalk-dust sneezing
decoys: The chalky air made children sneeze
A clean board is essential for good teaching
The teacher switched to a damp sponge

payload.passage: A foot pump fills an air bed without using your hands. You press the flat pedal down with your foot again and again. Each press squeezes a soft bellows and pushes a puff of air out through the hose. A one-way flap keeps the air from creeping back in. So a foot pump fills an air bed by squeezing a bellows with your foot.
payload.title: How a foot pump squeezes air into a bed
decoys: A one-way flap stops air creeping back
Air beds are comfy to sleep on

payload.passage: A weather vane on a roof shows which way the wind blows. It is a pointer that spins freely on an upright rod. When the wind blows, it pushes the broad tail of the vane around. The narrow head then ends up pointing into the wind. So a weather vane points out the wind's direction by turning freely on its rod.
payload.title: How a weather vane points to the wind
decoys: The wind pushes the broad tail round
The vane spins on an upright rod

payload.passage: Yashvi balanced a long ruler on her finger to find its middle. She slid it back and forth until it lay still and level on one point. She marked that spot and found it was right in the centre. Her teacher said every object balances at one special point. Yashvi learned that an object balances at its centre point.
payload.title: An object balances at its centre point
decoys: Rulers are used to measure things
She slid the ruler back and forth

payload.passage: Shaan wanted to learn how to hit a ball with a cricket bat properly. He kept missing the ball or hitting it weakly into the ground. His coach taught him to watch the ball closely and swing in time. His shots grew firmer and the ball flew off the bat sweetly. Soon Shaan was scoring runs and grinning at every clean hit.
payload.title: Watching the ball improved Shaan's batting
decoys: Shaan kept hitting the ball into the ground
Cricket is the favourite game of every Indian
Shaan grinned at every clean hit

payload.passage: A small green frog does not always look the way it does now. It begins life as a tiny egg floating in a pond. The egg hatches into a tadpole that swims with a long tail and breathes under water. Slowly it grows legs, loses its tail, and learns to breathe air. At last the tadpole has become a frog that can hop on land.
payload.title: A tadpole grows up to be a frog
decoys: A tadpole swims using its long tail
Pond animals change in many surprising ways
Frogs eat insects with their long sticky tongues

payload.passage: Nidhi was surprised that the river had built a fan of land where it met the sea. Her teacher explained that as a river slows down near the sea, it drops the mud and sand it has been carrying. Year after year, this dropped soil piles up into low, spreading land at the river's mouth. Nidhi learned that a river builds new land where it meets the sea.
payload.title: A river builds new land at the sea
decoys: The river dropped its mud near the sea
Rivers carry water to the ocean
Nidhi saw the spreading land on a map

payload.passage: A flat fever strip changes colour with heat to show how warm you are. It holds tiny bits along it that switch colour at certain set warmths. When you press it gently on your skin, it takes in some of your body's heat. The bits then light up at the number that matches your temperature. So a fever strip shows your temperature by changing colour with heat.
payload.title: How a strip shows temperature by colour
decoys: Tiny bits switch colour at set warmths
You press the strip on your skin

payload.passage: A traffic police officer keeps the busy roads in order. He stands at the crossing where many cars and bikes meet. With clear hand signals he tells some to stop and others to go. He also helps children and old people cross the road safely. So a traffic officer keeps the roads safe and moving smoothly.
payload.title: How a traffic officer keeps roads safe
decoys: The officer uses clear hand signals
Many helpers serve the busy city
Cars must stop when the light turns red

payload.passage: Dev had always thought the carved pillars in the temple were just decoration. The guide pointed out that each carving told a small story, like pages in a stone book. Long ago, when few people could read, these pictures taught lessons and old tales to everyone who came. Dev realised that the builders had turned the walls into a way of sharing stories with people who could not read.
payload.title: Temple carvings told stories to everyone
decoys: One carving showed a king riding an elephant
Temples are very old and beautiful places
Dev enjoyed walking around the cool temple

payload.passage: A drinking fountain sends up an arc of water to sip. When you press the pedal, water is pushed up a thin nozzle. The nozzle is angled so the water rises in a neat curving arc. You sip from the top of the arc without touching the spout. So a fountain lets you drink from a curving arc of pushed-up water.
payload.title: How a fountain sends up an arc to drink
decoys: The nozzle is angled to curve
Pressing the pedal pushes water up

payload.passage: A watering can sprinkles plants through a rose head. Water poured in is held in the round body of the can. When you tilt it, the water flows out through the spout into the rose head. The rose head is full of tiny holes that split the flow into a soft shower. So a watering can gives plants a gentle shower through its many small holes.
payload.title: How a watering can sprinkles a soft shower
decoys: The rose head is full of tiny holes
Tilting lets the water flow out

payload.passage: Priya wanted to see if air takes up space even though we cannot see it. She stuffed a dry paper ball into the bottom of an empty glass and pushed the glass straight down into a bucket of water. When she lifted it out, the paper was still completely dry. Her uncle said the trapped air had blocked the water from rushing in. Priya learned that air is real and takes up space in a glass.
payload.title: Trapped air keeps paper dry under water
decoys: Priya pushed the glass straight down into the bucket
Air is all around us wherever we go
Paper turns soft and weak when it gets wet

payload.passage: Esha set out a leaf, a feather and a coin and dropped each from the same height. The coin fell straight and fast, the feather drifted, and the leaf swung as it fell. She tried again with the same result each time. Her teacher said light, wide things are slowed by the air. Esha learned that light wide things fall slowly because air holds them back.
payload.title: Light wide things fall slowly in the air
decoys: The coin fell straight and fast
Esha used a leaf, feather and coin

payload.passage: A baby bird is helpless when it first hatches from its egg. It has no feathers, its eyes are shut, and it cannot fly at all. Its parents bring it food many times a day to help it grow. After a few weeks it grows feathers and strong wings. So a weak hatchling slowly grows into a bird that can fly.
payload.title: How a hatchling grows able to fly
decoys: A new hatchling has no feathers at all
Baby animals need much care to grow
Birds build their nests high in trees

payload.passage: Sia placed a sugar cube at one edge of a plate of water tinted with colour. The colour slowly crept towards and up into the cube as it began to dissolve. Bit by bit the cube soaked up the liquid and crumbled. Her teacher said the dry sugar pulled the water in. Sia learned that dry sugar soaks up water as it dissolves.
payload.title: Dry sugar soaks up water as it dissolves
decoys: The cube crumbled as it dissolved
Sia tinted the water with colour

payload.passage: Laksh kept getting cold while waiting for the school van each winter morning. The chilly wind made him shiver at the gate. His mother gave him a warm cap and gloves to wear while waiting. Bundled up, he stayed cosy until the van arrived. Laksh no longer caught colds from the morning chill.
payload.title: A cap and gloves solved Laksh's morning chill
decoys: The chilly wind made Laksh shiver
Warm clothes keep every child safe in winter
His mother gave him a cap and gloves

payload.passage: Earthworms do important work hidden under our feet. As they tunnel through the soil, they swallow bits of earth and leaves. They break this down and leave behind rich droppings that feed plants. Their tunnels also let air and water reach the roots below. So earthworms quietly keep the soil healthy for growing plants.
payload.title: Earthworms keep the soil healthy
decoys: Earthworm tunnels let air reach the roots
Small creatures help nature in many ways
Birds often hunt for worms after rain

payload.passage: A spin dryer flings water from washed clothes without any heat. The wet clothes are loaded into a metal drum full of small holes. A motor then spins the drum round and round very fast. The fast spin throws the water out through the holes, leaving the clothes much drier than before. So a spin dryer dries clothes by flinging water out as it spins.
payload.title: How a spinning drum flings water from clothes
decoys: Water is thrown out the holes
A motor spins the drum fast

payload.passage: The students wasted a lot of time hunting for sports gear before games. Bats, balls, and ropes lay jumbled in one big heap. The coach put up labelled hooks and bins for each kind of gear. Now the children grabbed what they needed in a moment. Game time started promptly and no minutes were lost any more.
payload.title: Labelled storage solved the lost sports-gear time
decoys: The gear lay jumbled in one big heap
Sports keep every child active and cheerful
The coach put up labelled hooks and bins

payload.passage: A delta forms where a big river finally meets the sea. As the river slows down near the coast, it can no longer carry its load of mud. The mud and sand settle and pile up into low, flat land. The river then splits into many small channels that wander through it. So a delta is the muddy land a river drops at its mouth.
payload.title: How a river builds a delta at its mouth
decoys: The slowing river drops its load of mud
Rivers shape the land all along their path
Rich delta soil is good for farming

payload.passage: Veer left a bowl of grapes on the table and forgot them for two weeks. When he came back the plump grapes had shrunk into wrinkled little raisins. He weighed them and found they were much lighter than before. His teacher said the water had slowly dried out of them. Veer learned that fruit shrinks and dries as it loses its water.
payload.title: Fruit shrinks and dries as it loses water
decoys: The grapes turned into wrinkled raisins

payload.passage: Aryan wanted to learn how to do a magic disappearing thumb trick. His first attempts were clumsy and his cousins easily caught on. He practised the hand bend in front of a mirror until it looked real. The trick grew smooth and his cousins gasped in surprise. Aryan felt like a real magician at the next family get-together.
payload.title: Mirror practice perfected Aryan's thumb trick
decoys: Aryan's cousins easily caught on at first
Magic always amazes a watching family
Aryan performed at a family get-together

payload.passage: The students set up an old-clothes box at the school gate. Children bring clothes they have outgrown but that are still good to wear. A charity comes and passes them on to families who need them. Nothing useful is thrown away, and many children are helped. The students learned that giving away old clothes is better than throwing them out.
payload.title: Giving away old clothes beats throwing them out
decoys: Children grow out of their clothes
The box stands at the school gate

payload.passage: Prisha laid out three leaves: a shiny one, a fuzzy one and a thin papery one. She dripped a drop of water onto each and watched. The water rolled off the shiny leaf in a bead but soaked into the papery one. Her teacher said different leaves handle water in different ways. Prisha learned that a leaf's surface decides how water sits on it.
payload.title: A leaf's surface decides how water sits on it
decoys: Water rolled off the shiny leaf in a bead
Prisha dripped water onto each leaf

payload.passage: A spinning globe lamp shows day and night. The round globe turns slowly on a slanted stand while a lamp shines on one side. The lit side stands for the part facing the sun in daytime. The shaded side stands for night on the far side of the globe. So a lamp and turning globe show how day and night follow each other.
payload.title: How a lamp and globe show day and night
decoys: The globe turns on a slanted stand
The Earth is round like a ball
A lamp shines on one side

payload.passage: Riya wanted to make a rainbow without rain, so she took a garden hose into the sunny yard. She stood with the sun behind her and sprayed a fine mist of water into the air. A small curved rainbow appeared in the floating droplets in front of her. Her brother said the water drops were splitting the sunlight into colours. Riya learned that water drops in sunlight can make a rainbow.
payload.title: Water drops in sunlight can make a rainbow
decoys: Riya sprayed a fine mist into the air
Sunlight reaches us all over the world
A garden hose is useful for watering plants

payload.passage: A mushroom spreads itself using a fine dust called spores. Under its cap are thin gills that make millions of tiny spores. When the mushroom is ripe, the spores drift away on the air. If a spore lands in a damp, dark place, it can grow into a new mushroom. So a mushroom scatters dust-like spores to make new ones.
payload.title: How a mushroom spreads with spores
decoys: Thin gills under the cap make the spores
Living things spread in many ways
Some mushrooms grow on rotting logs

payload.passage: Strong winds and water slowly carve rocks into strange shapes. Tiny bits of sand carried by the wind rub against the rock for years. Rivers and waves also scrape and wear the stone little by little. Over a very long time, this grinding shapes arches, caves, and pillars. So wind and water sculpt rock with great patience.
payload.title: How wind and water shape the rocks
decoys: Sand carried by wind rubs against the rock
The land keeps changing over time
Tourists visit strangely shaped rock arches

payload.passage: Bees do far more than just make sweet honey for us. As a bee lands on a flower to drink its sweet nectar, yellow pollen sticks to its furry body. The bee then flies to another flower and rubs some of that pollen onto it. This sharing of pollen helps the flowers make new seeds and fruit. So bees quietly help many plants to grow and spread.
payload.title: Bees help flowers grow new seeds
decoys: Yellow pollen sticks to the bee's furry body
Insects are useful to nature in many ways
Honey is sweet and good for our health

payload.passage: Reyansh's family used to let the tap run while waiting for the water to turn hot. All that cold water simply went down the drain. Now they keep a bucket under the tap to catch it. They use the saved water to wash the floor and water the plants. Over a week it added up to many litres, so the family learned that catching warming-up water saves a lot of water.
payload.title: Catching warming-up water saves litres
decoys: A bucket sits under the tap
Water is used in every home

payload.passage: A rubber suction hook sticks to a smooth wall. You press the soft cup hard against the tile to push out the air behind it. With the air gone, the outside air presses the cup tight to the wall. This press holds the hook in place so you can hang a towel. So a suction hook clings because air pressure holds the empty cup down.
payload.title: How air pressure holds a suction hook up
decoys: Hooks are handy for hanging things
The soft cup presses on the tile

payload.passage: Aman's class visited the ruins of an old town, where only low broken walls remained. The guide showed how the streets were laid out in a neat grid, with wide drains running beside them. This careful plan, she said, kept the town clean and easy to move around. Aman was surprised that people so long ago had planned their town as thoughtfully as a modern one.
payload.title: An ancient town was carefully planned
decoys: Wide drains ran beside the old streets
Towns from the past are interesting to study
Aman walked carefully over the broken walls

payload.passage: Ahana dropped a fat raisin into a glass of plain fizzy soda and watched. Tiny bubbles clung to the wrinkles of the raisin until it rose to the top. There the bubbles popped, and the raisin sank back down again. Her father said the gas bubbles lift the raisin and then let it fall. Ahana learned that gas bubbles can make a raisin dance up and down.
payload.title: Gas bubbles make a raisin dance in soda
decoys: Bubbles clung to the raisin's wrinkles
Fizzy drinks are full of bubbles

payload.passage: Nisha wanted to climb the tall rope in the gym like the senior girls. On her first attempt her arms gave way after barely a foot. Instead of feeling small, she did simple arm exercises at home each day. Her grip grew stronger and she climbed a little higher every week. By the sports day she reached the very top and rang the bell loudly.
payload.title: Building arm strength helped Nisha climb the rope
decoys: Nisha's arms gave way after one foot
Hard work always brings a prize in the end
The senior girls could climb the tall rope

payload.passage: The new boy in class sat alone every day and looked very sad. The other children did not know how to make him feel welcome. Sneha decided to invite him to join her group for lunch. Slowly the boy began to smile and join in the games. Soon the whole class made friends, and no one sat alone any more.
payload.title: A friendly invite ended the new boy's loneliness
decoys: The new boy looked very sad at first
Kindness can solve every problem in the world
Sneha invited him to her lunch group

payload.passage: A ramp helps roll a heavy drum up onto a truck. Instead of lifting the drum straight up, you push it up a long slope. The longer, gentler slope needs less force than a straight lift. You trade a longer push for an easier one. So a ramp lets you raise a heavy drum with a longer but easier push.
payload.title: How a ramp makes lifting a drum easier
decoys: The slope needs less force than a lift
You push the drum up the slope

payload.passage: Riya wanted to learn how to draw a perfect circle without any tool. Her circles always came out lumpy, like potatoes on the page. payload.title: Swinging her arm taught Riya to draw circles
decoys: Riya's circles looked like lumpy potatoes
Art needs no tools, only a steady hand
Riya needed circles for her art project

payload.passage: Ravi noticed that the river ran clear near the hills but turned muddy and grey near a busy town. His teacher explained that waste and loose soil wash into a river as it passes homes and factories. These cloud the water and harm the fish that live there. So the same river can be healthy in one place and sick in another. Ravi learned that a river can be clean and dirty in different places.
payload.title: A river can be clean and dirty in places
decoys: Om saw the factory by the river

payload.passage: A fig tree and a tiny wasp depend on each other to grow. The fig's flowers hide deep inside its round green fruit. A small wasp crawls inside to lay her eggs and spreads pollen as she goes. This pollen lets the fig make its seeds. So the fig and the little wasp help each other live and multiply.
payload.title: How a fig and a wasp help each other
decoys: The wasp spreads pollen inside the fig
Nature is full of clever partnerships
Birds enjoy eating ripe sweet figs

payload.passage: Naina's family started keeping a worm bin on the balcony. Into it they put their fruit and vegetable peels each day. The hungry worms eat the scraps and leave behind rich, dark soil. Naina's plants grow on the balcony

payload.passage: A drip coffee filter lets water trickle through grounds. Hot water is poured slowly over coffee grounds in a paper cone. The water soaks up flavour as it seeps through the grounds. payload.title: How a drip filter trickles water through grounds
decoys: The paper holds the grounds back
Hot water is poured over the grounds

payload.passage: Nidhi felt sleepy in class because she stayed up late watching shows. Her eyes drooped and she missed parts of the lessons. Her parents set a fixed time for switching off the screen at night. With proper sleep, Nidhi stayed bright and alert in class. Her understanding of lessons improved within just a few weeks.
payload.title: An early bedtime solved Nidhi's classroom sleepiness
decoys: Enough sleep keeps every child healthy
Her parents fixed a screen-off time

payload.passage: The colony elders and children together cleaned out the old well that had been left to fill with rubbish and weeds. They cleared the junk, fixed the wall, and used the well water for the garden again. Fresh, free water now flows where waste once lay. They learned that an old well can be cleaned and brought back to use.
payload.title: An old well can be cleaned and brought back

payload.passage: A hand winnowing fan helps clean grain. The farmer tosses mixed grain and light husk into the air above a tray. As it falls, a fan or the wind blows the light husk away to one side. decoys: The heavy grain drops straight down
Grain is tossed into the air

payload.passage: On the trip to the old observatory, Mira saw huge stone shapes built in the open air. payload.title: Giant stone shapes were used to study the sky
decoys: The instruments worked without any lenses
The sky has fascinated people forever
Mira found the shapes very large and odd

payload.passage: Esha watched the small hill stream tumble over rocks and froth white, while the river in town flowed slow and smooth. Esha learned that the slope of the land decides how fast a river flows.

decoys: The hill stream frothed white over rocks
Rivers can be calm or wild
Esha visited both the hill and the town

payload.passage: Ananya tried to learn calligraphy with a special slanted pen. Her first letters came out blotchy and the ink smudged everywhere. By the end of the month Ananya wrote a beautiful birthday card for her friend.
payload.title: Daily shape practice taught Ananya calligraphy
decoys: Ananya's first letters came out blotchy
Beautiful writing impresses everyone who sees it
Ananya made a birthday card for her friend

payload.passage: Pranav forgot his swimming kit at home before every practice. He missed sessions and his coach was not pleased. He packed his kit into his bag the night before each practice day. The ready bag meant he never forgot a thing again. Pranav attended every swimming session fully prepared after that.
payload.title: Packing the night before solved Pranav's forgotten kit
decoys: Good planning helps any sportsperson succeed
Pranav packed his bag the night before

payload.passage: Mira's class noticed birds getting tangled in loops of thrown-away thread, plastic rings and net pieces near the school. The trapped birds could not fly free. The class learned that clearing tangled waste keeps birds safe.
payload.title: Clearing tangled waste keeps birds safe
decoys: Birds got tangled in plastic rings

payload.passage: A bicycle brake slows the wheel by squeezing it tight. When you pull the lever on the handlebar, a cable tugs at the brake arms. decoys: A cable tugs at the brake arms
Bicycles need to be ridden safely
Rubber pads sit near the rim

payload.passage: A spring doorstop stops a door from banging into the wall. A small coiled spring is fixed firmly to the floor behind the door. payload.title: How a spring doorstop soaks up a door's push
decoys: The spring bends to take the push
It is fixed to the floor

payload.passage: Sana watched a big spinning storm called a cyclone form a swirl of clouds on the weather map. Her father explained that over the warm sea, rising moist air begins to turn in a huge circle, growing into a giant spinning storm with strong winds and heavy rain. When it reaches land, it can do great damage. Sana learned that a cyclone is a giant storm born over the warm sea.
payload.title: A cyclone is a giant storm from the sea
decoys: The storm made a swirl on the map
Sana watched the news with her father

payload.passage: Diya saw old phones and broken chargers piling up at home and asked her teacher about them. payload.title: Old gadgets must be recycled with care
decoys: Old gadgets hold metals worth saving
Diya saw broken chargers at home

payload.passage: The school's morning line was always crooked and slow to form. Children pushed and the teachers spent ages straightening it. decoys: Children pushed in the crooked line
Order and discipline matter in every school
The teachers painted footprints on the ground

payload.passage: Anika planted cress seeds on damp cotton and put them in a box with only one small hole for light. As the seedlings grew, they all bent and leaned towards that single hole. When she turned the box, they slowly bent the other way to follow the light. Her teacher said plants chase the light. Anika learned that seedlings bend towards the only light they can find.
payload.title: Seedlings bend towards the only light source
decoys: The seedlings leaned towards the hole
Anika used a box with one hole

payload.passage: Pihu noticed a snail leaving a shiny trail across the wet wall. She set a smooth glass tile and a rough brick in its path. Pihu learned that a snail moves more easily over a smooth surface.
payload.title: A snail moves more easily over smooth surfaces
decoys: The snail slowed on the rough brick
Pihu set a tile in its path

payload.passage: Arjun found long division the hardest part of his maths class. He often got the answer wrong and felt that numbers simply hated him. By the end of the month he could finish a whole page without panicking.
payload.title: A slow daily plan helped Arjun master division
decoys: Arjun used to get many sums wrong
Maths is a subject that troubles every student
Arjun's teacher gave the class ten sums daily

payload.passage: A rolling pin flattens dough into a thin sheet. The smooth round pin is held by a handle at each end. You press down and roll it back and forth over the lump of dough. payload.title: How a rolling pin flattens dough thin
decoys: A handle sits at each end
The pin rolls back and forth

payload.passage: Rian noticed that wet clothes dried faster on windy days. To check it, he hung two equal wet cloths, one in still air indoors and one in the breezy balcony. The balcony cloth dried much sooner than the indoor one. His mother said moving air carries the water away faster. Rian learned that wind helps wet things dry more quickly.
payload.title: Wind helps wet things dry more quickly
decoys: The balcony cloth dried much sooner
Clothes need washing and drying often
Rian hung two equal wet cloths

payload.passage: Krish wondered why the sea water tasted salty but the river water did not. His teacher explained that rivers slowly wash tiny bits of salt out of the rocks and soil and carry them to the sea. When sea water dries up in the sun, the water leaves but the salt stays behind, so the sea grows saltier. Krish learned that rivers carry salt that makes the sea salty.
payload.title: Rivers carry salt that makes the sea salty
decoys: Water covers most of the earth
Krish tasted the water at the beach

payload.passage: Saanvi tried to learn how to plait her own hair into a neat braid. The strands kept slipping and the braid came out lumpy and crooked. She practised on a doll's long hair until her fingers learned the pattern. Slowly her own braids turned smooth, tight, and even. Soon Saanvi plaited her hair every morning without any help at all.
payload.title: Practising on a doll taught Saanvi to braid hair
decoys: Saanvi's first braids came out lumpy
Looking neat is important for every child
Saanvi plaited her hair each morning now

payload.passage: Hailstones are balls of ice that fall during some strong storms. Strong winds inside a storm cloud carry water drops up very high. payload.title: How hailstones grow inside a storm
decoys: Strong winds toss the ice up and down
Storms bring many kinds of weather
Hail can damage crops in the fields

payload.passage: A waiter serves food to people at a restaurant. He greets guests and shows them to a clean table. He notes down what each person wants to eat and drink. He then brings the food from the kitchen and serves it with a smile. So a waiter's work is to serve guests their meals kindly.
payload.title: How a waiter serves guests their meals
decoys: He notes down what each person wants
Many helpers serve people each day
Restaurants get busy in the evening

payload.passage: Ishaan's group collected the school's scrap wood, metal and wire. Before this, it just lay in a heap in the yard and slowly rusted away. The group learned that sending scrap to be remade keeps it from going to waste.
payload.title: Sending scrap to be remade prevents waste
decoys: Scrap metal was rusting in a heap

payload.passage: A matchbox guitar plays soft notes from rubber bands. Bands of different thickness are stretched over an open box. Plucking a thin tight band gives a high note, a fat loose one a low note. The hollow box makes the sound louder than the bands alone. So a matchbox guitar plays notes as plucked bands shake over a hollow box.
payload.title: How plucked bands play a matchbox guitar
decoys: A thin tight band gives a high note
Bands stretch over the open box

payload.passage: A paper aeroplane glides on its folded wings. When you throw it, air slips over and under the flat wings. The smooth wings let it cut through the air and stay up for a while. A slight fold at the back keeps it from tipping over. So a paper plane glides because air flows smoothly over its folded wings.
payload.title: How folded wings let a paper plane glide
decoys: A fold at the back keeps it steady
Paper can be folded into shapes
Air slips over the flat wings

payload.passage: At home, Reva and her sister kept grabbing the same hairbrush each morning. The tug-of-war made them late and cross with each other. payload.title: A second hairbrush ended the sisters' morning fight
decoys: Sharing nicely keeps any family happy
Their mother bought a second brush

payload.passage: The colony planted a hedge of flowering plants all along the wall. They had noticed that bees and butterflies were growing scarce in the area. The colony learned that a flowering hedge brings back helpful bees.
payload.title: A flowering hedge brings back helpful bees

payload.passage: The guide took Hardik's class to a grand stone bridge built hundreds of years ago, still standing strong. payload.title: Stone arches gave a bridge a long life
decoys: The old bridge was made of round arches
Bridges help us cross rivers safely
Hardik walked across the wide bridge

payload.passage: The students collected dry leaves, twigs and grass cuttings from the whole school. They spread them as a soft cover over the garden soil. payload.title: A cover of leaves helps soil hold water
decoys: The cover is made of dry leaves

payload.title: A glass roof was built from tiny pieces

Art can be found in many old buildings

payload.passage: A coral island, or atoll, takes thousands of years to form. It begins when coral grows in a ring around the top of a sinking volcano. decoys: Coral grows in a ring around a volcano
The ocean shapes the land in many ways
Many sea birds rest on coral islands

Without rain, the crops wilted, the ponds shrank, and people had to carry water from far away. Meena understood that a drought is a long time with too little rain.
payload.title: A drought is a long spell with little rain
decoys: The village wells dried up completely
Water is precious in every village
Meena's grandfather knew about the weather

payload.passage: Esha wanted to learn how to make beaded bracelets to gift her friends. Her early bracelets kept breaking and the beads scattered everywhere. She learned to tie a strong double knot at each end of the string. Her bracelets held together and looked bright and colourful. Soon Esha had made a different bracelet for each of her close friends.
payload.title: Strong knots taught Esha to make lasting bracelets
decoys: A small gift can make any friend very happy
Esha made a bracelet for each close friend

payload.passage: A spinning top with a string winds up its own spin. You wrap the string round the body from bottom to top. With a sharp pull on the string, the body is set spinning very fast. As the string unwraps, it leaves the top whirling on the floor. So a string top spins fast as a quick pull unwinds the string.
payload.title: How a quick pull spins a string top
decoys: The string unwraps as you pull
You wrap the string round the body

payload.passage: A lever tap on a water cooler fills a glass with one press. You hold the glass below the spout and press the small lever. The press lifts a stopper inside and lets the cold water run. When you let go, the stopper drops back and the flow stops. So a lever tap pours water while pressed and stops when released.
payload.title: How a lever tap pours water on a press
decoys: Cold water is nice on hot days
You hold the glass below the spout

payload.passage: Saanjh dropped one sugar cube and one crushed sugar spoonful into two glasses of the same cool water and stirred each the same. The crushed sugar vanished quickly, while the whole cube took much longer to disappear. His teacher said small pieces meet more water at once. Saanjh learned that crushed sugar dissolves faster than a whole cube.
payload.title: Crushed sugar dissolves faster than a whole cube
decoys: The whole cube took longer to vanish
Saanjh stirred each glass the same

payload.passage: The guide stopped the class at a huge stone gateway with carved animals. She explained that long ago a king built it to mark a great victory, so that people passing through would remember it for years. The carvings showed the very battles he had won. Imran saw that the gateway was not just an entrance but a way of keeping a memory alive in stone.
payload.title: A stone gateway kept a victory remembered
decoys: The gateway had carved animals on it
Kings of old did many grand things
Imran walked under the gateway twice

payload.passage: Jay wanted to learn how to throw a flying disc straight to his friend. The disc kept curving away and landing far off to the side. He learned to flick his wrist and let go at just the right moment. The disc began to sail flat and straight across the park. Soon Jay and his friend could toss the disc back and forth easily.
payload.title: A good wrist flick taught Jay to throw the disc
decoys: The disc kept curving off to the side
Outdoor games are wonderful for every child
Jay and his friend played in the park

payload.passage: A telephone lineman keeps our phone and internet lines working. When a line breaks, he climbs the pole to reach the wires. He checks each wire to find where the trouble is. Then he joins or replaces the broken wire to restore the link. So a lineman's job is to keep our phones and internet connected.
payload.title: How a lineman keeps phones connected
decoys: He climbs the pole to reach the wires
Many skilled helpers serve our homes
The internet lets us talk to far-off friends

payload.passage: Ritika set out to learn freestyle football kicks she saw on a video. The ball flew off in odd directions during her early attempts. She practised one trick at a time on the soft grass after school. Her control improved as her feet learned to feel the ball. Within a month Ritika could flick the ball over her head and catch it.
payload.title: One-trick-at-a-time practice taught Ritika football kicks
decoys: The ball flew off in odd directions
Online videos can teach a child every sport
Ritika practised her kicks on soft grass

payload.passage: Diya saw the small stream behind her house grow into a wide river as it flowed toward the city. Her uncle explained that as a river travels downhill, many smaller streams join it from the sides, adding more and more water. By the time it reaches the plains, it is broad and powerful. Diya learned that a river grows wider as more streams flow into it.
payload.title: A river grows as streams join it
decoys: The river flowed toward the city
Rivers are found all over the land
Diya lives close to a small stream

payload.passage: The students fitted simple aerators on all the school taps. An aerator is a small piece that mixes air into the flowing water. This makes the water still feel strong while using much less of it. Hands and dishes get just as clean as before on far less water. The students learned that mixing air into the tap saves water.
payload.title: Mixing air into the tap saves water
decoys: The aerator mixes air into the water
Taps are used many times a day

payload.passage: The guide stopped Asha's class before a wall covered in faded paintings inside a cave. She explained that the colours had lasted so long because they were made from crushed rocks and earth, which do not fade quickly. The pictures showed hunters, animals and dances from thousands of years ago. Asha learned that the paintings were a window into the lives of very early people.
payload.title: Cave paintings show the lives of early people
decoys: The paint was made from crushed rocks
Painting is a very old kind of art
Asha liked the picture of a leaping deer

payload.passage: A spring bubbles out of the ground where underground water reaches the surface. Rain soaks deep into the soil and rock over many years. It collects below ground and moves slowly through tiny cracks. Where the rock dips low enough, the water seeps out as a clear spring. So a spring is hidden rainwater finding its way back to the open.
payload.title: How a spring rises out of the ground
decoys: Rain soaks deep into the soil and rock
Water travels around the Earth in many ways
People often collect spring water to drink

payload.passage: A bicycle gear chain needs to stay clean and oiled. The chain links must bend smoothly as they wrap round the toothed wheels. A drop of oil lets each link slide over the next with little rubbing. Grit and dust make the chain stiff and slow. So a well-oiled chain lets a bicycle's links bend smoothly round the gears.
payload.title: How oil keeps a bicycle chain moving smoothly
decoys: The links wrap round toothed wheels

payload.passage: The neighbourhood club painted their bins in three bright colours. On each one they wrote a simple word: wet, dry or recycle. Now even small children know exactly where to put their waste. So the rubbish goes to the right place and more of it is reused. The club learned that clear, coloured bins help everyone sort their waste.
payload.title: Coloured bins help everyone sort waste
decoys: The bins have three bright colours

payload.passage: The school notice board was so full that new notices got covered up. Children missed important news hidden under old papers. A monitor was asked to remove old notices every Monday morning. The board stayed clear, and fresh notices were easy to spot. Now nobody misses an announcement about tests or events.
payload.title: Clearing old notices solved the hidden-news problem
decoys: New notices got covered by old ones
Notice boards keep a school well informed
A monitor cleared the board each Monday

payload.passage: At home, the family could never find a pen when they needed one. Pens vanished into bags, drawers, and the bottoms of pockets. Mother kept a small jar of pens in the middle of the dining table. Anyone needing a pen simply took one from the jar. The frustrating pen hunts ended completely after that.
payload.title: A pen jar solved the vanishing-pen problem
decoys: Pens vanished into bags and drawers
A small idea can save a family much trouble
Mother kept a pen jar on the table

payload.passage: A potter shapes wet clay into useful pots and lamps. He places a lump of clay on his spinning wheel. As the wheel turns, he uses his hands to mould the clay into shape. He then dries and bakes the pot to make it hard and strong. So a potter's work is to turn soft clay into useful things.
payload.title: How a potter shapes clay into pots
decoys: He moulds the clay on a spinning wheel
Many skilled helpers serve our town
Clay lamps are lit during Diwali

payload.passage: Sara held a glass of icy water in the warm room and watched its outside. Tiny drops of water slowly formed on the cold surface, even though the glass had no leak. Her father said the warm air around it left its water on the cold glass. Sara learned that cold surfaces gather water drops from warm air.
payload.title: Cold surfaces gather water from warm air
decoys: Tiny drops formed on the cold glass
Water can appear in many ways
Sara held a glass of icy water

payload.passage: Vivek wanted to learn how to do simple sums in his head quickly. He always reached for paper and pencil even for tiny problems. His teacher taught him to round numbers and add the easy parts first. With practice the answers began to pop into his head fast. Soon Vivek solved mental sums quicker than many of his classmates.
payload.title: A rounding trick sped up Vivek's mental maths
decoys: Vivek reached for paper even for tiny sums
Quick thinking is the most useful skill ever
Vivek's teacher gave the class a new trick

payload.passage: Rudra wanted to see his own breath as fog. On a cold morning he breathed out hard and watched a little white cloud appear in front of him. Indoors in the warm room he breathed out and saw nothing at all. His mother said the warm breath turns to tiny drops only in cold air. Rudra learned that breath turns into mist when the air is cold.
payload.title: Breath turns into mist in cold air
decoys: A little white cloud appeared outdoors
Mornings can feel cold in winter
Rudra breathed out hard each time

payload.passage: The students collected the chalk stubs and broken crayons that were usually thrown away. They melted all the crayon bits together into bright new crayons. These fresh crayons went to the younger classes to use. They also ground the leftover chalk stubs to mark the lines on the playground. The students learned that even small bits and stubs can be made useful again.
payload.title: Even bits and stubs can be made useful again
decoys: Crayon bits were melted into new ones

payload.passage: Avni was surprised that the dry stream bed filled with a roaring flood within an hour of a faraway cloudburst. Her teacher explained that a sudden, very heavy rain can send a fast wall of water rushing down a narrow valley with little warning. This is called a flash flood and can be dangerous. Avni learned that a sudden heavy rain can cause a fast flash flood.
payload.title: Sudden heavy rain can cause a flash flood
decoys: The dry stream bed filled in an hour
Floods can happen in many ways

payload.passage: A drop of rain that lands on a high hill begins a long trip. It trickles down into a tiny mountain stream first. Many streams join to form a wider, faster river. That river flows on through plains and towns until it reaches the sea. So a single raindrop may journey all the way to the ocean.
payload.title: A raindrop's journey to the sea
decoys: Many streams join to form a wider river
Water moves about the Earth all the time
Rivers give us water for our farms

payload.passage: A pond can freeze on top yet stay alive underneath in winter. When the cold deepens, a layer of ice forms across the surface. This ice acts like a lid that keeps the cold out of the water below. Fish and frogs stay in the slightly warmer water under the ice. So a frozen lid keeps a pond's life safe through winter.
payload.title: How ice keeps a pond alive in winter
decoys: Fish stay in the water under the ice
Children sometimes slide on frozen ponds

payload.passage: A water tanker driver brings water to homes when the taps run dry. In the hot season some areas do not get enough water. The driver fills his big tanker at the station and sets off. He drives to each waiting street and fills the people's pots and tanks. So a tanker driver's work is to carry water to homes that need it.
payload.title: How a tanker driver carries water to homes
decoys: He fills the people's pots and tanks
We should not waste water in summer

payload.passage: Anjali decided to learn swimming during the summer holidays. The cold water frightened her, and for two days she only sat at the edge of the pool. Her coach was patient and showed her how to float on her back. Bit by bit Anjali grew braver and began to kick across the shallow end. By the last week she was swimming a full lap and smiling proudly.
payload.title: Anjali slowly overcame her fear of water
decoys: Anjali sat at the pool edge for two days
Every child must learn to swim in summer
Anjali had her holidays during the summer

payload.passage: The Clean Lane club gave every house a small basket for dry recyclable waste and arranged a weekly pickup by a recycler. Paper, glass and metal now leave the lane sorted and reused, instead of mixed in the dump. The lane is tidier too. The club learned that a weekly pickup makes recycling easy for a whole lane.
payload.title: A weekly pickup makes recycling easy
decoys: Each house got a small basket

payload.passage: A rainforest stays warm and wet in every season of the year. Rain falls almost every day, keeping the air thick and damp. The thick green roof of leaves traps heat and moisture below. Plants and animals there never face a cold winter or a dry spell. So a rainforest enjoys warm, wet weather all year round.
payload.title: Why a rainforest is warm and wet all year
decoys: A roof of leaves traps heat below
Forests grow in many parts of the world
Rainforests are home to countless animals

payload.passage: Vivaan noticed the school threw away lots of food every lunch break. His group decided to do something about it. They made a plan to cook only what is needed, and to give any extra to a shelter nearby. They also taught everyone to take small helpings first and come back for more. Soon almost no food was wasted, and the group learned that planning meals carefully stops good food being thrown away.
payload.title: Planning meals stops good food being wasted
decoys: Extra food goes to a nearby shelter

payload.passage: The school bell was so faint that children in far rooms never heard it. They often reached the assembly late and got into trouble. The principal had a louder bell fitted with a bigger speaker. Now the bell rang clearly to every corner of the building. The children gathered on time and the late marks disappeared.
payload.title: A louder bell solved the late-assembly trouble
decoys: Children in far rooms missed the faint bell
Punctuality is a virtue every student needs
The principal fitted a bigger speaker

payload.passage: A rain gauge at a weather post measures the rain. It is an open funnel that guides rain into a narrow marked tube below. Because the tube is thin, even a little rain shows clearly against the marks. A watcher reads the level each morning and notes it down. So a rain gauge measures rainfall by funnelling it into a thin marked tube.
payload.title: How a rain gauge funnels rain to be measured
decoys: A watcher reads the level each morning
An open funnel sits on top

payload.passage: A mercury-free thermometer shows heat with a rising liquid. A thin tube holds a coloured liquid in a tiny bulb at the bottom. When it grows warmer, the liquid swells and creeps up the narrow tube. The higher the liquid climbs, the higher the reading beside it. So a thermometer shows warmth by how far its liquid rises.
payload.title: How a thermometer shows warmth by rising liquid
decoys: The liquid sits in a tiny bulb
A thin tube holds the liquid

payload.passage: A baby elephant relies on its herd from the moment it is born. It can stand within an hour but still needs much help and care. The mother and other elephants guard it and guide it as it walks. It drinks its mother's milk and slowly learns to find its own food. So a young elephant grows up safely inside a caring herd.
payload.title: A baby elephant grows up in a herd
decoys: A baby elephant can stand within an hour
Animals look after their young in many ways
Elephants use their trunks to pick up food

payload.passage: A see-through soap dispenser pushes out soap with a small pump. When you press the top down, it squeezes a little chamber inside. The squeeze drives a dab of soap up the spout and out. As you let go, a spring lifts the top and pulls more soap up ready for next time. So a soap pump squirts soap by pressing a small chamber and refilling it.
payload.title: How a pump squirts soap from a bottle
decoys: A spring lifts the top back up

payload.passage: A young plant called a seedling is weak when it first appears. Its stem is thin and its first two leaves are small and soft. It must quickly make food and grow stronger roots to survive. With enough light and water it grows a tougher stem and bigger leaves. So a fragile seedling slowly grows into a sturdy plant.
payload.title: How a weak seedling grows sturdy
decoys: A seedling's first two leaves are small
Plants begin life in delicate ways

payload.passage: At home, the kitchen sink kept getting blocked with bits of food. Dirty water filled up and gave off a bad smell. Mother taught everyone to scrape their plates into the bin first. With no food going down the drain, the sink stopped clogging. The kitchen stayed clean and fresh from that day onwards.
payload.title: Scraping plates first solved the blocked sink
decoys: Dirty water gave off a bad smell
A clean kitchen keeps the whole family well
Mother taught everyone a simple habit

payload.passage: The guide took Roshni's class to a marble building shaped like a dome, glowing white in the sun. She explained that workers spent many years fitting the stones so perfectly that no gaps showed, and added gardens and pools to mirror the dome. Every part was planned to look balanced from all sides. Roshni learned that the monument was built with great care to look perfectly balanced.
payload.title: A marble monument was built to look balanced
decoys: Pools in the garden mirrored the dome
Roshni thought the white marble glowed

payload.passage: A plumber takes care of the pipes that carry water through our homes. When a tap drips or a pipe leaks, people send for him. He brings his tools and finds where the water is escaping. He tightens, seals, or changes the broken pipe to stop the leak. So a plumber's job is to keep the water flowing properly.
payload.title: How a plumber keeps the water flowing
decoys: He finds where the water is escaping
Many handy helpers serve our homes
Wasting water is bad in a dry season

payload.passage: A pumpkin starts its life as a bright yellow flower on a creeping vine. After a bee visits the flower, a tiny green fruit forms at its base. The young pumpkin then grows bigger and rounder week after week. As it ripens it turns from green to a deep orange colour. So a small flower slowly swells into a big round pumpkin.
payload.title: How a pumpkin grows from a flower
decoys: A ripe pumpkin turns a deep orange colour
Vines grow many kinds of fruit
Pumpkins are cooked into many dishes

payload.passage: Shreya saw long streaks of high, wispy white cloud one clear day and asked if it would rain. Her teacher explained that these thin, feathery clouds float very high up. The air there is so cold that water freezes. So the clouds are made of tiny ice bits, not water drops, and they hardly ever bring rain. Shreya learned that high feathery clouds are made of ice.
payload.title: High feathery clouds are made of ice
decoys: The clouds looked thin and wispy
Shreya looked up on a clear day

payload.passage: At the museum, Asma found a wall of old photographs of her city from a hundred years ago. The guide pointed out the empty fields where tall buildings now stand and the bullock carts where buses now run. Together the photos, she said, show how much the city has grown and changed. Asma learned that the old photos showed how her city changed over time.
payload.title: Old photos show how a city changed over time
decoys: One photo showed bullock carts on the road
Cities are busy and crowded places
Asma looked for her own street in the photos

payload.passage: At the museum, Gaurav found a case of old toys: clay animals, spinning tops and tiny carts. The guide said that long ago, children had no plastic or batteries, so toys were made from clay, wood and cloth by hand. Yet the games children played, like racing carts, were not so different from today. Gaurav saw that the toys showed how children have always loved to play.
payload.title: Old toys show children always loved to play
decoys: Some old toys were spinning wooden tops
Gaurav wished he could spin the top

payload.passage: The colony children noticed paint and oil being tipped into the open drain. The drain carried it to the pond, where it killed the fish. So the children told the grown-ups, who set up a safe place to collect such waste. The pond slowly began to recover. The children learned that keeping harmful waste out of drains protects the water.
payload.title: Keeping harmful waste out of drains protects water
decoys: Paint was tipped into the drain

payload.passage: At home, the family's wet towels lay in a damp heap and smelled musty. No one had a fixed place to hang them after a bath. Father put up a row of hooks on the bathroom wall. Each person hung their towel on a hook to dry properly. The towels stayed fresh and the musty smell disappeared.
payload.title: Towel hooks solved the musty-towel problem
decoys: A fresh home is a pleasure for everyone
Father put up hooks on the bathroom wall

payload.passage: The classroom's window curtain kept falling down on the children's heads. The loose rod slipped from its bracket whenever the wind blew. A worker screwed the bracket back tightly into the wall. The curtain rod held firm and stopped falling after that. The children sat safely without curtains dropping on them.
payload.title: Fixing the bracket solved the falling curtain
decoys: The rod slipped whenever the wind blew
A safe classroom is the right of every child
A worker screwed the bracket tightly

payload.passage: A ice-cream churn freezes a sweet mix with salt and ice. The mix sits in a small can set inside a bigger one of ice. Salt sprinkled on the ice makes it grow extra cold. As you turn the handle, the very cold can slowly freezes the mix into ice cream. So salt and ice grow cold enough to freeze the churning mix.
payload.title: How salt and ice freeze churning ice cream
decoys: The mix sits in a small inner can
Ice cream is a sweet treat
You turn the handle to churn

payload.passage: Ishaan filled three identical cups with the same hot water from one kettle. He wrapped the first cup in a woollen cloth, left the second one bare, and stood the third in a bowl of cool water. After half an hour he dipped his finger into each cup to compare them. The wrapped cup was still warm while the others had turned cool. Ishaan learned that wool keeps heat from escaping quickly.
payload.title: Wool slows heat from leaving warm water
decoys: Ishaan used the same hot water for each cup
Heat can travel in several different ways
Kettles are used to boil water at home

payload.passage: Shaurya poured warm water into a bottle and stretched a balloon over its neck. He stood the bottle in a bowl of hot water and waited. Slowly the limp balloon began to puff up on its own. His teacher said the warmed air inside grew and pushed into the balloon. Shaurya learned that air gets bigger and pushes out when it is heated.
payload.title: Air swells and pushes out when heated
decoys: The limp balloon puffed up on its own
Shaurya used warm water in the bottle

payload.passage: A tailor stitches clothes that fit each person just right. First he measures the customer carefully with his tape. Then he cuts the cloth to match those measurements. With his sewing machine he joins the pieces into a neat new outfit. So a tailor's work is to make clothes that fit us well.
payload.title: How a tailor makes clothes that fit
decoys: He measures the customer with a tape
Many skilled helpers serve our town
Festival time keeps tailors very busy

payload.passage: A storm on a summer afternoon can change the sky very fast. First white clouds pile up into tall dark towers. Then the wind grows strong, the sky darkens, and thunder rumbles. Lightning flashes and heavy rain pours down for a short while. After the storm passes, the air feels cool, clean, and fresh.
payload.title: How a summer storm builds and passes
decoys: Lightning flashes during a summer storm
The sky keeps changing all day long
Rain helps the dry garden plants grow

payload.passage: Reyansh planted the same flower seeds in two pots of equal soil. He gave the first pot a spoon of plant food each week and gave the second pot only plain water. After a month the fed plant stood tall with many buds while the other stayed short. His grandfather said the extra food helped the plant build strong stems and flowers. Reyansh learned that plant food helps a plant grow bigger and stronger.
payload.title: Plant food helps a plant grow bigger
decoys: The fed plant grew tall with many buds
Plants are living things that need care
Reyansh used two pots of equal soil

payload.passage: A level tool shows when a shelf is straight. A small tube of liquid with one air bubble lies along the tool. When the tool is tilted, the bubble slides towards the higher end. When the shelf is truly flat, the bubble rests right in the middle. So a level shows a flat surface when its bubble sits centred.
payload.title: How a bubble shows when a shelf is level
decoys: The bubble slides to the higher end
A tube of liquid holds the bubble

payload.passage: A caterpillar spends its early days doing just one thing, eating leaves all day long. When it has grown fat enough, it wraps itself in a hard case and stays very still. Inside that quiet case its whole body slowly changes shape. After some days the case splits and a butterfly with bright wings flies out. This is how a crawling caterpillar turns into a flying butterfly.
payload.title: A caterpillar changes into a butterfly
decoys: A caterpillar eats green leaves all day
Insects are some of the most interesting creatures
Butterflies help flowers by carrying their pollen

payload.passage: A telephone operator helps connect people who call for help. She sits at a busy board with many lines coming in. When someone rings, she listens and finds out what they need. She then joins their call to the right office or person. So an operator's job is to link callers to the help they need.
payload.title: How an operator connects callers
decoys: She joins each call to the right office
Many helpers serve people each day
A phone helps us reach far-off people

payload.passage: A spinning prism toy throws colours on the wall. A clear glass prism is set in a little stand by a sunny window. When sunlight passes through it, the prism bends the light and splits it. Bands of red through blue spread out across the far wall. So a prism makes a rainbow by splitting sunlight into its colours.
payload.title: How a prism splits sunlight into colours
decoys: The prism is set by a sunny window
It bends the light as it passes

payload.passage: The guide showed Veer's class a museum room of old masks used in village plays. She explained that each painted mask stood for a well-known character, so the audience knew at once who was good or wicked, even from far away. The masks helped tell stories to large crowds at night. Veer learned that old masks helped actors tell stories to a crowd.
payload.title: Old masks helped actors tell stories
decoys: Each mask stood for a known character
Plays are a popular kind of fun
Veer thought one mask looked rather scary

payload.passage: A school principal leads the whole school and looks after everyone in it. She makes the rules that keep the school running well. She helps the teachers plan and solves problems when they come up. She also greets parents and guides students who need help. So a principal's main work is to lead and care for the school.
payload.title: How a principal leads the school
decoys: She greets parents at the school
Many helpers work in a school
Schools hold a sports day each year

payload.passage: A simple sundial tells the time using the sun and a shadow. A flat plate is marked with hour lines around the edge. A slanted pointer in the middle casts a shadow as the sun moves. As the day goes on, the shadow swings from one hour line to the next. So a sundial shows the time by where the pointer's shadow falls.
payload.title: How a sundial tells time by a shadow
decoys: Hour lines run around the edge
The sun crosses the sky each day
A slanted pointer stands in the middle

payload.passage: Yug poured the same warm water into a metal cup and a clay cup and left both on the table. After half an hour he felt the water in each. The water in the clay cup had cooled more than the water in the metal one. His grandmother said clay lets warmth slip away through its tiny holes. Yug learned that water cools faster in a clay cup than a metal cup.
payload.title: Water cools faster in clay than in metal
decoys: The clay cup let warmth slip away
Yug used the same warm water

payload.passage: A see-through ball-point compass draws a neat circle on paper. One leg has a sharp point that you press into the centre of the page. The other leg holds a pencil at a set distance away. When you swing the pencil leg round, it traces a perfect circle. So a compass draws a circle by swinging a pencil round a fixed point.
payload.title: How a compass draws a circle round a point
decoys: One leg has a sharp point

payload.passage: Mira left a cut onion on a plate near her study table for an hour. Soon the whole room carried its sharp smell, even from far away. She covered it with a bowl and the smell faded. Her teacher said tiny bits of the onion floated through the air to her nose. Mira learned that smells travel because tiny bits spread through the air.
payload.title: Smells travel as tiny bits spread through air
decoys: Covering the onion made the smell fade
Mira left it near her table

payload.passage: A zip joins two edges of cloth with rows of tiny linking teeth. A small slider runs up and down along these teeth. As you pull the slider up, a wedge inside it hooks each tooth into the one opposite. Pulling it down does the reverse and parts the teeth again. So a zip works by a slider that locks or unlocks rows of little teeth.
payload.title: How a zip locks rows of tiny teeth
decoys: A wedge inside the slider hooks the teeth
Zips are found on bags and jackets
Two rows of teeth line each edge

payload.passage: On a freezing night, Anjali found the puddle outside turned to solid ice by morning. Her father explained that when the air gets cold enough, the tiny moving bits in water slow down and lock together into a hard solid. The water has not vanished; it has only changed into ice. When it warms, it melts back. Anjali learned that cold turns water into ice.
payload.title: Cold turns liquid water into solid ice
decoys: The puddle had frozen by morning

payload.passage: Bhuvan left a slice of lemon, a coin and a wet sponge on a metal tray near the kitchen window for a week. He checked the tray each day. A green-blue stain crept across the metal under the lemon and sponge but not under the dry coin. His teacher said sour, wet things slowly stain metal. Bhuvan learned that sour, damp things leave a stain on metal.
payload.title: Sour, damp things leave a stain on metal
decoys: Bhuvan checked the tray each day
He used a lemon, coin and sponge

payload.passage: The school's Green Roof team grew a thick mat of plants on the flat rooftop. The green leaves shade the building from the harsh sun. Because of this, the rooms below stay cooler and need fewer fans on hot days. The plants also soak up the rain that falls on the roof. The team learned that a roof of plants keeps a building cool and saves power.
payload.title: A roof of plants keeps a building cool
decoys: The team grew plants on the roof

payload.passage: A see-through sand timer for brushing teeth runs for two minutes. Fine sand sits in the upper of two joined glass bulbs.
