When you flip it, the sand slips through the narrow waist a few grains at a time. The amount of sand is set so the top empties in just two minutes. So a brushing timer marks two minutes with slowly falling sand.
payload.title: How a sand timer marks two brushing minutes
decoys: Sand slips through the narrow waist
Two glass bulbs hold the sand

payload.passage: A hermit crab does not grow its own shell to protect itself. Its soft back would be an easy meal without some cover. So it finds an empty sea snail shell and tucks itself inside. As the crab grows bigger, it leaves the small shell and finds a larger one. So a hermit crab keeps changing borrowed shells as it grows.
payload.title: How a hermit crab borrows its shells
decoys: The crab tucks into an empty snail shell
Hermit crabs live near the rocky shore

payload.passage: Kavya buried a peeled banana piece in one corner of a flowerpot and a plastic bottle cap in another corner. She dug them both up after three weeks to see what had happened. The banana had turned dark and soft and was breaking apart into the soil. The plastic cap looked exactly the same as before. Kavya learned that food rots away in soil but plastic does not.
payload.title: Food rots in soil but plastic does not
decoys: The banana turned dark and soft
We should take care of our environment
Kavya used a flowerpot for her test

payload.passage: After a rain shower, a rainbow sometimes appears across the sky. It is made when sunlight shines through tiny drops of water still floating in the air. The light bends inside each drop and splits into many colours. We then see a wide arch of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. So a rainbow is really sunlight and raindrops working together.
payload.title: How sunlight and rain make a rainbow
decoys: A rainbow shows red, green, and violet bands
The sky shows us many wonderful sights
Rain helps farmers fill their dry fields

payload.passage: A spirit stove burns a clean liquid fuel for cooking. The fuel sits in a small bowl with a soaked wick at the centre. When the wick is lit, it draws fuel up to feed the flame. The steady flame heats a pot placed on the stand above. So a spirit stove cooks with a flame fed by fuel rising up a wick.
payload.title: How a wick feeds a spirit stove flame
decoys: The fuel sits in a small bowl
A pot rests on the stand above

payload.passage: Nisha noticed that a sunflower in her garden always faced the morning sun. To check it, she marked the direction of the flower each day at breakfast and again at dinner. The flower head had clearly turned to follow the sun across the sky. By the next morning it had swung back to face the east again. Nisha learned that young sunflowers turn their heads to follow the sun.
payload.title: Young sunflowers turn to follow the sun
decoys: Nisha marked the flower's direction at dinner
Flowers make gardens look bright and cheerful
The sun rises in the east each morning

payload.passage: A rescue worker reaches people in danger during a flood. When water rises and traps families, he comes in a boat. He guides people gently into the boat and rows them to dry land. He brings food and blankets to those who have lost their homes. So a rescue worker's job is to save people caught in a flood.
payload.title: How a rescue worker saves flood victims
decoys: He rows people to dry land in a boat
Many brave helpers come to our aid
Heavy rain can cause sudden floods

payload.passage: Maya's family began saving their used water from washing vegetables and rinsing rice. Instead of letting it run down the drain, they pour it on the garden plants and the tulsi pot. The plants stay green even in summer, and the family uses much less fresh water. They learned that reusing water at home keeps a garden alive.
payload.title: Reusing home water keeps a garden alive
decoys: The family pours rinse water on plants
Maya's plants stay green in summer

payload.passage: The students made cloth bags from old bed sheets and washed them clean. They gave the bags away free at the market gate. They asked each shopper to use the cloth bag instead of taking a plastic one. Many people happily agreed, and the market saw far fewer plastic bags. The students learned that handing out cloth bags helps people give up plastic ones.
payload.title: Free cloth bags help people give up plastic
decoys: The bags were made from old sheets
The students gave bags away free

payload.passage: The school's Repair Club takes care of the torn library books. They mend the loose covers with tape and glue. They carefully re-stitch the pages that have come away. An old book that would have been binned can then serve many more readers for years. The club learned that mending old books keeps them in use for a long time.
payload.title: Mending old books keeps them in use for years

payload.passage: The guide led Sumit's class to an old town well with a roof and a wheel for the rope. She explained that this well was once the heart of the town, where people met every morning to draw water and share news. Around it grew shops and a small market. Sumit understood that the old well was once the busy meeting place of the whole town.
payload.title: An old well was the town's meeting place
decoys: The well had a wheel for the rope
Towns grow in many different ways
Sumit peered down into the deep well

payload.passage: Hardik saw a small whirl of dust spin across the dry field on a hot afternoon. His teacher explained that the ground heats up strongly in one spot, the hot air shoots up fast, and air rushing in to replace it begins to spin, picking up dust as it goes. It fades when the air mixes. Hardik learned that rising hot air can make a spinning dust whirl.
payload.title: Rising hot air can make a spinning dust whirl
decoys: The dust whirl crossed the field
Hardik watched it from the shade

payload.passage: Every June, dark clouds rolled in and the dry land came alive with rain. Kabir's teacher explained that the monsoon is a wind that changes direction with the seasons, carrying wet air from the warm sea onto the land for months. This rain fills the rivers and waters the crops that feed the country. Kabir learned that the monsoon is a season of wind that brings life-giving rain.
payload.title: The monsoon is a wind that brings rain
decoys: The monsoon clouds come every June
Rain is needed to grow food
Kabir lives where the monsoon arrives

payload.passage: Anjali wanted to know if plants really need light to grow. She kept one small bean pot on the sunny windowsill and hid a second pot inside a dark cupboard. She watered both pots the same amount every morning for two weeks. The sunny plant grew green and strong, but the cupboard plant turned pale and weak. Anjali learned that sunlight is food that green plants cannot do without.
payload.title: An experiment showed plants need sunlight to grow
decoys: Anjali watered both pots every single morning
All living things in the world need food
Beans are an easy seed to grow at home

payload.passage: Drishti put one plant in a room she kept quiet and another in a room with daily soft music as a fun test. She watered and lit them the same for three weeks. In the end both plants looked much the same height and colour. Her teacher said light and water mattered, not the music. Drishti learned that a fair test must change only one thing at a time.
payload.title: A fair test changes only one thing at once
decoys: Both plants ended up about the same

payload.passage: Krish noticed that wet sand sticks together but dry sand does not. He tried to build a tall tower with dry sand and it just slid down. Then he wet the sand and built a firm tower that held its shape. His teacher said the water glues the grains together. Krish learned that water helps sand grains hold together.
payload.title: Water helps sand grains hold together
decoys: The dry sand tower slid down
Krish wet the sand to build

payload.passage: At the museum, Naresh found a display of old farming calendars carved on stone and wood. The guide explained that farmers once marked the right days for ploughing, sowing and harvest by watching the stars and seasons, then carved them to remember. These calendars kept whole villages working in time with the land. Naresh learned that old calendars guided farmers through the year.
payload.title: Old calendars guided farmers through the year
decoys: Some calendars were carved on wood
Naresh tried to read the carved marks

payload.passage: A milkman brings fresh milk to many homes early each morning. While most people are still asleep, he loads his cans or packets. He cycles from house to house, leaving milk at each doorstep. He keeps the milk cool and clean so it is safe to drink. So a milkman's work is to deliver fresh milk to every home.
payload.title: How a milkman delivers fresh milk
decoys: He leaves milk at each doorstep
Many early helpers serve the street
Warm milk is a soothing bedtime drink

payload.passage: Krish wanted to learn how to do a proper push start on his skateboard. He kept losing his footing and the board shot out from under him. He practised pushing gently and placing his foot back slowly. His balance improved and the board rolled smoothly beneath him. Soon Krish glided down the smooth path with both feet on the board.
payload.title: A gentle push taught Krish to start his skateboard
decoys: The board kept shooting out from Krish's feet
Skateboarding is the coolest hobby for kids
Krish glided down a smooth path

payload.passage: Kavya struggled to learn the names of all the planets in order. They kept slipping out of her head right before the science quiz. She made up a funny sentence using the first letter of each planet. The silly sentence stuck in her mind and the order came easily. Kavya answered every planet question in the quiz without any trouble.
payload.title: A memory sentence helped Kavya learn the planets
decoys: The planet names slipped out of Kavya's head
Space is the most exciting subject to study
Kavya had a science quiz coming up soon

payload.passage: The colony's outdoor lamps used to burn brightly all morning long. Nobody ever remembered to switch them off after dawn. So the colony fitted simple shades and light timers to the lamps. Now they switch themselves off by themselves when the day breaks. The wasted electricity stopped and the bill dropped, so the colony learned that switching off lights on time saves power.
payload.title: Switching off lights on time saves power
decoys: The lamps switch off at dawn
Timers were fitted to the lights

payload.passage: Krish placed two equal blobs of butter on two plates. He set one plate in bright sunshine and kept the other in the shade. After twenty minutes the sunny butter had melted into a yellow puddle while the shaded blob held its shape. His mother said the sun's heat softened and melted the butter. Krish learned that heat melts a solid into a liquid.
payload.title: Heat melts a solid into a liquid
decoys: The sunny butter melted into a puddle
The sun gives off plenty of heat
Krish used two plates for his test

payload.passage: Avni wanted to learn how to do ten star jumps without getting tired. At first she ran out of breath after only three or four. She added one extra jump every other day and rested in between. Her legs and lungs grew stronger week by week. Soon Avni did ten star jumps easily and even challenged her friends.
payload.title: Adding jumps slowly built Avni's stamina
decoys: Avni ran out of breath after four jumps
Exercise keeps every body fit and healthy
Avni challenged her friends to a contest

payload.passage: A weighing balance on a market stall has a needle in the middle. As goods are placed in the pan, a spring inside stretches under the weight. The more the spring stretches, the further the needle swings across a marked dial. The shopkeeper reads the number the needle points to. So a spring scale shows weight by how far a spring stretches.
payload.title: How a spring scale shows weight on a dial
decoys: A needle swings across a marked dial
Markets sell many kinds of goods
A spring stretches under the load

payload.passage: The guide stopped Tarun's class at a tall stone pillar standing alone in a field. She explained that long ago a ruler carved his laws and wishes onto such pillars and placed them where many people passed, so the message would reach everyone. The words asked people to be kind and fair. Tarun learned that the pillar was an old way of sharing rules with the people.
payload.title: A carved pillar shared rules with the people
decoys: The pillar stood alone in a field
Rulers of old left many marks behind
Tarun ran his hand over the carved words

payload.passage: A pop-up toaster browns bread with hot glowing wires. When you push the lever down, the bread sinks between two heated grills. Power makes the wires glow red and toast both sides of the slice. A small timer counts the seconds and then springs the bread back up. So a toaster cooks bread with hot wires and pops it out on time.
payload.title: How a toaster browns and pops up bread
decoys: The wires glow red when toasting
A lever lowers the bread inside

payload.passage: A grain of wheat holds the whole future of a wheat plant. When it is planted in soft soil and watered, it begins to sprout. A green blade pushes up while roots dig down for water. The plant grows tall and forms a head full of many new grains. So each single grain can grow a plant bearing many more.
payload.title: One grain of wheat grows many more
decoys: A green blade pushes up from the wheat seed
Plants help feed people all over the world
Wheat is ground into flour for bread

payload.passage: The students collected old, broken umbrellas that were headed for the bin. They took apart the strong spokes and the cloth. From the spokes they made small garden stakes. From the cloth they made bird scarers. So the umbrellas found a new use in the garden, and the students learned that broken umbrellas can be reused in clever ways.
payload.title: Broken umbrellas can be reused in clever ways

payload.passage: Reva wanted to learn how to write with her left hand for fun. The letters came out shaky and backwards on her first try. She practised tracing simple shapes with her left hand each evening. Her control grew and the shaky letters turned neat and steady. Within a month Reva could write a whole sentence with either hand.
payload.title: Daily tracing taught Reva to write left-handed
decoys: Reva's left-hand letters came out backwards
Trying new things keeps the brain young and sharp
Reva could write with either hand at last

payload.passage: The school staircase grew dangerously crowded when the bell rang. Children pushed and a few small ones nearly tumbled down. The teachers made one staircase only for going up and one for coming down. The crowding eased as the children moved in one smooth direction. Now everyone walks the stairs safely without any pushing.
payload.title: Separate stairs solved the crowding danger
decoys: A few small children nearly tumbled down
Crowds are always dangerous in any building
The teachers split the staircase usage

payload.passage: Anaya's society used to throw away its garden trimmings and used tea leaves. Now they pile it all in a corner bin together with leaves and peels. Over weeks it slowly rots into dark, rich soil. The gardener spreads this soil on the flower beds, and the garden blooms. The society learned that garden waste can feed the garden itself.
payload.title: Garden waste can feed the garden itself
decoys: Tea leaves go into the corner bin

payload.passage: The students struggled to read the faded words in their old textbooks. The worn-out pages strained their eyes during lessons. The school replaced the most faded books with fresh new copies. The clear print made reading easy and pleasant again. The children read their lessons without squinting any more.
payload.title: New textbooks solved the faded-print problem
decoys: The worn pages strained the students' eyes
Good books are vital for proper learning
The school gave out fresh new copies

payload.passage: A spinning whisk of wires beats cream into froth. The loops of wire are turned round and round in the bowl. As they cut through the cream, they fold air into it again and again. The trapped air makes the cream grow thick and frothy. So a whisk froths cream by folding air into it with its spinning loops.
payload.title: How a whisk folds air to froth cream
decoys: The loops cut through the cream
The wires turn round the bowl

payload.passage: Aisha's society used to wash their cars with a running hose. The water splashed everywhere and a lot of it ran straight to waste. So they switched to using a bucket and a cloth instead. One bucket now cleans a whole car that the hose would have used many buckets for. Over the weeks the colony saved a great deal of water, and learned that a bucket saves a lot.
payload.title: Washing cars with a bucket saves water
decoys: One bucket cleans a whole car

payload.passage: A young oak tree grows from a single small acorn. A squirrel often buries acorns in the ground to eat later. Some are forgotten and left to rest through the cold winter. When spring comes, a buried acorn splits and sends up a tiny shoot. So a forgotten acorn can grow into a tall oak tree.
payload.title: How an acorn grows into an oak
decoys: A squirrel buries acorns to eat later
Trees grow from seeds in many ways
Oak trees give acorns to many animals

payload.passage: Vivek wondered why some clouds were flat and others piled up like towers. His teacher explained that flat, layered clouds spread out in calm, steady air and often bring light rain, while tall, puffy clouds grow where warm air rushes upward and can bring storms. The cloud's shape hints at the weather. Vivek learned that a cloud's shape can hint at the coming weather.
payload.title: A cloud's shape hints at coming weather
decoys: Some clouds piled up like towers
The sky is full of clouds
Vivek likes to watch the weather

payload.passage: Sneha tried to bake a cake all by herself for the first time. The first cake came out flat and the second one burned at the edges. She did not feel like baking again, but she read the recipe more carefully. On her third try she measured everything slowly and watched the oven closely. The cake rose softly and golden, and her family asked for a second slice.
payload.title: Careful reading helped Sneha bake a good cake
decoys: Sneha's first cake came out completely flat
Anyone can become a great cook with one recipe
Sneha's family enjoyed a second slice of cake

payload.passage: Reva placed two halves of an apple on a plate. She squeezed lemon juice over one half and left the other plain. After an hour the plain half had turned brown while the lemon half stayed pale and fresh. Her mother said the sour juice protects the cut fruit from the air. Reva learned that lemon juice keeps a cut apple from turning brown.
payload.title: Lemon juice keeps cut apple from browning
decoys: Fruit should be eaten while fresh
Reva used two halves of an apple

payload.passage: The school's craft scissors were always blunt and would not cut paper. Children tore their sheets and ruined their craftwork. The teacher had the scissors sharpened and counted them after each class. Sharp scissors made craftwork neat and the tearing stopped. The children enjoyed their craft lessons far more after that.
payload.title: Sharpening the scissors solved the torn craftwork
decoys: Children tore their sheets with blunt scissors
Craft lessons spark a child's imagination
The teacher had the scissors sharpened

payload.passage: A school bus helper looks after the children on the long ride. She stands at the door to help the little ones climb in safely. She makes sure each child sits down and stays in their seat. At each stop she sees that the right children get off. So a bus helper's work is to keep the children safe on the journey.
payload.title: How a bus helper keeps children safe
decoys: She helps the little ones climb in
Children should not stand in a moving bus

payload.passage: A drop of sap inside a tree can turn into hard, golden amber. Long ago, sticky sap oozed out of certain trees. Sometimes an insect got trapped in the sticky drop. Over millions of years the sap hardened into clear stone with the insect inside. So soft tree sap can slowly become solid amber.
payload.title: How tree sap becomes hard amber
decoys: An insect got trapped in the sticky sap
Nature changes things over long ages
Amber is polished to make jewellery

payload.passage: Nakul half-filled a balloon with water and put it in the freezer overnight. By morning the soft balloon had turned into a hard lump, and its skin felt stretched tight. He measured it and found the frozen ball was a little bigger than before. His teacher said water grows when it freezes into ice. Nakul learned that water takes up more room when it freezes.
payload.title: Water takes up more room when it freezes
decoys: The balloon turned into a hard lump

payload.passage: A grandfather clock keeps steady time with a long swinging weight called a pendulum. Each swing of the pendulum takes the very same amount of time. A little catch lets a toothed wheel move forward by one tooth on each swing. That wheel turns the gears that drive the hands. So a pendulum clock keeps time by counting its even swings.
payload.title: How a pendulum keeps a clock on time
decoys: Each swing takes the same time
Old clocks can be very tall
A catch moves a wheel one tooth

payload.passage: A whisk-broom and dustpan team up to clean a floor. You sweep the dust into a little pile with the soft bristles. Then you tilt the flat-edged dustpan against the floor near the pile. A few more sweeps push the dust up over the thin lip into the pan. So a dustpan and broom clear dust by sweeping it over a thin flat edge.
payload.title: How a broom and dustpan clear floor dust
decoys: The dustpan has a thin lip

payload.passage: Anvi's class adopted the dusty patch outside the school gate. First they cleared away all the rubbish that had piled up. Then they planted grass and flowers and put a low fence around it. Within months the bare patch became a small green corner. The class learned that a neglected patch can be turned into a pretty green spot.
payload.title: A neglected patch can become a green spot
decoys: The class cleared the rubbish first
Streets can look bare and dusty

payload.passage: A lotus grows in muddy ponds yet keeps itself clean and bright. Its roots sit in the dirty mud at the bottom of the water. Its long stem rises up until the flower opens above the surface. Its leaves have a waxy top so mud and water just roll off them. So a lotus stays clean and beautiful above the muddy water.
payload.title: How a lotus stays clean in muddy water
decoys: Waxy leaves let mud roll right off
Plants live in many kinds of places
The lotus is a much-loved flower in India

payload.passage: Rahul's home was often dark in the evenings because the bulb kept fusing. Doing homework in the dim light strained his eyes badly. His father studied the wiring and found a loose connection in the holder. He tightened it carefully and the flickering bulb stopped going out. Now Rahul does his homework in bright, steady light every night.
payload.title: Fixing the loose holder solved the flickering bulb
decoys: The dim light strained Rahul's eyes
Electrical faults can be dangerous in any house
Rahul's father studied the wiring carefully

payload.passage: Sumit kept missing the school announcements made over the speaker. The garbled, crackly sound was impossible to understand. The office had the old speaker replaced with a clear new one. Every announcement now came through loud and plain. Sumit never missed an important notice again after that.
payload.title: A new speaker solved the unclear announcements
decoys: The crackly sound was hard to understand
Clear notices keep a school well run
The office replaced the old speaker

payload.passage: A salmon makes one of the longest journeys of any fish. It is born in a cool river high in the hills. Then it swims all the way down to live for years in the wide sea. When it is grown, it swims back up the very same river to lay its eggs. So a salmon returns home to the river where it began.
payload.title: A salmon returns to its home river
decoys: A salmon is born in a cool hill river
Fish travel in many amazing ways
Bears like to catch leaping salmon

payload.passage: The school's lost-property pile grew into a huge mountain of unclaimed things. Children could not find their lost jackets and bottles in the heap. A teacher sorted the items and put up a list of what was found. Children checked the list and claimed their belongings easily. The mountain shrank as everyone got their things back.
payload.title: A found-items list solved the lost-property pile
decoys: Children could not find things in the heap
Schools collect a lot of forgotten belongings
A teacher put up a list of found items

payload.passage: Parth tried to learn the recorder for the school music period. His first notes were so shrill that even his dog ran away. He covered the holes carefully and blew softly instead of hard. Bit by bit the shrill sounds turned into a gentle, pleasant tune. By term-end Parth played a soft song that even his dog sat to hear.
payload.title: Blowing softly helped Parth play the recorder
decoys: Parth's first notes made his dog run away
Music can calm any animal in the house
Parth had a music period in his school

payload.passage: Mira and her father set out a bird feeder of seeds and watched which birds came. Tiny sparrows landed first and pecked quickly at the small seeds. Bigger crows tried but could not perch on the narrow ledge. Day after day only small birds fed there. Mira learned that a feeder's design decides which birds can use it.
payload.title: A feeder's design decides which birds feed there
decoys: Tiny sparrows landed first to peck

payload.passage: The teachers and students together started a no-litter rule in the school garden. Everyone now carries their wrappers to a bin, and a small team checks the garden each day. With no litter to clog it, the garden pond turned clear and the frogs returned to it. They learned that keeping a garden litter-free brings its small life back.
payload.title: A litter-free garden brings small life back
decoys: A team checks the garden each day
The school made a no-litter rule

payload.passage: A bottle opener lifts a metal cap with a clever lever. You hook its lip under the edge of the bottle cap. Then you press down on the long handle while the opener pushes up beneath the cap. The cap bends and pops off with very little effort. So a bottle opener pries off a cap by working as a lever.
payload.title: How a bottle opener pries off a cap
decoys: Its lip hooks under the cap edge
Bottles hold many kinds of drinks
The cap pops off with little effort

payload.passage: Meera blew up a balloon and rubbed it hard against her woollen sweater for a minute. Then she held the balloon close to tiny bits of torn paper on the table. The paper bits jumped up and clung to the balloon as if by magic. Her brother explained that rubbing fills the balloon with a hidden charge that pulls light things. Meera saw that static electricity can make a balloon grab paper.
payload.title: A rubbed balloon picks up paper with static
decoys: Meera rubbed the balloon on her sweater
Electricity is found all around us every day
Balloons can be blown up with a single breath

payload.passage: Anaya's group planted creepers and shady trees near the school water tank. The plants cover the tank and pipes from the harsh midday sun. Shaded from the heat, the stored water stays cooler. Because of this, much less of it dries away into the air. The group learned that shading water from the sun stops it drying away.
payload.title: Shading water from the sun stops it drying away
decoys: The midday sun is very hot

payload.passage: Mira's village had not seen rain for weeks, and the field was hard as stone. Her grandfather explained that when soil stays dry for too long, it loses all its softness. The dry ground splits into deep cracks that nothing can grow in. Even when rain finally comes, it runs off instead of soaking in. Mira learned that long dry weather makes the soil crack and harden.
payload.title: Long dry weather makes soil crack and harden
decoys: The field was hard as stone
Soil is important for growing food
Mira's village had not seen rain

payload.passage: Maitri planted the same flower in red clay soil in one pot and soft sandy soil in another. She watered both and watched over several weeks. The plant in the clay soil grew taller and greener than the one in the sandy soil. Her teacher said clay holds water and food better. Maitri learned that the kind of soil changes how well a plant grows.
payload.title: The kind of soil changes how a plant grows
decoys: Maitri used two kinds of soil

payload.passage: Geeta's class visited a fort gate covered in long iron spikes. She thought they were only for show, but the guide explained their real job. Long ago, enemies pushed huge elephants against gates to break them open, so the spikes were placed exactly at an elephant's head height to stop them. Geeta learned that even the sharp spikes were a clever part of the fort's defence.
payload.title: Spikes on a fort gate stopped elephants
decoys: The iron spikes were long and sharp
Geeta counted the spikes on the gate

payload.passage: Spring is the season when sleepy nature wakes up again. The cold of winter fades and the air turns mild and pleasant. Bare trees grow soft new leaves and gardens fill with bright flowers. Birds return and build their nests, and bees buzz busily from bloom to bloom. So spring is a time when fresh life appears all around us.
payload.title: Spring wakes up nature with new life
decoys: Bees buzz busily from one flower to the next
Every season has its own special weather
Many birds fly far away in the cold months

payload.passage: A bricklayer builds the walls of houses and shops. He spreads a layer of wet cement on the wall he is building. Then he lays bricks on top in neat, even rows. He checks that the wall stands straight and the bricks line up well. So a bricklayer's work is to raise the strong walls of buildings.
payload.title: How a bricklayer builds strong walls
decoys: He lays bricks in neat even rows
Many workers help build our town
Strong houses keep out wind and rain

payload.passage: Parth dropped a fizzy tablet into a glass of water and watched bubbles rush to the top. He tried it once in cold water and once in warm water, timing each with a clock. The tablet in warm water fizzed away much faster than the one in cold water. His teacher said warmth speeds up the bubbling. Parth learned that a fizzy tablet dissolves faster in warm water.
payload.title: A fizzy tablet dissolves faster in warm water
decoys: Parth timed each test with a clock
Water can dissolve many different things
Bubbles rose quickly to the top

payload.passage: Reyansh's colony faced a hard water shortage one dry season. Before, many small tankers came to each home, wasting fuel and time on the road. So the colony decided to share one big tanker for the whole lane instead. This meant fewer trips and water spread fairly among every family. The colony learned that sharing water fairly helps everyone through a shortage.
payload.title: Sharing water fairly helps everyone in a shortage
decoys: One tanker serves the whole lane

payload.passage: The children's drawings kept getting smudged before they dried in class. They touched them too soon and spoilt all the bright colours. The teacher made a drying rack with long wires for hanging the sheets. The drawings dried safely without anyone touching them. The colours stayed bright and the smudging stopped at once.
payload.title: A drying rack solved the smudged drawings
decoys: The bright colours got spoilt by touching
Children love drawing more than any subject
The teacher made a wire drying rack

payload.passage: The Compost Crew dealt with the school's wet kitchen waste. In the open bin it used to smell and draw many flies. Now they tip it into a covered compost pit instead. There it rots quietly into soil while the lid keeps smells and pests away. The crew learned that composting wet waste removes the smell and the pests.
payload.title: Composting wet waste removes smell and pests
decoys: The wet waste used to draw flies
Kitchens make a lot of waste
The crew uses a covered pit

payload.passage: A paper clip holds sheets without any glue. The thin wire is bent into two looping curves that press against each other. When you slide papers between the loops, the springy wire opens a touch. Its gentle squeeze then pinches the sheets and holds them. So a paper clip grips papers using the spring of its bent wire.
payload.title: How a bent wire makes a paper clip grip
decoys: The wire is bent into looping curves
Sliding papers in opens the loops

payload.passage: A storekeeper at a warehouse keeps track of many goods. Boxes of all kinds arrive and are stacked on tall shelves. He notes down what comes in and what goes out each day. When a shop needs goods, he finds them and sends them off. So a storekeeper's job is to keep the warehouse goods in order.
payload.title: How a storekeeper manages the warehouse
decoys: He notes what comes in and goes out
Shops order fresh stock every week

payload.passage: Ridhi watched a row of weaver ants pulling green leaves together high in a tree. Some ants held the leaf edges close while others joined them with sticky threads. Bit by bit a snug leaf nest took shape. Her teacher said the ants work as a team to build a home. Ridhi learned that weaver ants work together to build a leaf nest.
payload.title: Weaver ants work together to build a nest
decoys: Some ants held the leaf edges close
The nest was high in a tree

payload.passage: Kunal placed a magnet near a heap of mixed sand and tiny iron filings. He moved the magnet slowly across the heap without touching it. The iron bits jumped up and stuck to the magnet, leaving the clean sand behind. His teacher said a magnet pulls iron but not sand. Kunal learned that a magnet can separate iron from a mixture.
payload.title: A magnet can separate iron from a mixture
decoys: The iron bits jumped to the magnet
Mixtures can be split in many ways
Sand is made of tiny grains

payload.passage: A hot plate cooks food with a glowing coil beneath it. Power flows into a flat coil of special wire inside the plate. The wire fights the power and grows red-hot from it. That heat passes up through the plate into the pot and the food. So a hot plate cooks by heating a coil that warms the pot above.
payload.title: How a glowing coil heats a cooking plate
decoys: Power flows into a flat coil

payload.passage: Diya's group looked at how the school used plastic folders and files. They saw that new ones were bought every June. So they asked everyone to bring back their folders at the year's end. The next class then used them again. Hundreds of folders were reused, and the group learned that passing on old folders saves money and plastic.
payload.title: Passing on old folders saves money and plastic
decoys: Folders are returned at year's end

payload.passage: During a storm, Vihaan saw white balls of ice bounce off the road, even though it was not very cold. His teacher explained that strong winds inside a tall storm cloud toss raindrops high, where they freeze into ice. The wind keeps tossing them up until they grow heavy and fall as hail. Vihaan learned that hail forms when raindrops freeze high inside a storm.
payload.title: Hail forms when raindrops freeze in a storm
decoys: The white ice bounced off the road
Storms bring all kinds of weather
Vihaan watched the storm from the porch

payload.passage: Vanya soaked a hard dry sponge in a bowl of water and watched it swell. The flat thin sponge puffed up fat and soft as it drank the water. When she squeezed it, the water ran back out and it shrank again. Her teacher said the sponge has tiny holes that hold water. Vanya learned that a sponge soaks up water in its many tiny holes.
payload.title: A sponge soaks up water in its tiny holes
decoys: The sponge puffed up as it drank
Vanya squeezed the water back out

payload.passage: A pencil sharpener gives a pencil its point with a small slanted blade. When you push the pencil in and twist it, the wood turns against the fixed sharp edge. The blade shaves off a thin curling ribbon of wood with every turn. As more wood is peeled away, the soft lead in the centre is left standing out. So twisting the pencil against the blade slowly carves a sharp tip.
payload.title: How a sharpener carves a point on a pencil
decoys: The blade shaves off a curling ribbon
Pencils are used for writing and drawing
A sharpener has one small slanted blade

payload.passage: Kiara's family began buying loose vegetables and grains from the market. They stopped buying the packed ones wrapped in layers of plastic. To carry the loose goods home, they take their own steel boxes and cloth bags. Over time, far less packaging waste came into the house each week. The family learned that buying loose goods cuts down on packaging waste.
payload.title: Buying loose goods cuts packaging waste
decoys: Kiara's family changed how they shop

payload.passage: The colony set up a shared toolbox and a ladder for everyone to borrow. Before this, each home bought its own and rarely used them. Now neighbours borrow what they need for a day or two and return it. So fewer things are bought and left to gather dust. The colony learned that sharing tools means buying and wasting less.
payload.title: Sharing tools means buying and wasting less
decoys: Tools are useful for many jobs

payload.passage: Avantika put a slice of potato in plain water and another slice in very salty water for a few hours. The slice in plain water grew firm and crisp, while the salty-water slice turned limp and floppy. Her teacher said salty water pulls water out of the potato. Avantika learned that salty water makes a potato slice go limp.
payload.title: Salty water makes a potato slice go limp

payload.passage: A clay-pot cooler chills milk on a hot day. The rough clay pot is stood in a tray of water in a shady spot. Water creeps up the pot's walls and into the air around it. As it dries off, it carries heat away and cools the pot and milk. So a clay cooler keeps milk cold by letting water dry off its sides.
payload.title: How drying water cools milk in a clay pot
decoys: Water creeps up the pot walls
The pot stands in a water tray

payload.passage: On the class trip to the old stone fort, Ira learned that its high, thick walls were not built only to look grand. The guide explained that the walls kept enemies out, while narrow slits let guards watch the road and shoot arrows safely. A wide moat of water around the fort made it even harder to attack. By the end, Ira saw that almost every part of the fort was planned to protect the people inside.
payload.title: An old fort was built to protect people
decoys: A wide moat of water surrounded the old fort
Old buildings can be fun places to explore
The guide knew many facts about the fort

payload.passage: Aarav's group started a swap shelf in the school library. Children leave books, toys and games they no longer want on the shelf. In return they take home something another child has left behind. Nothing is bought or thrown away, yet everyone goes home with something new to them. The group learned that swapping old things gives them a happy second life.
payload.title: Swapping old things gives them a second life
decoys: Children leave books on the shelf

payload.passage: At home, the family fought over which channel to watch each evening. The shouting spoiled the relaxing hour after a long day. Mother made a simple chart so each person chose on a different night. Everyone now waited happily for their special viewing day. The peaceful evenings brought the whole family closer together.
payload.title: A viewing chart ended the channel fights
decoys: The shouting spoiled the relaxing hour
Watching together is good for any family
Mother made a chart for choosing nights

payload.passage: Aarav had always been afraid of speaking in front of the class. His voice shook and his hands turned cold whenever the teacher called his name. To beat this fear he began reading aloud to his pet dog every night. Bit by bit his voice grew steady, because the dog never laughed at him. When his turn came at the school assembly, Aarav spoke clearly and stood tall.
payload.title: Practice at home cured Aarav's stage fear
decoys: Aarav's hands turned cold during his turn
Every fear in life can be beaten by trying
Aarav read stories aloud to his pet dog

payload.passage: A tide pool is a small world left behind when the sea draws back. Twice a day the sea rises and covers the rocky shore. When it falls again, water stays trapped in dips among the rocks. Crabs, snails, and tiny fish live and hide in these little pools. So a tide pool is a tiny home shaped by the moving sea.
payload.title: How the sea shapes a tide pool
decoys: Crabs and snails hide in tide pools
The sea makes many interesting places
The tide rises and falls twice a day

payload.passage: A hot air balloon rises into the sky on warm air alone. A burner below heats the air inside the huge cloth bag. Warm air is lighter than the cool air outside, so it lifts the whole balloon. To come down, the pilot lets the air cool or opens a vent at the top. So a hot air balloon floats up because warm air inside lifts it.
payload.title: How warm air lifts a hot air balloon
decoys: A burner heats the air inside
Balloons can be many bright colours
Warm air is lighter than cool air

payload.passage: Aryan's family used to do many small washes of clothes through the week. Each wash used water and power of its own. So they changed to washing one full load at a time. One big wash uses far less than several small ones. Over time the savings grew, and the family learned that washing full loads saves water and power.
payload.title: Washing full loads saves water and power
decoys: One big wash replaces many small ones

payload.passage: A coral reef builds a calm, shallow lagoon behind it. The reef grows up like a wall against the open sea. It breaks the force of the big rolling waves. Behind the reef the water stays calm, warm, and shallow. So a reef shelters a quiet lagoon from the rough sea.
payload.title: How a reef shelters a calm lagoon
decoys: The reef breaks the force of the waves
The sea shapes the coast in many ways
Many fish swim in the calm lagoon

payload.passage: Misha held a thin sheet of paper over a comb and hummed a tune against it. The paper buzzed against her lips and made her voice sound funny and rough. When she hummed louder the buzzing grew stronger, and when she stopped it died away. Her teacher said her voice was shaking the thin paper very fast. Misha learned that a voice can make a thin paper buzz and change its sound.
payload.title: A voice can make thin paper buzz
decoys: The paper buzzed when she hummed
Sounds can be made many ways
Misha held paper over a comb

payload.passage: Ishita's colony planted trees and bushes along the noisy, dusty main road. Year by year the green wall grew thick and tall. The leaves trapped the dust before it reached the homes. They also softened the loud traffic noise. So the lane behind grew calmer and cleaner, and the colony learned that a wall of trees can shield homes from dust and noise.
payload.title: A wall of trees blocks dust and noise
decoys: The trees grew along the main road
Roads can be busy and noisy

payload.passage: The seasons change because the Earth is tilted as it circles the sun. For part of the year, one half of the Earth leans towards the sun. That half gets longer days and warmer weather, giving it summer. Months later it leans away, the days grow short, and winter arrives. So the Earth's tilt is the real reason we have seasons.
payload.title: The Earth's tilt gives us the seasons
decoys: One half of the Earth leans towards the sun
Our planet does many amazing things
Summer days feel longer than winter days

payload.passage: Myra noticed that the air felt sticky and heavy just before the monsoon rain. Her mother explained that warm air can hold a lot of invisible water vapour, and before a storm the air is packed full of it, which is why our skin feels damp and sweat does not dry. This dampness in the air is called humidity. Myra learned that humid air is full of invisible water vapour.
payload.title: Humid air is full of invisible water vapour
decoys: The air felt sticky before the rain
Myra felt the dampness on her skin

payload.passage: A river island slowly grows in the middle of a wide, slow river. As the river flows, it drops bits of sand and mud where the water is calm. These bits pile up little by little above the water. Grass and trees take root and hold the new land together. So a quiet river can build up its own small island.
payload.title: How a river builds a small island
decoys: Grass and trees root in the new land
Rivers shape the land in many ways

payload.passage: The Eco Club ran a fix-it day at the school. Children brought their broken toys, torn bags and loose chairs from home. Volunteers showed them how to glue, stitch and screw the things back together. Many items that were headed for the bin were saved instead. The club learned that mending broken things keeps them out of the dump.
payload.title: Mending broken things keeps them out of the dump
decoys: Children brought torn bags to mend
The Eco Club ran a fix-it day

payload.passage: Mishti rolled a ball of clay into a tight lump and dropped it into a bowl of water, and it sank at once. Then she flattened the same clay into a wide boat shape and floated it gently on the water. This time the clay boat stayed on top and even carried a coin. Her father said the shape pushed away more water. Mishti learned that shape can make heavy clay float.
payload.title: Shape can make heavy clay float
decoys: The clay lump sank at once
Clay can be moulded into shapes
Mishti floated a coin on the boat

payload.passage: A house help makes daily life easier for a busy family. She comes each day to clean the rooms and wash the dishes. She sweeps and mops the floors until they shine. She also helps with the washing so the home stays neat. So a house help's work is to keep the home clean and tidy.
payload.title: How a house help keeps a home tidy
decoys: She sweeps and mops the floors
Many helpers make our lives easier
A clean home is a healthy home

payload.passage: Roshni wanted to learn how to make soft chapatis that puffed up nicely. Her early ones came out hard, flat, and shaped like maps. She kneaded the dough longer and rolled each one into a round circle. Slowly her chapatis began to puff up like little balloons on the pan. Her father praised the soft, round chapatis at dinner that night.
payload.title: Patient kneading taught Roshni to make soft chapatis
decoys: Roshni's early chapatis came out hard and flat
Cooking warm food makes any family happy
Roshni's father praised her at dinner

payload.passage: A see-through kaleidoscope makes pretty patterns from a few beads. Inside the tube sit three long mirrors set in a triangle. A few loose beads lie at the end near a small window. When you look through and turn it, the mirrors reflect the beads many times. So a kaleidoscope turns a few beads into a pattern using mirrors.
payload.title: How mirrors make kaleidoscope patterns
decoys: Three mirrors sit in a triangle
Patterns are pleasing to look at
Loose beads lie at the end

payload.passage: A simple lift, or pulley, raises a bucket up a well with a rope over a wheel. The rope runs across a grooved wheel fixed at the top. When you pull one end down, the other end rises and lifts the bucket. The wheel lets the rope slide smoothly and changes the pull's direction. So a pulley lets you lift a load up by pulling the rope down.
payload.title: How a pulley lifts a bucket up a well
decoys: The rope runs over a grooved wheel
Pulling one end raises the other

payload.passage: Kabir poured a thin layer of cooking oil over a small bowl of water and watched it spread. The oil did not sink or mix but sat in a shiny film on the very top. However hard he stirred, it always rose back to the surface. His father said oil is lighter than water and will not blend with it. Kabir learned that oil floats on water and will not mix in.
payload.title: Oil floats on water and will not mix
decoys: The oil rose back to the surface
Oil is used in many dishes
Kabir poured oil over the water

payload.passage: A desert can burst into bloom after a rare and heavy rain. For most of the year the sandy ground looks dry and bare. Tiny seeds wait quietly in the soil for water to come. When a big rain finally falls, the seeds sprout and flower very fast. So a single rain can turn a bare desert into a field of flowers.
payload.title: How rain makes a desert bloom
decoys: Tiny seeds wait in the dry soil
Rain brings change to many places
Deserts feel very hot in the daytime

payload.passage: Sia hung a thick blanket of cotton wool over one half of a tray of ice cubes and left the other half open. After an hour she checked both halves. The covered ice cubes were still hard, while the open ones had melted into water. Her father said the cotton kept the warm room air away. Sia learned that a cover can keep ice from melting quickly.
payload.title: A cover keeps ice from melting quickly
decoys: The open ice cubes melted into water
Ice does not last in warm rooms
Sia used a tray of ice cubes

payload.passage: The classroom corner leaked rainwater that wet the children's bags. Their books got damp and the floor turned into a puddle. A worker climbed up and sealed the crack in the ceiling above. The leak stopped and the corner stayed dry in the rains. The children kept their bags there safely once more.
payload.title: Sealing the ceiling crack solved the leaking corner
decoys: Leaks cause damage in many old buildings
A worker sealed the crack in the ceiling

payload.passage: A pressure cooker cooks food fast by trapping steam inside. Its lid seals tightly so almost no steam can escape. As the water boils, the trapped steam builds up and pushes harder on the food, so it cooks at a higher heat than usual. A small weight on top lets out any extra steam safely. So a pressure cooker speeds up cooking by trapping hot steam.
payload.title: How a pressure cooker cooks food faster
decoys: A small weight lets out extra steam
The lid seals tightly on top

payload.passage: Dhruv wanted to learn how to whistle through two fingers loudly. For days only a weak puff of air slipped out between them. He kept adjusting his fingers and tongue while watching a clip. Suddenly a sharp, loud whistle burst out and startled his cat. After that Dhruv could call his friends from across the whole playground.
payload.title: Patient adjusting taught Dhruv to finger-whistle
decoys: Only a weak puff slipped out at first
A loud whistle can call anyone from far away
Dhruv startled his cat with the whistle

payload.passage: Saanvi's class learned about the thin blanket of air around the earth. It keeps us warm and lets every living thing breathe. But smoke and harmful fumes slowly dirty this precious air. So the class chose to walk more, plant trees and burn nothing at all. They learned that we must all work together to keep the earth's air clean.
payload.title: We must keep the earth's air clean
decoys: A blanket of air surrounds the earth

payload.passage: On the trip to the ancient caves, Priya saw rooms cut straight into a hill of solid rock. The guide explained that people long ago had no machines, so they chipped away the stone slowly with hand tools for many years. The smooth walls and pillars were all carved from the hill itself. Priya was amazed that such huge halls were made by patient hands and simple tools alone.
payload.title: Ancient caves were carved by patient hands
decoys: The cave walls had been rubbed smooth
People in the past made many great things
Priya found the caves cool and a little dark

payload.passage: A dairy worker turns fresh milk into many other foods. At the dairy he receives milk brought in from the farms. He checks that it is clean and cools it to keep it fresh. He then helps turn some of it into curd, butter, and cheese. So a dairy worker's job is to handle milk and make milk foods.
payload.title: How a dairy worker handles fresh milk
decoys: He turns some milk into curd and butter
Many helpers work to feed us
Milk is rich in goodness for bones

payload.passage: A water clock drips time away drop by drop. A container has a tiny hole in the bottom that lets water out slowly. Marks on the inside show how far the water has dropped over time. As the level falls past each mark, more time has passed. So a water clock measures time by water dripping out at a steady rate.
payload.title: How dripping water measures time in a clock
decoys: A tiny hole sits in the bottom

payload.passage: A blacksmith shapes hard metal into useful tools. He heats a piece of iron in his fire until it glows red and soft. Then he beats it with a hammer on his heavy anvil into shape. He makes things like spades, knives, and gate hinges. So a blacksmith's work is to forge metal into helpful tools.
payload.title: How a blacksmith shapes metal tools
decoys: He heats the iron until it glows red
Many skilled helpers serve our town
Iron tools last for many years

payload.passage: Dhruv wanted to catch some rain and measure it, so he cut the top off a clear bottle and marked lines along its side. He stood his homemade gauge in the open garden before the evening showers came. The next morning the water had risen to the second line he had drawn. He wrote the reading in a notebook to compare with other days. Dhruv learned that a simple bottle can measure how much rain falls.
payload.title: A bottle gauge measures how much rain falls
decoys: The water rose to the second marked line
Rain is very important for farms and rivers
Dhruv wrote his readings in a notebook

payload.passage: A drinking straw with a bend lets you sip lying back. The bend is a set of ridges that lets the top part tilt freely. You point the mouth end towards you while the cup stays upright. As you suck, the drink rises up the straw past the bend. So a bendy straw lets you sip from any angle through its flexible joint.
payload.title: How a bendy straw lets you sip at angles
decoys: Ridges let the top part tilt
Drinks are nicer through a straw
The cup stays upright as you sip

payload.passage: Tara kept forgetting her lunch box on the kitchen table at home. By midday she was hungry and could not focus in class. She began keeping her lunch box right on top of her school bag. Picking up the bag meant picking up the lunch too. Tara never went hungry at school again after that simple change.
payload.title: Lunch on the bag solved Tara's forgotten meals
decoys: Tara was hungry and could not focus
A good lunch is vital for every growing child
Tara kept her lunch box on her bag

payload.passage: A young plant uses sunlight to make its own food in its green leaves. The leaves take in sunlight, air, and water from the roots. Inside the leaf these are turned into a kind of sugar the plant can use. This food helps the plant build new stems, leaves, and flowers. So green leaves are like little kitchens that feed the whole plant.
payload.title: How green leaves make food for a plant
decoys: Leaves take in sunlight, air, and water
Tall plants give cool shade in summer

payload.passage: Hansa filled a clear bottle with water and stood it on a sunny windowsill near a wall. The curved bottle of water threw a brighter, bigger circle of light onto the wall behind it. When she looked through it, far things appeared larger. Her brother said the water bent the light like a lens. Hansa learned that a bottle of water can bend light like a magnifier.
payload.title: A water bottle can bend light like a lens
decoys: Far things looked larger through the bottle
Light does many useful things for us
Hansa stood the bottle on a windowsill

payload.passage: Aanya's family used to leave the tap running while brushing teeth or washing dishes. A lot of clean water simply ran away. Now they turn the tap off between rinses and open it only when needed. Over a month, the whole family used far less water without any trouble. The family learned that turning off the tap between uses saves plenty of water.
payload.title: Turning off the tap between uses saves water
decoys: They turn the tap off between rinses
Water is used many times a day

payload.passage: Aryan's colony set aside a small patch of wild grass and bushes in one corner. They chose not to mow or tidy it at all, leaving it to grow on its own. Soon butterflies, bees and small birds came there to feed and to nest among the leaves. The patch needs no water or care from anyone. The colony learned that leaving a wild patch gives small creatures a safe home.
payload.title: Leaving a wild patch gives creatures a home
decoys: Butterflies came to the wild patch

payload.passage: Gauri wanted to clean a dirty old coin without scrubbing. She soaked it overnight in a small cup of vinegar and salt. In the morning the coin came out far brighter and cleaner than before. Her grandfather said the sour vinegar had eaten away the dull layer. Gauri learned that vinegar can clean the grime off an old coin.
payload.title: Vinegar cleans the grime off an old coin
decoys: Old things can be made to look new
Coins are made of shiny metal

payload.passage: A spinning coin top is made from a coin and a matchstick. You push the stick through a hole in the centre of the coin. When you twist the stick and let go, the coin spins fast on its tip. The spin keeps it upright until it slows and topples. So a coin-and-stick top spins upright while it turns fast.
payload.title: How a coin-and-stick top spins upright
decoys: The stick goes through the coin's centre

payload.passage: The colony children noticed that paper, peels and plastic were all dumped together. Mixed up like that, nothing could be reused. So they taught every home to keep wet and dry waste apart in two bins. From then on, sorting was simple and more waste was recycled. The children learned that separating waste at home makes recycling work.
payload.title: Separating waste at home makes recycling work
decoys: Wet and dry waste are kept apart

payload.passage: A traffic warden helps children cross the road safely outside school. He stands at the busy crossing wearing a bright jacket. When children gather, he holds up his sign to stop the cars. Then he walks the children across to the other side safely. So a traffic warden's job is to help children cross the road.
payload.title: How a traffic warden helps children cross
decoys: He holds up his sign to stop the cars
Bright jackets are easy to see

payload.passage: On the visit to the old mint, Tanvi watched how coins were once made. The guide showed heavy metal stamps that workers pressed onto blank discs to print a king's face and words. Every coin had to be the same weight so people could trust it. Tanvi understood that the mint showed the careful way trusted coins were once made by hand.
payload.title: An old mint made coins people could trust
decoys: Workers stamped a king's face on the discs
Money is used by people everywhere
Tanvi liked the clinking sound of the coins

payload.passage: A drop of melted snow high in the Himalayas feeds great rivers. When the summer sun warms the mountain snow, some of it melts. The melted water trickles down and joins to form mountain streams. These streams grow into mighty rivers like the Ganga that flow far across the plains. So melting mountain snow keeps many big rivers full.
payload.title: How melting snow feeds the big rivers
decoys: Summer sun melts the mountain snow
Water moves around the land in many ways
Many people live along the Ganga's banks

payload.passage: A rolling log moves a heavy box across the floor. You set round logs under the box and push it forward. As the box rolls along, the logs turn under it like wheels. You keep moving the logs from back to front as it goes. So round logs let you roll a heavy box along instead of dragging it.
payload.title: How rolling logs move a heavy box
decoys: The logs turn under the box
Heavy boxes are hard to drag
You move logs from back to front

payload.passage: Vihaan's family set up a small drip system for their balcony plants. Thin pipes carry water drop by drop right to each plant's roots. Almost no water is lost compared with pouring it from a can. The plants thrive happily on far less water than before. The family learned that drip watering gives plants water without any waste.
payload.title: Drip watering gives plants water without waste
decoys: Water drops slowly at each root

payload.passage: A geared egg-timer rings out after a set number of minutes. You twist the top to wind a spring and choose how many minutes. Inside, a set of gears lets the spring slowly unwind tooth by tooth. When the set time runs out, a little bell rings to tell you. So a wind-up egg-timer counts down minutes and rings at the end.
payload.title: How a wind-up timer counts down minutes
decoys: A little bell rings at the end
You twist the top to wind it

payload.passage: Saira kept missing her bus because she dressed too slowly in the mornings. She dawdled over each button and ran late every day. She began laying out her full uniform the night before. Dressing took half the time with everything ready and waiting. Saira caught her bus with minutes to spare from then on.
payload.title: Laying out clothes solved Saira's slow mornings
decoys: Planning the night before helps everyone
Saira laid out her full uniform

payload.passage: A peacock changes its look completely when it wants to dance. Most of the time it folds its long tail feathers behind it. But when it shows off, it lifts and spreads them into a huge fan. The fan shines with blue and green eye-shaped spots in the sunlight. So a peacock turns its plain tail into a bright shimmering fan.
payload.title: A peacock spreads its tail into a fan
decoys: The fan shows blue and green eye-shaped spots
The peacock is the national bird of India

payload.passage: A oil lamp gives a steady light from a soaked wick. Oil is poured into the bowl at the bottom of the lamp. A cloth wick dips into the oil and slowly drinks it up to the top. The flame at the tip burns this oil as fast as the wick brings more. So an oil lamp burns steadily as its wick draws up oil to the flame.
payload.title: How a wick feeds oil to a lamp flame
decoys: Oil is poured into the bottom bowl
The wick dips into the oil

payload.passage: The classroom fan made a loud rattle that disturbed the lessons. Children covered their ears and could barely hear the teacher. The teacher reported it to the office, and a worker came to check. He tightened the loose blades and oiled the squeaky motor. The fan now spins quietly, and the class listens to lessons in peace.
payload.title: Repairing the fan brought quiet back to class
decoys: Children covered their ears in class
A worker tightened the loose fan blades

payload.passage: The guide led Harini's class to a fort with rows of round holes high in its walls. Harini guessed they were windows, but the guide explained they were built to pour hot oil or shoot arrows down on anyone trying to climb the wall. Their angle let guards aim straight below. Harini learned that even the small holes were part of the fort's defence.
payload.title: Holes in a fort wall helped its defence
decoys: The holes were placed high in the walls
Harini peered through one of the holes

payload.passage: Tiya wanted to know if sound can be felt. She rested her fingers lightly on a drum skin and asked her brother to bang it. Each beat made her fingertips buzz and tingle. When the drum fell silent, the buzzing stopped at once. Tiya learned that sound is a shaking that we can feel as well as hear.
payload.title: Sound is a shaking we can feel and hear
decoys: Tiya rested her fingers on the drum
Her brother banged the drum hard

payload.passage: A petrol pump worker fills fuel into vehicles all day. When a car or bike stops at the pump, he greets the driver. He asks how much fuel they want and fills the tank carefully. He then tells the cost and takes the money for it. So a pump worker's job is to fill vehicles with fuel safely.
payload.title: How a pump worker fills vehicles with fuel
decoys: Vehicles must switch off the engine at the pump

payload.passage: A clay water pot keeps drinking water cool in summer. The pot has tiny holes all through its baked clay walls. A little water seeps out through these holes to the outside. As that water dries in the air, it draws heat from the pot and the water within. So a clay pot cools its water by letting a little seep out and dry.
payload.title: How a clay pot keeps its water cool
decoys: Tiny holes run through the clay
Cool water is welcome in summer
Water seeps out to the outside

payload.passage: A silkworm makes a thread that people have prized for ages. After eating mulberry leaves, the fat caterpillar gets ready to change. It spins a single long silk thread around itself into a smooth cocoon. Inside the cocoon it slowly turns into a moth. So a humble silkworm spins the silk that we weave into cloth.
payload.title: How a silkworm spins silk thread
decoys: The silkworm spins a cocoon around itself
Silk cloth feels smooth and looks fine

payload.passage: At home, the family kept bumping into the dark hallway at night. Without a light, someone always stubbed a toe in the gloom. Father fixed a small night light that glowed softly in the hall. The gentle glow showed the way without waking anyone. The painful toe-stubbing in the dark stopped at once.
payload.title: A night light solved the dark hallway bumps
decoys: Someone always stubbed a toe in the gloom
A well-lit home keeps a family safe
Father fixed a soft night light

payload.passage: A school crossing helper guides children across the road at home time. When the bell rings, many children rush towards the gate. He stands in the road and signals the traffic to stop. Then he leads the children safely to the other side in small groups. So a crossing helper's job is to take the children safely across the road.
payload.title: How a crossing helper guides children home
decoys: He leads the children in small groups
Children should look both ways too

payload.passage: Reyansh's class made a rule to print only when something is truly needed. Instead of many copies, they now share one copy among a whole group. They also fixed the printer to use both sides of every sheet. Far less paper and ink were used after that change. The class learned that printing less and sharing copies saves a lot of paper.
payload.title: Printing less and sharing copies saves paper
decoys: The printer now uses both sides

payload.passage: A pilot flies an aeroplane carrying many people to far places. Before the flight he checks the plane and reads the weather. He guides the plane safely up into the sky and along its path. He talks to the control tower and lands the plane gently at the end. So a pilot's job is to fly passengers safely to their destination.
payload.title: How a pilot flies passengers safely
decoys: He talks to the control tower
Many skilled helpers carry us about
Aeroplanes fly high above the clouds

payload.passage: A watchman keeps a building and its people safe through the night. He sits near the gate and checks everyone who comes and goes. He walks around the grounds to make sure all doors are locked. If he sees anything wrong, he raises an alarm at once. So a watchman's main job is to guard the building day and night.
payload.title: How a watchman guards a building
decoys: He checks everyone who comes and goes
Many helpers keep our area safe
Some buildings have cameras as well

payload.passage: The sky changes its colours each day at sunrise and sunset. During the day the sun is high and the sky looks blue. As the sun drops low, its light travels through more air to reach us. This scatters the light and paints the sky orange, pink, and red. So the low sun gives the sky its evening colours.
payload.title: Why the evening sky turns orange and red
decoys: The low sun's light travels through more air
The sky shows many beautiful sights
People love to watch the sunset together

payload.passage: A matchstick bursts into flame the moment it is struck. Its small tip is coated with special chemicals that catch fire very easily. When you drag it quickly across the rough side of the box, the rubbing makes a little heat. That small bit of heat is enough to set the chemical tip alight at once. So a match lights because friction heats the chemicals on its tip.
payload.title: How friction lights a struck matchstick
decoys: The tip is coated with chemicals
Fire must be used with care
Dragging it makes a little heat

payload.passage: Sneha saw fat raindrops splash down while the sun still shone brightly. Her mother explained that sometimes a small rain cloud drifts overhead and drops its rain, even though the sky around it stays clear and sunny. The rain and sunshine happen in the same place at once. Sneha learned that rain can fall even while the sun is shining.
payload.title: Rain can fall while the sun is shining
decoys: Fat raindrops splashed on the ground
Sneha was outside when it happened

payload.passage: Aanya's group spread the word that wasting food also wastes much more. Growing food uses water, soil and a lot of hard work. So they asked everyone to take only what they would eat and to save any leftovers for later. Less food was thrown away each day after that. The group learned that wasting less food saves the earth's resources too.
payload.title: Wasting less food saves the earth's resources
decoys: Growing food uses water and soil

payload.passage: A bicycle reflector glows in a car's headlights at night. The red plastic disc is moulded with many tiny mirror-like corners. When light hits these corners, they bounce it straight back the way it came. So a driver sees a bright red glow even though the reflector makes no light of its own. So a reflector shines by bouncing a car's light right back.
payload.title: How a reflector bounces car light back
decoys: The disc has tiny mirror corners
Roads can be dark at night
The reflector makes no light itself

payload.passage: Aahana stood a candle at one end of a table and held a book upright a little way in front of it. Behind the book a clear dark shadow fell on the wall. When she moved the book closer to the candle, the shadow grew much bigger. Her teacher said a closer object blocks more light. Aahana learned that a shadow grows larger as an object nears the light.
payload.title: A shadow grows larger nearer the light
decoys: Aahana held a book in front of the candle
The shadow fell on the wall

payload.passage: A measuring jug shows how much liquid is inside. Lines are marked up the see-through side from bottom to top. As you pour liquid in, it fills up to one of these marks. You read the line the liquid reaches to find the amount. So a measuring jug tells how much liquid it holds by marked lines on its side.
payload.title: How a measuring jug shows the amount inside
decoys: Lines are marked up the side
Liquid fills up to a mark

payload.passage: Naveen tried to learn skating but the wheels made his legs slide everywhere. He fell so often that his knees were always dusty after practice. He borrowed knee pads and a helmet so the falls would not scare him. Free from worry, he glided a little further each evening on the smooth path. Soon Naveen was skating past the park with his arms out like wings.
payload.title: Safety gear gave Naveen courage to skate
decoys: Naveen's knees were always dusty after falls
Skating is the fastest way to travel anywhere
Naveen borrowed knee pads and a helmet

payload.passage: A bridge worker helps build the bridges that cross our rivers. His team sinks strong pillars deep into the riverbed. They lay heavy beams across the pillars to form the deck. Then they fix the road and railings so people can cross safely. So a bridge worker's job is to build safe ways across the water.
payload.title: How a bridge worker builds river crossings
decoys: They sink strong pillars into the riverbed
Many workers help build our country
Bridges save us a long walk around

payload.passage: A fan-shaped hand bellows pushes a strong puff of air at a fire. Two flat boards are joined by leather sides into a bag with a spout. When you pull the handles apart, air is drawn in through a flap. When you push them together, that air shoots out of the narrow spout. So a bellows blows air on a fire by squeezing it from a bag.
payload.title: How a bellows blows air onto a fire
decoys: Air is drawn in through a flap
Two boards join with leather sides

payload.passage: The school choir could never sing together because no one kept the beat. Some sang fast and others lagged, spoiling the song. The music teacher tapped a steady beat on a small drum. The singers matched the beat and their voices came together. The choir sounded lovely and won praise at the school show.
payload.title: A drum beat solved the choir's timing trouble
decoys: Some singers lagged and spoiled the song
Singing together is a joyful school activity
The teacher tapped a beat on a drum

payload.passage: Aniket wanted to learn how to do a forward roll without hurting himself. He kept landing crooked and rolling off to one side. His teacher showed him to tuck his head and push evenly with both hands. His rolls turned straight and smooth as he kept practising. By the end of the class Aniket rolled forward in a neat, straight line.
payload.title: Tucking his head taught Aniket the forward roll
decoys: Aniket kept rolling off to one side
Physical training keeps every child fit and strong
Aniket's teacher showed him the correct way

payload.passage: The school's drinking water tasted bad and children stopped using it. Many came to class thirsty and tired by midday. The principal had a clean filter fitted on the main water tank. The water turned clear and fresh, and children drank it gladly. Tiredness from thirst faded and the class felt more active.
payload.title: A water filter solved the bad-tasting water
decoys: Children came to class thirsty and tired
Clean water is the right of every person
The principal fitted a filter on the tank

payload.passage: Tara's group planted hardy native plants in the school garden. They left out the fancy ones that need lots of water. The native plants are used to the local weather, so they grow well with little watering. The garden stays green using far less water than before. The group learned that local plants need much less water to grow.
payload.title: Local plants need much less water to grow
decoys: The native plants grow with little water

payload.passage: A mixer tap blends hot and cold water from one spout. Two pipes feed in, one warm and one cool, behind the tap. When you turn the handle, it opens both a little and lets them join. The two streams mix together before they reach the spout. So a mixer tap gives warm water by blending hot and cold inside it.
payload.title: How a mixer tap blends hot and cold water
decoys: Two pipes feed in behind the tap
Warm water is nice for washing
The handle opens both a little

payload.passage: Bread does not rise on its own; a tiny living helper called yeast does the work. When yeast is mixed into warm wet dough, it begins to feed on the sugars in the flour. As it feeds, it lets out lots of tiny gas bubbles all through the dough. These bubbles get trapped and slowly puff the dough up bigger and softer. So yeast is what makes bread dough rise into a fluffy loaf.
payload.title: How yeast makes bread dough rise
decoys: Yeast feeds on the sugars in the flour
Bread is a food eaten around the world
Dough is made from flour and water

payload.passage: A potter's wheel helps shape a pot from wet clay. The flat wheel spins round and round on a central post. A lump of soft clay is placed in the middle as it turns. With wet hands the potter presses and lifts the spinning clay into a smooth pot. So a potter's wheel shapes clay by spinning it under steady hands.
payload.title: How a spinning wheel shapes a clay pot
decoys: A lump of clay sits in the middle
The wheel spins on a central post

payload.passage: A young tree grows a new ring of wood inside its trunk every year. In the warm wet season it grows fast, making a wide pale ring. In the cold dry season it grows slowly, making a thin dark ring. If you cut a trunk, you can count these rings to learn its age. So a tree quietly records its years inside its own wood.
payload.title: Tree rings show how old a tree is
decoys: A tree makes a wide ring in the wet season
Trees are full of hidden secrets
Old trees give shade to many travellers

payload.passage: Garv wanted to lift a heavy book easily, so he slid a fat pencil under a ruler to make a lever. He pressed down on the long end of the ruler and the book rose up with little effort. When he moved the pencil closer to the book, lifting it became even easier. His teacher said a lever helps us move heavy things. Garv learned that a lever makes lifting a heavy load easier.
payload.title: A lever makes lifting a heavy load easier
decoys: Garv slid a pencil under the ruler
Tools help us with daily work
Books can be quite heavy to lift

payload.passage: Atharv set out a saucer of sugar water, one of salt water and one of plain water in the garden. He watched all morning to see which butterflies and bees chose. Both insects kept returning to the sugar water and ignored the rest. His teacher said sweet food gives them energy. Atharv learned that bees and butterflies prefer sweet water.
payload.title: Bees and butterflies prefer sweet water
decoys: The insects ignored the salt water

payload.passage: Saira balanced a ruler on a round pencil to make a tiny see-saw. She placed one coin on the left end and the same coin slid towards the middle on the right. When both coins sat at equal distances, the ruler stayed perfectly level. Her teacher said the see-saw balances when the weights and distances match. Saira learned that a see-saw balances when both sides are evenly matched.
payload.title: A see-saw balances when both sides match
decoys: Saira balanced the ruler on a pencil
Toys can teach us useful ideas
Coins are small and round objects

payload.passage: Tanya planted a climbing bean and pushed a thin stick into the pot beside it. Over a few days she watched the soft tip of the plant reach out and curl around the stick. Soon it had wound itself tightly up the support. Her teacher said climbing plants feel for something to hold. Tanya learned that a climbing plant wraps itself around a support to rise.
payload.title: A climbing plant wraps around a support
decoys: The plant curled around the stick
Tanya pushed a thin stick in the pot

payload.passage: Hriday spread some salt on a cube of ice and watched closely. A little dip melted into the ice right where the salt sat. He touched it and found the puddle felt even colder than plain melting ice. His teacher said salt makes ice melt at a colder point than usual. Hriday learned that salt helps ice melt and turn extra cold.
payload.title: Salt makes ice melt and turn extra cold
decoys: A dip melted where the salt sat
Ice is frozen water that can melt
Salt is used in cooking food
