payload.passage: Bhavna wanted to memorise a long poem for the recitation contest. The verses kept slipping out of her head no matter how often she read them. She wrote each line on a card and stuck the cards along her bedroom wall. Reading them as she walked past, she soon knew the poem by heart. On the contest day Bhavna recited every line without a single pause.
payload.title: Wall cards helped Bhavna memorise the poem
decoys: The verses kept slipping out of Bhavna's head
Poetry can sharpen the memory of any person
Bhavna took part in a recitation contest

payload.passage: The colony had a leaking pipe deep under the road that wasted water for months. No one could see it from above. The children noticed a damp patch that never dried and reported it. A plumber dug down, found the leak, and mended it. After that the colony's water lasted much longer, so they learned that finding hidden leaks saves a lot of water.
payload.title: Finding hidden leaks saves a lot of water
decoys: A plumber found the leaking pipe
The children spotted a damp patch

payload.passage: Tanvi placed a strong bar magnet under a sheet of paper and sprinkled iron filings on top. The little grey bits did not lie still but lined up in curving paths around the two ends. She tapped the paper gently and the pattern grew even neater. Her teacher said the filings were showing the hidden magnetic field around the magnet. Tanvi learned that a magnet has an invisible force that has a clear shape.
payload.title: Iron filings reveal a magnet's invisible field
decoys: The filings lined up around the two ends
Magnets are useful in many machines and toys
Tanvi used a sheet of paper on top

payload.passage: A straw oboe makes a buzzing note from a flat straw. You press one end of the straw flat and snip the corners to a point. When you blow hard, the flat tip flaps quickly and buzzes. Cutting the straw shorter makes the buzz go higher. So a flattened straw buzzes a note as its flapping tip shakes the air.
payload.title: How a flattened straw buzzes a note
decoys: A shorter straw gives a higher buzz
You snip the corners to a point

payload.passage: Bina wanted to play badminton without missing the shuttle each time. Her racquet swung at the air while the shuttle dropped past her. She practised gentle taps against a wall to learn the timing. Her eyes and hand slowly learned to meet the shuttle just right. Soon Bina could rally many shots back and forth with her brother.
payload.title: Wall taps improved Bina's badminton timing
decoys: Bina's racquet kept swinging at the air
Badminton is the most popular game everywhere
Bina rallied shots with her elder brother

payload.passage: Tejas wanted to know if cold slows a plant down. He kept one small plant on a warm shelf and put a twin plant in the cool, dim veranda. He watered both the same and watched for two weeks. The warm plant grew new leaves while the cool one barely changed. Tejas learned that plants grow more slowly in cold conditions.
payload.title: Plants grow more slowly when it is cold
decoys: The warm plant grew new leaves
Plants react to where they are kept
Tejas watered both plants the same

payload.passage: Samaira planted bean seeds in two pots and gave both the same water and the same sunlight each day. She fed one pot with a little compost every week and gave the other none at all. After a month the compost pot had bushier, greener plants with many more leaves. Her teacher said compost adds food to the soil. Samaira learned that compost makes plants grow bushier and greener.
payload.title: Compost makes plants grow bushier and greener
decoys: The compost pot had greener plants
Samaira used two pots of beans

payload.passage: A barber keeps people's hair neat and tidy. People come to his shop when their hair grows too long. He seats them in his chair and drapes a clean cloth around them. With scissors and comb he trims the hair into a neat shape. So a barber's work is to cut and style people's hair.
payload.title: How a barber cuts and styles hair
decoys: He drapes a clean cloth around the customer
Many helpers serve people each day
His shop gets busy before festivals

payload.passage: A vegetable seller brings fresh produce close to our homes. Early in the morning he buys crates of vegetables from the big market. He arranges them neatly on his cart in bright, tempting heaps. Then he pushes the cart through the lanes, calling out his goods. So a vegetable seller's work is to bring fresh food to our doorstep.
payload.title: How a vegetable seller brings fresh food
decoys: He arranges vegetables in neat heaps
Fresh vegetables keep us strong and healthy

payload.passage: Autumn is a season of slow change and rich colours. The hot summer fades and the air turns cool and crisp. Leaves on many trees turn yellow, orange, and red before they fall. Farmers gather the crops they planted earlier in the year. So autumn is a time of harvest and falling leaves.
payload.title: Autumn brings harvest and falling leaves
decoys: Leaves turn yellow, orange, and red in autumn
Every season looks different from the last
Cool air feels nice after a hot summer

payload.passage: Bhavya tipped a little powder paint into a glass of still water and did not stir it. Slowly the colour spread out on its own until the whole glass was evenly tinted. He found the same thing happened every time he tried. His teacher said tiny bits drift about and mix by themselves. Bhavya learned that colour spreads through still water all on its own.
payload.title: Colour spreads through still water on its own
decoys: The whole glass became evenly tinted
Bhavya did not stir the glass

payload.passage: Samaira spun a bucket with a little water in it round in a fast circle, with her arm going right over the top. To her surprise the water stayed in the bucket even upside down. When she slowed down, the water began to fall. Her teacher said fast spinning holds the water against the bottom. Samaira learned that fast spinning keeps water in an upturned bucket.
payload.title: Fast spinning keeps water in an upturned bucket
decoys: The water fell when she slowed down

payload.passage: At home, the family's morning tea always spilled on the crowded table. Plates, cups, and books left no room to set things down. Mother cleared the table fully before serving breakfast each day. With plenty of space, the cups sat safely and nothing spilled. The morning breakfast became calm and free of mess.
payload.title: Clearing the table solved the breakfast spills
decoys: Books left no room on the table
A peaceful breakfast sets up a good day
Mother cleared the table before serving

payload.passage: Dough rises in a warm spot more quickly than in a cold one. The tiny yeast in the dough works fastest when it is warm and fed. As the yeast feeds, it makes many gas bubbles trapped in the dough. These bubbles swell the dough until it has doubled in size. So warm yeast bubbles puff the dough up into a bigger lump.
payload.title: How warmth helps yeast puff up dough
decoys: Gas bubbles get trapped in the dough
Bread is baked in an oven

payload.passage: Aadya scattered some breadcrumbs near an ant hole and sat back to watch. A single ant found a crumb too big to carry alone and hurried home. Soon a whole team of ants came and lifted the crumb together. Her teacher said ants share heavy loads as a group. Aadya learned that ants carry big loads by working as a team.
payload.title: Ants carry big loads by working as a team
decoys: One ant found a crumb too big to carry
Ants are everywhere in the garden
Aadya scattered breadcrumbs near the hole

payload.passage: The class struggled to hear the teacher over noise from the road. Honking and traffic drowned out the lessons all day. The school fixed thick glass panes on the windows facing the road. The new glass kept most of the street noise outside. The children could finally hear every word the teacher said.
payload.title: Thick glass panes solved the road-noise trouble
decoys: City schools always face problems with noise
The school fixed thick glass on the windows

payload.passage: At home, Aisha could never finish her milk because it turned cold. The cold milk sat half-finished and her mother was upset. Aisha began drinking it right away while it was still warm. The warm milk went down easily and the glass was emptied. Her mother was happy to see no milk wasted any more.
payload.title: Drinking it warm solved Aisha's wasted milk
decoys: Milk gives strength to every growing child
Aisha drank her milk while warm

payload.passage: At home, the family kept stepping on small toys left on the stairs. A nasty fall nearly happened more than once on the steps. Mother made a rule that no toys could be kept on the staircase. The children carried their toys away and the stairs stayed clear. The dangerous falls were avoided from that day on.
payload.title: A no-toys rule made the stairs safe
decoys: A nasty fall nearly happened on the steps
Stairs are a common danger spot in homes
Mother made a rule about the staircase

payload.passage: Esha kept tripping over the long wire of her study lamp at home. The loose wire snaked across the floor near her chair. She used a small clip to fix the wire neatly along the table leg. The floor cleared up and the tripping stopped at once. Esha studied safely without any wire in her way.
payload.title: Clipping the wire solved Esha's tripping problem
decoys: The loose wire snaked across the floor
A tidy space prevents many small accidents
Esha clipped the wire along the table leg

payload.passage: Yuvan was curious whether colours fade in sunlight. He cut a bright paper square in half and taped one half inside a dark drawer. He stuck the other half on the sunny windowpane and waited a few weeks. The window half had turned pale and washed-out, while the drawer half stayed bright. Yuvan learned that strong sunlight slowly fades the colour out of paper.
payload.title: Strong sunlight slowly fades paper's colour
decoys: The window half turned pale and washed-out
Sunlight changes many things over time
Yuvan taped one half inside a drawer

payload.passage: Ira poured cold water into one bowl and warm water into another and gently added a drop of ink to each. In the warm bowl the ink spread out and mixed in very quickly. In the cold bowl it sank slowly and took much longer to blend. Her sister said warmth makes the tiny water bits move faster. Ira learned that colour mixes into warm water faster than into cold water.
payload.title: Ink mixes faster in warm water than cold
decoys: The ink spread quickly in the warm bowl
Water can be warm, cold or anywhere between
Ira added a single drop of ink

payload.passage: Ananya dropped a little washing soda into a glass of hard tap water and stirred it slowly with a spoon. At first the water was perfectly clear, but soon it began to turn cloudy and white. The more she mixed, the milkier the water became in the glass. Her teacher said the soda joined with the hardness to make tiny solid bits. Ananya learned that washing soda makes hard water turn cloudy.
payload.title: Washing soda makes hard water turn cloudy
decoys: The clear water slowly turned white
Water can be soft or hard

payload.passage: A seedling reaches towards the light as soon as it sprouts. If light comes mostly from one side, the plant bends that way. The cells on the dark side grow longer and tip the stem over. This keeps the leaves pointed at the brightest light they can find. So a young plant leans and grows towards the sunlight.
payload.title: How a young plant leans towards light
decoys: Cells on the dark side grow longer
Plants do many clever things to live
Green leaves use sunlight to make food

payload.passage: A coconut crab is a land crab that climbs trees to find food. It starts life in the sea like other crabs. As it grows, it moves onto land and breathes air through special parts. It climbs palm trees and uses its strong claws to crack open coconuts. So a coconut crab leaves the sea and lives a clever life on land.
payload.title: How a coconut crab lives on land
decoys: The crab uses strong claws to crack coconuts
Sea creatures live in surprising ways
Coconut palms grow along sandy beaches

payload.passage: Sumit wanted to learn how to whistle a long, steady note for fun. At first his breath ran out and the note kept breaking. He practised breathing slowly from his belly while he whistled. His note grew longer and steadier with each passing day. Soon Sumit could whistle a whole tune without stopping for breath.
payload.title: Belly breathing taught Sumit to whistle steadily
decoys: Sumit's note kept breaking at first
Whistling is a happy habit anyone can pick up
Sumit could whistle a whole tune at last

payload.passage: A windlass on a deep well winds up a heavy bucket. A rope is wound around a thick round bar fixed across the top. When you turn the crank handle, the bar rolls and winds the rope in. As the rope shortens, the full bucket is lifted up the shaft. So a windlass raises a bucket by winding rope around a turning bar.
payload.title: How a windlass winds a bucket up a well
decoys: Rope is wound around a thick bar
Wells are dug deep for water
Turning the crank rolls the bar

payload.passage: The school's Bottle Brigade keeps a big drum for empty glass and plastic bottles. Children drop their used bottles in it instead of the bin. Once a week a recycler comes to collect the full drum. The money the school earns is saved for the garden. The teacher explained that recycled glass and plastic save energy and materials, so the brigade learned that saving bottles for recycling saves energy.
payload.title: Saving bottles for recycling saves energy
decoys: The drum holds glass and plastic bottles

payload.passage: The monsoon brings heavy rain to most parts of India every year. Dark clouds roll in, the wind picks up, and water pours down for hours. Dry brown fields slowly turn green as thirsty plants drink deeply. Rivers and wells fill up again, giving people water to use for many months. So the monsoon rains bring new life back to the land.
payload.title: Monsoon rain brings new life to the land
decoys: Dry brown fields slowly turn green
Weather changes a lot all through the year
Farmers grow rice and wheat in their fields

payload.passage: Air feels lighter and cooler the higher you climb up a mountain. At the bottom, the air is thick, warm, and easy to breathe. As you go up, there is less air pressing down, so it grows thin and cold. High peaks can be freezing even on a sunny day. So climbing a mountain takes you into thinner, colder air.
payload.title: Why mountain air is thin and cold
decoys: High mountain peaks can be freezing cold
The weather changes from place to place
Climbers carry warm clothes up the mountain

payload.passage: A mousetrap snaps shut with a stored spring. You pull a metal bar back against a tight spring and rest it on a little catch. A bit of food sits on the catch as bait. When the catch is nudged, the spring throws the bar over in a flash. So a mousetrap works by a catch that releases a loaded spring.
payload.title: How a catch releases a mousetrap's spring
decoys: Bait sits on the little catch
A bar is pulled back against a spring

payload.passage: A two-bottle tornado shows a swirling funnel of water. Two bottles are joined neck to neck, with water in the top one. When you swirl it and let the water drain, it spins into a narrow whirling funnel. Air rushes up the middle as the water goes down. So a bottle tornado forms a spinning funnel as water drains through.
payload.title: How draining water makes a bottle tornado
decoys: Two bottles join neck to neck

payload.passage: A coconut sprouts in a way unlike most other seeds. After it lands on warm sand, it stays still for some weeks. Then a thick green shoot pushes out through a soft eye in the shell. At the same time strong roots grow down into the sandy soil. So a whole coconut palm slowly springs from one floating nut.
payload.title: How a coconut sprouts into a palm
decoys: A green shoot pushes out of the shell
Seeds sprout in many different ways
Coconut palms line many warm beaches

payload.passage: A delivery rider brings parcels and food to our doors. He picks up the packets from the shop or kitchen. He reads the address and rides his bike through the busy lanes. He hands the parcel to the right person with a friendly smile. So a delivery rider's work is to bring our orders to our doorstep.
payload.title: How a delivery rider brings our orders
decoys: He reads the address on each parcel
Hot food should reach us quickly

payload.passage: Tanish blew up a balloon and let it go without tying the neck. It shot across the room, hissing as the air rushed out of the back. He tried it again and the balloon flew the other way when he turned it round. His teacher said the air pushing out backwards drives the balloon forwards. Tanish learned that escaping air can push a balloon forward.
payload.title: Escaping air pushes a balloon forward
decoys: The balloon hissed as air rushed out
Balloons are fun to play with
Tanish let the balloon go untied

payload.passage: A soap bubble forms a perfect round ball in the air. A thin skin of soapy water traps a puff of your breath inside. The stretchy skin pulls itself in as tight and small as it can. The smallest, neatest shape it can make around the air is a ball. So a bubble becomes round because its skin pulls into the tightest shape.
payload.title: How a bubble's skin pulls it into a ball
decoys: A thin skin traps your breath
The skin pulls itself in tight

payload.passage: The Nature Watch club set up a small pond in a corner of the school garden. They lined the dug pit with clay and let it slowly fill with rain. Soon frogs, dragonflies and birds came there to drink and to live. The dull, empty corner became full of busy life. The club learned that a small pond brings many creatures to a garden.
payload.title: A small pond brings many creatures to a garden
decoys: The pond was lined with clay

payload.passage: A can telephone works best when the string is tight. Two cans are joined by a long string through small holes. When the string is pulled tight, a voice shakes it and carries clearly. When the string goes slack, the shaking dies and little is heard. So a can phone carries a voice only while its string is held tight.
payload.title: How a tight string carries a can-phone voice
decoys: A slack string carries little sound
The string runs through small holes

payload.passage: Diya put a small magnet near a pile of coins, paper clips and buttons on the table. The steel paper clips jumped to the magnet, but the coins and plastic buttons did not move. She tried each object one by one to be sure. Her teacher said a magnet pulls only certain metals. Diya learned that a magnet pulls some things but not others.
payload.title: A magnet pulls some things but not others
decoys: The paper clips jumped to the magnet
Magnets are fun to play with
Diya tested each object one by one

payload.passage: A flight attendant looks after travellers on an aeroplane. She greets them as they board and helps them find their seats. She shows everyone how to stay safe during the flight. She brings food and drinks and helps anyone who feels unwell. So a flight attendant's work is to keep passengers safe and comfortable.
payload.title: How a flight attendant helps travellers
decoys: She shows everyone how to stay safe
Planes serve meals during long flights

payload.passage: At the museum, Bhumi found an old kitchen set up just as it was a century ago. The guide showed a clay stove, stone grinders and brass pots, and explained that cooking once took hours of hard work without gas or mixers. Even boiling water meant lighting a fire first. Bhumi understood that the kitchen showed how much harder daily cooking was in the past.
payload.title: An old kitchen shows how hard cooking once was
decoys: The kitchen had a clay stove
Kitchens are an important part of a home
Bhumi liked the shiny brass pots

payload.passage: The art class always ran short because clearing the paint took ages. Children fought over the one tap to wash their brushes. The teacher placed buckets of water on each table for quick rinsing. Cleaning up grew fast and the fighting at the tap stopped. Now the children get plenty of time to finish their paintings.
payload.title: Water buckets solved the slow art clean-up
decoys: Children fought over the one tap
Art class is the most enjoyable lesson of all
The teacher placed buckets on each table

payload.passage: A spinning newspaper fan keeps a baby cool. A sheet is folded back and forth into many pleats and tied at one end. When you spread it open, it forms a wide pleated fan. Waving it pushes a good gust of air with each sweep. So a pleated paper fan moves plenty of air because its folds open out wide.
payload.title: How folds make a paper fan move more air
decoys: It opens into a wide pleated shape
The sheet is folded into pleats

payload.passage: The guide led Pranav's class along a long, high stone wall that ran over the hills as far as they could see. Pranav learned that the great wall was built to protect a kingdom's border.
payload.title: A great wall guarded a kingdom's border
decoys: Soldiers walked along the top of the wall
Walls are built for many reasons
Pranav could not see the end of the wall

payload.passage: Kabir's homework papers were always getting mixed up and lost. He handed in the wrong sheet more than once and felt embarrassed. He bought a folder with named sections for each subject. Every paper now went straight into its proper section. Kabir never handed in the wrong homework again after that.
payload.title: A sectioned folder solved Kabir's mixed-up papers
decoys: Kabir once handed in the wrong sheet
Being organised is the secret to doing well
Kabir bought a folder with named sections

payload.passage: A young mango tree takes many years to grow tall and strong. It starts from a single large seed planted in warm soil. Slowly it grows a thick trunk, spreading branches, and a wide leafy top. After several years it finally blooms and grows its first sweet mangoes. So patience is needed before a mango tree can give fruit.
payload.title: A mango tree takes years to fruit
decoys: A mango tree starts from one large seed
Trees are an important part of nature
Mangoes taste sweet and juicy in summer

payload.passage: A bus conductor helps the driver run the bus smoothly. As people get on, he collects the fare and hands them a ticket. He calls out the name of each stop so no one misses theirs. He also signals the driver when it is safe to start again. So a bus conductor's job is to look after the passengers.
payload.title: How a bus conductor helps passengers
decoys: He collects the fare and gives a ticket
Many workers keep the city moving
Buses are a cheap way to travel

payload.passage: A river can change its path after years of flowing. As the water bends round a curve, it wears away the outer bank. On the inner side it drops sand and the bank builds up. Over time the bends grow larger and the river slowly shifts sideways. So a winding river slowly moves across the flat land.
payload.title: How a winding river shifts its path
decoys: The water wears away the outer bank
Rivers change the land all the time
Boats sail along the winding river

payload.passage: The youth group planted a long row of trees along the crumbling riverbank. The bare bank had been falling into the water bit by bit. As the trees grew, their roots gripped the soil and held it firm. So much less mud washed into the river. The group learned that tree roots hold a riverbank firm and clean.
payload.title: Tree roots hold a riverbank firm and clean
decoys: The youth group planted the trees

payload.passage: Harsh wanted to learn how to fix a flat bicycle tyre himself. The first time he tried, he pinched the tube and made the hole worse. He watched his father carefully and then tried again very slowly. He found the leak, patched it, and pumped the tyre to just the right level. Harsh felt grown up knowing he could mend his own bicycle now.
payload.title: Careful practice taught Harsh to mend a tyre
decoys: Harsh pinched the tube and made it worse
Bicycles always break down at the wrong time
Harsh learned the repair from his father

payload.passage: At the old harbour, Diya looked at a giant stone lighthouse standing at the edge of the sea. The guide said that before radios and lights on ships, sailors found the coast at night by its bright, turning lamp. The tall tower kept ships from crashing on hidden rocks. Diya realised the lighthouse was built as a safe guide for sailors in the dark.
payload.title: A lighthouse guided ships safely at night
decoys: The lighthouse stood right beside the sea
Sailors have always faced danger at sea
Diya counted the steps inside the tower

payload.passage: The children kept hurting their fingers on the splintered classroom door. The rough old wood scratched them as they passed through. A carpenter sanded the door smooth and gave it a coat of paint. The smooth surface no longer caught at anyone's hands. The children walked through the doorway safely after that.
payload.title: Sanding the door solved the splinter problem
decoys: The rough wood scratched the children
Old doors often need care and repair
A carpenter sanded the door smooth

payload.passage: A pair of scissors cuts paper using two blades that cross in the middle. They are joined at a single point by a small screw or pin. When you press the handles together, the two sharp edges slide past each other. The paper caught between them is squeezed and sliced along that line. So scissors cut by pinching paper between two crossing blades.
payload.title: How scissors cut by crossing two blades
decoys: The two blades meet at a single pin
Sharp edges can slice through paper

payload.passage: Veer mixed a spoon of baking soda into a little vinegar inside a tall glass. At once the mixture began to hiss and bubble up like a tiny volcano. He held an unlit matchstick near the foam and the flame went out the moment it reached the top. His teacher said the fizzing made a gas that does not let things burn. Veer learned that soda and vinegar make a gas that puts out fire.
payload.title: Soda and vinegar make a gas that smothers flames
decoys: The mixture bubbled up like a tiny volcano
Chemicals can do many surprising things together
Vinegar has a strong and sour smell

payload.passage: Sneha was curious about how a seed turns into a plant, so she lined a glass jar with wet cotton. She tucked two bean seeds against the glass where she could watch them every day. After three days a tiny white root pushed out and curled downwards. Soon a pale shoot rose up and opened its first green leaves towards the light. Sneha learned that a seed sprouts a root first and then a shoot.
payload.title: A sprouting seed grows its root before its shoot
decoys: The first root curled downwards into the cotton
Plants are an important part of our world
Sneha placed the seeds against the glass jar

payload.passage: Ayaan stood at the bottom of a hill and clapped his hands hard while facing a far cliff. A moment later he heard his own clap come bouncing back to him. He clapped again from the open field and heard no echo at all. His uncle said sound bounces off the hard cliff but spreads away in the open. Ayaan learned that an echo happens when sound bounces back off a hard surface.
payload.title: An echo is sound bouncing off a hard surface
decoys: Ayaan clapped his hands towards the cliff
Sound is something we hear all the time
Hills are fun places to explore

payload.passage: A see-saw style hand drill bores a hole with a turning bit. When you crank the handle, a set of gears spins the sharp bit fast. The spinning bit is pressed against the wood and cuts in slowly. Tiny shavings curl out as the hole grows deeper. So a hand drill makes a hole by spinning a sharp bit into the wood.
payload.title: How a hand drill bores a hole in wood
decoys: Shavings curl out of the hole

payload.passage: Tushar wanted to learn how to tie his shoelaces into a neat double knot. His loops kept coming undone before he even reached the gate. He practised on a big shoe with thick laces sitting on the floor. Once his fingers learned the loops, he tied the knot quickly and tightly. Tushar was thrilled that his shoes no longer came loose while running.
payload.title: Practice taught Tushar a knot that stays tied
decoys: Shoes are always coming loose at the worst time
Tushar practised on a shoe with thick laces

payload.passage: At home, the family's shoes got soaked and muddy near the gate. The mud was tracked into the house and dirtied the floors. Father laid a rough mat and a small rack just outside the door. Everyone wiped and parked their shoes there before stepping in. The house floors stayed clean even on the muddiest days.
payload.title: A mat and rack solved the muddy-shoe mess
decoys: Mud was tracked into the house
A clean home reflects a caring family
Father laid a rough mat outside the door

payload.passage: Inaya watched a long row of ants cross the veranda each evening. One day she gently wiped the path with a damp cloth where they walked. The next ants reached the wiped patch and milled about in confusion before finding the trail again. Her teacher said she had rubbed away their smell path. Inaya learned that wiping the path erases the ants' scent trail.
payload.title: Wiping the path erases an ant scent trail
decoys: The ants milled about in confusion
Inaya wiped the path with a cloth

payload.passage: Vikram wanted to balance on his cricket bat handle as a fun trick. He tried for days and the bat toppled over again and again. He learned to fix his eyes on one steady point in front of him. Once his focus held, the bat stayed upright for longer and longer. By the weekend Vikram balanced the bat for a full minute and grinned.
payload.title: Steady focus helped Vikram balance the bat
decoys: The bat toppled over again and again
Cricket teaches children patience and teamwork
Vikram balanced the bat on its handle

payload.passage: A kite climbs into the sky on the push of moving air. When you run or the wind blows, air slides under the slanted face of the kite. This air pushes the kite upward as it slips past. The string in your hand holds the kite at the right tilt against the breeze. So a kite flies because slanted air lifts it while the string holds it steady.
payload.title: How wind and string lift a kite
decoys: The string holds the kite at a tilt
Flying kites is a popular pastime
Air pushes against the kite's face

payload.passage: Arjun's scout troop noticed the stream behind their school choked with bags and bottles. One weekend they pulled out three sacks of rubbish and put up signs asking people not to throw waste in the water. Within weeks, small fish came back to the clear stream. The troop learned that cleaning a stream can bring its life back.
payload.title: Cleaning a stream brings its life back
decoys: The troop pulled out three sacks of waste
Arjun is a member of a scout troop

payload.passage: Harini saw the wide river break into many smaller channels as it neared the sea, spreading like the fingers of a hand. Her teacher explained that a river drops a lot of mud near its mouth. The piled-up soil blocks its path and slows it down. So the water finds many smaller ways around the mud. Harini learned that a river splits into many channels near the sea.
payload.title: A river splits into many channels near the sea
decoys: Harini saw the split on a map

payload.passage: Stuti dropped a single ink drop into a bowl of warm water and one into cold water at the same time. In the warm bowl the ink raced out in swirling clouds, while in the cold bowl it crept down slowly. Her teacher said warm water bits jiggle faster. Stuti learned that ink spreads quicker in warm water than cold.
payload.title: Ink spreads quicker in warm than cold water
decoys: The ink raced out in the warm bowl
Stuti dropped ink into both bowls

payload.passage: Riya's group noticed that the school threw out hundreds of plastic ink pens. Each empty pen went straight into the bin. So they switched the whole school to refillable pens. With these, only the tiny ink tube is changed, not the whole pen. Far fewer pens now reach the bin, and the group learned that refillable pens cut down on plastic waste.
payload.title: Refillable pens cut down on plastic waste
decoys: Only the ink tube is changed
Pens are used in every class

payload.passage: A museum guide helps visitors learn about the things on show. She walks with the group from one display to the next. She explains where each old object came from and why it matters. She answers questions so people understand what they are seeing. So a museum guide's work is to help visitors learn from the displays.
payload.title: How a museum guide teaches visitors
decoys: She explains where each object came from
Many helpers share knowledge with us
Museums keep very old things safe

payload.passage: The school field had a deep pit where children sometimes twisted their ankles. The hidden hole was hard to spot during fast games. The groundsman filled the pit with earth and pressed it flat and firm. The field became level and the twisted ankles stopped. The children played their games safely from that day on.
payload.title: Filling the pit solved the twisted-ankle danger
decoys: A safe field is needed for all sports
The groundsman filled the pit with earth

payload.passage: The hostel students set a rule of short showers using a small bucket and mug. They gave up long showers under the running tap. To help, they timed themselves and reminded one another. Over a month, the hostel used much less water and less power to heat it. The students learned that shorter showers save both water and energy.
payload.title: Shorter showers save water and energy
decoys: Students use a bucket and mug

payload.passage: A forest guard protects the trees and animals of the forest. He walks long paths through the trees, keeping a careful watch. He stops people from cutting trees or harming the wild animals. He also warns of fires and helps lost travellers find their way. So a forest guard's job is to keep the forest and its life safe.
payload.title: How a forest guard protects the forest
decoys: He stops people from cutting trees
Forests are home to many wild animals

payload.passage: Pooja saw a small canal carry river water all the way to dry fields far from the river. Her uncle explained that people dig such canals on purpose. They lead water from a full river or dam to farms that get little rain. In this way crops can grow even in dry places. Pooja learned that canals carry river water to thirsty fields.
payload.title: Canals carry river water to dry fields
decoys: The canal reached the far fields
Farms need water to grow crops

payload.passage: A crab must shed its shell in order to grow bigger. Its hard shell cannot stretch, so it becomes too tight in time. The crab cracks open the old shell and backs slowly out. Underneath is a soft new shell that soon hardens to fit its larger body. So a crab leaves its old shell behind each time it grows.
payload.title: Why a crab sheds its old shell
decoys: A crab backs slowly out of its old shell
Sea animals grow in many ways
Crabs walk sideways along the sandy beach

payload.passage: A hand fan cools you with nothing but a folded sheet of paper. When you wave it back and forth, it pushes the still air near your face. This moving air sweeps away the warm, damp layer sitting on your skin. As that layer is carried off, fresh cooler air takes its place. So a hand fan cools you by keeping the air around your face moving.
payload.title: How a hand fan cools you by moving air
decoys: Waving pushes the still air about
Fans come in many shapes and sizes
Warm air sits in a layer on skin

payload.passage: Lata saw dew sparkling on the grass one cool morning, though it had not rained. Her grandmother explained that on clear, calm nights the grass cools down quickly, and the water vapour in the air turns into tiny drops on the cold leaves. By midday the sun dries them away. Lata learned that dew forms when night air cools on cold leaves.
payload.title: Dew forms when night air cools on leaves
decoys: Mornings can feel fresh and cool
Lata walked on the grass barefoot

payload.passage: A banyan tree can spread out to cover a huge piece of ground. From its high branches it drops long thin roots towards the soil. When these roots reach the earth, they grow thick and become new trunks. Over many years one banyan can look like a whole little forest. So a single banyan tree slowly grows many trunks of its own.
payload.title: How one banyan grows many trunks
decoys: Hanging roots reach down and become trunks
Trees grow in many wonderful shapes
Travellers rest under a shady banyan

payload.passage: Ishaan wished to write neatly, but his letters tumbled all over the page. The teacher returned his notebook with a note about messy handwriting. Ishaan bought a fresh four-lined book and copied one paragraph slowly every evening. His letters began to stand straight and sit on the lines. Within a month his teacher praised the neat work in front of the whole class.
payload.title: Slow daily copying improved Ishaan's handwriting
decoys: Ishaan's letters tumbled all over the page
Good handwriting is the key to success in life
Ishaan bought himself a fresh four-lined book

payload.passage: Sara stuck a thin straw into a glass of juice and tried to sip. Then she made a tiny hole in the side of the straw and tried again. With the hole, no juice came up no matter how hard she sucked. Her father said the leaking air stopped the straw from pulling the juice. Sara learned that a straw works only when no air can leak into it.
payload.title: A straw works only without an air leak
decoys: Sara made a tiny hole in the straw
Drinks can be sipped in many ways
Juice is a sweet and tasty drink

payload.passage: A hand-held hole punch makes neat holes in paper. When you press the top down, a sharp metal pin is driven downward. The pin pushes through the stacked paper into a small round hole below. A tidy little disc of paper drops out into a tray. So a hole punch makes a hole by driving a sharp pin through the paper.
payload.title: How a punch drives a hole through paper
decoys: A little disc drops into a tray

payload.passage: A warm bag of rice is heated and used to ease aches. A cloth bag is filled with dry rice and warmed for a short while. The many grains soak up the heat and hold it well. Laid on a sore shoulder, the bag gives off its warmth slowly for a long time. So a rice bag eases aches by holding and slowly giving off heat.
payload.title: How a rice bag holds and gives off heat
decoys: The grains soak up the heat
A cloth bag is filled with rice

payload.passage: Faizan wanted to fix his own kite so it would fly higher than the rest. His first kite kept spinning down and crashing into the ground. He studied how the string and the tail balanced the kite in the wind. After adjusting the tail length, the kite rose smoothly and stayed up. Faizan felt proud that his own careful changes had solved the problem.
payload.title: Adjusting the tail helped Faizan's kite fly
decoys: Faizan's first kite kept crashing down
Kites can teach children all about the wind
Faizan studied the string and the tail

payload.passage: The guide led Trisha to a giant stone wheel-shaped temple carved to look like a chariot. payload.title: A carved temple wheel could tell the time
decoys: The temple was carved to look like a chariot
Trisha walked all the way around the wheel

payload.passage: A coral reef slowly recovers after a strong storm. Big waves can break off pieces of the brittle coral. But the living polyps that survive keep building new stony cups. Tiny bits of broken coral can also settle and grow into fresh colonies. So over many years a damaged reef can slowly grow back.
payload.title: How a coral reef grows back after a storm
decoys: Surviving polyps keep building new cups
Nature can heal itself over time
Bright fish return to a healthy reef

payload.passage: Samar dropped a coin into a bowl and stepped back until the rim just hid the coin from view. He asked a friend to slowly pour water into the bowl. payload.title: Water bends light to reveal a hidden coin
decoys: The hidden coin seemed to lift into view
Samar dropped a coin in the bowl

payload.passage: Pankaj saw the river wind in big loops across the flat plain instead of running straight. His teacher explained that on level land a slow river pushes harder on the outside of each bend, wearing it away, while it drops soil on the inside. Over years the loops grow bigger and curvier. Pankaj learned that a slow river bends into loops on flat land.
payload.title: A slow river bends into loops on flat land
decoys: The river looped across the plain
Rivers shape the land they cross
Pankaj saw it from the bridge

payload.passage: A chef plans and cooks the meals served at a restaurant. He decides what dishes will be on the menu each day. He gathers fresh items and cooks them with skill and care. He tastes each dish to make sure it is just right before it is served. So a chef's work is to prepare tasty meals for the guests.
payload.title: How a chef prepares meals for guests
decoys: He tastes each dish before it is served
Many helpers serve people each day
Fresh items make food taste better

payload.passage: A hand drill for making fire spins a stick fast. You press a pointed stick into a notch on a flat board. Rolling the stick quickly between your palms rubs it against the board. The rubbing makes heat and a little glowing dust at the notch. So a fire drill makes heat by rubbing a spinning stick on a board.
payload.title: How a spinning stick rubs up fire heat
decoys: Glowing dust forms at the notch
You roll the stick between your palms

payload.passage: The students could not see the board clearly because of the glare. Sunlight bounced off the shiny board straight into their eyes. payload.title: Tilting the board solved the blinding glare
decoys: Sunlight bounced into the students' eyes
A clear board is the heart of every lesson
The teacher shifted the board from the window

payload.passage: Aryan filled a balloon with air and another with water and held each one over a candle flame for a moment, well away from his face. The air-filled balloon popped almost at once. Aryan learned that water can carry away heat and stop a balloon from bursting.
payload.title: Water absorbs heat and protects a balloon
decoys: The air-filled balloon popped almost at once
Fire must always be handled with great care
Balloons can be filled with air or water

payload.passage: Devansh wanted to grow a plant from a kitchen scrap. He stood the cut base of a spring onion in a glass of water on the windowsill. Within days fresh green shoots sprang up from the old white base. He snipped the green tops to use and the plant grew more. Devansh learned that a spring onion base can grow new green shoots.
payload.title: A spring onion base grows new green shoots
decoys: Devansh stood the base in water
Spring onions are used in cooking

payload.passage: Ravi poured water into a clear glass and dropped a straight pencil inside it. From the side the pencil suddenly looked broken at the spot where it entered the water. He lifted the pencil out and saw that it was still whole and straight. His teacher told him that water bends the light coming from the pencil, which fools our eyes. Ravi learned that light changes direction when it passes into water.
payload.title: Water bends light and tricks our eyes
decoys: The pencil looked broken at the water line
Our eyes can be fooled in many surprising ways
Ravi used a clear glass for his experiment

payload.passage: A stapler joins sheets of paper with a small bent wire staple. When you press down hard, a thin metal arm pushes one staple out from the row inside. The two legs of the staple are driven through the stacked paper. A shaped plate underneath bends the legs flat so they grip. So a stapler clips paper by pushing a staple through and folding its legs.
payload.title: How a stapler clips paper with a staple
decoys: A plate bends the staple legs flat
Paper can be joined in many ways

payload.passage: The students wasted time at lunch fighting over the few washing taps. The long wait left many with no time to eat properly. The school fitted three extra taps along the washing area. The children washed their hands quickly and sat down to eat. Lunch became calm and everyone finished their meal in time.
payload.title: Extra taps solved the lunch-time washing rush
decoys: The long wait left no time to eat
Clean hands keep every child free from illness
The school fitted three extra taps

payload.passage: When the cold season ends, many birds fly back to their old homes. During winter they had travelled far to warmer lands to find food. Now that spring has come, they return to the lakes and trees they left behind. They build fresh nests, lay eggs, and raise their young in the milder weather. So the change of season tells these birds when to fly home.
payload.title: Seasons tell birds when to fly home
decoys: Birds build fresh nests when they return
Animals do clever things to stay alive
Some birds can fly across whole oceans

payload.passage: Yash decided to learn juggling with three small balls. At the start he could not even keep two balls in the air for long. He practised over a soft bed so the balls would not roll far when dropped. Drop after drop, his hands learned the rhythm of the throws. Within a month Yash juggled all three balls in a steady, smooth circle.
payload.title: Patient practice taught Yash to juggle three balls
decoys: Yash could not keep two balls up at first
Circus skills can be learned by absolutely anyone
Yash practised juggling over a soft bed

payload.passage: The classroom got muddy footprints all over the floor in the rains. The dirty floor made the room look untidy and damp. The teacher placed a coir mat right inside the door for wiping feet. Children wiped their shoes and the floor stayed clean. The classroom looked neat and dry even on rainy days.
payload.title: A coir mat solved the muddy classroom floor
decoys: Rains create extra cleaning work everywhere
The teacher placed a coir mat inside

payload.passage: A zip-line lets you slide down a sloping wire. A small wheel rides along a tight wire stretched between two posts. You hold the handle that hangs below the wheel and lift your feet. Gravity then pulls you down the slope as the wheel rolls along. So a zip-line carries you down by a wheel rolling on a sloping wire.
payload.title: How a wheel carries you down a zip-line
decoys: A small wheel rides the tight wire
You hold a handle below the wheel

payload.passage: Sumit noticed dark clouds far over the sea moving toward the shore one evening. His uncle, a fisherman, explained that the weather at sea can change very fast. So he watches the clouds, the wind and the waves before he takes his boat out. If a storm looks near, he waits safely on land. Sumit learned that fishermen read the sky to stay safe at sea.
payload.title: Fishermen read the sky to stay safe
decoys: Dark clouds moved toward the shore

payload.passage: When Yash sold homemade greeting cards, he set the price by counting only the paper and glitter he had bought. His sister pointed out that he had forgotten the most precious ingredient: his own time. The hours spent cutting and drawing were worth something too, she said, and a fair price should cover them. Yash had been quietly working almost for free. He raised his prices a little, and customers still bought happily. Yash learnt that the value of any handmade thing includes the labour hidden inside it.
payload.title: Why a fair price must value your time
decoys: Yash made greeting cards from paper and glitter
Hard work deserves to be respected
He had forgotten to count his own hours

payload.passage: A simple solar water heater warms water using only the sun. On the roof sit dark panels through which water slowly flows. The dark colour soaks up the sun's warmth and passes it to the water inside. The heated water rises and gathers in a storage tank. By evening, a family has a tank of hot water without burning any fuel.
payload.title: How a solar water heater warms water free of fuel
decoys: Dark panels soak up the sun's warmth
Clean ideas save fuel and money
Heated water gathers in a tank

payload.passage: Long before fridges, salt was a precious way to keep food from rotting. Salting works by drawing the water out of meat or fish. Germs that spoil food cannot grow without water to live in. Packed in salt, food stays safe to eat for many months. This old trick let people store and trade food across long, hot journeys.
payload.title: How salting keeps food from rotting
decoys: Salt draws the water out of meat
Old ideas helped people store food

payload.passage: Every year the great wildebeest herds make a vast circular journey across the African plains, and there is real safety in their numbers. Over a million animals move together in search of fresh grass and rain. When they reach a crocodile-filled river, they must cross all at once in a thundering rush. Many are lost, but by crossing in such a huge crowd, the great majority make it over before the hunters can take more than a few. The herd's enormous size means most survive. Travelling as a multitude is their oldest defence.
payload.title: How the wildebeest herd survives by sheer numbers
decoys: Wildebeest cross rivers full of crocodiles
Herds move to find fresh grass
Over a million animals travel together

payload.passage: Almost all life on Earth runs, in the end, on the light of the sun. Green plants catch sunlight and store its energy as food. Plant-eating animals gain that energy when they eat the plants. Meat-eaters then take it in by eating the plant-eaters. Even decomposers feed on the remains of these creatures. From the smallest seed to the largest beast, the energy that powers life can be traced back to a single distant star; so the great web of life on Earth rests, in the end, upon the steady light of a single star.
payload.title: How sunlight feeds nearly every living thing
decoys: Plant-eating animals gain energy from the plants
The sun supports life across the planet
Even decomposers feed on the remains of creatures

payload.passage: An electric fan brought relief from the heat to millions of homes. Inside its hub a small motor spins a set of slanted blades. As the blades turn, their slant pushes the air forward in a steady stream. The moving air does not chill the room, but it helps your sweat dry faster. That drying is what makes the breeze from a fan feel so cool on a hot day.
payload.title: How a ceiling fan brings relief from heat
decoys: A motor spins a set of slanted blades
Inventions help us face hot weather
Slanted blades push the air forward

payload.passage: On a dark night, a lighthouse warns ships away from dangerous rocks. High in its tower burns a very bright lamp. Curved mirrors and glass gather this light and aim it into one strong beam. The beam sweeps slowly around so sailors far out at sea can spot it. By its steady flash, a captain knows where the coast and its hidden rocks lie.
payload.title: How a lighthouse guides ships away from danger
decoys: Mirrors aim the lamp into one strong beam
The beam of a lighthouse sweeps slowly around

payload.passage: A single shower seems harmless, but rain is a patient sculptor of the Earth. Falling water washes tiny grains of soil and rock downhill bit by bit. Over countless years this slow carrying carves valleys and smooths hillsides. Streams gather the loosened material and lay it down far away, building flat plains. So the shape of much of the land around us is the slow handiwork of rain and flowing water; given enough time, the gentle work of rain and rivers can grind down whole hills and build broad valleys and plains.
payload.title: How rain shapes the land over long ages
decoys: Streams lay down material to build flat plains
Nature changes the world over long stretches of time
Falling water washes grains of soil downhill

payload.passage: When you spin around quickly and then stop, the room seems to keep turning for a moment. Deep inside each ear are tiny curved tubes filled with fluid. As you spin, the fluid sloshes around and tells your brain that you are moving. When you stop suddenly, the fluid keeps swirling for a few seconds. Your brain still thinks you are turning, and that mixed-up message makes you feel dizzy.
payload.title: Why spinning around makes you feel dizzy
decoys: Fluid swirls inside tiny tubes in the ear
The brain controls everything we feel
The ear helps the body keep its balance

payload.passage: Rain that soaks the ground does not stay there forever. The sun warms the wet earth, the puddles and the rivers. Slowly this water turns to vapour and rises invisibly into the sky. High up, the vapour cools and gathers into clouds once more. In time those clouds grow heavy and release the water as fresh rain. The very rain that fell yesterday may climb back up and fall again another day; so the rain of one day may rise and fall once more, again and again, through the endless cycle.
payload.title: How rain returns to the sky to fall again
decoys: The sun warms the wet earth and rivers
Vapour cools and gathers into clouds again

payload.passage: The trap-jaw ant carries jaws that snap shut faster than almost any movement in the animal world. It holds these huge jaws wide open, locked like a loaded spring, while tiny hairs feel for prey. The instant an insect touches a trigger hair, the jaws slam closed in a flash, seizing or stunning the victim at once. Even more cleverly, the ant can snap its jaws against the ground to fling itself backward through the air, escaping a sudden danger. By using its jaws both to hunt and to leap away, the trap-jaw ant thrives.
payload.title: How the trap-jaw ant uses its jaws to hunt and escape
decoys: The trap-jaw ant's jaws snap shut very fast
It can fling itself backward with its jaws

payload.passage: The moon may glow softly in our sky, but its surface is a barren, dusty place. It has no air and no liquid water at all. Without these, there are no plants, no rivers and no weather of any kind. Grey dust and rocky craters stretch in every direction under a black sky. Nothing grows or stirs upon it. The gentle-looking moon is in truth a silent, lifeless desert hanging in space; so the soft glow we admire belongs, in truth, to a silent and utterly lifeless world.
payload.title: Why the moon is a desert world of dust
decoys: The moon's surface has no air or liquid water
Other worlds differ greatly from Earth
Grey dust and craters stretch under a black sky

payload.passage: Ishita was thrilled when a fancy new toy promised hours of fun in its advertisement, and she spent all her savings on it at once. By the next week it lay forgotten in a corner, and her money was gone. Her brother asked whether the toy had truly given the joy it promised. Honestly, it had not. Ishita realised that some purchases feel exciting for a moment but leave you poorer and no happier. She learnt to ask, before spending, whether a thing would still matter to her a week later.
payload.title: Asking if a purchase will still matter later
decoys: The new toy lay forgotten within a week
She spent all her savings at once

payload.passage: Throwing all rubbish into one bin wastes more than we realise. Old paper can be turned into new notebooks, and glass can be melted into fresh bottles. Even kitchen scraps can rot down into rich food for plants. When we sort our waste, far less of it ends up piled in a dump. Sorting and reusing waste saves materials and keeps our towns much cleaner.
payload.title: Why sorting and reusing our waste is important
decoys: Old paper can be made into new notebooks
Cleanliness is a good habit to have
Kitchen scraps can rot into plant food

payload.passage: Keeping a wild animal as a pet may seem exciting, but it does great harm. A parrot or a monkey taken from the forest loses the free life it was meant to have. In a small cage it often grows sad and sickly. Taking wild creatures from their homes also leaves fewer of them in the forest. Wild animals belong in the wild, not behind the bars of a cage.
payload.title: Why wild animals should not be kept as pets
decoys: A caged animal often grows sickly
Taking animals leaves fewer in the forest

payload.passage: A digital camera stores a photo as a vast grid of tiny dots. Each dot, called a pixel, records the colour and brightness of one speck of the scene. Millions of these pixels together build up the whole picture. Because the image is just numbers, it can be copied or shared without ever wearing out. The digital camera made photographs cheap, instant and endlessly shareable.
payload.title: How a digital camera stores a photo as dots
decoys: Each pixel records colour and brightness
Modern devices changed how we take photos
A digital photo can be copied without wearing out

payload.passage: Why does a bicycle stay upright when you ride it but topple when it stops? The secret lies in the spinning wheels. A spinning wheel does not like to change the way it is leaning, so it keeps the bicycle steady. The faster you ride, the more strongly the wheels resist tipping over. This is why learning to balance feels much easier once you start moving.
payload.title: Why a moving bicycle stays balanced
decoys: Spinning wheels resist a change in their lean
Riding a bicycle is a useful skill to learn
A bicycle is harder to balance when standing still

payload.passage: Before printing reached the common home, the typewriter let people produce neat, clear pages. Each key was joined to a small metal arm that carried a single letter. Pressing a key swung the arm up to strike an inked ribbon against the paper. Letter by letter, a tidy printed page took shape. Offices, writers and schools soon depended on this quick and steady machine.
payload.title: How the typewriter produced neat printed pages
decoys: Each key swings a metal arm with one letter
Inventions changed how work is done
An inked ribbon makes the letters on the page

payload.passage: A windmill captures the unseen power of moving air. Its wide blades are tilted so the passing wind pushes against them. The push makes the blades spin around a central shaft. That spinning shaft can turn a heavy grindstone or drive a pump. For centuries, windmills ground grain and lifted water using nothing but the free wind.
payload.title: How a windmill turns wind into useful work
decoys: Tilted blades are pushed by the passing wind
Nature offers many sources of power
A windmill can grind grain or lift water

payload.passage: Ishita's craft stall did well, and a friend urged her to spend all her profit at once on a flashy new sign. Ishita paused and thought about what would truly help her sell more. Instead of the sign, she bought better materials that let her make finer crafts customers loved. The wise spending grew her business, while the flashy sign would have only looked pretty. Ishita learnt that money put back into a business should be spent on what actually helps it earn, not merely on what looks impressive to others.
payload.title: Why reinvested money should help you earn
decoys: A friend urged a flashy new sign

payload.passage: A flower marks the first step toward a plant's fruit. Once pollen reaches it, tiny seeds begin to form deep inside the flower. The bright petals, having done their work, wither and drop away. The base of the flower then swells and ripens around the growing seeds. In time it becomes a fruit that protects and feeds those seeds. A juicy fruit is really a flower that has grown up to guard the next generation; so the fruit in your hand is really a flower grown up to protect the plant's next generation.
payload.title: How a plant's flower becomes its fruit
decoys: Tiny seeds form inside the flower after pollen reaches it
The base of the flower swells into a fruit

payload.passage: The mother crocodile looks fierce, yet she is one of the most careful parents in the animal world. When her eggs hatch in the sandy bank, the tiny calls of her babies reach her at once. She scoops the squeaking hatchlings gently into her enormous mouth, the very jaws that crush bones, and carries them softly to the water. There she opens up and lets the little ones swim free in the shallows under her watchful eye. For many weeks she guards them from herons and fish. Her frightening mouth becomes a cradle.
payload.title: How a fierce crocodile gently guards her babies
decoys: A crocodile carries its young in its mouth
The hatchlings call out from the sandy bank

payload.passage: Aarav's small printing business was busy, yet at the end of each month barely any money was left. Puzzled, he finally wrote down every single cost: ink, paper, electricity and a helper's wage. The list revealed that he was charging customers less than the job actually cost him to do. He had been working hard only to lose money quietly. Aarav raised his prices to cover his true costs, and at last the business began to profit. He learnt that knowing your real costs is the only way to set a price that keeps you afloat.
payload.title: Why knowing true costs sets the right price
decoys: Aarav listed ink, paper and wages
Hard work alone is not always enough
He charged less than the job cost

payload.passage: Ayaan thought the hospital's vaccination drive was only about the children who got the jabs. The doctor showed him a wider picture. When most children in a town are protected against a disease, the germ can hardly find anyone to infect, so it cannot spread. This shields even the few babies too young or too sick to be vaccinated. The protection of the many quietly guards the vulnerable few. Ayaan realised that a vaccine is not only a private shield; it is a wall the whole community builds together.
payload.title: How vaccinating many protects the vulnerable few
decoys: Some babies are too young to be vaccinated
Doctors do a lot of good in society
A germ cannot spread without people to infect

payload.passage: When rain falls, not all of it runs into rivers; much of it sinks downward. It trickles through soil and tiny cracks until it reaches a layer of rock it cannot pass. There it collects in the spaces between grains of sand and stone, forming a hidden store called groundwater. Wells and pumps reach down to lift this water for drinking and farming. Slowly, fresh rain refills the store, keeping the underground water alive; because it refills slowly, people must use this hidden water carefully, or the wells may run dry faster than the rain can replace them.
payload.title: How groundwater hides beneath our feet
decoys: Wells and pumps lift water from underground
Water is one of nature's most useful gifts
Rain sinks until it meets a layer it cannot pass

payload.passage: Why do your hands and feet feel cold first on a chilly day? Your body cares most about keeping its inner organs warm. When the cold bites, it pulls warm blood away from the edges towards the centre. Your hands and feet, far from the warm core, lose their heat first. This is the body sacrificing warm fingers to protect the vital organs within.
payload.title: Why hands and feet feel cold first
decoys: The body pulls warm blood towards the centre
The body protects its vital parts
Hands and feet are far from the warm core

payload.passage: Saira learnt at school that the town's water, roads and streetlights were not magically free but paid for by money the council collected and spent. When she carelessly left a public tap running, her teacher reminded her that the wasted water was paid for by everyone, including her own family. Wasting a shared thing was like wasting a little of each neighbour's money. Saira began turning off taps and lights with new care. She learnt that public services are paid for by all, so wasting them quietly burdens the whole community.
payload.title: Why wasting public services wastes shared money
decoys: She left a public tap running
Wasted water is paid for by everyone

payload.passage: When you switch on a fan, you do not really see how it works. Electricity flows into a small coil of wire inside the motor and turns it into a spinning magnet. The spinning magnet pulls the blades around, and the tilted blades push air forward as they turn. Your skin feels cooler because the moving air carries away your sweat faster. So a fan does not actually chill the room; it only helps your body lose heat more quickly.
payload.title: How an electric fan cools you down
decoys: The blades of a fan are tilted at an angle
Electricity can power many machines in a home
Moving air feels nice on a hot afternoon

payload.passage: An escalator carries crowds up and down without anyone climbing a step. It is really a staircase whose steps move on a loop. A motor drives a chain that pulls the steps along in an endless belt. As you step on, the moving stairs carry you smoothly to the next floor. Busy stations and malls move thousands of people this way every hour.
payload.title: How an escalator carries crowds between floors
decoys: A chain pulls the steps in an endless loop
An escalator is a staircase that moves

payload.passage: The stick insect avoids being eaten not by running, but by doing almost nothing at all. Its long, thin brown body looks exactly like a dry twig among the branches. When a bird passes, the insect freezes utterly still, and even sways a little if the wind moves the real twigs. Some kinds can stay motionless for hours, fooling the sharpest eyes. If a leg is grabbed, it can even shed the limb and slip away. By pretending to be a lifeless stick, this fragile creature hides in full view of its hungry enemies.
payload.title: How the stick insect hides by pretending to be a twig
decoys: A stick insect can shed a grabbed leg
Birds hunt insects among the branches
Its thin brown body looks like a twig

payload.passage: A row of potted plants on a window ledge does more than brighten a flat. The leaves quietly take in stale air and breathe out fresh oxygen indoors. They trap a little dust and damp from the room. A touch of green has even been shown to calm and cheer the people nearby. So a few simple pots make a small flat healthier to live in.
payload.title: How indoor plants make a home healthier
decoys: Leaves breathe out fresh oxygen indoors
Indoor plants trap a little dust

payload.passage: On a freezing morning, grass and leaves may wear a coat of delicate white. This frost forms on very cold, clear nights. The water vapour in the air touches surfaces that have chilled below freezing. Instead of forming dew, the vapour turns straight into tiny ice crystals on leaves and roofs. As the sun rises and warms the air, the fragile frost melts and vanishes within minutes; because it forms only on cold, calm nights, frost is one of the first quiet signs that winter is on its way.
payload.title: How frost paints the ground on cold nights
decoys: Vapour turns to ice on freezing surfaces
Cold weather decorates the world in many ways
The fragile frost melts within minutes of sunrise

payload.passage: The platypus hunts in muddy rivers where it cannot see its prey at all, yet it never goes hungry. When it dives, it shuts its eyes, ears and nose tightly and relies on a stranger sense. Its broad, rubbery bill can detect the faint electric signals given off by the tiny muscles of shrimp and worms hidden in the mud. Sweeping its bill from side to side, it senses these signals and snaps up the prey it cannot see. By feeling for electricity, this odd animal finds its food in the darkest, muddiest water.
payload.title: How the platypus hunts by sensing electric signals
decoys: The platypus shuts its eyes underwater
River water can be muddy and dark
Its bill detects faint electric signals

payload.passage: Mihika was puzzled that the new public park was free for everyone, even though it cost a great deal to build and keep clean. Her father explained that some things are made free on purpose, paid for by the whole town's taxes, so that even the poorest child can enjoy them. A park open only to those who could pay would shut out many. The free gate was a deliberate gift of fairness. Mihika learnt that a caring town spends shared money to give everyone, rich or poor, a place they can equally enjoy.
payload.title: Why some public places are kept free
decoys: The park was paid for by taxes
A paid gate would shut out the poor

payload.passage: Aarav noticed that the postman in his lane always carried a heavy bag yet somehow knew exactly which house wanted which letter. The secret was the careful sorting done before he ever set out that morning. At the office, letters were arranged in the precise order of the houses along his route, so he never doubled back or wasted a step. A walk that looked random was really planned to the last corner. Aarav learnt that the smooth ending of a delivery was shaped by quiet, clever planning long before the postman knocked.
payload.title: How route sorting makes a postman's walk efficient
decoys: The postman carried a very heavy bag
Planning helps in all kinds of work
Letters were arranged in the order of houses

payload.passage: Why is it healthier to play outside than to sit indoors all day? Outdoor play lets your body move freely and your muscles grow strong. Fresh air and sunshine are good for your lungs and your mood. Running and games keep your heart fit and burn off restless energy. A child who plays outdoors each day tends to be both happier and healthier.
payload.title: Why playing outdoors is good for health
decoys: Outdoor play makes muscles grow strong
Fresh air is good for the lungs

payload.passage: The pangolin is a gentle, ant-eating animal with no teeth and no claws fit for fighting. Yet a leopard can rarely make a meal of it. The pangolin's whole body is covered in tough, overlapping scales as hard as fingernails. When a predator threatens, it simply rolls into a tight, armoured ball, tucking its soft face and belly safely inside. The sharp scales point outward in every direction, and the ball is far too hard to bite or open. The frustrated hunter soon gives up. By rolling up behind its armour, the pangolin defends itself without a single blow.
payload.title: How the pangolin's scales protect it from predators
decoys: The pangolin rolls into an armoured ball
Its scales are as hard as fingernails

payload.passage: Tara collected old stamps and was delighted when the post office released a fresh set marking the country's railways. Each tiny picture showed a different engine, from a puffing steam train to a sleek modern one. The clerk told her that such stamps are printed in limited numbers, so collectors hurry to buy them on the first day. More than decoration, the set quietly taught buyers a slice of the nation's history. Tara saw that a stamp can be a stick-on storybook, carrying memory and pride in a square the size of a thumbnail.
payload.title: Special stamps tell a nation's story
decoys: The new stamps pictured many kinds of trains
Collecting things can be a rewarding hobby
Limited stamps sell quickly on the first day

payload.passage: A simple pair of spectacles for reading helps older eyes see close print. As people age, the lens inside the eye grows stiff and cannot bend enough. Small letters held nearby then look blurred. A reading lens does the extra bending the eye can no longer manage. Slipping them on, a grandparent can once again enjoy a book or a newspaper.
payload.title: How reading glasses help older eyes see close up
decoys: The eye's lens grows stiff with age
A reading lens does the extra bending

payload.passage: Ira's small candle business made a tidy sum during the festival season, and she was tempted to relax once the rush ended. Her mother warned that the quiet months would come, when few people bought candles at all. Wisely, Ira set aside part of her festival earnings to carry her through the lean weeks ahead. When sales dipped, she was not caught short. Ira learnt that a steady business saves from its good months to survive its slow ones, smoothing out the ups and downs of an uneven year.
payload.title: Saving in good months to survive lean ones
decoys: Ira set aside part of her festival earnings
Candle sales dipped in the quiet months

payload.passage: Two boys set up rival juice stalls on the same street, and at first Reyansh simply tried to shout louder than the other. It barely helped. Then he noticed that customers wanted shade and a clean glass more than noise, so he added a small umbrella and washed his cups carefully. Soon his stall drew the bigger crowd, not because it was cheaper but because it served people better. Reyansh learnt that in a fair competition, the winner is often the one who listens to what customers truly want.
payload.title: Winning customers by serving them better
decoys: Reyansh added a small umbrella for shade
Competition pushes people to try harder
Two boys ran rival juice stalls

payload.passage: A kite needs more than just wind to climb into the sky. As you run, the kite tilts so that air rushes past it. The flat face of the kite pushes the rushing air downwards. In return, the air pushes the kite upwards with a force called lift. The string in your hand holds the kite at the right tilt so the lift keeps it high. Aeroplane wings rise into the air using this very same force.
payload.title: How lift keeps a kite up in the sky
decoys: The kite pushes rushing air downwards
Flying things have always amazed people
Aeroplane wings rise using lift too

payload.passage: Why do doctors warn against eating in a great hurry? When you gulp food too fast, you swallow large pieces and a lot of air. Your stomach then has to work much harder to break the big chunks down. Eating fast also stops your body from noticing it is full, so you may eat too much. Slow, careful eating is gentler and healthier for the body.
payload.title: Why eating slowly is better for the body
decoys: Gulping food swallows large pieces and air
Eating fast hides the full feeling

payload.passage: Veer had promised to help his friend move house on Sunday, but a much better invitation to a cricket match arrived. He was sorely tempted to make an excuse and go to the match instead. He pictured his friend waiting, counting on his help with the heavy boxes. He turned down the match and spent the day lifting and carrying. His tired friend was deeply grateful. Veer learnt that a promise stays binding even when a brighter offer comes along to tempt you.
payload.title: A promise binds even when better offers tempt
decoys: Veer kept his promise to help move house
Moving house means lifting heavy boxes
A cricket match invitation tempted him

payload.passage: Why do you blink without ever deciding to? Blinking is far too important to leave to your busy thoughts. A part of your brain keeps your eyes blinking on their own, again and again. Each blink spreads tears and keeps the eye clean and clear. So your eyes are cared for all day long, even when your mind is on other things.
payload.title: Why we blink without thinking about it
decoys: A part of the brain keeps us blinking
Each blink keeps the eye clean

payload.passage: Ira noticed that her town set aside money each year for a thing called maintenance, spent on roads and pipes that already worked fine. She thought it a waste until a neighbouring town's neglected bridge collapsed. Her father explained that a little spent on regular care prevented a huge cost from sudden ruin. Fixing small cracks early was far cheaper than rebuilding after a disaster. Ira learnt that wise spending includes caring for what you already have, and that ignoring upkeep to save money today often costs far more tomorrow.
payload.title: Why spending on upkeep prevents costly ruin
decoys: Money was set aside for maintenance
Fixing small cracks early is cheaper

payload.passage: A green roof, covered in plants, does more than just look pretty. The layer of soil and leaves keeps the building cooler in the hot months. It soaks up rain that would otherwise rush into the drains. The plants clean the air and give bees and butterflies a place to feed. A roof full of greenery turns wasted space into a small helper for the city.
payload.title: How a green roof helps cool and clean a city
decoys: A green roof keeps a building cooler
Plants are nice to have around
A green roof soaks up the rain

payload.passage: A pond near a village is busier than it first looks. Frogs, fish and dragonflies all make their homes in and around the water. Birds visit to drink and to hunt for insects among the reeds. The plants give shelter and clean the water as they grow. When people dump waste into the pond, this whole web of life is put in danger.
payload.title: Why a pond is a home worth protecting
decoys: Frogs and fish live in the pond
Water is needed by all living things
Dumping waste harms the pond's life

payload.passage: The stars overhead in winter are not the same as those we see in summer. As the Earth circles the sun through the year, our night side faces out toward different parts of space. In one season we look toward one set of distant stars. Half a year later, on the far side of our orbit, we face the opposite way and see quite different ones. So the slow journey of the Earth gradually changes the show of stars on display each season. People once used these shifting patterns to tell the time of year.
payload.title: Why we see different stars in different seasons
decoys: Our night side faces different parts of space
The sky is always slowly changing
Winter stars differ from the stars of summer

payload.passage: Scattered through space are vast clouds of gas and dust, the nurseries of stars. Here gravity slowly draws the thin material together into thickening clumps. As a clump packs ever tighter, its centre grows hotter and denser. When it becomes hot enough, it begins to shine, and a new star is born. From such quiet clouds came our own sun, long ago in the deep past; so every star, including our sun, has a birthplace among these vast, drifting clouds scattered through space.
payload.title: How stars are born inside clouds of gas and dust
decoys: Gravity draws thin material into thickening clumps
The universe is always making something new
Our own sun was born from such a cloud long ago

payload.passage: In some hillsides, clear water flows out of the ground on its own. This is a spring, fed by rain that soaked into the earth long before. The water sinks through soil and rock until it meets a layer it cannot pass. Where that layer reaches the surface, the trapped water seeps out as a spring. From there it trickles away to join streams, returning to the water cycle; so a clear hillside spring is really old rain, returning to the surface to rejoin the endless cycle of water.
payload.title: How a spring bubbles up from underground water
decoys: Water sinks until it meets a layer it cannot pass
Water finds many paths through nature
Spring water trickles away to join the streams

payload.passage: The Emperor penguin father takes on one of the hardest jobs in the animal world. After the mother lays a single egg, she returns to the distant sea to feed, leaving the egg with him. Through the darkest, coldest weeks of the Antarctic winter, the father balances the egg on his feet and covers it with a warm flap of skin.
