He eats nothing for two whole months, huddling with other fathers against the killing wind. When the chick finally hatches, the mother returns with food. The father's long, patient fast keeps the chick alive.
payload.title: How the penguin father guards the egg through winter
decoys: The father penguin balances the egg on his feet
Penguins lay eggs in the cold Antarctic
He eats nothing for two months

payload.passage: Aadhya was surprised that the panchayat spent a whole evening simply writing down its decisions in a register instead of acting at once. Her father explained that a written record stopped future quarrels about what had really been agreed. Months later, when someone claimed a different decision, the elders just opened the book and settled it. Memory could be argued over; the written page could not. Aadhya learnt that careful records were not a waste of an evening but a shield against confusion and dishonesty in the years to come.
payload.title: Why a council writes down its decisions
decoys: The elders wrote decisions in a register
Memory can be argued over later

payload.passage: Oil spilled into the sea spreads into a thin, shining film on the water. This film blocks the sunlight and air that sea creatures need. Seabirds get their feathers soaked in the sticky oil and can no longer fly or stay warm. Fish and other animals fall sick or die in the poisoned water. A single spill can harm a stretch of coast for many years.
payload.title: Why oil spills are so harmful to the sea
decoys: Oil spreads into a thin film on the water
The sea is full of life
Seabirds get their feathers soaked in oil

payload.passage: Rehan saw two stalls selling identical umbrellas, yet one was always busier than the other. Curious, he watched closely and saw that the busy seller greeted each shopper warmly, answered questions patiently and let buyers test the umbrellas. The other seller barely looked up from his phone. The goods were the same, but the service was not. Rehan learnt that when products are alike, the way a seller treats people can quietly decide who wins the customer and who watches them walk past.
payload.title: How friendly service wins identical-goods customers
decoys: The busy seller greeted each shopper warmly

payload.passage: Sneha discovered a shortcut in the maths test: she could glance at a clever girl's answers in the next row. For a few questions she was tempted as the clock ticked down. Then she shut her eyes for a moment and chose to attempt them herself, right or wrong. She got two wrong but the rest were truly hers. When the teacher later explained those two, Sneha finally understood them. She learnt that honest mistakes teach you, while copied answers leave you just as lost as before.
payload.title: Honest mistakes teach more than copied answers
decoys: Sneha attempted the maths questions herself
Tests are taken against the clock
She got two of the questions wrong

payload.passage: Our sun is not alone; a family of planets keeps it company. Each planet follows its own oval path, called an orbit, around the sun. The sun's strong gravity holds them all in place, like an invisible string. Planets close to the sun race around quickly, while those far away take many years for one loop. Together the sun and these circling worlds make up our solar system; astronomers have studied these paths for centuries and can now predict exactly where each planet will be far into the future.
payload.title: How the planets travel around the sun
decoys: Planets close to the sun race around quickly
Space is a vast and wonderful place
The sun's gravity holds the planets in their paths

payload.passage: Kabir kept hearing the word inflation on the news and finally asked his sister what it meant. She explained that over time the same note tends to buy a little less, as prices slowly creep upward. A coin that bought two sweets for their mother once buys only one for them. This is why simply hiding cash in a tin for ten years can quietly shrink its real worth, even though the number stays the same. Kabir understood that money must usually grow at least as fast as prices, or its true power gently melts away.
payload.title: How rising prices quietly shrink saved cash
decoys: A coin once bought more sweets than today
The world keeps changing over the years
Inflation means prices slowly creep upward

payload.passage: When the council planned a new well, a clever young member insisted they ask the women who fetched water exactly where it should be dug. The men had wanted it near the temple, but the women knew a spot closer to most homes and to good underground water. The council listened, and the well served far more people. Krish saw that those who used a thing daily often understood it best. He learnt that asking the people closest to a problem can turn a fair plan into a truly good one.
payload.title: Why asking daily users improves a plan
decoys: The women knew the best spot for water
The men preferred a site near the temple

payload.passage: A flower's beauty is not just for our enjoyment; it has a purpose. Bright colours and sweet scents are signals aimed at insects and birds. These visitors come seeking the flower's sugary nectar as food. As they feed, they brush against the flower and pick up dusty pollen. They then carry that pollen to the next flower, helping it form seeds. A flower's display is really an invitation, offering a meal in return for help making seeds; so the loveliness of a flower is, in the end, a clever bargain struck between the plant and its visitors.
payload.title: Why flowers use bright colours and sweet smells
decoys: Visitors come seeking the flower's sweet nectar
Nature is full of clever partnerships
Pollen carried to the next flower helps form seeds

payload.passage: Why does a runner take deep breaths even before the race begins? A hard race will soon ask the muscles for a great deal of oxygen. By breathing deeply at the start, the runner fills the lungs and loads the blood with oxygen. The heart can then deliver this oxygen the moment the sprint begins. Preparing the breath this way helps the body meet the sudden demand.
payload.title: Why deep breaths prepare the body for effort
decoys: Deep breaths load the blood with oxygen
The body readies itself for action
A hard race demands much oxygen

payload.passage: When the moon appears cut neatly in half, it reveals exactly where the sunlight is coming from. At this phase, the moon sits at a right angle to the line between the Earth and the sun. The sun lights one side of the moon while the other stays dark, and we see the boundary edge-on. That straight line down the middle marks where day meets night on the moon. So a half moon is really a clear lesson in how sunlight falls upon it.
payload.title: Why a half moon shows the sunlight's angle
decoys: The lit and dark sides meet in a straight line
The night sky teaches us many things
The moon sits at a right angle to the sun's line

payload.passage: Myra's grandfather still remembered when the railway first reached their small town, and how it changed everything. Before the line, their famous mangoes rotted because no cart could carry them far enough in time. Once the trains came, the fruit reached distant cities fresh, and farmers earned far more for the same crop. New shops, jobs and visitors followed the tracks into the once-sleepy town. Myra understood that the railway had brought not merely faster travel but a wave of trade and prosperity that reshaped her family's fortunes.
payload.title: How a railway line transformed a small town
decoys: Mangoes once rotted before reaching distant cities
Transport plays a big part in any economy
New shops and visitors followed the tracks

payload.passage: The stars on a winter night are not the same as those of a summer one. As the Earth circles the sun across the year, our night side faces different parts of space. In one season we gaze toward one set of distant stars. Half a year later, on the opposite side of our orbit, we face the other way. So the show of constellations slowly changes with the seasons. People once used these shifting stars to tell the time of year.
payload.title: Why a starry sky looks different each season
decoys: Our night side faces different parts of space
The sky changes slowly over time
People used shifting stars to tell the time of year

payload.passage: Sneezing is a sudden, powerful blast that your body does on purpose. When dust or pollen tickles the inside of your nose, tiny sensors raise the alarm. Your body answers by taking a deep breath and then forcing it out in a rush. This blast shoots the dust and germs back out of your nose. A sneeze is really your nose cleaning itself in an instant.
payload.title: Why we sneeze to clear the nose
decoys: Dust tickling the nose raises an alarm
A sneeze forces air out in a rush

payload.passage: Bones may look dry and dead, but inside you they are very much alive. A living bone has a hard outer shell for strength. Deep inside lies a soft, jelly-like part where new blood is made every day. Bones also store minerals the body can call on when needed. And like skin, a broken bone can slowly mend and grow strong again.
payload.title: How living bones grow, mend and make blood
decoys: A soft part inside the bone makes blood
The body is full of living surprises
A broken bone can slowly mend

payload.passage: A pair of binoculars brings a faraway bird close enough to study. Inside each tube sit lenses that bend light to make things look larger. Two tubes work together so you see with both eyes at once. Small angled mirrors fold the light inside, keeping the tubes short. With binoculars, watchers can enjoy distant birds, hills and games in fine detail.
payload.title: How binoculars make distant things look near
decoys: Lenses bend light to make things look larger
Inventions widen what we can see
Angled mirrors fold the light inside

payload.passage: When the new shopping mall opened, the small shops on Aarush's street feared they would all be wiped out. Yet the old tailor survived, because he stitched clothes to each customer's exact measurements, something the giant mall could never match. The local grocer survived by knowing every family's name and delivering to their door. The mall won on price and variety, but the small shops won on personal care. Aarush learnt that a tiny business can stand beside a giant by offering the close, human touch that bigness cannot copy.
payload.title: How small shops survive beside a big mall
decoys: The tailor stitched clothes to exact measurements
Big and small businesses both exist
The mall won on price and variety

payload.passage: Step out of a dark cinema hall into bright daylight and you squint for a while. Your eyes hold a tiny round window called the pupil that lets light inside. In the dark, the pupil opens wide to gather every bit of light. In bright sunshine it shrinks small so that too much light does not flood in. This is why your eyes need a few seconds to adjust each time the light changes.
payload.title: How the eye adjusts to bright and dim light
decoys: The pupil opens wide in the dark
The eye is a remarkable part of the body
Bright daylight can make you squint

payload.passage: Many seeds drop in autumn but do not sprout right away. If they grew at once, the harsh winter cold would kill the tender shoots. So the seeds rest quietly in the cool soil, biding their time. When spring brings warmth and moisture, the resting seeds finally stir and germinate. By waiting out the cold, they give their young plants a far better chance to thrive; this patient waiting, set off by the warmth of spring, helps a plant give its seedlings the best possible start.
payload.title: How seeds rest through winter and wake in spring
decoys: Tender shoots would die in the winter cold
Living things adapt to the world around them
Spring warmth and moisture wake the resting seeds

payload.passage: Why does your nose sometimes bleed in very dry weather? The inside of your nose is lined with delicate skin and many tiny blood vessels. In dry air, this lining can crack like dry ground. A small crack can break one of the fine vessels just beneath. A little blood then trickles out until the tiny break seals itself again.
payload.title: Why the nose can bleed in dry weather
decoys: Dry air can crack the lining of the nose
A crack can break a fine blood vessel

payload.passage: A simple thermometer rises and falls to tell us how warm things are. Inside the thin glass tube sits a slim thread of liquid. When the air or water around it warms up, the liquid spreads out and creeps up the tube. When it cools, the liquid shrinks and slides back down. By reading where the thread stops against the marked scale, we learn the temperature.
payload.title: How a thermometer measures temperature
decoys: The liquid spreads out when it warms
Measuring things is useful in many ways
A thermometer has a marked scale on it

payload.passage: The sloth moves so slowly through the rainforest trees that it seems an easy meal, yet it is hard for hunters to find. The secret lies in its slowness itself. Because the sloth barely moves, tiny green algae grow right in its shaggy fur, tinting it the colour of the leaves around it. Hanging still among the branches, the sloth looks like just another clump of green foliage. Sharp-eyed eagles searching for movement glide right past it. By being slow and greenish, the sloth hides in plain sight high in the canopy.
payload.title: How the slow sloth hides among green leaves
decoys: Green algae grow in the sloth's fur
Sloths live high in rainforest trees

payload.passage: A tall tree is far more than a quiet green giant; it is a working part of the water cycle. Its roots drink up huge amounts of water from deep in the soil. Most of that water travels up the trunk and slips out of the leaves as invisible vapour. This vapour rises to help form the very clouds that will later rain. When the rain returns, the tree drinks again, and the loop goes on. So a forest is not just fed by the cycle but helps to drive it.
payload.title: How a single tree takes part in the water cycle
decoys: Water slips out of the leaves as vapour
Trees are useful to the world in many ways
A forest helps to drive the water cycle along

payload.passage: The flounder is a flat fish that spends its life lying on the seabed, and it has become a master of vanishing. Its skin can change colour and even pattern to copy the sand or pebbles beneath it almost exactly. If it settles on speckled gravel, dark spots appear on its body within minutes. Lying still and flat, it becomes nearly invisible to both the prey it waits for and the hunters that seek it. Only its watchful eyes, raised on top, give any hint it is there. By matching the very floor of the sea, the flounder hides in the open.
payload.title: How the flounder vanishes against the seabed
decoys: A flounder's skin can match speckled gravel
Many fish live on the floor of the sea
Its eyes sit on top of its body

payload.passage: When the dry season scorches the African plains, most animals must search far and wide for shrinking water. The elephants, however, carry a map in their memory. The oldest female, the matriarch, has lived through many droughts and remembers distant water holes that still hold a little to drink. She leads the thirsty herd across the cracked earth straight to these hidden places. Without her old knowledge the young ones might wander and die. The herd's survival in the worst times rests on the long memory of its eldest member.
payload.title: How an old elephant's memory saves the herd
decoys: The matriarch remembers distant water holes
Droughts dry up water on the plains
The oldest female leads the thirsty herd

payload.passage: The Alaskan blackfish lives in shallow pools that freeze nearly solid every winter, a death sentence for most fish. But this hardy little fish has a way to endure. As the water turns to ice around it, the fish slows its body almost to a stop and can survive being trapped in the freezing mud and ice for long spells. It carries a special ability to take in oxygen even from the icy slush. When the spring thaw frees the pool, the blackfish swims on as if nothing had happened. By enduring the freeze, it survives where others perish.
payload.title: How the blackfish survives in nearly frozen pools
decoys: The blackfish endures being trapped in ice
Shallow pools can freeze in winter
It swims on after the spring thaw

payload.passage: When the class chose teams for the project, no one wanted the slow worker, Bittu, who was always picked last. Riya was team leader and could have left him out. Instead she welcomed him and gave him a task that suited his careful nature. Bittu, trusted at last, did his part beautifully. The team did well, and Bittu beamed all week. The others, who had always picked him last, looked at Bittu with new eyes. Riya learnt that giving an overlooked person a real chance can bring out a talent no one expected.
payload.title: Giving the overlooked a chance reveals hidden talent
decoys: Riya welcomed Bittu onto her team
Slow workers are often picked last

payload.passage: Arjun begged his parents for the newest phone the moment an advertisement filled the television screen with its glow. His mother asked him to wait one week and see if he still wanted it as badly. Within days the thrilling feeling faded, and he realised his old phone worked perfectly well. The advertisement, she explained, was designed to make a passing wish feel like an urgent need. Arjun learnt that pausing before a big purchase lets a clever advertisement's spell wear off, saving both money and regret.
payload.title: How a short wait defeats an advert's spell
decoys: His old phone worked perfectly well
His mother asked him to wait a week

payload.passage: The change from day to night feels gentle, but it springs from a steady, ceaseless motion. Our planet spins like a slow top, turning once roughly every twenty-four hours. As it turns, the side facing the sun enjoys daylight. Slowly that side rotates away, and dusk falls as the sun sinks from view. Then comes night, until the same spin brings the sun back at dawn. So the daily round of light and dark is the simple result of the turning Earth.
payload.title: How day turns to night as the Earth spins
decoys: The side facing the sun enjoys daylight
The Earth's movements shape our lives
The same spin brings the sun back at dawn

payload.passage: A simple funnel pours liquid into a narrow bottle without a spill. Its wide mouth catches the liquid easily as you pour. The sides slope down to a small spout that fits the bottle's neck. The liquid is guided smoothly from the wide top to the narrow bottom. Thanks to this little cone, even a clumsy pour reaches the bottle cleanly.
payload.title: How a funnel guides liquid into a narrow bottle
decoys: The sides slope down to a small spout
The wide mouth catches the liquid

payload.passage: The moon does more for us than light the night; it quietly steadies our whole planet. As the Earth spins, it tends to wobble slightly on its axis. The steady pull of the moon helps to hold that wobble in check. With the wobble kept small, the Earth's tilt stays fairly even over long ages. A steady tilt means our seasons remain dependable rather than wild. So the faithful moon helps keep the Earth a calm and livable world; in this quiet way, our nearest neighbour in space helps make life on Earth more settled.
payload.title: How the moon's gentle pull steadies the Earth
decoys: The moon's pull holds the Earth's wobble in check
The moon affects our planet in many ways
A steady tilt keeps the seasons dependable

payload.passage: Why does the doctor tap your knee with a small hammer? When the hammer taps just below the knee, it stretches a muscle in your leg. Your body answers in a flash, before you can even think, by kicking the leg out. This automatic action is called a reflex. Reflexes protect you by reacting far faster than careful thought ever could.
payload.title: How reflexes make the body react in a flash
decoys: The tap stretches a muscle in the leg
The body protects us in clever ways
A reflex reacts faster than thought

payload.passage: A simple stethoscope lets a doctor listen to sounds inside the body. Its round end rests against your chest and picks up faint sounds. These quiet sounds travel up through hollow tubes to the doctor's ears. The tubes shut out other noise and make the body's sounds clearer. By listening, a doctor can check whether the heart and lungs are working well.
payload.title: How a stethoscope lets doctors hear inside us
decoys: Sounds travel up the hollow tubes
The round end rests against the chest

payload.passage: Inside a tall earthen mound, millions of termites live and work with no leader giving orders. Some workers tend the eggs, some gather plant matter, and some build endless tunnels of mud and spit. The mound itself is a marvel, with narrow shafts that let hot air rise and escape, keeping the nest cool in the fierce sun. Soldier termites with huge jaws guard every crack against ants. Each tiny insect does only one small job, yet together they raise a structure taller than a person. Their shared, silent labour is their strength.
payload.title: How tiny termites build a great mound together
decoys: Termite mounds have shafts that release hot air
Many insects live together in large groups
Soldier termites guard the nest with big jaws

payload.passage: Geeta had trained all year to win the long-distance run and was leading near the finish. Then she saw a younger runner faint from the heat by the track's edge. The finish line was just steps away and the trophy almost hers. Geeta turned aside, called for help, and stayed with the fainting girl until she was safe. She lost the race but won the crowd's heart. The fainting girl recovered soon, thanks to the help Geeta had called for. Geeta learnt that a trophy is never worth more than a person's safety.
payload.title: No trophy is worth more than a person's safety
decoys: Geeta stopped to help a fainting runner
Long-distance runs are tiring in heat
She was leading near the finish line

payload.passage: Keeping food fresh for months without a fridge once seemed impossible. The invention of canning solved this neatly. Food is sealed inside an airtight metal tin and then heated strongly. The heat kills the germs that would spoil it, and the seal keeps new germs out. Sealed this way, food can be stored and carried safely for a very long time.
payload.title: How canning keeps food safe for months
decoys: Heat kills the germs inside a sealed tin
Clever ideas help us store our food
Canned food can be carried far away

payload.passage: Asha's grandmother could no longer thread a needle, and her beloved hobby of stitching was slipping away. The cousins thought the old lady's complaints tiresome and ignored them. Asha quietly began threading the needles for her each evening and sitting nearby as she sewed. Her grandmother's joy in stitching returned. Each night the soft scratch of her needle filled the quiet room once more. Asha learnt that a little patience and a small helping hand can give back to someone a happiness they thought was lost for good.
payload.title: A small hand can restore a lost happiness
decoys: Asha threaded needles for her grandmother
Old eyes find threading needles hard
The cousins ignored the old lady

payload.passage: Birds have hollow bones, which seems strange for animals that must be strong. Bones full of air would surely be weaker than solid ones. But these light bones make the bird's whole body much lighter to carry. A lighter body is far easier to lift into the air and keep flying. So the hollow bones are a clever trade that helps birds rule the sky.
payload.title: How hollow bones help birds fly
decoys: Birds have bones that are full of air
Animals are wonderfully suited to their lives
Hollow bones make a bird's body lighter

payload.passage: A simple key and lock guard our homes with a clever puzzle inside. Within the lock sit small pins of different heights blocking the turn. The correct key has a jagged edge cut to match those exact heights. When the right key slides in, it lifts each pin to just the right level. Only then can the lock turn and the door open.
payload.title: How a key and lock keep a door secure
decoys: Small pins inside the lock block the turn
Inventions help keep our homes safe
The right key lifts each pin to the right level

payload.passage: Hriday felt rich the moment a relative handed him a thick bundle of small notes for the festival. Within a single afternoon, however, the bundle had melted into snacks, toys and games he barely remembered the next day. His older cousin asked what he had to show for it, and Hriday had nothing. Spending without a thought, he realised, made money vanish faster than it ever came. Hriday learnt that having money and keeping money are two different skills, and that the second one needs a little planning and self-control.
payload.title: Why having money differs from keeping money
decoys: The bundle melted into snacks and toys
He had nothing left to show by evening

payload.passage: Why does your body make tears even when you are not crying? A thin layer of tears bathes your eyes all the time. These tears keep the surface smooth, clean and free of dust. They also carry helpful substances that fight germs trying to settle on the eye. So tears are not only for sadness; they quietly guard your eyes every moment.
payload.title: Why tears protect the eyes all the time
decoys: A thin layer of tears bathes the eyes
The body protects its delicate parts
Tears fight germs on the eye

payload.passage: Cool air-conditioning feels wonderful, yet it asks a lot of the planet. The machine uses a great deal of electricity, most of it made by burning coal. It also pumps warm air out into the street, heating the city a little more. Setting the temperature a notch higher and using fans can cut this cost. Using the cooler less often is a kindness to the earth as well as the bill.
payload.title: Why we should use air-conditioning sparingly
decoys: An air-conditioner uses a lot of electricity
Cooling machines warm the city outside

payload.passage: Reyansh saw the council plant rows of young trees along the dusty main road and grumbled that the money could have bought something useful now. An elder smiled and said the trees were a gift to the future. In ten years they would shade the road, cool the air and shelter birds, long after today's small cost was forgotten. Some spending, the elder said, plants benefits that ripen slowly. Reyansh learnt that wise communities, like wise savers, sometimes spend today on things whose true reward will only be enjoyed by tomorrow.
payload.title: Why some spending is a gift to the future
decoys: The council planted young roadside trees
The trees would shade the road in time

payload.passage: Why do doctors say a few minutes of quiet rest can help a tired mind? Your brain works hard all day, taking in sights, sounds and lessons. Like a muscle, it grows tired if it never gets a pause. A short, quiet rest lets the brain settle and refresh itself. After even a brief break, you can often think more clearly and feel less weary.
payload.title: Why short rests refresh a tired mind
decoys: The brain grows tired without a pause
A break helps you think more clearly

payload.passage: Earth has just one moon, but some planets are circled by dozens. A planet's gravity decides how many it can hold. The giant gas planets are so massive that their strong pull can capture and keep many moons. Smaller, rocky planets have weaker pulls and so gather few or none. The number of moons a planet keeps is closely tied to how large and heavy that planet is; so counting a planet's moons can give a rough clue to its size, with the giants keeping crowds and the smaller worlds keeping few.
payload.title: Why some planets have many moons
decoys: Giant gas planets can capture and keep many moons
There is endless variety among the planets
Smaller rocky planets have only a few moons or none

payload.passage: Why does your stomach sometimes make a loud rumbling sound? Your stomach and the long tube below it are always gently squeezing. When they are empty, this squeezing moves mostly air and juices about. The trapped air sloshing through the empty tube makes that rumbling noise. The sound is louder when you are hungry and the stomach has little food inside.
payload.title: Why an empty stomach rumbles
decoys: The stomach is always gently squeezing
The body makes many curious sounds
Trapped air sloshing makes the noise

payload.passage: A single dripping tap wastes far more water than most people guess. One slow drip may seem like nothing at all. But those drips add up, drop by drop, hour after hour, all through the day and night. In a single week a leaky tap can waste a whole bucket or more. Fixing the drip is a small repair that saves a great deal of precious water.
payload.title: Why fixing a dripping tap saves so much water
decoys: One slow drip seems like nothing
We must care for natural resources
A leaky tap wastes a bucket each week

payload.passage: The orb of a golden silk spider is so large and strong it can trap not just insects but sometimes even small birds. The spider spins its silk from special glands, and this thread is astonishingly tough for its thinness, stronger than a strand of steel of the same width. The spider lays sticky spirals to catch prey and dry lines to walk on safely. The golden colour of the silk may even lure insects in the dappled sunlight. By weaving such powerful silk, this spider builds a trap that few flying creatures can break free from.
payload.title: How the golden silk spider weaves a powerful trap
decoys: The spider's silk is stronger than steel of its width
Spiders spin webs to catch prey
It lays sticky spirals and dry lines

payload.passage: Naveen was trusted to carry the day's collection from the school fair to the office. A torn note fell out unseen on the path, and he found it later in his pocket. He could have kept the stray rupees for himself, sure no one would ever count so closely. Instead he added it back and reported the exact amount. The teacher praised his careful honesty before the whole committee. Naveen learnt that when others trust you with money, every single coin is a small test of your word.
payload.title: Trust with money tests you coin by coin
decoys: Naveen carried the fair collection to the office
School fairs collect money for the school
A torn note fell out on the path

payload.passage: Far out at sea, a single sardine is an easy meal for any larger fish. So when danger nears, thousands of sardines suddenly swirl together into a huge, shimmering ball. The shoal twists and folds as one, flashing silver in the sunlight to confuse the hunter's eye. A predator that darts in finds it almost impossible to fix on any single fish in the whirling crowd. By moving as one giant shape, the tiny sardines turn their weakness into a shared defence. There is real safety in their dazzling numbers.
payload.title: How sardines confuse hunters by swimming as one
decoys: Sardines swirl into a huge shimmering ball
Small fish are eaten by larger fish
The shoal flashes silver in the sunlight

payload.passage: Ishaan watched the panchayat invite a college student to teach the villagers how to use a new banking app on their phones. He thought the old folk would never bother, but many came eager to learn. With the app, they could send money or check balances without a long trip to town. The council had spent a little to open a big new door. Ishaan learnt that helping people gain a new skill could matter as much as building roads, and that a wise community invests in its people's knowledge too.
payload.title: Why a village invests in new skills
decoys: A student taught a banking app
Villagers could now send money easily

payload.passage: Why do you breathe in through your nose rather than your mouth when you can? Your nose is built to prepare the air before it reaches your lungs. It warms the cold air, adds moisture, and traps dust and germs in its lining. Air taken through the mouth skips all this cleaning and arrives raw. So nose breathing gives your lungs cleaner, gentler air.
payload.title: Why breathing through the nose is better
decoys: The nose warms and moistens the air

payload.passage: The lyrebird of the forest cannot fight or flee very well, but it owns one of nature's strangest gifts. It can copy almost any sound it hears with astonishing accuracy. A male lyrebird's song may weave together the calls of twenty other birds, one after another. It can even imitate sounds like a barking dog or a distant axe. The bird uses these borrowed songs to impress a mate and to claim its patch of forest. By collecting and replaying the voices around it, the clever lyrebird makes itself heard above all the rest.
payload.title: How the lyrebird survives by copying many sounds
decoys: A lyrebird can imitate a barking dog
Birds use songs to attract mates
Its song copies many other birds

payload.passage: Lata was certain her neighbour's son had stolen her bicycle bell, since he had admired it the day before. She nearly marched over to accuse him in front of his mother. First, though, she searched her own house once more and found the bell under a cushion. She felt cold at how close she had come to a false charge. She felt grateful she had checked her own house before saying a single word. Lata learnt that fairness means being absolutely sure before you accuse anyone, for a wrong accusation is hard to take back.
payload.title: Be sure before you accuse anyone
decoys: Lata found her bell under a cushion
Bicycle bells can be small and easy to lose
Her neighbour's son had admired the bell

payload.passage: The planets nearest the sun bask in far more warmth than the distant ones. This is simply a matter of distance. Close to the sun, its rays arrive strong and concentrated, heating the nearby worlds. Farther out, the same rays spread thin and weak across the cold gulf of space. So the inner planets can be hot while the outer ones stay frozen. A planet's distance from the sun is the main reason for its warmth or chill; so a planet's distance from the sun is the main reason it bakes in heat or lies locked in ice.
payload.title: Why the inner planets are warmer than the outer ones
decoys: Close to the sun, the rays arrive strong
The solar system holds great variety
Outer planets stay frozen in the cold of space

payload.passage: Salt seems to vanish when you stir it into a glass of water, but it is not truly gone. The water pulls the salt apart into pieces far too small for your eyes to see. These tiny pieces spread out evenly and slip between the bits of water. The salt is still there, which is why the water tastes salty. Leave the glass in the sun, the water drifts off as vapour, and the salt is left behind.
payload.title: Where salt goes when it dissolves in water
decoys: Water can do many surprising things
Water pulls salt into tiny pieces

payload.passage: Why does a wound feel warm and look red while it heals? When you hurt yourself, the body rushes extra blood to the spot. The fresh blood brings cells that fight germs and begin repairs. All that busy blood near the surface makes the area feel warm and look red. This swelling and warmth are signs that the body is hard at work mending the wound.
payload.title: Why a healing wound feels warm and looks red
decoys: Extra blood rushes to the hurt spot

payload.passage: Why does a cup of cold milk leave drops of water on its outside? The air around us holds a great deal of invisible water vapour. When this damp air touches the chilly surface of the cup, it cools quickly. The cooling makes the hidden vapour change into tiny drops of liquid water. Those drops cling to the cold cup, making it look wet.
payload.title: Why a cold cup gets wet on the outside
decoys: Damp air touches the chilly cup
Cold drinks leave drops on the glass

payload.passage: Every meal in nature can be traced back to the sun. Green plants catch sunlight and store its energy in their leaves and seeds. A grasshopper eats the plant and takes in some of that energy; a frog then eats the grasshopper and gains a share too. Finally a snake may eat the frog, passing the energy along once more. Step by step, the sun's energy travels up the chain from plant to animal to animal; at each step, though, much of the energy is used up, so only a little is left for the creatures higher up.
payload.title: How energy passes along a food chain
decoys: A frog can eat a grasshopper for its meal
Everything in nature is joined to everything else
Green plants store the sun's energy in their leaves

payload.passage: When a forest is cleared, the loss reaches far beyond the missing trees. Animals that lived there lose their homes and their food all at once. The bare ground bakes hard and washes away in the rains. Without the trees to soak it up, less rain returns to the clouds, so even the weather can shift. One cleared forest sends ripples through the whole living web.
payload.title: Why clearing a forest harms far more than the trees
decoys: Animals lose their homes when a forest goes
Bare ground washes away in the rains

payload.passage: Nidhi was tempted to spend her savings the moment they reached a tidy sum, but her grandfather told her a small story. A farmer who eats his seed grain has nothing to plant, while one who saves it reaps a whole field. Money, like seed, could either be eaten today or planted to grow more tomorrow. Nidhi decided to keep her savings growing instead of spending them at once. She learnt that the patient choice to hold and grow money, rather than consume it, was what slowly built real wealth.
payload.title: Why saved money is like seed to plant
decoys: A farmer who eats his seed has nothing

payload.passage: A pressure cooker did more than speed up cooking; it changed busy kitchens everywhere. By trapping steam under a tight lid, it lets water grow hotter than usual. The extra heat softens hard grains and lentils in a fraction of the normal time. Families saved both fuel and hours of waiting at the stove. This handy pot quickly became a treasured tool in millions of homes.
payload.title: How the pressure cooker reshaped busy kitchens
decoys: Trapped steam lets water grow hotter
Kitchen tools have changed home life
A pressure cooker saves fuel and time

payload.passage: A sunny meadow is a vast machine for turning light into living things. The grass and flowers catch the sunshine and build food within their leaves. Grasshoppers and rabbits feed on this greenery and grow. Foxes, birds and snakes then feed on the plant-eaters. When creatures die, tiny decomposers return their goodness to the soil for new plants. The whole busy meadow runs, from start to finish, on the energy of the sun; so a sunny field is, in a sense, a great green machine for turning light into living things.
payload.title: How a green meadow turns sunlight into life
decoys: Grasshoppers and rabbits feed on the greenery
Sunlight supports life across the land
Decomposers return goodness to the soil

payload.passage: A simple loud siren warns a whole town of coming danger. A motor spins a disc with many slots past a stream of air. As the slots open and close the air over and over, they chop it into a wailing sound. The sound rises so loud that it carries for miles around. People hear the siren and quickly take shelter from a storm or fire.
payload.title: How a siren warns a whole town of danger
decoys: Slots chop the air into a wailing sound
The siren carries for miles around

payload.passage: Why does eating too many sweets harm your teeth? Sweets leave sugar clinging to the surface of your teeth. Tiny germs in your mouth feed greedily on this sugar. As they feed, they make an acid that slowly eats into the hard outer layer of the teeth. Over time this leads to holes and toothache, which is why sweets are best eaten rarely.
payload.title: Why too many sweets damage the teeth
decoys: Germs feed on the sugar left on teeth
What we eat affects our health
Acid slowly eats the teeth's outer layer

payload.passage: Isha's little brother broke their mother's favourite vase and began to cry in fear. When their mother asked what happened, the boy looked desperately at Isha to take the blame for him. Isha knew lying to shield him would only teach him to hide his faults. Gently she told her brother to speak the truth himself, and she stood beside him while he did. Their mother forgave him for his honesty. Isha learnt that real love sometimes means letting someone face their own small mistakes.
payload.title: Real love lets others own their mistakes
decoys: Isha's brother broke their mother's vase
Small children fear scolding for breakages
Mothers often have a favourite vase

payload.passage: Why does the body need a mix of foods rather than one favourite dish? No single food carries everything the body needs to thrive. One gives energy, another builds muscle, and a third protects you from illness. Eating only one thing, however tasty, leaves gaps your body cannot fill. A varied plate covers all these needs and keeps you truly well.
payload.title: Why a varied diet keeps the body well
decoys: One food gives energy, another builds muscle

payload.passage: Why does your body sometimes get goose bumps when you are cold or scared? Tiny muscles at the base of each hair can pull the hair upright. Long ago, raised hair helped trap warmth and made animals look bigger. In us, the same muscles still tug, raising small bumps on the skin. Goose bumps are a leftover from our distant past that the body still keeps.
payload.title: Why the body gets goose bumps
decoys: Tiny muscles pull each hair upright

payload.passage: Harsh had bragged to everyone that he would top the maths exam without any help at all. When a tricky chapter defeated him, his pride almost stopped him asking his sister to explain it. Swallowing that pride, he finally admitted he was stuck and asked her to teach him slowly. She did, patiently, and he understood the topic at last. He scored well, but more importantly he learnt that asking for help is not weakness; it is the wiser, humbler path to actually getting better.
payload.title: Asking for help is wisdom, not weakness
decoys: Harsh asked his sister to teach him maths
A tricky chapter can defeat a confident student
Bragging about exams can be embarrassing later

payload.passage: On a school trip to the bank, Ira expected to see only counters and queues, but the manager showed her something deeper. He explained that when a farmer deposits the money from his harvest, the bank can lend it to a young woman opening a tailoring shop across town. Neither of them ever meets, yet the farmer's idle money becomes the tailor's new sewing machine. The bank quietly links a saver in one place to a borrower in another. Ira realised that a bank weaves strangers' fortunes together without their even knowing it.
payload.title: How a bank links savers to far-off borrowers
decoys: A farmer deposits his harvest money
Banks are interesting places to visit
The tailor buys a new sewing machine

payload.passage: Atharv was curious why some platforms had a long yellow line that everyone was told to stand behind. A railway officer explained that a fast train rushing through created a powerful gust and suction that could pull a careless person off balance. The yellow line marked a safe distance from that hidden danger. It looked like a mere stripe of paint, yet it quietly saved lives every day. Atharv learnt that a simple painted line, obeyed by all, was a small but vital rule protecting the careless from an unseen force.
payload.title: Why a yellow line keeps the platform safe
decoys: A fast train creates a powerful gust
The line marked a safe distance

payload.passage: Climb a tall mountain or fly high in the sky and the air becomes thin and hard to breathe. Gravity is the cause. It pulls the air down, so most of it gathers in a dense layer near the ground. The higher you go, the less air remains pressing above you. With fewer particles around, each breath holds less to use. The comfortable, thick air we breathe is kept low by the Earth's steady pull; so the comfortable, dense air we breathe is held close to the ground by the Earth's quiet pull.
payload.title: Why the air grows thinner higher above the Earth
decoys: Gravity pulls most of the air down near the ground
The Earth shapes its surroundings in many ways
Each high breath holds fewer particles to use

payload.passage: High inside a winter cloud the air can be far below freezing. There the water vapour does not make liquid droplets at all. Instead it freezes straight onto specks of dust, building delicate six-sided ice crystals. As these crystals bump and stick together, they grow into soft flakes of snow. When the flakes become heavy enough, they drift gently down to cover the ground in white; in this way the same water cycle that brings summer rain can paint a winter morning in glittering, silent white.
payload.title: How snow forms when clouds grow very cold
decoys: Ice crystals always grow with six neat sides
Winter brings many beautiful changes to the land
Snowflakes form when raindrops freeze on the way down

payload.passage: Why is it important to brush your teeth before bed each night? During the day, bits of food and a sticky film gather on your teeth. While you sleep, your mouth makes less saliva to wash this away. The film and food then slowly attack the teeth through the long night. A good brush before bed clears them away and guards your teeth till morning.
payload.title: Why brushing before bed protects the teeth
decoys: A sticky film gathers on the teeth by day
The mouth makes less saliva in sleep

payload.passage: Why does your body droop and slow down late at night? As the night wears on, your inner clock prepares you for deep rest. It slows your heartbeat and cools your body a little. It also makes you feel heavy-eyed and dull so you will lie down to sleep. Fighting this natural slowing only leaves you tired and out of step the next day.
payload.title: Why the body slows down late at night
decoys: The inner clock slows the heartbeat at night
The body follows its own rhythm
Heavy eyes make us lie down to sleep

payload.passage: Nikhil broke a window with a wild, looping cricket shot in an empty courtyard one evening. He looked quickly around, and it was clear that nobody had seen him do it. The other boys urged him in whispers to slip away before anyone came out. Nikhil stood frozen for a moment, the broken glass glittering on the floor. Then he walked over, knocked on the owner's door, owned up to the damage, and offered to pay for it from his small savings. The owner, moved by such rare honesty, asked only that he be more careful next time. Nikhil learnt that facing the music yourself is far lighter than carrying a guilty secret.
payload.title: Facing your fault is lighter than hiding it
decoys: Nikhil broke a window with a cricket shot
Cricket balls can easily break glass windows
Boys sometimes run away after breaking things

payload.passage: Nikita practised the high jump all season but could never clear the top bar. The other girls had given up trying to beat her own best mark, calling it her limit. Nikita refused to accept any limit and adjusted her run-up a little each day. On sports day she soared clean over the bar at last. The crowd gasped. Her coach hugged her and said he had always known she could do it. Nikita learnt that the limits others set for us are often just the point where they themselves stopped trying.
payload.title: Others' limits are just where they stopped
decoys: Nikita finally cleared the high-jump bar
High jump needs a good run-up
The other girls called her best her limit

payload.passage: Aarav and his sister both got the same pocket money, yet by month's end she always had some left while he had none. Curious, he watched how she handled hers. She set aside a small amount the moment she received it, then spent only what remained, while he spent first and tried to save whatever was left, which was nothing. The order made all the difference. Aarav learnt that the secret was saving before spending, not after, because money left for last has a way of disappearing.
payload.title: Why saving first beats saving last
decoys: His sister set money aside immediately
He spent first and saved nothing

payload.passage: Knowing exactly where you are in a strange place was once very hard. A satellite navigation device solved this neatly. It listens to signals beamed down by several satellites high above. By measuring how long each signal takes to arrive, it works out your exact spot. A map on the screen then shows you the way to your destination.
payload.title: How a navigation device finds where you are
decoys: The device listens to satellite signals
A map shows you the way to go

payload.passage: A streak of light darts across the night, and someone cries out about a shooting star. In truth it is no star, but a tiny speck of rock or dust from space. As it plunges into our air at great speed, it rubs against the air and heats up fiercely. The glowing trail we see is this speck burning away high above. Most are no larger than a grain of sand; on a clear, dark night you might spot several of these brief, glowing streaks, especially during a meteor shower.
payload.title: How a shooting star is not a star at all
decoys: Most shooting stars are no bigger than a sand grain
The night sky is full of surprises
A speck of rock heats up as it rubs the air

payload.passage: A drop of medicine poured down the sink does more harm than good. Old or unused medicines should never be flushed away. Through the drains they can reach rivers and ponds and harm the fish and water life. They may even slip into the water that people drink. Returning old medicines to a chemist for safe disposal keeps these chemicals out of nature.
payload.title: Why old medicines should not be flushed away
decoys: Medicines can reach rivers through drains
Such chemicals can harm water life

payload.passage: A roadside hedge of bushes does quiet work for a busy street. Its thick green leaves catch some of the dust and soot from passing traffic. The bushes muffle a little of the harsh road noise as well. Small birds nest within the branches, safe from the cars. So a simple hedge cleans the air, calms the noise and shelters life, all at once.
payload.title: How a roadside hedge helps a busy street
decoys: Hedge leaves catch dust from traffic
Small birds nest within the hedge

payload.passage: Ananya had spent all week building a tall tower of blocks for the model competition. Just before judging, a careless boy knocked it flat by accident and turned pale with worry. Ananya's first feeling was hot anger at the ruin of her work. Then she saw how sorry and frightened the boy truly was. She swallowed her anger and told him it was only an accident, then began rebuilding with a calm smile. Ananya learnt that forgiving a genuine mistake is harder, and finer, than holding on to anger.
payload.title: Forgiving a genuine mistake beats holding anger
decoys: A boy knocked over Ananya's block tower
Ananya rebuilt her tower after it fell

payload.passage: A simple ramp built beside steps lets a wheelchair reach the door. Steps are easy for walking feet but impossible for wheels. A gentle ramp turns a sharp climb into a smooth, rolling slope. A person can wheel themselves up little by little instead of facing a wall of stairs. Such ramps let many more people enter shops, schools and homes.
payload.title: How a ramp lets wheelchairs reach the door
decoys: A ramp turns a climb into a rolling slope

payload.passage: Frogs are sometimes called the messengers of a healthy wetland. Their thin skin soaks up whatever is in the water and air around them. When the water is clean, frogs thrive and sing loudly on rainy nights. When pollution creeps in, the frogs grow sick and quietly disappear. So watching how the frogs are doing tells us a lot about the health of a place.
payload.title: How frogs reveal whether a place is healthy
decoys: A frog's thin skin soaks up the water
Frogs sing loudly on rainy nights

payload.passage: Trees do far more than give us cool shade on a hot day. Their leaves take in a harmful gas from the air and give back fresh oxygen for us to breathe. Their deep roots hold the soil together, so it is not washed away in heavy rain. Birds, insects and squirrels make their homes among the branches. By planting and protecting trees, we look after the air, the soil and many living things at once.
payload.title: Why protecting trees helps the whole environment
decoys: Tree roots hold the soil in place
Nature gives us many gifts to enjoy
Trees give shade on a hot day

payload.passage: Each day feels reliably the same length, and the spinning Earth is why. Our planet turns at a remarkably even pace, completing one rotation in about twenty-four hours. This steady spin gives us a dependable rhythm of light and dark. People long ago used it to divide the day into hours. So the clock on your wall is really keeping time with the turning of the whole Earth; because the spin is so dependable, the rhythm of day and night has served as nature's oldest and most trusted clock.
payload.title: How the Earth's spin gives us a steady day length
decoys: People long ago divided the day into hours
The Earth completes one turn in about twenty-four hours

payload.passage: A leaf drifting down in autumn is not the end of its usefulness. Once on the ground, it begins to break apart with help from worms and fungi. Slowly it crumbles into dark, rich material full of nutrients. Rain washes these nutrients down into the soil where roots can reach them. New plants then take up this goodness to grow strong and green. A single fallen leaf completes a small circle, feeding the living plants around it; so even in falling, a leaf keeps serving the tree it came from and the forest all around.
payload.title: How a falling leaf returns life to the soil
decoys: Worms and fungi help the leaf break apart
New plants take up the goodness to grow strong

payload.passage: The vervet monkey troop in the African bush has worked out a clever way to warn of danger. The monkeys use different alarm calls for different enemies. One special bark means an eagle is overhead, and on hearing it the troop dives down into the bushes. A different chirp means a leopard prowls below, sending them rushing up into the safety of the trees. A third call warns of a snake in the grass, and they stand and peer at the ground. Because each danger has its own word, the monkeys always know exactly where to flee.
payload.title: How vervet monkeys use special calls for each danger
decoys: One vervet call means an eagle is overhead
A different call warns of a leopard

payload.passage: Why does laughing hard sometimes leave your tummy aching? A big laugh makes the muscles around your stomach squeeze again and again. These muscles are not used to working so fast for so long. After a long fit of laughter they grow tired and feel sore, much like after exercise. The friendly ache simply shows how hard those muscles worked.
payload.title: Why hard laughing makes the tummy ache
decoys: Laughing makes the stomach muscles squeeze
The body reacts in surprising ways
Tired muscles feel sore after laughing

payload.passage: Before refrigerated ships, no one in a cold country could taste a fresh tropical fruit. The invention of cold storage on ships changed world trade. Huge chilled rooms kept fruit, meat and fish cool throughout a long sea voyage. Food that would have rotted now arrived fresh on the far side of the world. People could enjoy foods grown thousands of miles away.
payload.title: How cold storage let food travel the world
decoys: Chilled rooms kept food cool at sea
New ideas have changed how we trade
Food once rotted on long sea voyages

payload.passage: In the queue for the new library books, the boys jostled and cut ahead of the smaller children. Karan had waited long and was nearly at the front. He noticed a tiny girl shoved to the back, near tears. He stepped out of his place and walked her to the front beside him, telling the others to let the little ones go first. Some grumbled, but they made way. Karan learnt that fairness often means using your own advantage to protect those who cannot push back.
payload.title: Use your advantage to protect the weak
decoys: Karan let a small girl go ahead of him
Children queue for new library books
Bigger boys cut ahead in the line

payload.passage: When a fierce storm tore the roof off a poor family's hut in the colony, the children gathered to watch. Most simply felt sorry and went home. Dev, though, emptied his money box and went door to door asking neighbours to give what they could. By evening he had gathered enough to help mend the roof. The family blessed him tearfully. The neighbours, shamed by a child's effort, gave more than he had hoped. Dev learnt that feeling pity changes nothing, but turning that feeling into action can truly change a life.
payload.title: Pity changes nothing until it becomes action
decoys: Dev collected money to mend a roof
Storms can tear roofs off huts
He emptied his own money box first

payload.passage: Why does your heart need valves inside it? The heart pumps blood out with every strong squeeze. Without a way to stop it, the blood would simply rush back in again. Small flaps called valves act like one-way doors between the heart's rooms. They snap shut after each beat so the blood can flow only one way around the body.
payload.title: How heart valves keep blood flowing one way
decoys: Valves act like one-way doors in the heart
The heart pumps blood with each squeeze

payload.passage: The praying mantis is a patient hunter that lets its disguise do half the work. Some kinds look exactly like green leaves, while the flower mantis is shaped and coloured like the petals of a bloom. It sits utterly still among the flowers, swaying gently in the breeze. Insects searching for nectar see only a pretty blossom and land right beside it. In a blur too fast for the eye, the mantis snaps out its spiny front legs and seizes the unsuspecting visitor. By dressing as a flower, the mantis brings its dinner straight to its arms.
payload.title: How the flower mantis lures prey by looking like a bloom
decoys: The flower mantis is shaped like petals
Insects land beside it seeking nectar

payload.passage: A simple knife may be the oldest tool of all. Its thin, sharp edge presses a great force onto a tiny line. That concentrated force slices easily through food, rope and wood. A blunt edge spreads the force out and only crushes instead of cutting. This is why a sharp knife cuts cleanly while a dull one struggles.
payload.title: Why a sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one
decoys: A sharp edge presses force onto a tiny line
Tools have served us for ages
A blunt edge only crushes things

payload.passage: On counting day, the result in Aarush's ward came down to just a handful of votes between the two candidates. Because the gap was so tiny, the officers carefully counted the same votes a second time to be absolutely sure. Every single ballot mattered. The recount confirmed the first result, and the winner was declared with full confidence. Aarush saw how seriously a close contest was treated. He learnt that in a fair election, even one vote can decide an outcome, and so every vote is counted with the greatest of care.
payload.title: Why a close result is counted twice
decoys: The gap was just a handful of votes
The officers counted the votes again

payload.passage: A simple thermometer for a fever is a small but vital invention. Inside its thin tube lies a liquid that creeps up when warmed. When the tip touches a feverish body, the liquid rises along a marked scale. The doctor reads where it stops to learn the body's exact temperature. From this single number, a doctor can tell how serious an illness might be.
payload.title: How a fever thermometer reads body heat
decoys: The liquid rises along a marked scale
A high reading hints at illness

payload.passage: A summer meadow looks peaceful, but it hums with a web of connected lives. Grasses and flowers catch the sunlight and make food from it. Insects sip nectar and nibble leaves, while spiders and frogs hunt the insects. Birds swoop in to catch the frogs and insects in turn. Beneath it all, worms and tiny creatures break down the dead and feed the soil. Every living thing in the meadow is tied to the others in one busy food web; pull out any one of these creatures and the others would surely feel the change.
payload.title: Why a meadow buzzes with linked lives
decoys: Spiders and frogs hunt the meadow's insects
Nature connects living things in countless ways
Worms break down the dead to feed the soil

payload.passage: The cuttlefish wears its feelings and its disguises on its skin. In a single second it can flash waves of changing colour across its body, like a moving screen of light. It uses this to vanish against the seabed, to startle a predator with a sudden bright pattern, or to signal to other cuttlefish. A hunting cuttlefish may send hypnotic stripes rippling down its body to dazzle a crab before striking. No paint could move so fast. This living light-show lets the soft, shell-less creature both hide and hunt in the busy sea.
payload.title: How the cuttlefish hides and hunts with changing skin
decoys: A cuttlefish flashes colour across its skin
Sea animals must both hide and hunt
It dazzles crabs with rippling stripes

payload.passage: A microphone does the opposite job of a loudspeaker. It turns the sound of your voice into an electric signal. Sound waves strike a thin part inside and make it tremble. This trembling is changed into a matching pattern of electricity. That signal can then be made louder, recorded or sent far away. Without the microphone, radio, films and recordings could not exist.
payload.title: How a microphone turns sound into a signal
decoys: Sound waves make a thin part tremble
Clever devices changed how we share sound
A microphone is the opposite of a speaker

payload.passage: Long before a star shines, it begins as a cold, dark cloud of gas and dust. Gravity slowly draws this thin material inward upon itself. As the cloud shrinks, its centre packs together and grows hotter and hotter. When the core becomes hot and dense enough, it begins to glow with its own light. A new star has been born and starts to shine across space. Our own sun arose from such a cloud in the distant past; so every shining star, near or far, traces its beginning to a quiet, collapsing cloud.
payload.title: How a star is born from a cloud in space
decoys: Gravity draws the thin material inward
Space is always creating something new
Our own sun arose from such a cloud long ago

payload.passage: Beavers do not simply find a good home; they build the river to suit themselves. Working through the night, a beaver family gnaws down trees with their strong front teeth and drags the logs into the stream. They pile branches, mud and stones to make a sturdy dam that slows the water and forms a deep, calm pond. In the middle of this safe pond they raise a snug lodge with an underwater door no land hunter can use. By reshaping the land itself, the busy beavers create the very habitat they need to survive.
payload.title: How beavers reshape a river to build a home
decoys: Beavers gnaw down trees with strong teeth
Many animals build shelters to live in
Their dam forms a deep, calm pond

payload.passage: A pair of crutches lets a person with a hurt leg still move about. The crutches reach from under the arms or hands down to the ground. When the leg is sore, the body's weight is passed through the crutches instead. The strong arms take over the work the leg cannot do. With this simple aid, an injured person can walk while the leg heals.
payload.title: How crutches help an injured person walk
decoys: Crutches pass the body's weight to the ground
Strong arms do the work the leg cannot

payload.passage: The tiny tardigrade, no bigger than a grain of sand, may be the toughest animal alive. When its watery home dries up, it does not die. Instead it pulls in its legs, curls into a hard little ball, and drains almost all the water from its body. In this dried, deathlike state it can survive boiling heat, freezing cold and years without a drink. Add a single drop of water, and the tardigrade swells, uncurls and crawls away as if nothing happened. By shutting itself down, this minute creature outlasts conditions that would destroy almost anything else.
payload.title: How the tiny tardigrade survives by drying out
decoys: A tardigrade curls into a hard ball

payload.passage: Tara saw that the town library lent books, magazines and even tools for free, and she could not see how it survived. The librarian explained that the town paid for it from shared funds, judging it worth the cost because a reading, learning community grew stronger and wiser. The money spent on books today, she said, returned as better-educated citizens tomorrow. The library was an investment, not a waste. Tara learnt that a town sometimes spends shared money on things whose true value shows up slowly, in the people it helps grow.
payload.title: Why a town invests in a free library
decoys: The library lent books for free
Shared funds paid for the library

payload.passage: A simple cloth or clay water filter can change lives in a village. Water from a pond or river often hides dirt and tiny germs. When this water is passed slowly through fine sand and cloth, the dirt is caught and held back. Boiling the filtered water then kills the germs that are left. Clean water like this keeps families safe from many sicknesses.
payload.title: How filtering makes pond water safe to drink
decoys: Sand and cloth catch the dirt

payload.passage: Your ears do two important jobs at the same time. The outer part catches sound and funnels it deep inside, where it becomes signals for the brain to hear. Hidden further in are tiny curved tubes filled with fluid. As your head moves, the fluid shifts and tells the brain which way is up. So your ears help you both hear and keep your balance.
payload.title: How the ears help us hear and keep balance
decoys: Tiny tubes of fluid sense which way is up
The outer ear funnels sound inside

payload.passage: When a herd of musk oxen on the frozen tundra is threatened by a pack of wolves, the adults do not flee and abandon the young. Instead they swiftly form a tight ring, their broad bodies facing outward and their great curved horns lowered like a wall. The calves are gathered safely into the centre of this living shield. Any wolf that dashes in meets a sweep of sharp horns. Faced with this unbroken wall, the wolves usually give up and move off. By standing together as one fortress, the musk oxen guard their calves from the pack.
payload.title: How musk oxen form a ring to guard their calves
decoys: Musk oxen face outward with horns lowered
Wolves hunt animals on the tundra
The calves stand in the centre

payload.passage: Repairing a torn shirt or a wobbly chair is greener than buying new. Every new thing we buy took materials, water and energy to make. A small repair gives the old item many more months or years of use. It also keeps the broken thing out of the rubbish heap. Mending what we have is a simple, thrifty way to ease the strain on nature.
payload.title: Why mending things is kinder to nature than buying new
decoys: A new thing takes materials to make
A repair keeps an item out of the rubbish

payload.passage: Aryan's little brother kept knocking over his carefully built block towers, again and again, laughing each time. Aryan's patience wore thin, and he wanted to shout him away. Instead he took a breath and built a small, separate tower just for his brother to knock down as he pleased. The little one was delighted, and Aryan's own tower stood safe at last. His mother, watching from the doorway, smiled quietly at his cleverness. Aryan learnt that patience often finds a clever, kind solution where anger only makes more noise.
payload.title: Patience finds solutions where anger makes noise
decoys: Aryan built a tower for his brother to topple
Small children love knocking over blocks

payload.passage: Why does the body sometimes get a cramp in the leg at night? A cramp is a muscle that suddenly tightens hard and will not let go. It can happen if a muscle is tired, low on water, or short of certain minerals. The tight muscle gives a sharp, gripping pain for a moment. Gently stretching and rubbing the leg usually eases the cramp away.
payload.title: Why a leg muscle cramps at night
decoys: A cramp is a muscle that tightens hard

payload.passage: Aadi started selling paper kites and counted only the cost of paper and string when setting his price, ignoring the glue, the time and the torn ones he threw away. At month's end he was puzzled to find almost no profit. His aunt helped him list every hidden cost he had forgotten. Once all were counted, he saw his price was far too low. Aadi raised it fairly and finally earned. He learnt that a price must cover every cost, even the small and hidden ones, or a busy business can still earn nothing at all.
payload.title: Why a price must cover every hidden cost
decoys: He ignored glue and wasted kites
His price was far too low

payload.passage: On a cool morning, you may see wisps of mist drifting up from a calm river. This soft cloud forms close to the water. Overnight the air above the river grows cool, while the water stays a little warmer. As the warm water gives off vapour into the chilly air, that vapour quickly turns into tiny droplets. These droplets hang just above the surface as low mist. Once the sun warms the air, the mist thins and lifts away into the clearing sky.
payload.title: How morning mist rises off a warming river
decoys: Tiny droplets hang just above the water's surface
Mornings can look very different from day to day
Warm water gives off vapour into the cool air

payload.passage: Why do you yawn when you are sleepy or have sat still for too long? A yawn is a big, slow breath that pulls in plenty of air. Some scientists think it helps cool a tired brain. Others believe it brings in a little extra oxygen when your breathing has grown shallow. Whatever the exact reason, a yawn is the body's gentle nudge to wake you up.
payload.title: Why we yawn when we are tired
decoys: A yawn pulls in plenty of air
The body sends us many signals
A yawn may help cool a tired brain

payload.passage: Travel far across the world and the stars overhead are not quite the same. From the northern lands you can see certain patterns and the steady Pole Star. Far to the south, different stars rise that northerners never glimpse. This happens because the round Earth tips each region toward a different part of space. Your view of the heavens depends on where you stand on the globe. A traveller meets new stars as well as new lands; so part of the wonder of travel is finding fresh patterns of stars overhead at each new home.
payload.title: Why the night sky differs from place to place
decoys: Northern lands can see the steady Pole Star
The world holds many differences to discover
Your view depends on where you stand on the globe

payload.passage: Meena's drawing won the contest, but she saw that the judges had wrongly disqualified a rival's entry over a tiny rule. The rival was the only one who could truly have beaten her. Meena could have stayed silent and kept her prize. Instead she told the judges the disqualification was unfair and asked them to reconsider. They did, and the result became a shared first place. Meena learnt that wanting fair treatment even for a rival is the real meaning of justice.
payload.title: Wanting fairness even for a rival is justice
decoys: Meena defended her rival's disqualified entry
Contests can disqualify entries over rules
The rival might have beaten her

payload.passage: On a clear night the ground loses its warmth quickly and turns cool. The air just above the grass cools too, and cool air cannot hold all its vapour. The spare water settles onto blades of grass as tiny, shining beads. We call this dew, and it forms best on calm, cloudless nights. By mid-morning the sun warms the grass again, and the dew quietly evaporates back into the air; so the dew you see at dawn is simply water that left the air for a few hours and will soon return to it.
payload.title: Why morning dew appears on cold grass
decoys: Dew beads form best on calm, cloudless nights
Cold weather changes the world in many ways
Grass cools down faster than the air above it

payload.passage: Why does the body need protein from foods like beans, eggs and milk? Protein gives the body the building blocks to grow and repair. Your muscles, skin and even your hair are built from it. While you are young and growing fast, you need a steady supply. Eating some protein each day helps your body build new parts and mend old ones.
payload.title: Why protein helps the body grow and repair
decoys: Muscles and skin are built from protein
Growing children need a steady supply

payload.passage: The viceroy butterfly is perfectly good to eat, yet birds avoid it all the same. The reason is a clever copycat trick. The viceroy has almost exactly the same orange and black pattern as the monarch butterfly, which tastes foul and makes birds sick. A bird that has once tried a monarch remembers the colours and will not touch anything that looks like one. So the tasty viceroy is left in peace, protected by its likeness to a bad-tasting cousin. By copying a creature birds have learnt to fear, the viceroy keeps itself off the menu.
payload.title: How the viceroy butterfly copies a foul-tasting cousin
decoys: The viceroy looks like the monarch butterfly
Birds eat many kinds of butterfly

payload.passage: The puff adder is a thick, slow snake that could never chase down its prey, so it lets the prey come to it. It lies coiled and perfectly still among dead leaves, its blotchy brown skin blending so well that even a careful eye slides past. It can wait there, motionless, for hours or even days. A mouse or frog wanders close, noticing nothing, until the snake strikes in a blur too fast to see. By relying on stillness and disguise rather than speed, the patient puff adder catches its meals.
payload.title: How the puff adder catches prey by lying still
decoys: The puff adder's skin blends with dead leaves
It can wait motionless for days

payload.passage: Migrating cranes travel thousands of kilometres each year, and they survive the journey by sharing knowledge across generations. Young cranes do not know the long route to the wintering grounds; they learn it by following experienced elders. Flying together in great flocks, the older birds lead the way along rivers and coasts, stopping at the same safe wetlands their kind have used for ages. The young watch and remember every landmark. One day they will guide their own chicks the same way. By passing on the route, the cranes keep the great migration alive.
payload.title: How young cranes learn their migration from elders
decoys: They stop at the same safe wetlands

payload.passage: Ravi found a purse on the bus seat, fat with notes and a few loose coins. For one long moment he imagined the shiny cricket bat he could finally buy with it. Then he pictured the worried face of whoever had lost their hard-earned savings, and the daydream lost its shine. He handed the purse straight to the conductor without another thought. The owner, an old farmer, returned weeping with thanks and pressed a reward into his hand. Ravi shook his head and said the calm settling in his chest was reward enough, and he saw that an honest choice can feel far better than any prize.
payload.title: Honesty brings a peace no reward can buy
decoys: Ravi found a fat purse on a crowded bus
Old farmers often carry their savings as cash
Returning lost money is the polite thing to do

payload.passage: A pen that never needs dipping was once a wonderful new tool. The fountain pen carries its own supply of ink inside a small chamber. A thin channel lets the ink creep down to the nib at a steady rate. As the nib glides over paper, the ink flows out just enough to write smoothly. Writers could now scribble for pages without stopping to dip a quill in an inkpot.
payload.title: How the fountain pen freed writers from the inkpot
decoys: Ink creeps down a thin channel to the nib
Tools for writing have improved over time
A fountain pen holds its own ink supply

payload.passage: Why do you feel thirsty after running about in the sun? Playing hard makes you sweat, and sweating takes water from your body. As your water level drops, your body sends a strong thirst signal. This thirst pushes you to drink and refill what you lost. By answering thirst quickly, you keep your body working at its best.
payload.title: Why the body makes us thirsty after exercise
decoys: Sweating takes water from the body
The body guides us with signals

payload.passage: Across a month the moon swings from a barely-there sliver to a dazzling full disc and back. This rise and fall of brightness follows how much of its lit side we can see. Near new moon, almost none of the sunlit half faces us, so it is faint. As it moves along its orbit, more of that bright half turns our way, until at full moon we see it all. Then it slowly turns away once more; so the slow brightening and dimming of the moon is simply a changing view of how much sunlit surface it shows us.
payload.title: Why the moon brightens and dims through the month
decoys: Near new moon almost none of the lit half faces us
The sky changes steadily over time
At full moon we see the whole sunlit half

payload.passage: Bees not only gather food but also keep their crowded hive clean and free of disease, and they do it as a team. Certain worker bees take on the job of housekeepers. They drag out dead bees and bits of rubbish, carrying them far from the hive. They polish the wax cells and even coat cracks with a sticky plant gum that fights germs. Sick or dying bees often leave on their own to protect the rest. Through this constant tidy housekeeping, the colony stays healthy where filth would spread sickness fast.
payload.title: How worker bees keep the whole hive healthy
decoys: Some bees drag out dead bees and rubbish
Bees live crowded together in a hive
They coat cracks with germ-fighting gum

payload.passage: At the village well, two families had quarrelled for years over whose turn it was to draw water first each morning. Little Asha grew tired of the daily shouting that echoed across the lane. One quiet morning she drew a full pot of water herself and carried it carefully to the rival family's frail old grandmother. The simple, unexpected gesture seemed to shame the grown-ups into silence. Within days they agreed at last to share the well fairly, by turns. Asha had shown everyone that fairness sometimes begins with just one person choosing to give rather than to fight.
payload.title: Fairness can start with one giving heart
decoys: Asha carried water to the rival grandmother
Two families quarrelled over the village well
Drawing water from a well is hard work

payload.passage: The tailorbird builds a nest so cleverly that it seems made by human hands. Choosing one or two large green leaves still growing on a plant, the little bird pierces tiny holes along their edges with its sharp beak.
