Then it draws plant fibre or spider silk through the holes, stitching the leaves together into a neat pouch. Inside this living green cradle it builds a soft nest, hidden among the foliage. Snakes and crows pass right by, seeing only leaves. By sewing its nest into the leaves themselves, the tailorbird keeps its eggs safely out of sight.
payload.title: How the tailorbird sews leaves into a hidden nest
decoys: The tailorbird stitches leaves with fibre
Birds build nests to hold their eggs
It pierces holes in green leaves

payload.passage: Plants and animals trade the very air between them in a neat partnership. Animals breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. Plants, by day, take in that carbon dioxide to make their food and give back fresh oxygen. So each side produces what the other needs. This quiet exchange keeps the air balanced and helps both plants and animals stay alive together; so plants and animals are quiet partners, each one helping to refresh the very air that the other needs to live.
payload.title: How plants and animals depend on each other for air
decoys: Animals breathe out carbon dioxide that plants use
Living things are linked in countless ways
The exchange keeps the air balanced for all

payload.passage: The weaverbird builds one of the most remarkable nests of any creature, and the male does it to win a mate. Using thin strips of grass and reed, he knots and weaves a hanging nest with a narrow entrance tube below to keep out snakes. He works for days, tightening every strand. When a female arrives, she inspects the nest closely, and if the weaving is poor she rejects it. The male must then tear it down and build a better one. Only fine, careful work wins him a partner and a family.
payload.title: How the weaverbird's careful nest wins a mate
decoys: A male weaverbird knots a hanging nest
Birds build nests from grass and reed
The female inspects the finished nest

payload.passage: A healthy pond, forest or meadow holds itself in a quiet balance. Plants make food, plant-eaters feed on them, and hunters keep the plant-eaters in check. Decomposers recycle the dead, returning nutrients to feed new plants. If one part grows too large or too small, the others shift to set it right. Through these links, the whole community keeps itself steady year after year; this natural balancing act is delicate, though, and a single large disturbance can take a long time to settle again.
payload.title: How an ecosystem stays in balance
decoys: Hunters keep the plant-eaters in check
Nature has ways of keeping itself in order
Decomposers return nutrients to feed new plants

payload.passage: A planet rushes through space at enormous speed, so why does it not shoot off into the dark? The answer is the sun's gravity, a pull that reaches across vast distances. This pull constantly bends the planet's path into a curve around the sun. The planet keeps trying to fly straight, but gravity keeps tugging it back. The balance between the two holds the planet forever circling its star; without this steady pull, the planets would simply drift off into the darkness, and the solar system would slowly fall apart.
payload.title: How gravity keeps the planets from flying away
decoys: The sun's gravity reaches across vast distances
Forces shape everything that happens in space
A planet keeps trying to fly straight ahead

payload.passage: A desert can roast you at noon yet leave you shivering after dark. The dry air is the reason. With little moisture and few clouds, sunlight pours straight down and bakes the sand all day. But once the sun sets, that same clear, dry air lets the heat escape quickly into the sky. With nothing to trap the warmth, the desert cools fast and nights turn cold; so the desert's huge swing from baking days to chilly nights comes down mostly to its dry, nearly cloudless air.
payload.title: Why deserts are hot by day but cold by night
decoys: Clear dry air lets desert heat escape at night
The weather can change a great deal in one place
Sunlight bakes the desert sand all day long

payload.passage: Spiders are often swept away in fear, but a house spider is a quiet helper. It spins its web in a still corner and waits patiently. Into the web blunder the flies and mosquitoes that trouble us. In a single week one spider may catch many such pests. By letting a corner spider be, you keep the home freer of biting insects.
payload.title: Why a house spider is a helpful guest
decoys: A spider spins its web in a corner
A spider catches flies and mosquitoes

payload.passage: Aadi loved buying small toys on credit at the corner shop, telling the owner he would pay later. The little debts felt harmless until they piled into a sum he could not repay. The kindly owner gently stopped his credit until the old amount was cleared. Working it off from his pocket money was a slow, uncomfortable lesson. Aadi learnt that buying on credit is borrowing in disguise, and that many small 'pay later' purchases can quietly trap you in a debt far heavier than any single toy was worth.
payload.title: How small credit purchases pile into debt
decoys: Aadi bought toys on credit at the shop
Toys can be very tempting to children
The owner stopped his credit for a while

payload.passage: When the teacher mistakenly gave Varun extra marks on his paper, he saw it at once. The higher score would have placed him first in class, ahead of his rival. He looked at the red figures for a while, then walked up and pointed out the mistake himself. The teacher corrected it, and Varun slipped to second place. Yet his teacher's quiet nod of respect meant more than any rank. Varun learnt that honesty can cost you a position but win you something far more lasting.
payload.title: Honesty may cost a rank but earns respect
decoys: Varun pointed out his own extra marks
Teachers sometimes add up marks wrongly
Being first in class feels very good

payload.passage: For years the women of the village had to walk far for clean water, while the council spent money on other things. Then a brave woman named Sunita won a seat on the panchayat and spoke up at every meeting. She pressed the members until a new water tank was built right in the village. Other women, encouraged, began attending the meetings too. Ayaan learnt that when those who feel a problem most sit at the decision table, the village's spending finally turns toward their real needs.
payload.title: A woman's voice reshapes village spending
decoys: Sunita pressed for a new water tank
Everyone deserves access to clean water
Women once walked far to fetch water

payload.passage: The class trip leader asked for a volunteer to carry the heavy first-aid bag up the long trail. Everyone looked away, hoping not to be picked. Karan, though tired, raised his hand without being asked. The bag weighed on his shoulders the whole climb. But near the top a boy sprained his ankle, and Karan's bag had exactly what was needed. The leader thanked him warmly. Karan learnt that willingly taking on a hard, thankless task can quietly turn into the most useful choice of all.
payload.title: Taking on thankless tasks can prove most useful
decoys: Karan volunteered to carry the first-aid bag
First-aid bags can be heavy to carry
A boy sprained his ankle on the trail

payload.passage: Water seems endless when it flows from the tap, but clean water is truly precious. Most of the water on earth is salty sea water that we cannot drink. Only a tiny share is fresh and fit to use. In many places people walk far each day to fetch a single pot. By closing taps tightly and fixing drips, we can save this scarce and valuable resource for everyone.
payload.title: Why saving clean water matters for everyone
decoys: Most of the earth's water is salty
Nature provides for all our needs
Some people walk far to fetch water

payload.passage: A simple search box on a screen can answer almost any question. Behind it, a search engine has already visited millions of pages and made a giant index. When you type a few words, it hunts through this index in an instant. It then ranks the pages that best match your words and lists them for you. In one moment you are pointed to answers gathered from across the world.
payload.title: How a search engine finds answers in an instant
decoys: A search engine makes a giant index of pages
The internet changed how we find facts
It ranks the pages that match your words

payload.passage: Why does a wet umbrella dry out faster on a windy day? The water on the cloth slowly drifts off into the air as vapour. On a still day, this damp air lingers right next to the wet cloth and slows things down. The wind sweeps the damp air away and brings fresh, dry air to the surface. With dry air always arriving, the water leaves the cloth much faster.
payload.title: Why wet things dry faster in the wind
decoys: Water on the cloth drifts off as vapour
Rainy days can be messy and wet
Wind brings fresh, dry air to the cloth

payload.passage: Two friends, Jaya and Sara, both wanted the single window seat on the school bus. They argued every morning until the ride was spoilt for both. One day Jaya suggested they swap seats at the halfway stop, so each got the window for part of the trip. The quarrels stopped at once, and mornings became cheerful again. Soon the two were chatting and laughing all the way to school. Jaya learnt that a fair compromise can turn a daily fight into a daily friendship, where stubbornness only made both unhappy.
payload.title: A fair compromise ends a needless quarrel
decoys: Jaya and Sara argued over the window seat
School buses have popular window seats
Swapping seats at the halfway stop is clever

payload.passage: A simple ban on plastic bags in one town can change much. Shops begin to hand out paper or cloth instead. Shoppers grow used to carrying their own bags from home. The drains stay clearer without bags to choke them, and the streets look tidier. Cows and stray animals no longer swallow stray plastic, so a single rule ripples out into many small gains.
payload.title: How banning plastic bags helps a whole town
decoys: Shops hand out paper or cloth bags
Clearer drains stop the streets flooding

payload.passage: Lata's family ran into a hard month when the rains ruined their crop, but they did not panic. Years earlier they had quietly built an emergency fund, a separate pile of savings touched only in trouble. That cushion paid for food and school fees while they waited for the next harvest, so they never had to borrow at a heavy cost. Lata noticed how calm her parents stayed compared with neighbours who had saved nothing. The lesson stuck with her: money set aside for bad days buys something priceless, which is peace of mind.
payload.title: Why an emergency fund brings peace of mind
decoys: The family's crop was ruined by heavy rain
Families should plan carefully for the future
The fund covered food and school fees

payload.passage: The old footbridge over the railway line had grown dangerously rusty, and the townspeople wanted it replaced quickly. The council, however, could not simply spend on a whim. The members had to gather the money from the town's funds, invite fair bids from builders, and make sure the work was safe and honestly priced. The careful process took longer than people liked, but it stopped both waste and cheating. Saira understood that spending public money well means following slow, open steps rather than rushing to please an impatient crowd.
payload.title: Why spending public money follows careful steps
decoys: The footbridge had grown dangerously rusty
The council invited bids from builders

payload.passage: Manav's grandmother always carried a cloth bag to the market and frowned at the thin plastic ones the sellers offered. She explained that those plastic bags were used for minutes but littered the drains and fields for years. Her sturdy cloth bag, washed and reused, did the same job a thousand times over. Slowly other shoppers in the lane copied her, and a few stalls began keeping cloth bags for sale. Manav understood that one small, stubborn habit, repeated by many, could quietly clean up an entire market.
payload.title: A cloth bag habit that cleans the market
decoys: Thin plastic bags litter the drains for years
Caring for nature is everyone's duty
Grandmother always carried a sturdy cloth bag

payload.passage: Saanvi heard a loud villager demand that the panchayat spend most of its money on his own crowded lane. The members listened politely but then spread the funds across all the lanes that needed help, not just the loudest one. Some grumbled, yet the fairness was plain to see. Saanvi realised that good leaders must weigh the whole village's needs against one strong voice. She learnt that a wise council serves everyone fairly rather than simply rewarding whoever shouts the longest and loudest.
payload.title: Why fair leaders serve all, not the loudest
decoys: A villager demanded money for his lane
The funds were spread across all lanes

payload.passage: Why does a swing slow down and stop if you stop pumping your legs? Each push you give adds a little energy to the swing. But the air pushes against the swing and the chains rub at the top. These rubbing forces steal a small bit of energy on every pass. Without fresh pushes from you, the energy fades and the swing settles to a stop.
payload.title: Why a swing slows down without pushing
decoys: Air pushes against a moving swing
Playgrounds are wonderful places to be
Each push adds energy to the swing

payload.passage: A weather balloon climbs high into the sky to study the air above us. Hanging beneath it is a small box of instruments. As the balloon rises, the box measures the temperature, the moisture and the wind at each height. It sends these readings back to a station on the ground by radio. With this data, forecasters can warn us of storms before they arrive.
payload.title: How a weather balloon helps forecast storms
decoys: A box of instruments hangs beneath the balloon
Science helps us understand the world
The box measures temperature and wind

payload.passage: An umbrella keeps you dry, yet folding it small was once impossible. The folding umbrella uses thin rods joined at clever hinges. When you push the runner up the shaft, the rods swing out and stretch the cloth into a dome. Pull the runner down and the rods fold neatly together again. This handy design lets a large shield against rain shrink to fit inside a bag.
payload.title: How a folding umbrella opens and shuts
decoys: Thin rods swing out to stretch the cloth
An umbrella keeps a person dry

payload.passage: When a comet nears the sun, it often grows not one tail but two. The sun's heat frees both gas and dust from the comet's icy body. The light gas is pushed straight away from the sun in a faint, glowing streak. The heavier dust trails behind along the comet's curved path. So the two tails point in slightly different directions across the sky. Watching them shows the gentle push of sunlight upon the comet's escaping material; so the next bright comet you read about may well trail both a gas tail and a dust tail across the sky.
payload.title: Why a comet has two parts to its glowing tail
decoys: The sun's heat frees gas and dust from the comet
Space objects can be strange and beautiful
The dust tail trails along the comet's curved path

payload.passage: Every week Aarav put a few coins into a clay piggy bank instead of spending the whole of his pocket money on snacks. His friends teased him for missing out on small treats. But months later, when a wonderful kite went on sale, Aarav had exactly enough saved to buy it himself. His friends, who had eaten all their money, could only watch. Aarav learnt that saving is really patience with a reward: giving up a tiny pleasure now to afford a bigger joy later.
payload.title: Saving means trading small treats for bigger joys
decoys: Aarav put coins into a clay piggy bank
Money can buy many things we enjoy
His friends teased him for missing snacks

payload.passage: An empty plot left wild can become a small refuge for nature. Without mowing, grasses grow tall and wildflowers spring up on their own. Bees and butterflies come to feed among the blooms. Beetles, frogs and birds soon follow to share the space. What looks like an untidy patch is in truth a busy little home for many creatures.
payload.title: How a wild empty plot becomes a home for nature
decoys: Empty plots are common in towns
Bees and butterflies feed among the blooms

payload.passage: When the late train finally rolled in two hours behind schedule, angry passengers blamed the staff on the platform. The station master calmly explained that a landslide far up the hills had blocked the track, and crews had worked all morning to clear it. The delay was not laziness but a careful choice to keep everyone safe rather than risk the broken line. Slowly the crowd's anger cooled into understanding. Kiara, watching nearby, saw that an honest explanation could turn a furious mob back into patient travellers.
payload.title: An honest explanation calms angry passengers
decoys: A landslide had blocked the hill track
Patience is needed when plans go wrong
The train arrived two hours late

payload.passage: Vihaan wondered why his town held a public meeting before raising the small fee charged for the weekly market stalls. The officer explained that the sellers had a right to know why their costs were rising and to say whether they could bear it. After the meeting, the fee was raised only a little, with the sellers' grudging agreement. Forcing it through silently might have sparked anger and distrust. Vihaan learnt that even a money decision goes more smoothly when those who must pay are first heard and their reasons weighed.
payload.title: Why a fee rise is discussed before deciding
decoys: Sellers had a right to know the reason
The fee was raised only a little

payload.passage: On Earth a year is the time we take to circle the sun once. But each planet has its own year of a very different length. Planets near the sun have short paths and move fast, so their years are brief. Far-off planets travel huge, slow loops, so a single year there can last many Earth years. The length of a planet's year simply depends on how far it sits from the sun; so while a year flashes by on the nearest planet, it crawls along on the farthest, all from the same simple rule of distance.
payload.title: Why a year is different on every planet
decoys: Planets near the sun finish their year quickly
Every world in space has its own ways
A far-off planet's year lasts many Earth years

payload.passage: When a letter Tara sent came back marked 'insufficient postage', she was confused, since she had stuck a stamp on it. The clerk gently showed her that her thick, heavy envelope needed more than one stamp's worth. A single stamp covered only a light letter; her bulky one had been short-paid. She added the right value, and off it went. Tara learnt that postage is a fair price for the weight carried, and that a stamp is not a magic pass but a measured payment.
payload.title: Why a heavy letter needs enough postage
decoys: Her envelope was thick and heavy
One stamp covers only a light letter

payload.passage: Why does the body have so many tiny blood vessels, not just a few big ones? The big tubes carry blood quickly over long distances. But every tiny part of you also needs its own supply of oxygen and food. So the large tubes branch into smaller and smaller ones, until they are finer than a hair. These tiny vessels reach right up to every single cell.
payload.title: Why the body needs countless tiny blood vessels
decoys: Big tubes carry blood over long distances

payload.passage: Look at the moon on any night and you will see the same familiar markings. This is because the moon turns just once for every loop it makes around the Earth. Its spin and its orbit are perfectly matched, so the same side always faces us. The far side, which we never glimpse from home, is sometimes called the hidden face. It is not dark, but simply always turned away from Earth; only with spacecraft have people ever been able to photograph the far side that always points away from our planet.
payload.title: Why we always see the same face of the moon
decoys: The moon's spin and its orbit are perfectly matched
There is always more to learn about space
The far side of the moon points away from Earth

payload.passage: When the aeroplane first flew, many people refused to believe a heavy machine could rise into the sky. The secret lay in the shape of its wings. Air rushing over the curved top of a wing moves faster than the air below it. This difference creates an upward push called lift that holds the plane up. The aeroplane shrank the world, letting people cross oceans in a single day.
payload.title: How the aeroplane lets heavy machines fly
decoys: Air moves faster over the curved top of a wing
Bold inventions can change how we travel
Planes let people cross oceans in a day

payload.passage: Why do we feel out of breath after climbing stairs quickly? Your busy muscles burn through oxygen fast and make extra waste gas. Your body senses this and tells you to breathe harder and faster. The quick breaths rush more oxygen in and push the waste gas out. Once your muscles have caught up, your breathing slowly settles back to normal.
payload.title: Why we breathe faster after hard exercise
decoys: Busy muscles burn through oxygen fast
Exercise is good for our health
Quick breaths push out the waste gas

payload.passage: Almost every leaf you see is some shade of green, and there is a reason for it. Inside the leaf is a colouring that captures the energy in sunlight. This colouring soaks up most colours of light but bounces green light back. The green that returns to our eyes is the colour we see. It is this same colouring that lets the leaf make food from light. So a leaf looks green precisely because of the part that powers its hidden work.
payload.title: Why a leaf is green and not some other colour
decoys: The colouring bounces green light back to us
Nature is full of colours to notice
The colouring captures the energy in sunlight

payload.passage: Why does your body have a sense of hot and cold on the skin? Tiny sensors spread through your skin watch the temperature around you. Some fire when things grow warm, and others fire when they grow cold. They send these messages straight to the brain. This lets you pull back from a hot flame or reach for a coat before the cold harms you.
payload.title: How the skin senses hot and cold
decoys: Some sensors fire for warmth, others for cold
The body has many useful senses
Messages go straight to the brain

payload.passage: Why does the body make ear wax inside your ears? Deep in the ear canal, small glands make a sticky yellow wax. This wax is not dirt; it does a useful job. It traps dust, tiny insects and germs before they reach the delicate inner ear. The old wax slowly moves outward on its own, carrying the trapped dirt away with it.
payload.title: Why the body makes wax to guard the ear
decoys: Small glands in the ear make sticky wax
The body protects its delicate parts
The wax traps dust and germs

payload.passage: Why does chewing gum or food on only one side feel odd over time? Your jaw and face muscles work best when used evenly on both sides. If you always chew on one side, those muscles grow uneven and can begin to ache. The teeth on the busy side also wear faster than the others. Chewing on both sides keeps your jaw balanced and comfortable.
payload.title: Why chewing evenly on both sides is healthier
decoys: Jaw muscles grow uneven from one-sided chewing
Teeth wear faster on the busy side

payload.passage: Although the sun is highest at midday, the air often feels hottest a little after. Still, noon brings the most direct and powerful sunlight of the day. At that hour the sun's rays strike the ground most steeply and concentrate their heat. The ground soaks up this warmth and then shares it with the air. Because heating takes a little time, the air keeps warming past noon. The strongest sunshine at midday leads to the warmest part of the afternoon; so the most powerful sunshine of the day shapes the warmth of the whole afternoon.
payload.title: Why noon is the hottest part of a sunny day
decoys: The sun's rays strike most steeply at noon
The day changes in temperature from hour to hour
The ground soaks up warmth and shares it with air

payload.passage: Why does keeping your nails clean help keep you well? Dirt and germs love to hide in the small gap beneath your fingernails. When you touch your mouth or food, those germs can slip inside and make you ill. Trimming and washing your nails sweeps these hidden germs away. Clean, short nails are a simple but powerful guard for your health.
payload.title: Why clean nails help keep us healthy
decoys: Germs hide in the gap beneath the nails
Germs can slip in when we touch food

payload.passage: When the town council had to decide where to build a new clinic, Reyaan expected the members to simply pick the spot nearest their own homes. Instead they studied a map showing where the most people lived far from any doctor. The clinic was placed where it would help the greatest number, not where it was most convenient for the powerful. Some grumbled, but the choice was fair. Reyaan learnt that a good public decision looks at the whole community's need rather than the comfort of a chosen few.
payload.title: Placing a clinic where the most need it
decoys: The members studied a map of the town
Many people lived far from any doctor

payload.passage: After the picnic, the field was littered with wrappers and empty bottles, and the group hurried to catch the bus home. Everyone stepped over the mess, sure the cleaners would handle it. Only Ravi turned back and began gathering the rubbish into a bag. A few ashamed friends joined him, and soon the field was spotless. They caught a later bus, but the clean field felt worth the wait. Ravi learnt that taking responsibility for a shared mess, instead of leaving it to someone else, is what keeps a place worth enjoying.
payload.title: Cleaning a shared mess is everyone's duty
decoys: Ravi gathered the picnic rubbish into a bag
Picnics often leave wrappers and bottles behind
Friends joined Ravi to clean the field

payload.passage: Nisha always wondered why grown-ups trusted a bank with their hard-earned money. Her father explained that a bank does not lock every rupee in a vault and leave it there. Instead it lends most of the deposits to families building homes or shops starting up, and charges them a fee called interest. Some of that fee comes back to savers like her father as a small reward for keeping money in the bank. So a bank is really a careful go-between, gathering idle money and putting it to work for the whole community.
payload.title: How a bank turns savings into useful loans
decoys: Savers earn a small reward called interest
Money plays an important role in modern life
A bank lends money to families building homes

payload.passage: When you cut your finger, the bleeding soon stops by itself. Tiny pieces in your blood, called platelets, rush to the wound. They stick together and to the torn edges, building a soft plug. Fine threads then weave across to make the plug stronger. Slowly this plug dries into a hard scab that shields the cut while new skin grows beneath.
payload.title: How the body stops bleeding and heals a cut
decoys: Platelets stick together to build a plug
The body can heal many small hurts
A scab shields the cut while it heals

payload.passage: A simple choice to walk past the lift and take the stairs adds up. A lift draws electricity each time it rises and falls. The stairs use only the energy of your own legs. Climbing them keeps the heart strong and the body fit. When many people choose the stairs for a floor or two, a building quietly saves a fair bit of power.
payload.title: Why taking the stairs saves power and builds health
decoys: A lift draws electricity each trip
Climbing stairs keeps the heart strong

payload.passage: A butterfly garden is more than a patch of pretty flowers. Butterflies need certain plants to lay their eggs upon and others to feed from. By growing the right mix, you give them a full home for every stage of life. As the butterflies flit from bloom to bloom, they help the flowers make seeds. A garden planned for butterflies helps these gentle insects survive.
payload.title: How a butterfly garden helps butterflies thrive
decoys: Butterflies lay eggs on certain plants
Flowers are beautiful to look at

payload.passage: Vivaan was surprised that the cobbler, the tailor and the barber on his street each did only one kind of work instead of trying to do everything. His father explained that by focusing on one craft, each grew highly skilled and fast at it. Such a specialist did a far better job than a jack-of-all-trades could. People came to each for what he did best, and all of them earned a living. Vivaan learnt that specialising, rather than spreading thin, lets each worker become expert and serves everyone better than a crowd of amateurs.
payload.title: Why focusing on one craft serves everyone
decoys: Each worker did only one kind of job
People came to each for his specialty

payload.passage: A handful of native creepers grown over a balcony rail brings cool and life. The green leaves shade the wall from the harsh afternoon sun. They take in the dust and breathe out fresh air for the flat. Small birds and butterflies come to rest among the vines. With little space and care, a creeper turns a bare rail into a cool, living screen.
payload.title: How a balcony creeper cools and greens a flat
decoys: Green leaves shade the wall from the sun

payload.passage: Sara never understood why her cousin booked train tickets weeks before the journey until a holiday trip went wrong. Every seat was full, and the family had to crowd into a packed unreserved coach. Her cousin explained that popular trains fill up fast, and a confirmed seat is a promise the railway cannot easily break. Booking early was not over-worry; it was simply claiming a spot before thousands of others did. After that uncomfortable ride, Sara learnt that planning ahead can be the difference between a restful journey and a long, tiring squeeze.
payload.title: Why booking train tickets early pays off
decoys: Popular trains fill their seats very fast
Planning ahead is a wise thing to do
The family crowded into an unreserved coach

payload.passage: Aarohi made handmade soaps and was tempted to lower her price below every rival to grab all the customers. Her aunt warned that if she sold below what the soap cost her to make, every sale would lose money, and more sales would only deepen the loss. A full order book could still ruin her. Aarohi set a price that covered her costs and left a fair profit instead. She learnt that being the cheapest is pointless if each sale drains money, and that a business must price above its true costs to survive.
payload.title: Why being cheapest can still ruin a business
decoys: Selling below cost loses money each time
A full order book could still ruin her

payload.passage: Why does your stomach use such strong juices on your food? The food you swallow is often in lumps too big to use. The stomach pours out a powerful juice that breaks these lumps apart. The same juice also kills many germs that ride in on the food. A special lining keeps the stomach itself safe from its own strong juice.
payload.title: Why the stomach uses strong juices on food
decoys: Stomach juice breaks the food lumps apart
The body processes what we eat
A lining keeps the stomach safe

payload.passage: Why is fresh, home-cooked food often better than packaged snacks? Fresh food keeps more of the vitamins and goodness the body needs. Packaged snacks are often heavy with salt, sugar and fat but light on nourishment. Eating them too often can crowd out the foods that truly help you. A plate of fresh, simple food keeps the body far better fed.
payload.title: Why fresh food is better than packaged snacks
decoys: Fresh food keeps more of its vitamins
What we eat shapes our health
Snacks are heavy on salt and sugar

payload.passage: Twins Riya and Diya were given just one bright kite to share between the two of them. Each one wanted desperately to fly it first, and a sharp tug-of-war over the string nearly ripped the fragile kite in half. Riya suddenly let go of her end and suggested they take it in turns instead, one holding the spool while the other ran. Working together like this, they sent the kite climbing higher than either of them could have managed alone. Both girls laughed in delight. The twins learnt that sharing something fairly often brings far more joy than winning it outright.
payload.title: Sharing fairly brings more joy than winning
decoys: Riya and Diya shared a single kite
Kites fly higher with two people helping
Twins sometimes quarrel over one toy

payload.passage: Saanvika asked why the hospital made every visitor wait outside the operation room instead of letting family stay close. A nurse explained that the room was kept extremely clean, almost free of germs, to protect the patient whose body lay open during surgery. Even a single visitor could carry in dust and disease. Keeping the room sealed was part of the cure itself. Saanvika learnt that what felt like a cold rule was really a careful shield, guarding a helpless patient from the unseen germs that crowd ordinary air.
payload.title: Why an operation room stays sealed and clean
decoys: Visitors waited outside the operation room
A visitor could carry in germs

payload.passage: When children in the north are wrapped up for winter, children far in the south are enjoying summer. This curious swap comes from the Earth's tilt. At any time, the half of the Earth leaning toward the sun has summer, while the half leaning away has winter. Since the two halves always lean in opposite ways, their seasons are flipped. One half's snowfall matches the other half's sunny beach days; so friends living far apart on the two halves of the world can be enjoying completely different seasons on the very same day.
payload.title: Why the North and South have opposite seasons
decoys: The half leaning toward the sun enjoys summer
The Earth is a place full of differences
The two halves of Earth always lean opposite ways

payload.passage: Wherever you stand on Earth, you will always see the sun appear in the east. This is not luck but the result of how the Earth turns. Our planet spins steadily toward the east, so each new place rolls to face the sun on that side first. As your spot turns away again, the sun appears to sink in the west. The direction of the spin sets the same sunrise side for everyone; this dependable east-to-west journey of the sun has guided travellers and timekeepers for thousands of years.
payload.title: How the sun rises in the east everywhere on Earth
decoys: Each place rolls to face the sun on its eastern side
Some things on Earth are true for all people
The sun appears to sink down in the west

payload.passage: During the long power cut, Aditya found a torch with working batteries in the dark stairwell. He knew his frightened neighbours, an old couple, were stumbling about with no light at all. He could have kept the torch for his own family's comfort. Instead he carried it up and lent it to the worried couple for the night. His own home stayed dark, lit only by one small candle. Aditya learnt that responsibility means sharing what you have with those who need it more.
payload.title: Responsibility means sharing with those in greater need
decoys: Aditya lent his torch to an old couple
Power cuts leave stairwells very dark
Old people fear stumbling in the dark

payload.passage: Why do you feel sleepy at around the same time every night? Inside your body runs a kind of natural clock that follows the day and night. As it grows dark, this clock tells your body to prepare for rest. You start to feel drowsy and your body slows down for sleep. Keeping regular bed and waking times keeps this inner clock running smoothly.
payload.title: How the body's inner clock guides our sleep
decoys: Darkness tells the clock to prepare for rest
Regular times keep the inner clock smooth

payload.passage: Ananya noticed that the fruit sellers all clustered together on one side of the market, while she thought they would spread out to avoid competing. Her grandmother explained that buyers came to that corner precisely because so many fruit sellers gathered there. A shopper could compare ten stalls in a minute and find the freshest at the best price. The crowd of sellers actually drew a bigger crowd of buyers for them all. Ananya learnt that sometimes sellers gain more by clustering together than by hiding apart.
payload.title: Why similar sellers gather in one place
decoys: Fruit sellers clustered on one side
Buyers could compare many stalls quickly

payload.passage: A seed will not grow just anywhere; it waits for the right conditions. Warmth wakes the tiny life resting inside it. Water softens the seed coat and swells the seed so the root can push out. Air provides the oxygen the seed uses to release the energy stored within. Give a seed all three and it sprouts, but deny even one and it stays asleep, sometimes for years; because all three must be present, a seed can wait safely in dry or cold ground until the right season finally arrives.
payload.title: Why a seed needs warmth, water and air to sprout
decoys: Water softens the seed coat so the root can push out
Living things need the right conditions to grow
Deny one condition and the seed stays asleep

payload.passage: Buying fruits and vegetables that grow in your own season is a wise green habit. Crops grown nearby and in their right season need no long, fuel-hungry journeys. They are fresher, tastier and often cheaper than fruit flown in from afar. Out-of-season produce must travel far or grow in heated sheds, both of which harm the earth. Eating with the seasons quietly helps the planet and the farmer.
payload.title: Why eating seasonal local food helps the earth
decoys: Local crops need no long journeys
Seasonal food is fresher and cheaper

payload.passage: Nikhil thought that the cleanest street in town stayed clean simply by luck. Then he learnt that the residents there paid a small monthly sum into a shared fund for a sweeper and a rubbish van. Each family gave only a little, but pooled together it paid for a service none could afford alone. Streets where people refused to chip in stayed dirty. Nikhil understood that many small contributions, gathered for a common purpose, could buy a clean, pleasant neighbourhood that benefited every single home.
payload.title: How pooled money buys a cleaner street
decoys: Each family paid a small monthly sum
The fund paid for a sweeper and a van

payload.passage: Wild animals have no calendars, yet they sense the turning of the year. As autumn cools and days shorten, some birds set off for warmer lands. Others grow thicker coats or store food for the lean months ahead. When spring warms the world again, many animals raise their young. They read signs like day length and temperature to know when to act. The steady march of the seasons quietly guides the lives of creatures everywhere; so the turning year acts as a silent timetable that wild creatures everywhere learn to follow.
payload.title: How animals use the changing seasons as a guide
decoys: Some animals grow thicker coats for the cold months
Nature follows patterns through the year
Animals read day length to know when to act

payload.passage: A simple drip irrigation pipe waters crops without wasting a drop. Thin pipes run between the rows of plants in a field. Tiny holes let water seep out slowly, right at the roots of each plant. Because the water goes straight to the roots, very little dries up in the sun. Farmers in dry lands grow far more using far less water this way.
payload.title: How drip irrigation waters crops without waste
decoys: Tiny holes let water seep out slowly
Water goes straight to the roots

payload.passage: After rain, the ground does not simply let all the water rush away. Soil acts like a great sponge, holding water in the tiny spaces between its grains. Plant roots can then sip this stored water slowly over many days. Without this store, plants would dry out quickly between showers. The soil also keeps the water from running off and being lost at once. Good soil is a quiet reservoir that helps plants survive the gaps between rains; so healthy, spongy soil is one of the quiet secrets behind a green and thriving garden.
payload.title: Why the soil holds water for plants to use
decoys: Roots sip the stored water over many days
Soil is important for life on land
Soil keeps water from running off all at once

payload.passage: The peppered moth taught the world a striking lesson about hiding. In clean countryside the moth was mostly pale, blending with light, lichen-covered tree bark so birds could not find it. When soot from factories darkened the trees, the pale moths suddenly stood out and were eaten, while rare dark moths now blended in and survived. Over the years the dark form became common in sooty areas. When the air grew clean again, the pale moths returned to favour. The moth's survival always depended on matching whatever colour its world had become.
payload.title: How the peppered moth survives by matching its world
decoys: Soot once turned tree bark dark
Birds eat moths resting on bark
Pale moths blend with light bark

payload.passage: The cactus wren makes its home in a place that would seem far too dangerous: among the cruel spines of a desert cactus. Far from fearing the sharp needles, the little bird uses them as a fortress. It weaves a bulky nest deep inside the prickly arms of the cactus, where the spines surround it on every side. Snakes, foxes and other raiders cannot push through the wall of needles to reach the eggs. The wren slips in and out through one careful gap. By nesting inside the thorns, the cactus wren keeps its young perfectly safe.
payload.title: How the cactus wren nests safely among sharp spines
decoys: The cactus wren nests deep in a spiny cactus
Deserts are home to many birds

payload.passage: Before the election, two candidates went from house to house making grand promises about roads, water and free gifts. Anvi's father listened politely but reminded her not to be dazzled by the loudest voice. He compared what each candidate had actually done before, not just what they pledged now. One had quietly built a clinic years earlier; the other had only made speeches. On voting day he chose the doer over the talker. Anvi learnt that a wise voter weighs a person's past actions far more heavily than their shiny promises.
payload.title: Why voters should judge deeds over promises
decoys: One candidate had quietly built a clinic
Honesty matters a great deal in life
Candidates went house to house with promises

payload.passage: Why is it healthier to climb stairs than to always take the lift? Climbing stairs makes your heart beat faster and your lungs work harder. It also uses the strong muscles in your legs and middle. This little burst of exercise fits easily into a busy day. Taken often, the stairs quietly keep your heart and legs stronger than the lift ever could.
payload.title: Why taking the stairs keeps the body fitter
decoys: Climbing stairs makes the heart beat faster
Stairs use the strong leg muscles

payload.passage: Animals living along the seashore arrange their lives around the rise and fall of the tide. When the tide comes in, crabs and shellfish feed in the fresh seawater. When it goes out, they shelter in damp sand or rocky pools to stay moist. Some time their hunting, hiding and even egg-laying to the tides. The whole rhythm is set, far overhead, by the pull of the moon. Shore creatures keep careful time with the distant moon; so the small, tough animals of the shore keep careful time with the distant, pulling moon.
payload.title: How creatures of the shore live by the tides
decoys: Crabs feed in the seawater when the tide comes in
The seashore is full of fitted life
The tide's rhythm is set by the pull of the moon

payload.passage: Set a paper boat on water and gently drop in a few grains of soap behind it, and the boat scoots forward. Water has a thin, tight skin on its surface that pulls in every direction. Soap weakens this skin wherever it touches. With the pull suddenly weaker behind the boat, the stronger pull in front drags it ahead. The boat darts off across the water all on its own.
payload.title: How soap pushes a paper boat across water
decoys: Soap weakens the skin on the water
Water has a thin, tight skin on top

payload.passage: One large tree is far more than a plant; it is a bustling home. Birds build nests among its branches, while insects burrow into its bark. Squirrels store food in its hollows, and fungi spread through its roots. Even fallen leaves beneath it shelter worms and beetles. So a tree feeds and houses a whole crowd of creatures, all linked in the web of life around it; for this reason, cutting down even one old tree can scatter or harm a surprising number of living things.
payload.title: How a single tree shelters a whole community of life
decoys: Birds build their nests in the tree's branches
Nature connects living things in many ways
Fallen leaves shelter worms and beetles below

payload.passage: Why does the body keep a store of fat even in a healthy person? Fat is the body's way of saving energy for times of need. When you eat more than you use, the body tucks the extra away as fat. Later, if food is short or you work hard, it draws on this store. A sensible amount of stored fat is a useful and natural part of a healthy body.
payload.title: Why the body stores fat as saved energy
decoys: The body tucks extra food away as fat
The body plans for the future
Stored fat is drawn on when food is short

payload.passage: A simple bridge of rope and planks lets villagers cross a deep ravine. Thick ropes are stretched tightly from one bank to the other. Wooden planks are tied across them to make a path for the feet. The ropes carry the weight of each person down to the strong anchors at each side. With this swaying bridge, places once cut off by a gorge are joined.
payload.title: How a rope bridge joins two banks of a ravine
decoys: Wooden planks make a path for the feet
The ropes carry the weight to the anchors

payload.passage: Cows and other grazing animals shape the grasslands they live in. As they nibble the grass, they keep it short and let new shoots spring up. Their droppings fall to the ground and feed the soil with fresh goodness. Seeds caught in their hooves and fur are carried to new spots to grow. In their own quiet way, grazing animals help keep the grassland alive and green.
payload.title: How grazing animals keep grasslands healthy
decoys: Animals are part of the land

payload.passage: Among the stars, a few steady lights are planets, yet planets are not burning like stars. Stars blaze with their own fierce light made deep inside. Planets are cold, dark worlds that make no light at all. We see them only because they catch sunlight and reflect it back to us. A glowing planet in the evening sky is really just lit up by our own sun; so a bright planet in the evening sky is not a flame at all, but a distant world quietly lit by our own sun.
payload.title: Why the planets shine without being on fire
decoys: Planets catch sunlight and reflect it to us
The night sky holds many kinds of lights
Planets are cold worlds that make no light

payload.passage: Of all the planets, Earth alone is bursting with life, and its position helps explain why. It orbits at a comfortable distance from the sun, neither scorching nor freezing. This gentle warmth lets water stay liquid, which living things need. A blanket of air keeps the warmth steady and shields the surface. Set Earth much closer or farther, and this delicate balance for life would be lost; for this reason, many scientists call Earth's gentle position the comfortable zone where life has the best chance to begin.
payload.title: How Earth sits in just the right place for life
decoys: A blanket of air keeps Earth's warmth steady
Earth is a very special place in space
Earth orbits at a comfortable distance from the sun

payload.passage: The leaf insect looks so exactly like a green leaf that even hungry birds fly right past it. Its flat body has the shape of a leaf, complete with fake veins and even tiny brown spots like old blemishes. When a breeze blows, the insect rocks gently from side to side, just as a real leaf would sway on its stem. Predators searching the branch see only ordinary foliage and move on hungry. This perfect disguise lets the slow, soft insect survive in a forest full of sharp eyes. Its whole safety rests on simply not being noticed at all.
payload.title: How the leaf insect survives by hiding in plain sight
decoys: The leaf insect has fake veins on its body
Many forest creatures are hunted by birds
The insect sways gently like a real leaf

payload.passage: Stand in a grassland and you will see far more grass than gazelles, and far more gazelles than lions. This is no accident. At each step up a food chain, most of the energy is used up for living and moving, and only a little passes on. So it takes a great many plants to feed the plant-eaters, and many plant-eaters to feed a single hunter. That is why top hunters are always rare; this neat pyramid, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, is found in almost every habitat on Earth.
payload.title: Why there are fewer hunters than plant-eaters
decoys: Most energy is used up at each step of the chain
Big animals need a lot of food to survive
There are more gazelles than lions in a grassland

payload.passage: A plastic bag may be used for only a few minutes, yet it can trouble the earth for hundreds of years. Unlike a banana peel, plastic does not rot away in the soil. When thrown carelessly, it blocks drains, chokes rivers and harms animals that swallow it. Cows and sea turtles often mistake floating plastic for food. By carrying a cloth bag instead, each of us can cut down this lasting harm.
payload.title: Why we should use less plastic in daily life
decoys: Plastic does not rot away in the soil
Pollution is a problem all over the world

payload.passage: Choosing things with less packaging is a quiet way to help the earth. Many goods come wrapped in layers of plastic and card that we throw away at once. All that wrapping took resources to make and now adds to the waste heap. Buying loose fruit or refilling a jar skips much of this rubbish. Less packaging means less waste from the very start.
payload.title: Why choosing less packaging cuts down waste
decoys: Goods come wrapped in layers of plastic
Shopping is part of daily life
Buying loose fruit skips the wrapping

payload.passage: The big cats of the forest, like tigers, do more than look grand. As the top hunters, they keep the number of deer and other grazers in check. Without them, too many grazers would eat the forest bare. A healthy forest with its trees and grasses depends on these hunters at the top. Saving the tiger therefore helps save the whole forest around it.
payload.title: Why saving the tiger helps the whole forest
decoys: Tigers keep the number of deer in check
Too many grazers would eat the forest bare

payload.passage: Watch one meadow across a year and it seems to change its clothes. In spring fresh green shoots and bright flowers spread over the ground. Summer fills it with tall grass and busy insects under a high sun. Autumn turns the leaves gold and scatters seeds on the wind. Winter then strips it bare and quiet, until the cycle of seasons brings the colours round once more; so a single field, watched patiently across a year, tells the whole story of the turning seasons in its colours.
payload.title: How the seasons paint a changing landscape
decoys: Spring brings fresh shoots and bright flowers
Nature is forever shifting and changing
Winter strips the meadow bare and quiet

payload.passage: Your skin is far more than a simple wrapping around the body. It forms a tough barrier that keeps germs and dirt outside. It holds in the body's water so you do not dry out. Tiny sweat holes let you cool down on a hot day. Your skin even senses touch, heat and pain to warn you of danger.
payload.title: The many ways skin protects the body
decoys: Skin keeps germs and dirt outside
The body has many useful organs
Tiny sweat holes help you cool down

payload.passage: Why should you not stare at a bright screen late into the night? Bright light in the evening tricks your brain into thinking it is still day. Your body then delays the sleepy feeling it normally makes at night. You lie awake longer and lose precious rest. Dimming screens and lights before bed helps your body wind down and fall asleep on time.
payload.title: Why bright screens at night spoil our sleep
decoys: Bright light tricks the brain into thinking it is day
Good habits help us rest well
Dimming lights helps the body wind down

payload.passage: A simple bar of soap and clean water became a great defence against disease. Once doctors learned that unseen germs spread illness, washing took on new meaning. Soap loosens the germs and grease on the skin, and water rinses them away. Hospitals that began washing carefully saw far fewer patients fall sick. This humble habit has saved more lives than many grand inventions.
payload.title: How washing with soap fought the spread of disease
decoys: Soap loosens germs and grease on the skin
Hospitals saw fewer patients fall sick

payload.passage: It seems hard to believe that a giant oak begins as a small acorn. Inside the acorn lies a baby plant and a store of food. When it falls to moist ground, warmth and water wake it, and a root pushes down. A shoot rises and unfolds leaves that start making food from sunlight. Year after year the seedling grows taller and stronger until it becomes a towering tree; it can take many decades for that small acorn to become a full-grown oak spreading its branches over the land.
payload.title: How a tiny acorn grows into a mighty oak
decoys: An acorn holds a baby plant and stored food
Big things in nature start from small beginnings
Warmth and water wake the acorn on moist ground

payload.passage: Why does the body keep growing new blood all the time? Your blood cells do not last forever; old ones wear out and are cleared away. To keep your blood healthy, the body must make fresh cells every day. Deep inside certain bones, a soft tissue quietly builds these new cells. In this steady way, your blood stays fresh throughout your life.
payload.title: Why the body keeps making fresh blood
decoys: Soft tissue in bones builds new blood cells
Old blood cells wear out and are cleared

payload.passage: When you press a key on a calculator, the answer appears at once, as if by magic. Inside the calculator are countless tiny switches that can each be on or off. Pressing the keys turns groups of these switches on and off in patterns. The patterns stand for numbers, and clever rules change them step by step. The final pattern lights up the screen as the answer you wanted.
payload.title: How a calculator works out an answer
decoys: A calculator holds many tiny switches
Machines can do amazing things today
Pressing a key shows an answer on the screen

payload.passage: Why does a runner's face turn red during a hard race? Hard exercise heats the body up quickly from the inside. To cool down, the body widens the tiny blood vessels near the skin. More warm blood rushes close to the surface, making the face glow red. The warmth is then carried away into the air, helping the runner stay cool.
payload.title: Why a runner's face turns red with effort
decoys: Blood vessels near the skin widen during exercise
The body cools itself in clever ways
Warm blood near the surface glows red

payload.passage: The mother octopus gives up everything to protect her eggs. After laying thousands of them in a sheltered den, she stays beside them without leaving, even to find food. For weeks or months she gently blows fresh water over the eggs to keep them clean and supplied with oxygen, and she fends off any hungry crab or fish. Slowly she grows weak from never eating. By the time the eggs hatch and the tiny young drift away, the mother has spent her last strength. Her complete devotion gives her young their start in life.
payload.title: How a mother octopus gives all to guard her eggs
decoys: The octopus blows water over her eggs

payload.passage: Why does your body feel heavy and slow when you are unwell with a cold? Fighting germs takes a great deal of the body's energy. To win that battle, the body saves its strength for the fight. It makes you feel tired and sleepy so that you will rest. This forced rest is the body's clever way of helping itself recover faster.
payload.title: Why illness makes the body feel tired
decoys: Fighting germs takes much of the body's energy
Tiredness makes us rest while ill

payload.passage: Ananya was thrilled when a shop offered a huge discount, until her father pointed at the original price printed on the tag. The 'old price', he showed her, had been quietly raised just before the sale, so the discount only brought it back to normal. The big red sign made an ordinary price look like a bargain. Ananya felt cheated by the trick. She learnt that a discount means little unless you know the true, honest price first, and that a clever sign can dress up no real saving at all.
payload.title: Why a discount needs a true starting price
decoys: The old price had been quietly raised
A big sign made it look like a bargain

payload.passage: When the new boy Aman could not afford the cricket club fee, the captain wanted to leave him out of the team. Several players agreed, since rules were rules. Quiet Mohan suggested instead that they each contribute a little so Aman could play. Some grumbled, but they gathered the small sum together. Aman turned out to be their best bowler that season. The whole team cheered him after the first match. Mohan learnt that fairness sometimes means bending a rule so that nobody is shut out just for being poor.
payload.title: Fairness can mean making room for everyone
decoys: The boys gathered money for Aman's club fee
Cricket clubs often charge a joining fee
Aman turned out to be a fine bowler

payload.passage: When the mango season arrived in full, the market was suddenly buried under sweet golden fruit. With so many crates piled up, sellers had to drop their prices just to clear the day's stock before it spoiled. Months later, when mangoes were rare and out of season, the few available cost far more. Yash noticed the same fruit swinging between cheap and dear across the year. His grandfather explained the simple rule behind it: when something is plentiful it grows cheap, and when it is scarce it grows expensive.
payload.title: Why plenty makes fruit cheap and scarcity dear
decoys: Sellers dropped prices to clear the mango stock
Seasons bring many changes to daily life
Out-of-season mangoes cost a great deal more

payload.passage: Wherever there is light and a solid object, a shadow falls on the far side. Light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around things easily. When an object blocks the light, it leaves a dark patch behind it. That patch always lies on the side away from the light source. Move the light, and the shadow swings to the opposite side. A shadow is simply the dark space where an object has blocked the light's straight path; so by noticing where a shadow falls, you can always tell which way the light is coming from.
payload.title: Why a shadow points away from the light
decoys: Light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around
Light and dark follow simple rules
The dark patch lies on the side away from the light

payload.passage: Why is drinking enough water so important every single day? Your body is mostly made of water, and it uses water for almost everything. Water carries food and oxygen around in your blood. It helps wash away waste and keeps your body cool when you sweat. When you drink too little, you feel tired and dull, so sipping water through the day keeps you fresh.
payload.title: Why drinking enough water matters every day
decoys: Water carries food and oxygen in the blood
Healthy habits help us feel good
Water helps wash away the body's waste

payload.passage: Rehan was puzzled that the same shirt cost much less in the open market than in the shiny mall down the road. His aunt explained that the mall pays heavy rent, bright lights, air conditioning and many staff, and all those costs hide inside the price tag. The market stall, with its simple cloth roof and one owner, carries almost none of that burden. Neither place was cheating; each merely passed on its own running costs. Rehan saw that a price tag tells the story of everything it took to put the shirt in front of him.
payload.title: Why the same shirt costs more in a mall
decoys: The mall pays heavy rent and electricity bills
Prices can differ from one place to another
A market stall has just a simple cloth roof

payload.passage: Rohit kept losing track of his savings because he mixed them with the money he spent every day. His mother gave him two jars, one labelled 'spend' and one labelled 'save', and told him to split his money the moment he got it. Suddenly he could see exactly how much was for keeping and how much for using. The 'save' jar grew steadily because he never raided it for snacks. Rohit learnt that simply separating money into clear purposes made saving almost effortless and spending far easier to control.
payload.title: How two labelled jars make saving easy
decoys: His mother gave him two labelled jars
The save jar grew because he never raided it

payload.passage: The largest animals in the sea are fed, in the end, by some of the smallest. Near the surface drift clouds of tiny plants and animals called plankton. These soak up sunlight or graze on those that do. Vast numbers of them are swept up by great whales straining seawater through their mouths. The mighty whale survives on the countless specks at the very base of the ocean food chain; so the greatest creatures of the sea depend, in the end, on the countless tiny lives drifting near the sunlit surface.
payload.title: How tiny plankton support giant whales
decoys: Whales strain seawater to catch the plankton
The ocean links the small and the large
Plankton soak up sunlight near the surface

payload.passage: Why should children spend time playing and running outdoors? Active play makes the heart and lungs grow stronger with use. Moving about keeps the muscles and bones firm and healthy. Running and jumping also burn off extra energy and lift your mood. A child who plays actively each day sleeps better and stays fitter than one who only sits.
payload.title: Why daily active play keeps children fit
decoys: Active play makes the heart stronger
Children should look after their bodies

payload.passage: When leaves fall and turn brown on the ground, it may look like simple rubbish. In truth, those leaves begin a useful second life. Worms, fungi and tiny creatures slowly break them down into rich, dark matter. This crumbly material mixes into the soil and feeds the roots of growing plants. The very trees that dropped the leaves are nourished by them once more. Fallen leaves quietly return their goodness to the living forest around them; so the litter of brown leaves on a forest floor is really a quiet store of food for the trees to come.
payload.title: Why dead leaves are not really wasted
decoys: Worms and fungi break the leaves down slowly
Nature wastes very little of anything
The rich matter feeds the roots of growing plants

payload.passage: Far up in the snowy mountains lived just a handful of voters, yet the election came to them too. A small team trekked for two days carrying a voting machine to a single tiny hut so that even one distant villager could cast a vote. The effort cost far more than the few votes gathered. Bhavya was puzzled until her teacher explained the principle: in a true democracy no citizen is too remote or too few to be left out. Every single voice, she said, must be allowed to count.
payload.title: Why no voter is too remote to count
decoys: A team trekked two days carrying a machine
Mountains are hard and lonely places to live
Only a few voters lived in the hills

payload.passage: Clean drinking water was once a luxury that caused much illness when it was missing. The water filter became a quiet life-saver. It passes dirty water through layers of sand, gravel and fine material. These layers trap mud, grit and many harmful germs as the water seeps through. The water that drips out the bottom is far safer to drink than before.
payload.title: How a water filter makes water safe to drink
decoys: Layers of sand and gravel trap the dirt
Dirty water once caused much illness

payload.passage: When you pour hot water into a cold glass too quickly, it may crack with a sharp snap. The inside of the glass meets the hot water and warms up at once. As it warms, the inside spreads out and grows a little bigger. But the outside is still cold and has not spread yet. This uneven tug between the hot and cold parts pulls the glass apart and cracks it.
payload.title: Why a cold glass cracks with hot water
decoys: The inside of the glass warms first
Glass is a useful but fragile material
Warm glass spreads out and grows bigger

payload.passage: Priya was surprised that the bank charged her uncle a higher interest rate than her aunt for almost the same loan. The manager explained that her aunt had always repaid past loans on time, while her uncle had once delayed for months. A steady record of repaying told the bank he was a safer bet, so it offered a gentler rate. Past behaviour, not just promises, shaped what each borrower paid. Priya learnt that keeping your word about money quietly earns you a kind of reputation that can be worth real savings later.
payload.title: How a good repayment record lowers borrowing cost
decoys: Her aunt always repaid loans on time
Her uncle once delayed his repayments

payload.passage: Sunlight cannot reach the dark depths of the sea, yet fish live there all the same. Near the surface, tiny floating plants soak up the sunlight and make food. Small creatures eat these plants and are eaten by bigger fish in turn. When scraps and bodies drift down, they feed the strange animals far below. Even in the lightless deep, life still runs on energy that began with the distant sun; so even creatures that never glimpse a single ray of light still owe their meals, in the end, to the distant sun.
payload.title: How the sun feeds even the deepest ocean fish
decoys: Tiny floating plants make food near the surface
The ocean is full of surprising kinds of life
Scraps drift down to feed the deep-sea animals

payload.passage: Watch the stars for hours and they appear to wheel slowly around one fixed spot. That spot lies directly above the Earth's axis of spin. As our planet turns through the night, the whole sky seems to rotate about it. Stars near that point trace small circles, while those farther away sweep wider arcs. The star closest to the point, the Pole Star, barely moves at all. So the circling of the stars is really a reflection of the Earth turning below.
payload.title: Why stars seem to circle a single point at night
decoys: Stars near the point trace small circles
The sky is always slowly changing
The Pole Star barely moves all night long

payload.passage: Ishita borrowed a little money from her father to start selling beaded bracelets, promising to pay him back from her earnings. The first month she made just enough to repay part of the loan and bought more beads with the rest. Slowly the debt shrank and the business grew side by side. Some friends who had borrowed but spent the money on sweets had nothing to repay. Ishita learnt that borrowing can help you start something, but only if the borrowed money is put to work earning more than it costs.
payload.title: Borrowing wisely to start a small business
decoys: Ishita sold beaded bracelets to repay her father
Friends matter a lot when growing up
She bought more beads with her earnings

payload.passage: Why does the body need you to look after your eyes carefully? Your eyes are delicate and cannot fully heal if badly hurt. Bright light, sharp objects and long screen use can all strain or harm them. Simple care, like resting them and shielding them from danger, keeps them safe. Healthy eyes looked after now can serve you clearly for a lifetime.
payload.title: Why caring for the eyes protects our sight
decoys: The eyes cannot fully heal if badly hurt
Long screen use can strain the eyes

payload.passage: When the Earth passes between the sun and the moon, it casts a shadow on the moon's face. People long ago noticed something telling about that shadow. Its edge always curves the same gentle, round way. Only a ball-shaped object can cast a round shadow from every angle. This simple fact was one of the first clues that the Earth is a sphere, not a flat plate; so a lunar eclipse offered our ancestors one of their earliest and clearest proofs that the Earth is shaped like a ball.
payload.title: Why the Earth's shadow is round during an eclipse
decoys: The shadow's edge always curves the same way
Careful watching reveals truths about our world
A round shadow showed the Earth is a sphere

payload.passage: Pooja was given the marker to award house points fairly during the contest. Her own house was losing, and adding a few extra points in secret would have pushed it ahead. The marker felt heavy in her hand as the temptation rose. She wrote down only the points truly earned, and her house finished last. Yet the teacher praised her honest scoring before everyone. Pooja learnt that being fair when cheating would help your own side is the hardest and finest kind of fairness.
payload.title: Being fair when cheating would help you is hardest
decoys: Pooja scored only the points truly earned
Houses earn points in school contests

payload.passage: When you run hard, your breathing speeds up without you trying. Your lungs are two soft, spongy bags inside your chest. As you breathe in, they fill with air and grab the oxygen your body needs. The oxygen slips into your blood to fuel your busy muscles. When you breathe out, the lungs push away the waste gas your body no longer wants.
payload.title: How the lungs take in oxygen for the body
decoys: The lungs are two soft, spongy bags
The human body works in amazing ways
Breathing speeds up when you run hard

payload.passage: Drop an ice cube into a glass and it bobs at the surface rather than sinking. Most things grow heavier and shrink when they freeze, but water is unusual. As water turns to ice, its particles lock into a roomy pattern that takes up more space. This makes ice lighter than the same amount of liquid water. Because it is lighter, ice floats, which is why frozen ponds carry a lid of ice on top; this unusual habit of water is lucky for fish, since the floating ice forms a roof that keeps the water below from freezing solid.
payload.title: Why ice floats on top of water
decoys: Ice particles lock into a roomy pattern
Water behaves in some surprising ways
Frozen ponds carry a lid of ice on top

payload.passage: Not every night shows the stars equally well; the best ones share a few traits. A clear sky with no clouds lets starlight reach your eyes. A dark place far from city lights keeps faint stars from being washed out. A night with little or no moon leaves the sky darker still. When clear skies, dark surroundings and a faint moon all meet, the heavens blaze with countless stars; so choosing a clear, dark, moonless night away from the city can turn an ordinary sky into a breathtaking one.
payload.title: Why some nights are perfect for stargazing
decoys: City lights wash out the faintest stars
Good conditions matter when watching nature
A clear sky with no clouds lets starlight through

payload.passage: On a sunny coast, a cool wind often blows in from the sea by afternoon. The sun is the hidden cause of this pleasant breeze. Land heats up faster than water under the sunshine. The warm air over the land rises, leaving a gap below. Cooler air from over the sea then flows in to fill that gap, and we feel it as a sea breeze. The gentle coastal wind is really the sun stirring the air into motion; so the refreshing wind that cools a beach in the afternoon is really a gift of the warming sun.
payload.title: How a sea breeze is born from the sun
decoys: Land heats up faster than water in the sun
The sun shapes the weather in many ways
Warm air over the land rises and leaves a gap

payload.passage: Why does the doctor ask you to take a deep breath and hold it? A deep breath fills your lungs right to the edges with air. Held still, the lungs are stretched out fully for the doctor to examine. By listening then, the doctor can hear how clearly air moves through them. This simple test helps show whether the lungs are healthy and clear.
payload.title: Why a deep breath helps a doctor check the lungs
decoys: A deep breath fills the lungs to the edges
Doctors check the body in many ways
Held breath stretches the lungs out

payload.passage: When the new bus route to the village was first proposed, some council members worried it would never earn back its cost. Others argued that the bus was not meant to make a profit at all. With it, children could reach school and the sick could reach the hospital, things no price tag could measure. The council finally ran the bus, even at a small yearly loss. Ishaan understood that some public services are judged not by the money they earn but by the good they do for people who need them.
payload.title: Why some services serve people, not profit
decoys: The bus let children reach their school
The route ran at a small yearly loss

payload.passage: Veer wanted both a new video game and a cricket bat, but his savings could buy only one. His father told him this was a trade-off, a choice every spender must make. Whatever Veer picked, he would have to give up the other for now. He thought hard about which he would use more, and finally chose the bat he could play with friends all summer. Veer learnt that money is limited, so spending wisely means facing the honest question of what matters most.
payload.title: Why limited money forces honest trade-offs
decoys: Veer finally chose the cricket bat
He could buy only one of the two

payload.passage: When the class went to plant trees, most children dug a quick, shallow hole and dropped the sapling in carelessly. Bhuvan took his time, digging deep, adding compost, and tying the young plant to a stake so the wind would not bend it. The others teased him for being so slow. Months later, only Bhuvan's tree stood tall while many others had withered. The teacher pointed to his sturdy tree as an example for the whole class. Bhuvan learnt that a job worth doing is worth doing carefully, even when others rush and laugh.
payload.title: A job worth doing is worth doing carefully
decoys: Bhuvan planted his sapling with great care
Schools take children to plant trees
Many of the other saplings withered

payload.passage: Why do you breathe in and out without ever having to think about it? Breathing is far too important to be left to your busy thoughts. A special part of your brain keeps the breathing going on its own, day and night. It speeds up your breath when you run and slows it when you rest. Thanks to this, you keep breathing even while you sleep.
payload.title: Why we breathe without having to think
decoys: A part of the brain keeps breathing going
Breathing speeds up when you run

payload.passage: Before the school council election, Yuvan and Dia ran very different campaigns. Yuvan promised wild things he could never deliver, like a swimming pool and no homework ever. Dia promised only small, real improvements, such as a longer library hour and a cleaner playground. When the votes came in, the students happily chose Dia's modest but believable plan over the empty dream. Yuvan was stunned by the result. He learnt that voters can usually sense an empty boast, and that promising less but possible often beats promising the impossible.
payload.title: Believable promises beat impossible boasts
decoys: Yuvan promised a swimming pool and no homework
Dia offered a longer library hour

payload.passage: A small boy fell off his cycle near the school gate and sat dazed as students streamed past, late for class. Manoj was hurrying too, afraid of a scolding for being late. He stopped anyway, helped the boy up, dusted him off, and walked him to the nurse. Manoj reached class late and was scolded, but he did not mind. The little boy waved at him cheerfully for weeks afterward in the corridor. He learnt that helping someone hurt is worth a small punishment, and that kindness should not wait for a convenient moment.
payload.title: Kindness should not wait for a convenient moment
decoys: Manoj helped a fallen boy to the nurse
Children can fall off their cycles
He was scolded for being late

payload.passage: On a clear night, a few bright points shine with a calm, unwavering light among the twinkling stars. These steady lights are planets. The stars twinkle because they are so distant they appear as single points, easily disturbed by our moving air. Planets sit much closer and show as tiny discs, so their light steadies out. Both shine in our sky, but only the far-off stars seem to flicker. So a steady glow is a handy clue that you are seeing a planet.
payload.title: Why the planets glow steadily among twinkling stars
decoys: Planets show as tiny discs rather than points
The night sky holds many kinds of lights
A steady glow is a clue that it is a planet

payload.passage: Lata's little brother was blamed by their mother for breaking a plate that Lata herself had dropped. The boy said nothing, too scared to defend himself. Lata could have let him take the scolding and saved her own skin. Instead she spoke up at once and admitted the plate was hers. Her mother, surprised by her honesty, forgave the small accident. Her little brother gave her a grateful look she would remember for a long time. Lata learnt that letting someone else suffer for your fault is a worse wrong than the fault itself.
payload.title: Letting others suffer for your fault is worse
decoys: Lata admitted she broke the plate

payload.passage: Look at a thin crescent moon and you may notice the rest of it glowing faintly. This gentle light has a charming source. Sunlight strikes the Earth and a good deal bounces off our clouds and seas into space. Some of that reflected light reaches the moon and lights its dark part dimly. From the moon, the Earth would look bright in the sky, casting this glow. So the soft shine on the dark moon is really sunlight that has bounced off our own planet.
payload.title: How earthshine softly lights the dark moon
decoys: Sunlight bounces off our clouds and seas
Light travels between worlds in surprising ways
From the moon, the Earth would look bright

payload.passage: Choosing a paper straw or none at all over plastic is a small green step. A plastic straw is used for one cool drink and then tossed for good. It never truly rots and often ends up in rivers and the sea. There it can harm fish, birds and turtles. Skipping the straw, or picking paper, keeps one more bit of plastic out of the water.
