payload.title: Why skipping plastic straws helps our waters
decoys: A plastic straw is used just once
Plastic straws can harm sea turtles

payload.passage: A heavy storm flooded the school field, and the football match everyone awaited was cancelled. The captain, Dev, had trained his team for weeks and felt crushed. He could have spent the day sulking at home. Instead he gathered his team to help the staff clear fallen branches and drain the field. By evening the field was nearly playable again. His teammates went home tired but strangely proud of their muddy afternoon. Dev learnt that turning a disappointment into useful action eases the sting far better than sulking ever could.
payload.title: Turning disappointment into action eases its sting
decoys: A storm flooded the school football field
Dev's team helped clear fallen branches
Football matches are cancelled in heavy rain

payload.passage: Kabir caught his very best friend quietly copying answers from a neighbour during the class test. Telling the teacher might well cost him the friendship he treasured most. He stayed silent in the classroom but pulled his friend aside privately afterwards. There he explained, kindly but firmly, that real friends help each other do what is right, not hide what is wrong. His friend listened, went red with shame, and chose to own up to the teacher himself the next day. Kabir learnt that honesty and friendship can walk together side by side, when they are handled with care.
payload.title: Real friendship gently guides others toward honesty
decoys: Kabir spoke to his friend about cheating
Students sometimes copy answers in a test
Telling a teacher can cost a friendship

payload.passage: A magnet seems almost magical, yet its power follows simple rules. Every magnet has two ends called poles, a north pole and a south pole. Two unlike poles pull strongly towards each other, but two like poles push firmly apart. A magnet also tugs on objects made of iron, steel and a few other metals. This pulling power is why a compass needle always swings to point towards the north.
payload.title: How the poles of a magnet attract and repel
decoys: A magnet pulls on objects made of iron
Many forces in nature are invisible to the eye
A compass needle points towards the north

payload.passage: Every evening on his way home Vikram passed a blind beggar who sang the same gentle, wavering tune. The other boys liked to mock the old man, and one day Vikram laughed along just to fit in with them. That night the melody kept circling in his head, and a deep shame for his own laughter settled over him. The next day he sat down beside the singer, listened to the whole song properly, and dropped his pocket money into the cup. The man's blind eyes turned toward him with a tired smile. Vikram learnt that it takes far more strength to be kind in front of a crowd than to mock along with one.
payload.title: Choosing kindness over the crowd takes strength
decoys: Vikram gave his pocket money to a singer
Blind people sometimes earn money by singing
It is wrong to laugh at people in need

payload.passage: In the height of summer, the sky stays bright well past the time school lets out. This happens because your half of the Earth leans toward the sun. With that lean, the sun climbs high and stays above the horizon for many hours. The long hours of strong sunlight warm the land and stretch the daylight late into the evening. Only slowly does the sun sink and the sky dim. So the lingering warm evenings of summer flow straight from the Earth's friendly tilt.
payload.title: Why summer brings long, warm evenings
decoys: The summer sun stays above the horizon for hours
The seasons change daily life in many ways
Long sunlight hours warm the land in summer

payload.passage: Why does the body sometimes shake or jump when you are startled? A sudden fright sets off the body's quick alert reaction. In a flash, signals tense your muscles and ready you to move. This can make you jump, gasp or shiver before you even think. The reaction is an old, fast way the body prepares for sudden danger.
payload.title: Why a sudden fright makes the body jump
decoys: Signals tense the muscles in a flash
The body reacts before we think
A fright readies the body to move

payload.passage: The four seasons do not simply happen once; they return again and again. As the tilted Earth travels around the sun, each part leans toward it and away in turn. This brings summer, then autumn, then winter, then spring, year after year. When one full loop is finished, the cycle quietly begins anew. There is no last season and no first; they flow forever into one another. The turning of the seasons is a wheel that never stops; so we can always be sure that after the coldest winter, spring will come round once more.
payload.title: Why the seasons turn in an endless cycle
decoys: The tilted Earth leans toward the sun and away
Nature is full of cycles that repeat
When one loop ends, the cycle begins again

payload.passage: When you blow up a balloon and let it go, it darts across the room. The puffed-up balloon is packed with squeezed air pushing out in every direction. The moment you release the neck, the air rushes out of the open end in a fast stream. As the air shoots backwards, it pushes the balloon forwards. A rocket flies into space using this very same idea, only with burning fuel instead of air.
payload.title: How escaping air pushes a balloon forward
decoys: Air rushes out of the open neck of a balloon
Many everyday things work in surprising ways
Rockets use this idea to fly into outer space

payload.passage: A small fish tank can teach a child to care for living things. The fish need clean water, the right food and gentle handling to thrive. A child soon learns that too much food or dirty water makes the fish unwell. Watching the fish glide about brings calm and wonder. Looking after even a small tank grows a habit of care for all of nature.
payload.title: How caring for a fish tank teaches care for nature
decoys: Fish need clean water to thrive

payload.passage: A simple paper fan cools your face on a hot, still day. As you wave it, the broad sheet pushes the air against your skin. The moving air sweeps away the warm, damp layer clinging to you. With fresh air arriving, your sweat dries faster and you feel cooler. A folded paper fan costs almost nothing yet brings welcome relief.
payload.title: How a hand fan cools you on a hot day
decoys: The waving sheet pushes air against your skin
Moving air helps your sweat dry

payload.passage: Why does the doctor shine a light into your eye? At the front of your eye is a small window that lets light reach the parts within. A bright beam lets the doctor peer through this window. By watching how the eye answers the light, the doctor learns whether it is working well. This quick, painless check tells a great deal about your health.
payload.title: Why a doctor shines a light into the eye
decoys: A small window lets light into the eye
Doctors examine the body in many ways
The eye's answer to light reveals its health

payload.passage: The next customer found the machine working properly, never knowing why. Rohan discovered that the vending machine had given him two snacks for the price of one by mistake. His friends urged him to grab the free snack and walk off quickly. He held the extra packet, tempted. Then he took it to the office and reported the fault so it could be fixed and the shop not cheated. The clerk thanked him in surprise. Rohan learnt that honesty means caring about a stranger's loss as much as your own easy gain.
payload.title: Honesty cares about a stranger's loss
decoys: Rohan reported the faulty vending machine
His friends urged him to keep it

payload.passage: Why does the body keep healing slowly rather than all at once? Mending a wound or a broken bone is careful, detailed work. The body must clear away the damage, then build new tissue piece by piece. Rushing this work would leave the repair weak and likely to fail. By healing steadily, the body makes the mended part strong and lasting.
payload.title: Why the body heals slowly and steadily
decoys: The body builds new tissue piece by piece
Rushing would leave the repair weak

payload.passage: Two cousins, Rohan and Veer, were given a basket of mangoes to share, and Rohan, being older, divided them. He kept the bigger share for himself out of habit. Seeing Veer's quiet disappointment, something pricked his conscience. He stopped, counted the fruit again, and shared them out equally this time. Veer's face lit up at once. Rohan learnt that being older or stronger does not give you the right to a larger share, and that fairness means an equal hand for all.
payload.title: Being older gives no right to a larger share
decoys: Rohan shared the mangoes equally in the end
Cousins sometimes share a basket of fruit
Rohan was the older of the two boys

payload.passage: Why does a balanced day of work, play and rest keep you healthy? Study and work feed your mind but tire it if they never stop. Play and exercise keep your body strong and lift your spirits. Rest and sleep let both body and mind repair and refresh. A day that balances all three keeps you healthier and happier than too much of any one.
payload.title: Why balancing work, play and rest keeps us well
decoys: Study tires the mind if it never stops
Good habits keep us in good shape

payload.passage: On the moon there are no clouds, no wind and no rain, only grey stillness. The moon is far too small and its gravity too weak to hold onto a blanket of air. Without air there can be no clouds or weather of any kind. The sky there stays black even by day, and there is no sound at all. So the moon's surface remains a silent, airless world quite unlike our own; because of this airless stillness, footprints left by visiting astronauts may stay sharp on the moon for millions of years.
payload.title: Why the moon has no air or weather
decoys: The moon's weak gravity cannot hold onto air
Other worlds can be very different from Earth
The moon's sky stays black even in the daytime

payload.passage: Penguins in the frozen south face winds cold enough to freeze a bird solid, yet they endure together. When the worst storms hit, hundreds of emperor penguins shuffle into a huge, tight huddle, pressing close to share their body warmth. The birds on the chilly outer edge are not left to suffer; the huddle slowly turns, so each one takes a turn in the warm middle. By rotating in this fair way, the whole group survives temperatures that would kill a lone bird. Their warmth, like their hardship, is shared by all.
payload.title: How huddling penguins share warmth to survive
decoys: Penguins shuffle into a tight huddle in storms
The far south is bitterly cold
The huddle turns so each bird warms up

payload.passage: Priya's uncle wanted to expand his furniture workshop but did not have enough money for new machines. The bank agreed to lend him the sum on the promise that he would repay it in small monthly amounts over three years, plus interest. Before saying yes, the manager studied his sales records to be sure he could really pay it back. The loan let the workshop grow far sooner than waiting and saving ever would. Priya saw that a bank loan is a tool: helpful when used for something that can earn the money to repay it.
payload.title: A bank loan as a tool for growth
decoys: The manager checked his sales before agreeing
Hard work helps a small business grow
He would repay the loan in monthly amounts

payload.passage: Sending a picture across the world once meant posting a photograph and waiting for days. The scanner and the screen changed this completely. A scanner reads a picture as thousands of tiny dots, each given a number for its colour. These numbers travel quickly across the internet to a far-off screen. There the screen rebuilds the dots, and the same picture appears in seconds.
payload.title: How pictures travel the world in seconds
decoys: A scanner reads a picture as tiny dots
A picture once took days to post

payload.passage: Ananya loved watching her mother bargain at the cloth market, almost like a friendly game. The seller named a high price, her mother offered a low one, and slowly they met somewhere in the middle. Far from being rude, this back-and-forth let both sides feel they had struck a fair deal. The seller still made a profit, and her mother still paid less than the first asking price. Ananya realised that bargaining is not about cheating anyone; it is a polite dance that finds a price both people can happily accept.
payload.title: Bargaining as a fair dance over price
decoys: The seller still earned a profit on the cloth
Shopping with family can be enjoyable
Her mother offered a low starting price

payload.passage: The wood frog of the far north faces winters so cold that it actually freezes solid, yet it does not die. As the temperature drops, the frog floods its body with a natural sugar that protects its vital parts. Then ice spreads through it until its heart stops and it lies stiff as a stone, looking quite dead. It can stay frozen for weeks. When spring warms the ground, the frog slowly thaws, its heart starts beating again, and it hops away alive. By freezing and thawing safely, the wood frog survives the deadly northern winter.
payload.title: How the wood frog survives by freezing solid
decoys: The wood frog floods its body with sugar
It thaws and revives in spring

payload.passage: Why does the body need clean, fresh air to breathe? Each breath brings oxygen that every part of you needs to work. Dirty air carries dust, smoke and tiny harmful bits along with the oxygen. Breathed in often, these can settle in the lungs and slowly harm them. Fresh, clean air keeps the lungs healthy and the whole body well supplied.
payload.title: Why clean air keeps the lungs healthy
decoys: Each breath brings the oxygen we need
The body depends on its surroundings
Dirty air carries dust and smoke

payload.passage: The town council announced it would build either a new library or a new playground, but not both, since the budget allowed only one. Heated arguments broke out at the meeting between book lovers and sports lovers. In the end the members held a vote and chose the library, while promising the playground for the following year. Some were disappointed, yet all accepted the fair decision. Saira understood that when money is limited, a community cannot have everything at once and must choose together, in order, what comes first.
payload.title: Choosing together when the budget allows one
decoys: The council chose the library by a vote
The budget allowed only one project

payload.passage: Rain falling from the sky is always fresh and clean, yet the sea is salty. The answer is in the journey water makes. As rivers flow over land, they pick up tiny amounts of salt from rocks and soil and carry it to the sea. When seawater later evaporates, only the pure water rises, leaving the salt behind. Over millions of years this salt has built up, which is why the ocean tastes of it while the rain does not; so the freshness of rain and the saltiness of the sea are really two sides of the same patient, endless cycle of water.
payload.title: Why the sea stays salty while rain is fresh
decoys: Only pure water rises when the sea evaporates
Everything in nature takes a very long time to change
Rivers carry salt from rocks down to the sea

payload.passage: The newspaper warned that a clever false story about a candidate was spreading fast on people's phones before the election. Saira's father did not forward it; instead he checked the claim against two trusted news sources and found it was made up. He gently told his friends to do the same before sharing. A lie, he said, can swing votes long before the truth catches up. Saira understood that a careful voter must guard not only the vote itself but also the facts on which that vote is based.
payload.title: Why voters must check facts before sharing
decoys: Her father checked the claim against two sources
We should not believe everything we read
A false story spread fast on phones

payload.passage: A young elephant grows up in a herd that is almost entirely female, and there it learns everything it needs to know. The older aunts and grandmothers patiently show the calf where to find water, which plants are safe, and how to behave with the group. When the calf slips into mud or trips on a slope, gentle trunks reach out at once to help it up. It learns by watching its elders year after year. This shared raising, where every female helps mind the young, gives each calf the wisdom and care it needs to thrive.
payload.title: How a whole elephant herd helps raise each calf
decoys: Older elephants show the calf where water is
Trunks help a fallen calf get up

payload.passage: Why do doctors say breakfast is the most important meal? While you slept, your body used up the fuel from the night before. By morning your energy store is running low and your brain feels foggy. A good breakfast refills that store for the busy day ahead. Children who eat breakfast think more clearly and have the energy to learn and play.
payload.title: Why breakfast fuels the body for the day
decoys: The body uses up fuel during the night

payload.passage: Rub a plastic comb on your dry hair and it will pick up tiny bits of paper. The rubbing scrapes off an invisible charge onto the comb. This charge is called static electricity, which simply means electricity that stays in one place. A charged object can pull lightly on light things nearby, like scraps of paper or loose hair. The same charge makes your hair stand up when you remove a woollen cap.
payload.title: How static electricity makes a comb pick up paper
decoys: Rubbing a comb scrapes a charge onto it
Electricity is a powerful force in our world
A woollen cap can make your hair stand up

payload.passage: Tara had spent days perfecting a clay model for the art contest, and it stood far better than her rival Sonia's. Just before judging, she noticed a deep crack forming on Sonia's piece that Sonia had not seen. Tara could have kept silent and let her rival's model crumble before the judges. Instead she quietly warned Sonia in time to mend it. Sonia fixed the crack and they tied for first place. Tara learnt that winning by warning a rival of danger feels far cleaner than winning by their bad luck.
payload.title: Helping a rival is finer than winning by luck
decoys: Tara warned Sonia about the crack
Clay models can crack before drying
They tied for first place in the contest

payload.passage: A simple clay water pot keeps drinking water cool in summer heat. The pot's walls are slightly porous, so a little water seeps through to the outside. There it slowly dries off into the air. As the water dries, it carries away heat from the pot. This gentle cooling keeps the water inside pleasantly cold without any electricity at all.
payload.title: How a clay pot keeps water cool in summer
decoys: A little water seeps through the porous walls
Old ideas can be very clever

payload.passage: On the morning of the festival rush, the town post office looked like a small factory. Sacks of greeting cards arrived faster than the staff could open them, and extra workers were called in for the week. Each card still had to be stamped, sorted by area and bundled for the right route, no matter how high the pile grew. The clerks knew that one missed bundle could mean a family's wishes arriving a day too late. Their steady teamwork, not luck, was what kept thousands of cards flowing out on time.
payload.title: Teamwork keeps the festival post moving on time
decoys: Extra workers were called in for the busy week
Festivals bring a lot of excitement to a town
Greeting cards arrive in large sacks during festivals

payload.passage: Manish had been trusted with the key to the school store cupboard for the whole term. One sleepy afternoon he discovered a brand-new football tucked inside and longed to borrow it without asking anyone first. He picked the ball up, turned it over in his hands, and felt its smooth panels. Then, with a small sigh, he set it down again and locked the cupboard tight. When the teacher later praised him for his careful handling of the key, Manish felt prouder than any stolen game could have made him. He understood that being trusted is a duty you protect, not a chance you exploit.
payload.title: Being trusted is a duty, not a chance
decoys: Manish kept the key to the store cupboard
School cupboards often hold sports equipment
A new football is tempting to any child

payload.passage: Stretch a rubber band and let it go, and it springs back at once. This snap-back is thanks to a stored kind of energy. While you pull the band, your muscles do work and that work is locked inside the stretched rubber. The instant you let go, the band releases the stored energy and zips back to its old shape. A wind-up toy and a pulled bowstring keep their energy in the very same way.
payload.title: How a stretched rubber band stores energy
decoys: A rubber band snaps back to its old shape
Energy is an important idea in all of science
Wind-up toys store energy before they move

payload.passage: Keep a green plant away from light for a while and it grows pale and feeble. Light is what a plant needs to make its food. In darkness its leaves cannot carry out the work that keeps them green. The plant uses up its stored food and slowly weakens. Its leaves may yellow and its stem grow thin and stretched. Without light, even a healthy plant cannot feed itself and begins to fade; so light is not a luxury for a plant but a need it cannot live without for long.
payload.title: Why a plant left in the dark turns pale
decoys: Leaves in the dark cannot do their green work
Living things need the right conditions
Stored food runs out and the plant weakens

payload.passage: A drone is a small flying machine that needs no pilot inside it. Several spinning blades lift it straight up into the air. A person on the ground guides it with a remote control or a phone. Tiny computers keep the drone steady and level as it hovers. People now use drones to film from above, deliver parcels and check faraway fields.
payload.title: How a drone flies without a pilot on board
decoys: Spinning blades lift the drone upward
New machines keep changing daily life
People use drones to film from above

payload.passage: A pile of dry autumn leaves is a treasure, not a nuisance. Swept into a corner, the leaves slowly break down into soft, dark mould. This leaf mould feeds the garden soil and helps it hold water. Spread under plants, the leaves also keep weeds down and roots cool. Far from being rubbish, fallen leaves are nature's free gift to the gardener.
payload.title: Why fallen leaves are a gift to the garden
decoys: Leaves break down into dark mould
Leaf mould helps the soil hold water

payload.passage: Dia wanted to sell her drawings but had no idea what price to ask. Her teacher suggested she look around first: how much did others charge for similar drawings, and what would buyers happily pay? A price set too high would scare everyone off, while one set too low would barely cover her paper and pens. After watching the market for a week, she settled on a fair middle figure, and her drawings began to sell. Dia learnt that a good price is found by studying both the customer and the competition.
payload.title: How to set a fair price by studying the market
decoys: Dia checked what others charged for drawings
A high price would scare buyers off

payload.passage: Out on the windswept savanna, a lone zebra is hard to defend, but the herd has a hidden trick built into its very skin. When zebras bunch tightly together, their bold black-and-white stripes blur into one dizzying, moving pattern. A charging lion finds it hard to tell where one zebra ends and the next begins, or to single out a target. The herd seems like one huge, confusing shape rather than many separate meals. By standing close and letting their stripes merge, the zebras protect each other through sheer confusion.
payload.title: How a zebra herd confuses lions with its stripes
decoys: Zebras' stripes blur together in a herd
Lions hunt animals on the savanna
A lone zebra is easier to catch

payload.passage: A forest is alive with energy that began as sunlight. The trees and plants catch the sun's light and store it as food in their leaves and wood. Insects and deer feed on the plants, taking in that energy. Birds and larger animals then feed on the plant-eaters. When any of them die, small creatures break them down and free their nutrients. The energy of the sun flows through the whole forest, link by link; so a whole woodland, from the tallest tree to the smallest beetle, runs on the energy of the sun.
payload.title: How the sun's energy moves through a forest
decoys: Insects and deer feed on the forest plants
Small creatures break down the dead and free nutrients

payload.passage: Mixing dough by hand for a large family was once slow and tiring. The electric mixer took over this heavy work. A small motor inside spins a pair of beaters very fast. The whirling beaters fold air into the batter and blend it smooth in moments. What once took long minutes of stirring is now done in seconds, leaving the cook free for other tasks.
payload.title: How an electric mixer speeds up the cook's work
decoys: A motor spins a pair of fast beaters
Inventions ease the work of the kitchen
The beaters fold air into the batter

payload.passage: The air in a busy city can grow thick and grey with smoke. Cars, buses and factories all pour out fumes as they run. Breathing this dirty air can give people coughs and make it hard to see far ahead. Trees and parks help by filtering some of the smoke from the air. Cleaner vehicles and more green spaces can let everyone breathe easier.
payload.title: Why clean air matters in our crowded cities
decoys: Cars and factories pour out fumes
Cities are crowded and busy places
Trees help filter smoke from the air

payload.passage: The archerfish has found a way to hunt insects that rest on leaves above the water, well out of reach. It rises just below the surface and takes careful aim at a bug on a branch overhead. Then it shoots a sharp jet of water from its mouth, knocking the surprised insect off its perch and into the river. As the bug tumbles down, the archerfish darts over and gulps it up. It must even allow for the way light bends in water to aim true. By turning water into a weapon, this clever fish reaches food no ordinary fish could.
payload.title: How the archerfish shoots water to catch insects
decoys: The archerfish shoots a jet of water
Fish must find clever ways to eat
It knocks insects off branches above

payload.passage: Tara kept all her money in cash until the day she lost a whole week's savings through a hole in her pocket. Her older brother showed her how a bank card and a passbook keep a careful record of every rupee. With money in the bank, a lost card could be blocked, but lost cash was simply gone forever. The record also helped her see exactly where her money went. Tara learnt that tracking and safekeeping money is not dull paperwork; it is a shield against losing what you worked for.
payload.title: Why tracking money guards against losing it
decoys: Tara lost a week's savings through a hole
A lost bank card can be blocked

payload.passage: Picking up litter on a beach or in a park is a small act with a big reach. Every wrapper or bottle left lying about can harm an animal or wash into the sea. When you carry your rubbish to a bin, you keep that harm from ever happening. A clean beach is safer for crabs, birds and barefoot children alike. One person's tidy habit can inspire many others to do the same.
payload.title: Why picking up litter protects animals and people
decoys: A wrapper can wash into the sea
We should keep our surroundings clean
A clean beach is safer for crabs and birds

payload.passage: By day the sun blazes alone, looking nothing like the tiny stars of night. Yet the sun is itself a star, just a very close one. The other stars seem small only because they lie unimaginably far away. If we could travel to one, it would blaze as fiercely as our sun. So the difference between the sun and the night stars is mostly a matter of distance; realising this turns the night sky into a field of distant suns, each one perhaps warming worlds of its own.
payload.title: Why the sun is really a nearby star
decoys: Other stars lie unimaginably far from Earth
Space stretches farther than we can imagine
A distant star would blaze as fiercely as our sun

payload.passage: Suresh was the strongest boy in the lane and always won the arm-wrestling games. One day a thin, quiet boy challenged him, and Suresh laughed at the very idea. To everyone's surprise the quiet boy held firm, then slowly pinned Suresh's arm down. Instead of sulking or making excuses, Suresh stood up, grinned, and shook the winner's hand warmly. The watching boys clapped for his good spirit more than for the win. Suresh learnt that losing gracefully can win you more respect than any easy victory ever could.
payload.title: Losing gracefully wins more respect than victory
decoys: A thin boy beat the strongest boy

payload.passage: Look closely at the night sky and the stars are not all plain white. Some shine faintly blue, others golden or reddish. A star's colour reveals how hot its surface is. The hottest stars burn with a blue-white glow, while cooler ones gleam orange or red. So by simply noting a star's tint, you can guess whether it is one of the sky's hottest or coolest fires; astronomers use a star's colour as a quick way to judge its temperature long before measuring it in any other way.
payload.title: Why stars come in different colours
decoys: The hottest stars glow with a blue-white light
The night sky is richer than it first appears
A star's colour reveals how hot its surface is

payload.passage: A simple ramp can help a person move a heavy box more easily. Lifting a box straight up takes a lot of strength all at once. A ramp lets you push the box up a gentle slope instead. You use less force at any moment, though you push it over a longer distance. This is why builders use ramps and slopes to roll heavy loads up to higher places.
payload.title: How a ramp makes lifting a heavy load easier
decoys: A ramp is a kind of gentle slope
Clever tools make hard work simpler
Pushing a box up a ramp covers a longer distance

payload.passage: Most of the time a comet is just a quiet lump of ice and dust drifting in the cold dark. But as its long orbit carries it close to the sun, things change. The sun's heat melts some of the ice, releasing gas and dust. This material streams away from the comet, lit up into a long, glowing tail. As the comet moves off again into the cold, the tail fades and the comet sleeps once more; because of these rare, glowing visits, comets were once feared as strange omens before people understood what they truly were.
payload.title: How a comet grows a glowing tail near the sun
decoys: The sun's heat melts some of the comet's ice
Space is full of strange and beautiful objects
A comet's tail always streams away from the sun

payload.passage: During the long power cut, the whole hostel had only one charged lantern to study by. The senior boys claimed it for themselves each night. Gopal, a senior too, saw the juniors struggling in the dark before their exams. He set up a rota so the lantern passed to every room in turn, his own included only at its proper time. The juniors thanked him warmly. Gopal learnt that sharing a scarce thing fairly matters far more than grabbing it by seniority.
payload.title: Sharing scarcity fairly beats grabbing by rank
decoys: Gopal set up a rota for the lantern
Senior boys claimed the lantern first

payload.passage: A seed looks dead and dry, yet it holds a tiny sleeping plant inside. When the seed lands in warm, damp soil, it begins to wake. It drinks in water and swells until its hard coat splits open. A little root pushes down to grip the soil, while a tender shoot reaches up towards the light. With sun and water, that small shoot grows into a full plant.
payload.title: How a tiny seed grows into a plant
decoys: A seed swells when it drinks in water
Nature is full of living wonders
A root pushes down into the soil

payload.passage: Ice cream melts on a hot day, but the same cup can freeze again in the fridge. This is because water can take three forms depending on its warmth. When it is very cold it stays as hard ice, a solid. As it warms up it turns into flowing liquid water. Heat it further and it rises as an invisible vapour, a gas. The water itself does not change; only its form shifts with temperature.
payload.title: How water changes between solid, liquid and gas
decoys: Ice is the solid form of water
Temperature affects almost everything around us
Ice cream melts quickly on a hot day

payload.passage: The camera once seemed like magic, freezing a moment so it could be kept forever. Light from a scene enters the camera through a small opening at the front. A curved lens bends this light and draws a sharp picture onto a surface inside. There the image is captured and saved, whether on film or in a chip. With a camera, people could share faces and places they had never been able to show before.
payload.title: How a camera captures and saves a picture
decoys: A lens bends the light entering the camera
Inventions can make life feel almost magical
A camera lets people share faces and places

payload.passage: Some nights the moon seems to vanish completely from the sky. At this time, called the new moon, it sits almost between the Earth and the sun. Its lit side faces fully away from us, so the side we see stays dark. It also rises and sets close to the sun, lost in the daytime glare. A few nights later a thin curve appears, and the moon slowly returns to view; so the moon does not really vanish at new moon, but simply turns its dark face toward us, lost in the sun's glare.
payload.title: How a new moon hides in the daytime sky
decoys: A thin curve appears a few nights later
The sky is always changing above us
At new moon the lit side faces fully away from us

payload.passage: Every move you make, from a smile to a sprint, is the work of muscles. A muscle works by pulling, never by pushing. When your brain sends a signal, the muscle tightens and grows shorter. As it shortens, it tugs on a bone and moves that part of you. Because a muscle can only pull, the body uses muscles in pairs that take turns.
payload.title: How muscles pull on bones to move the body
decoys: A muscle tightens and grows shorter
The body is full of clever parts
Muscles work in pairs that take turns

payload.passage: When Nikhil missed the announcement for his train, a uniformed porter came to his rescue. The porter not only carried the heavy trunk on his head but knew every platform, shortcut and timing in the station by heart. He guided the worried boy through tunnels and up stairs, reaching the right coach with a minute to spare. Nikhil's father paid the agreed fee gratefully. Nikhil saw that the porter sold far more than muscle; he sold a deep, practical knowledge of the station that no map could replace.
payload.title: A station porter sells knowledge, not just muscle
decoys: The porter carried the trunk on his head
Kind strangers can help us when we struggle
Nikhil's father paid the porter a fee

payload.passage: On cool mornings the grass may be wet with dew or white with frost, and the two are closely linked. Both form when air cools and gives up its hidden vapour overnight. If the surface is above freezing, the vapour settles as liquid dew. If it is below freezing, the same vapour turns straight into icy frost. The only difference is the temperature of the chilled surface. So dew and frost are really the same event happening on either side of freezing.
payload.title: How dew and frost are two sides of one change
decoys: Dew forms when the surface is above freezing
Cold weather changes the world in many ways
Vapour turns to frost below the freezing point

payload.passage: Geckos and many lizards have a startling way of escaping a hunter's grip. If a bird or cat seizes the lizard by its tail, the tail simply breaks off and is left behind. The dropped tail keeps wriggling on the ground for a while, drawing the confused predator's attention. Meanwhile the lizard itself dashes away to safety, losing only a tail it can manage without. In time a new tail slowly grows back in place of the old one. By sacrificing a small part of itself, the lizard saves the whole.
payload.title: How a lizard drops its tail to escape
decoys: A lizard's dropped tail keeps wriggling
Birds and cats hunt small lizards
A new tail slowly grows back

payload.passage: Tanish was puzzled that the ballot paper showed not only names but also little pictures beside them, like a lamp or a tree. His teacher explained that not everyone could read, yet every citizen had the right to vote. The simple symbols let a person who knew no letters still find and choose their candidate with confidence. The picture was a bridge across the gap of reading. Tanish learnt that a truly fair election bends to include even those who cannot read, so that no voice is silenced by a lack of letters.
payload.title: Why ballot symbols include non-readers
decoys: The ballot showed pictures beside names
A symbol helps a non-reader choose

payload.passage: When a young shoot pushes up through the soil, it often bends into a little hook. This clever bending protects the tender tip. As the hook leads the way, it shields the soft growing point from being scraped by the rough soil. Once the shoot breaks into the open air and light, it straightens up. Then it spreads its first leaves to catch the sun. The bend is a brief but useful trick for getting safely above ground; so this small, clever bend helps the young plant reach the open air without harm.
payload.title: Why a sprouting seed bends its stem as it rises
decoys: The hook shields the soft growing point
Living things have many clever habits
The shoot straightens once it reaches the light

payload.passage: Every autumn, huge flocks of bar-headed geese leave the cold northern plains and fly all the way to warmer Indian wetlands. They do not wander aimlessly; they follow the same ancient routes their parents used, guided by rivers, mountains and the angle of the sun. Flying in a neat V-shape, each bird rides on the gentle draft made by the one ahead, saving precious energy. The leader at the point works hardest and is swapped often so no single goose tires out. In this clever, shared way the whole flock crosses thousands of kilometres to reach food and gentler weather.
payload.title: How migrating geese travel far by working together
decoys: Geese fly in a neat V-shaped formation
Many birds travel south when winter arrives
The lead goose is swapped when it tires

payload.passage: Rain does not just fall from nowhere; it is part of a never-ending journey of water. The sun heats lakes, rivers and the sea, and the water rises as an invisible vapour. High in the cool sky this vapour gathers into tiny droplets that form clouds. When the droplets grow heavy, they tumble down as rain, sleet or snow. The water then flows back to the rivers and sea, ready to rise once more.
payload.title: The water cycle that gives us rain
decoys: Water vapour rises when the sun heats the sea
Nature is full of patterns that repeat over time
Clouds are made of many tiny water droplets

payload.passage: A colony of prairie dogs lives in a vast network of burrows beneath the grassland, and they keep one another safe through constant chatter. When one prairie dog spots a hawk or a coyote, it gives a sharp bark to warn the rest. Remarkably, their calls seem to differ for different dangers and even for the size and speed of the threat. Hearing the warning, the others dash for their burrow openings. Lookouts pop up and scan the horizon in turns. Through this shared watchfulness and detailed calling, the whole town stays alert and alive.
payload.title: How prairie dogs warn each other of danger
decoys: A prairie dog barks to warn of a hawk
Prairie dogs live in underground burrows
Lookouts scan the horizon in turns

payload.passage: Why does your body need rest days between hard exercise? When you exercise hard, you make tiny tears in your muscles that need time to heal. On a rest day, the body repairs these tears and builds the muscle stronger. Without enough rest, the muscles stay tired and sore and cannot grow well. So rest is as much a part of training as the exercise itself.
payload.title: Why the body needs rest days after exercise
decoys: Rest days let the body repair tiny tears

payload.passage: Young Aditi was surprised that the village schoolchildren could influence the panchayat at all. Their teacher helped them write a polite letter asking for a safe footpath to the school, since cars sped along the muddy road. The children read the letter aloud at the open meeting, and the elders, moved, agreed to lay a path. It appeared within two months. Aditi learnt that taking part in village affairs was not only for grown-ups; even children, by speaking up the right way, could shape the place they lived in.
payload.title: How schoolchildren can shape village decisions
decoys: The children asked for a safe footpath
Cars sped along the muddy road

payload.passage: Earth is circled by a single large moon, neither many nor none. Scientists think this moon was born from a giant crash in the early days. A huge object is thought to have struck the young Earth, flinging out a ring of hot debris. Over time this debris gathered under its own gravity into one round moon. Since then that lone moon has faithfully circled the Earth for billions of years; whatever its exact beginning, that single companion has shaped our tides, our nights and even our calendars ever since.
payload.title: Why the Earth has just one moon
decoys: Debris gathered under gravity into one round moon
Space holds many tales of long ago
A huge object struck the young Earth long ago

payload.passage: Why does your body shiver and your teeth chatter in a high fever? When germs attack, the body sometimes raises its own temperature to fight them better. To climb to this higher level, the body first makes itself feel cold. It shivers and shakes to make heat and push the temperature up. That is why a rising fever can begin with chills and chattering teeth.
payload.title: Why a rising fever begins with chills
decoys: Shivering makes heat to push the temperature up
The body fights germs in clever ways
A fever helps the body fight germs

payload.passage: A simple periscope lets you see over a wall or around a corner. Inside a long tube sit two mirrors set at slanted angles. Light from above strikes the top mirror and bounces down the tube. The lower mirror then bends that light into your waiting eye. With it, a person can peer over a fence or out of a submarine without being seen.
payload.title: How a periscope lets you see around corners
decoys: Two slanted mirrors bounce the light down
Clever devices widen what we see
A periscope can peer out of a submarine

payload.passage: Bread dough seems to swell up as if by magic before it is baked. Bakers add a tiny living thing called yeast to the dough. As the yeast feeds on the sugars in the flour, it gives off a gas. This gas gets trapped inside the soft, stretchy dough and forms many little bubbles. The bubbles push the dough up and make it rise, leaving the baked bread soft and full of holes.
payload.title: Why bread dough rises before it is baked
decoys: Yeast gives off a gas as it feeds
Baking is a skill that takes lots of practice
Tiny bubbles make holes inside the bread

payload.passage: On sports day, Veer was leading the sack race when he saw the boy beside him topple and get tangled in his sack. The finish line was close, and the medal almost his. Veer hopped back, helped untangle the boy, and they finished together near the end. He won no medal, but the crowd clapped longest for him. Long after the medals were forgotten, people still spoke of what Veer had done. Veer learnt that an act of kindness can be remembered far longer than the name of whoever crossed the line first.
payload.title: Kindness is remembered longer than who won
decoys: Veer helped a fallen boy in the sack race
Sack races can leave runners tangled
He was leading near the finish

payload.passage: Kavya was the best singer in school and was certain of winning the solo contest. On the day, a shy newcomer sang with surprising beauty and took the first prize. Kavya's first feeling was bitter disappointment. Then she saw the newcomer standing alone, unsure and friendless. Swallowing her envy, Kavya went over and warmly congratulated her, and the two became close. From that day the two girls practised their songs together after school. Kavya learnt that choosing graciousness over envy can turn a rival into a friend and a loss into a gain.
payload.title: Graciousness turns a rival into a friend
decoys: A newcomer beat Kavya in the singing contest
Singing contests award a first prize
Kavya was the best singer in school

payload.passage: A simple pile of stones in a garden corner can shelter many small lives. The gaps between the stones stay cool and damp in the heat. Frogs, beetles and even small lizards creep in to rest and hide. The pile gives them shade in summer and a refuge from the cold. From a heap of leftover stones grows a tiny, lively home.
payload.title: How a pile of stones shelters garden creatures
decoys: Gaps between stones stay cool and damp
Frogs and lizards hide in the stones

payload.passage: Why does the body grow thirsty before it grows truly short of water? Your body does not wait until it is badly dry to warn you. It senses a small drop in water and sends thirst as an early nudge. Drinking then keeps you topped up before any harm begins. This early warning is the body protecting you well ahead of trouble.
payload.title: Why thirst warns us early about water
decoys: The body senses a small drop in water
The body guards us with signals
Thirst comes before any harm begins

payload.passage: When a seed first sprouts, it has no leaves and so cannot make food from light. Yet it still manages to send out a root and a shoot. The secret is a store of food packed inside the seed by its parent plant. The tiny seedling lives on this supply until its first green leaves open. Only then can it begin cooking its own meals from sunlight, and the packed store runs out just in time; this neat arrangement is why a healthy seed can sprout in dark soil long before it ever sees a ray of sunlight.
payload.title: Why a seed carries its own packed lunch
decoys: The seedling uses stored food before its leaves open
Parents in nature often care for their young
A new seedling cannot yet make food from light

payload.passage: In one busy ward, fewer than half the voters bothered to come out, and a weak candidate slipped into office on a thin handful of votes. Years later the same people complained loudly about his poor work. Reyaan's mother pointed out the quiet irony: those who had stayed home had handed their share of the decision to a small, unrepresentative few. Their silence on voting day had echoed for five long years. Reyaan learnt that skipping a vote is itself a choice, and often a costly one.
payload.title: How skipping a vote carries a cost
decoys: Fewer than half the ward's voters turned out
People often complain about their leaders
A weak candidate won on few votes

payload.passage: A simple solar street light needs no wire from the town supply. By day a small panel on top soaks up the sun and fills a battery. The battery stores this energy quietly through the daylight hours. When darkness falls, a sensor switches on the lamp from the stored power. Villages with no power line can now light their streets with the sun alone.
payload.title: How a solar street light works without wires
decoys: A panel fills a battery during the day
A sensor switches the lamp on at dark

payload.passage: At the fish market, Diya noticed the boldest cries came from sellers whose catch was beginning to dull. Fresh fish almost sells itself, but a stall with ageing stock must work harder to attract a buyer before the day ends. So those sellers shout louder, smile wider and offer to throw in a little extra. Diya found that the noisiest corner was often the most anxious one. She learnt to read the market not just by the prices on display but by the urgency behind each seller's voice.
payload.title: Reading a market by the sellers' urgency
decoys: Sellers with old stock shout the loudest
Markets are full of interesting sounds
Fresh fish hardly needs any selling

payload.passage: The Arctic ground squirrel faces a winter so long and cold that no food can be found for months. To survive, it does something almost unbelievable. It curls up in its burrow and lets its body cool until it is nearly freezing, far colder than any other warm animal can bear. Its heart barely beats and it scarcely breathes during this deep, deathlike sleep. Every few weeks it briefly warms and shivers, then chills again. Living slowly off its stored fat, it sleeps right through the brutal winter and wakes thin but alive in spring.
payload.title: How the ground squirrel survives a freezing winter
decoys: The ground squirrel cools nearly to freezing
Arctic winters last for many months
It lives off stored fat while it sleeps

payload.passage: The mantis shrimp, no longer than a finger, carries one of the fastest weapons in all of nature. Folded beneath its body are two club-like arms held under enormous spring tension. When it spots a crab or snail, it unleashes a strike so fast and powerful it can crack a hard shell in an instant, even sending out a tiny shock in the water. Few prey can withstand such a blow. The little shrimp smashes open meals that look far too tough for its size. By striking with astonishing force, the mantis shrimp eats what others cannot.
payload.title: How the mantis shrimp smashes open tough shells
decoys: The mantis shrimp strikes with great force
Many sea creatures have hard shells
Its club arms are held under tension

payload.passage: A spider does not chase its dinner across the forest; it lets the dinner come to it. With great patience it spins a wide web of silk between two branches, each thread placed with care. Some strands are sticky to trap, while others are dry so the spider itself can walk without getting caught. When an insect blunders in and struggles, the trembling threads carry the news straight to the waiting spider. It rushes out and wraps its meal in silk. The web is both a clever trap and a quiet message line, built by patience rather than chase.
payload.title: How a spider's web catches food through patience
decoys: Some web threads are sticky and others dry
A trapped insect makes the web tremble

payload.passage: Vivaan watched a worker tap the train's heavy wheels with a hammer at every long stop and thought it a strange habit. The man explained that a healthy wheel rings clear, while a cracked one gives a dull thud. By listening, he could catch a hidden flaw before it caused a terrible accident far down the track. The simple test, done again and again, quietly kept thousands safe. Vivaan learnt that careful checking, even of something as humble as a wheel, was a steady guard standing between travellers and disaster.
payload.title: How tapping wheels keeps a train safe
decoys: A cracked wheel gives a dull thud
A worker tapped the wheels with a hammer

payload.passage: A rising moon close to the rooftops can look huge, almost startling in size. Yet measure it and you will find it is no bigger than usual. The change is a trick of the mind, not of the moon. Near the horizon we compare the moon with trees and buildings, which makes it seem large. High in the empty sky there is nothing to compare it to, so it looks smaller again; so the giant rising moon that startles us is really an illusion of the mind rather than any true change in the sky.
payload.title: Why the moon looks bigger near the horizon
decoys: Near the horizon we compare the moon with buildings
Our eyes can fool us in surprising ways
High in the sky there is nothing to compare the moon to

payload.passage: The water a plant needs is in the soil, but its leaves are far above. To solve this, fine roots soak up water from between the soil grains. The water then climbs through thin tubes inside the stem, almost like a drink rising through a straw. As water escapes from the leaves into the air, it gently pulls more water up behind it. In this quiet way the whole plant stays fed and firm from root to tip; so the simple act of a plant getting a drink involves the roots, the stem and the leaves all working quietly together.
payload.title: How a plant drinks water from the ground up
decoys: Thin tubes inside the stem carry water upward
Plants depend on many parts working together
Roots soak up water from between the soil grains

payload.passage: A choked drain after a heavy rain often holds a sad story. People toss plastic wrappers and bags onto the street without a thought. When the rain comes, all this litter washes into the drains and blocks them. The water then has nowhere to go and floods the roads. Simply throwing rubbish into a bin would keep the drains clear and the streets dry.
payload.title: Why littering leads to blocked drains and floods
decoys: Litter washes into the drains in the rain
Blocked drains make the roads flood

payload.passage: A simple kettle that switches itself off was a small but welcome invention. Inside it lies a strip made of two metals stuck together. As the water boils, rising steam heats this strip. The two metals grow at different rates, so the strip bends. The bending strip flicks a switch that cuts the power, and the kettle turns off before it boils dry.
payload.title: How a kettle switches itself off when boiling
decoys: A strip of two metals bends when heated
Rising steam heats the metal strip

payload.passage: The Canada goose and many shorebirds raise chicks that must feed themselves almost from birth, and timing is everything. The parents arrange for the eggs to hatch exactly when the brief summer fills the marshes with insects and fresh shoots. A few weeks early or late and the chicks would find little to eat. The downy young can walk and feed within a day, racing to fatten up before the cold returns. By matching the hatching to the burst of food, the parents give their fast-growing chicks the best chance to survive the short season.
payload.title: How birds time their eggs to the burst of food
decoys: Chicks hatch when insects are plentiful
Some chicks feed themselves from birth
The young can walk within a day

payload.passage: A clean beach is more than a pretty place to play. The sand and shallows are home to crabs, tiny shellfish and nesting birds. Bottles and plastic left behind can trap or poison these creatures. Sharp glass also puts barefoot children at risk. When everyone carries their litter home, the beach stays safe and alive for all who visit.
payload.title: Why keeping beaches clean protects shore life
decoys: Crabs and shellfish live in the sand

payload.passage: Why does your body sweat even when you sit quietly in the heat? Your body works hard to stay at one warm temperature inside. On a hot day, even resting can let too much heat build up. So the skin lets out sweat to carry that heat away as it dries. This is why you can grow damp on a sultry afternoon without moving at all.
payload.title: Why we sweat even while resting in the heat
decoys: The skin lets out sweat to carry heat away
The body keeps its inside steady
Heat builds up even while resting

payload.passage: Yash had trained all summer long to climb the steep, rocky hill that rose behind his village. Halfway up the slope his legs began to burn, and a small voice inside him begged him to turn back and go home. He sat on a boulder, rested, and drank a little water instead of giving in. Then he rose and took one slow, deliberate step after another up the path. When he finally reached the very top, the whole valley lay spread out golden and glowing below him. Yash learnt that the hardest part of any climb often comes just before the great view opens up.
payload.title: The hardest climb ends just before the view
decoys: Yash trained all summer to climb the hill
Climbing a steep hill makes your legs burn
The valley looked golden from the hilltop

payload.passage: The sun looks the same round shape every day, while the moon keeps changing. The difference is in how they shine. The sun makes its own light, so we always see its whole glowing face. The moon only reflects sunlight, and we see different amounts of its lit half as it orbits us. That is why the moon has phases and the steady sun does not; so the changing moon and the steady sun, side by side in our sky, shine in two completely different ways.
payload.title: Why the moon has phases but the sun does not
decoys: The moon reflects light from the sun
The sky is full of contrasts to notice
The sun makes its own light and shows its whole face

payload.passage: Long before printed calendars, people kept track of time by watching the moon. The moon slips through its phases in a steady cycle of about a month. From one full moon to the next, roughly four weeks go by. By counting these cycles, early people could mark the passing months of the year. Many old calendars were built directly around this lunar rhythm. The slow change of the moon's face served as one of humankind's first clocks; so our very word 'month' is a lasting echo of the time people kept by the moon.
payload.title: How the changing moon once marked the months
decoys: From one full moon to the next is about four weeks
People have always tried to measure time
Old calendars were built around the moon's rhythm

payload.passage: A simple wheel with teeth, called a gear, passes movement from one part to another. When two gears meet, the teeth of one push the teeth of the next. A small gear turning a large one makes the large one move slowly but with great force. Swap them around and you trade force for speed instead. Gears like these run inside clocks, cycles, mills and countless machines.
payload.title: How gears pass movement between machine parts
decoys: The teeth of one gear push the next
Machines are built from clever parts
Small and large gears trade force for speed

payload.passage: Why does a regular sleeping time help children grow well? Much of a child's growing happens during the deep hours of night sleep. A steady bedtime lets the body settle into that deep sleep more easily. Sleeping and waking at the same times keeps the inner clock smooth and reliable. Children with a regular routine tend to grow, learn and feel better.
payload.title: Why a regular bedtime helps children grow
decoys: Much growing happens during deep night sleep
A steady bedtime aids deep sleep

payload.passage: Old Mrs Iyer's heavy shopping bags split open right in the middle of the busy footpath, scattering vegetables everywhere. Crowds of people streamed past her, all far too hurried to stop and help. Schoolboy Amit was already running late for his tuition class. Even so, he knelt down on the dusty pavement and gathered up every last rolling tomato and onion. Then he walked the grateful old lady safely home before hurrying on, missing the first part of his lesson. Amit learnt that responsibility to a fellow human being can sometimes matter more than being perfectly on time.
payload.title: Helping someone can matter more than being punctual
decoys: Amit helped Mrs Iyer carry her vegetables
Shopping bags can split on a footpath
Crowds are often too busy to stop

payload.passage: A simple bar of glass called a prism splits sunlight into colours. White light is really a mix of many colours travelling together. As the light passes through the angled glass, it bends. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount and fans out. A band of colours, like a small rainbow, spreads across the wall beyond the prism.
payload.title: How a prism spreads sunlight into a rainbow
decoys: Each colour bends by a different amount
White light is a mix of many colours

payload.passage: Old Mr. Banerjee sold the same plump guavas in the market for thirty years, and customers walked past fresher-looking stalls to reach him. He never cheated on weight, never sold a hidden rotten fruit, and remembered each regular by name. Younger sellers offered lower prices, yet his loyal crowd stayed put. Slowly the lane learnt his lesson the hard way: a vendor caught cheating once lost buyers forever. Mr. Banerjee proved that honest weighing and steady kindness are a kind of wealth no quick trick can match.
payload.title: Honest dealing builds a loyal market following
decoys: Mr. Banerjee never cheated on the weight
Kind people are liked wherever they go
He remembered each regular customer's name

payload.passage: Neha's drawing was chosen over her close friend Sara's for the school magazine cover that term. Sara tried hard to hide her sharp disappointment, but she went very quiet for the rest of the day. Neha noticed the silence at once. Instead of boasting about her win, she asked Sara to help her colour in the final picture together. The two girls worked side by side, and Neha made sure they signed both their names below the drawing. The magazine looked all the brighter for it. Neha learnt that true success feels fuller and warmer when you make room in it for a friend.
payload.title: Success feels fuller when shared with a friend
decoys: Neha's drawing was chosen for the magazine
School magazines need a cover picture
Losing a contest can make a friend quiet

payload.passage: When a honeybee finds a thief or a wasp at the hive door, it cannot fight a much larger foe alone. So Japanese honeybees use a remarkable group trick against an attacking hornet. Dozens of bees swarm over the intruder in a tight, buzzing ball. Then they all vibrate their bodies hard, raising the heat inside the ball higher and higher. The hornet can stand far less heat than the bees can, and it slowly cooks while the bees survive. By turning their own warmth into a weapon together, the small bees defeat a giant enemy.
payload.title: How honeybees cook a hornet by working together
decoys: Bees swarm over the hornet in a ball
The bees vibrate to raise the heat

payload.passage: A cloud may hold tonnes of water, yet it drifts overhead without dropping like a stone. Its water is split into countless droplets so tiny they are almost weightless. Gentle currents of rising warm air also push up against them. As long as the droplets stay small and the air keeps lifting, the cloud floats. Only when droplets join and grow heavy enough does the cloud release its water as rain; so a cloud is best thought of not as a solid object but as a vast, slowly shifting crowd of tiny floating droplets.
payload.title: Why clouds float instead of falling
decoys: Rising warm air pushes up against the droplets
The sky holds many things we take for granted
Cloud droplets are so tiny they are almost weightless

payload.passage: On a sunny day you may watch white, puffy clouds slowly grow and swell over the warm land, born from rising warm air. The sun heats the ground, and the ground in turn warms the air resting just above it. This warm air, being light, floats steadily upward into the sky. As it climbs, it cools, and its vapour gathers into tiny droplets. Those droplets clump together as a fluffy white cloud. So a fair-weather cloud is really a sign of warm air quietly rising from the land below.
payload.title: How rising warm air builds a fluffy cloud
decoys: The sun heats the ground, which warms the air
The sky is shaped by many processes
Cooling vapour gathers into tiny droplets

payload.passage: Aryan was learning to ride a bicycle and fell off again and again, scraping his knees each time. His friends had all learnt quickly and teased him for being so slow. He wanted to give up and push the bicycle into the shed for good. But each evening he wheeled it out and tried once more. One golden evening he suddenly found his balance and rode the whole length of the lane. Aryan learnt that the only true failure is stopping before the last try that would have worked.
payload.title: The only real failure is giving up early
decoys: Aryan kept falling off his bicycle
Learning to cycle means scraped knees
His friends teased him for being slow

payload.passage: Devika was nearly at the very front of the long ration queue after standing an hour in the blazing sun. A frail old woman behind her began to sway, faint from the heat and clearly unable to stand much longer. Devika looked at the short distance left to the counter, then quietly stepped aside and let the woman take her place. She walked all the way to the back of the line again. She waited a second hour in the sun, but she carried home far more than rice that day. Devika realised that true patience can be the willingness to wait so that someone weaker need not.
payload.title: Patience can be a quiet act of mercy
decoys: Devika gave her queue place to a frail woman
Ration queues can be long and tiring
Standing in the sun makes people feel faint

payload.passage: A river that flows past a town carries the marks of how people treat it. Where waste and dirty water are poured in, the river turns murky and begins to smell. Fish struggle to breathe, and the water is no longer safe to use. Where people keep the banks clean and treat their waste first, the river runs clear and lively. The state of a river mirrors the care of its people.
payload.title: How a river reflects the care of its people
decoys: Waste makes a river murky and smelly

payload.passage: Sunlight pours down on a leaf, but the leaf does not simply waste it as heat. The green colouring inside captures the light and locks its energy into sugar. That sugar is like a battery the plant can use later to grow, flower and make fruit. When an animal eats the plant, it takes in that stored energy too. In this way the energy of distant sunlight ends up powering creatures all across the land; in this way the green leaf becomes the doorway through which the sun's energy first enters almost every living thing.
payload.title: Why green leaves turn the sun into stored energy
decoys: Green colouring inside a leaf captures sunlight
The sun gives energy to everything on Earth
Animals get energy by eating green plants

payload.passage: The planets near the sun and those far away are strangely different. The four closest, including Earth, are small and made mostly of rock and metal. Far out, where the sun's warmth is weak, the giant planets are huge balls of gas and ice. Long ago, the heat near the young sun let only rocky bits survive close by. Lighter gases drifted outward, where the cold let them gather into giant worlds; so the orderly split between small rocky worlds nearby and huge gassy ones far off goes back to the birth of the solar system.
payload.title: Why inner planets are rocky and outer ones gassy
decoys: The four planets closest to the sun are made of rock
The solar system is full of variety
Lighter gases gathered into giant worlds far from the sun

payload.passage: On a hot, dry day you may see streaks falling from a cloud that simply fade away. This strange sight has a simple cause. The raindrops do leave the cloud, but the air below is so warm and dry that they evaporate on the way down. Long before they can land, the drops turn back into invisible vapour. So the rain seems to vanish in mid-air. It is really the water cycle at work, lifting the water back up before it ever touches the earth.
payload.title: Why some rain never reaches the ground
decoys: Warm, dry air below evaporates the falling drops
Weather can behave in surprising ways
The drops turn back into vapour before landing

payload.passage: A simple electric switch lets you control power with one finger. Inside it sit two metal pieces that can touch or part. When you flick it on, the pieces meet and complete the path for the current. The electricity then flows on to the light or fan. Flick it off and the pieces part, breaking the path so the power stops.
payload.title: How a switch turns electric power on and off
decoys: Two metal pieces touch to complete the path
Inventions put power in our hands
Flicking off breaks the path for current

payload.passage: Why does the body need you to drink water rather than only sweet drinks? Your body uses plain water for nearly every task inside it. Sweet drinks carry a lot of sugar with little real benefit. Drinking them in place of water can harm the teeth and add unhealthy weight. A glass of clean water serves the body far better than a sugary one.
payload.title: Why plain water serves the body better than sweet drinks
decoys: The body uses plain water for almost everything
What we drink affects our health
Sweet drinks can harm the teeth

payload.passage: High in cold mountains, snow piles up and packs into thick, heavy ice called a glacier. Pulled by gravity, this great mass of ice creeps slowly downhill. As it grinds along, it scrapes rock and carries away stones beneath it. Over ages this slow scouring gouges out a wide, U-shaped valley. Long after the ice melts away, the carved valley remains as a sign of its passage; so a wide, gently curved mountain valley is often the lasting signature of a great river of ice that vanished long ago.
payload.title: How a glacier slowly carves a valley
decoys: The glacier scrapes rock and carries away stones
Nature can reshape mountains over long ages
A glacier gouges out a wide U-shaped valley

payload.passage: A simple hand drill makes a neat hole where a nail would split the wood. The drill holds a sharp twisted bit at its tip. As you turn the handle, the bit spins and bites into the wood. Its spiral shape carries the chips up and out of the hole. Slowly a clean, round hole appears, ready for a screw or a peg.
payload.title: How a drill bores a clean hole in wood
decoys: The spinning bit bites into the wood
Tools help us build and mend
The spiral carries the chips out

payload.passage: The whole hostel wanted to watch one channel, but little Sunny wanted his cartoon at the same hour. The older boys simply took the remote, ignoring his pleas. Ravi, the eldest, could have sided with his friends. Instead he suggested cartoons for half an hour first, then the match, so everyone got a turn. The boys grumbled but agreed, and Sunny beamed. When the cartoon ended, even Sunny cheered loudly for the cricket match. Ravi learnt that fairness sometimes means standing up for the smallest voice, even against your own friends.
payload.title: Fairness stands up for the smallest voice
decoys: Ravi gave Sunny half an hour of cartoons
The older boys grabbed the remote

payload.passage: Pouring a bucket of waste water onto the garden is wiser than letting it run off. Water used to wash rice or vegetables still carries goodness the plants can use. Given to the garden, it waters the plants without drawing more from the tap. This way one lot of water does two jobs before it is done. Reusing such water is a simple way to save a precious resource.
payload.title: How reusing waste water helps a garden grow
decoys: Reused water saves drawing from the tap

payload.passage: Sometimes a summer storm pelts the ground with icy balls of hail. These are made high inside towering storm clouds. Strong updraughts carry water droplets up to freezing heights, where they turn to ice. The lumps fall, catch more water, and are tossed up to freeze again, growing layer by layer. When they finally become too heavy for the updraught to lift, they crash down as hail; if you ever cut a large hailstone in half, you can see the rings of ice that show how many times it rose and fell.
payload.title: Why hail forms inside tall storm clouds
decoys: Updraughts carry droplets up to freezing heights
Storms can bring unexpected kinds of weather
Hailstones grow layer by layer as they rise and fall

payload.passage: Arjun could not understand why a bank would pay him interest just for keeping his money there. His teacher turned the question around: why would the bank want his money at all? Because, she explained, the bank lends that money to others at a higher rate and keeps the difference. To attract savers like Arjun, it shares a small slice of its earnings with them. The interest was really a thank-you for the use of his money. Arjun learnt that both saver and bank gain when idle money is put to work.
payload.title: Why a bank pays you to keep money there
decoys: The bank lends money at a higher rate
Interest is a reward for saving

payload.passage: In a colony of honeypot ants, food is plentiful in the rainy season but scarce in the long dry spell. To survive the lean months, the colony uses some of its own workers as living storehouses. These special ants are fed so much that their bellies swell into great golden globes, far too heavy to move. They hang from the ceiling of the nest, holding the stored food inside their own bodies. When food runs out above ground, the other ants stroke them and they give back the stored nectar. The colony survives the drought on its living larder.
payload.title: How honeypot ants store food inside living workers
decoys: Some honeypot ants swell into golden globes
Ant colonies face dry, foodless seasons
The stored ants hang from the ceiling

payload.passage: The hognose snake has no venom strong enough to frighten a serious enemy, so it puts on a startling act instead. First it flattens its neck, hisses loudly, and pretends to strike, hoping to scare the threat away. If the bluff fails, it suddenly flips onto its back, lets its tongue loll out, and lies perfectly still as if dead. It even gives off a foul smell to seem like rotting meat. Most hunters want nothing to do with a dead, smelly snake and leave. By acting dead, this harmless snake fools its way to safety.
payload.title: How the hognose snake plays dead to escape
decoys: The hognose snake flips onto its back
Snakes have many ways to avoid enemies
It hisses and pretends to strike first

payload.passage: When the class collected money for a sick teacher, Preeti was put in charge of the box. Day by day it filled with coins and notes, and no one kept an exact count. It would have been easy to slip a little out for sweets. Preeti instead noted every contribution carefully and handed over the full amount, down to the last rupee. The teacher's family thanked the class for its honesty. Preeti learnt that when people place their trust and their money in your hands, guarding both is a sacred duty.
payload.title: Guarding others' trust and money is a duty
decoys: Preeti counted every coin in the box
Classes collect money for sick teachers
No one kept an exact count of the box

payload.passage: A simple stapler joins sheets of paper with a small metal staple. When you press down, a thin strip of metal is pushed against the papers. The metal pierces straight through the stacked sheets. A shaped plate below bends the two ends flat against the back. The bent ends lock the pages firmly together in a single quick press.
payload.title: How a stapler binds sheets of paper
decoys: A plate below bends the staple ends flat
Small inventions help us at work
The metal pierces through the sheets

payload.passage: A simple woven mat over the soil in a pot does quiet, useful work. The cover of straw or dry leaves is called a mulch. It shades the soil and keeps it from drying out too fast in the sun. It also smothers the weeds that would steal the plant's water. As the mulch slowly rots, it even feeds the soil beneath. A layer of mulch saves water and labour at once.
payload.title: How a layer of mulch saves water in a pot
decoys: A mulch shades the soil from the sun

payload.passage: Young Tarun was put in charge of his baby sister for one whole afternoon while their mother went out to work. Halfway through, his friends called up to him to come and play cricket in the cool evening lane. The shouts and the thud of the ball tempted him sorely. He leaned out of the window, then turned back and stayed home, gently rocking the cradle and watching over her nap instead. When his mother returned to find a safe, peacefully sleeping baby, she trusted Tarun with much more from that day onward. He learnt that responsibility often means giving up your own fun for someone who depends on you.
payload.title: Responsibility often means giving up your own fun
decoys: Tarun watched his baby sister all afternoon
Mothers sometimes leave children to mind babies
Cricket in the lane is hard to resist

payload.passage: Anjali had saved for a whole year to buy a fancy pen she had longed for since the start of school. On her way to the shop she met a classmate whose torn schoolbag had spilled all his books into a muddy puddle. Without much thought, Anjali used most of her carefully saved money to buy the shaken boy a sturdy new bag instead. She walked home that evening without the pen, yet with a lightness in her step she could not quite explain. The boy's grateful smile kept returning to her mind. Anjali realised that money spent on someone in need can bring a joy nothing on a shop shelf ever could.
payload.title: Giving to others outshines spending on yourself
decoys: Anjali saved for a year to buy a pen
A torn schoolbag can ruin a child's books
Saving money slowly takes a lot of patience

payload.passage: We count birthdays once a year, but where does a year come from? It is the time the Earth needs to travel one full loop around the sun. This journey takes a little over three hundred and sixty-five days. To keep the calendar neat, we add an extra day every fourth year, called a leap year. A year is really one complete trip of our planet around its star; so a birthday really marks one more complete journey that you and the whole Earth have made together around our star.
payload.title: Why a year is one trip around the sun
decoys: We add a leap day every fourth year
People measure time in many different ways
Earth takes a little over 365 days to loop the sun

payload.passage: The daily rise and fall of the sea is shaped by both the moon and the sun. The moon's pull is the stronger of the two and leads the tides. The sun adds a gentler pull of its own. When the sun and moon line up, their pulls combine to make especially high and low tides. When they pull from different directions, the tides are milder. The sea's changing height is a duet played by these two distant bodies; so the sea's daily rise and fall is a quiet record of two distant bodies pulling upon our world.
payload.title: How the moon and sun together stretch the tides
decoys: The moon's pull is the stronger of the two
The sea is shaped by forces from afar
Lined-up pulls make especially high and low tides

payload.passage: Some nights the moon is a full bright circle, other nights only a thin curve. The moon itself never truly changes; it is always a round ball of rock. The sun lights up one half of it, but as the moon circles the Earth we see that lit half from different angles. Sometimes we face the whole bright side, sometimes only a sliver of it. These changing views are what we call the phases of the moon; so the moon never truly grows or shrinks, and we are simply catching its sunlit half from a slightly new angle each night.
payload.title: Why the moon seems to change its shape
decoys: The sun lights up one half of the moon
