The night sky is full of changing sights
We see the lit half of the moon from different angles

payload.passage: Why does the body feel tired if you study with no breaks for hours? Your brain works like a muscle and grows weary with long, steady effort. Without a pause, it finds it harder to take in and hold new facts. A short break lets the brain rest and the body stretch. After a few minutes away, you can return able to learn far better.
payload.title: Why study breaks help the brain learn
decoys: The brain grows weary with long effort
A break lets the body stretch

payload.passage: A simple change from harsh cleaners to gentle ones helps the water downstream. Strong chemical cleaners wash off the floor and down the drain into rivers and ponds. There they can harm fish and the tiny lives of the water. Gentler cleaners, made from mild ingredients, do the job with far less harm. Choosing them keeps our homes clean without poisoning the water.
payload.title: Why gentle cleaners protect rivers and ponds
decoys: Strong cleaners wash down into rivers

payload.passage: A single careless cigarette or spark can undo a whole forest. In the dry season the leaves and grass turn to tinder, ready to burn. A small flame can race through the trees faster than anyone can run. Birds, animals and ancient trees are lost in the blaze. Putting out every spark and never lighting fires in dry woods guards the forest from this swift destruction.
payload.title: Why a single spark can destroy a whole forest
decoys: Dry grass turns to tinder in the heat
Fire races through the trees fast

payload.passage: The polar bear lives where the cold could kill in minutes, yet it stays cosy through it all. Beneath its fur lies a thick layer of fat that holds in warmth like a blanket. Its fur is not truly white but made of clear, hollow hairs that trap heat and scatter light so the bear looks snowy. Even its black skin underneath soaks up what little sun there is. Wide, furry paws spread its weight on thin ice and grip the slippery surface. Every part of the bear is shaped to defeat the deadly Arctic cold.
payload.title: How the polar bear stays warm in the Arctic
decoys: A polar bear's fur is made of hollow hairs
The Arctic is a freezing place to live
Fat under its skin keeps the bear warm

payload.passage: A simple ink pen with a metal nib once replaced the feather quill. The nib has a fine slit and a tiny hole at its tip. Dipped in ink, the slit holds a small store of liquid by a gentle pull. As the nib glides on paper, the ink flows out evenly through the slit. This neat tip let people write smoother, finer lines than a ragged quill.
payload.title: How a metal nib improved the writing pen
decoys: The slit holds a small store of ink
Ink flows out evenly through the slit

payload.passage: Why does your heart sometimes beat slow and sometimes fast? Your heart works like a clever pump that matches your body's needs. When you rest, your muscles need little oxygen, so the heart beats slow and steady. When you run, your muscles cry out for more oxygen, so the heart speeds up to deliver it. This way, the heart always sends just enough blood for the moment.
payload.title: Why the heartbeat changes with the body's needs
decoys: The heart is a wonderful organ
The heart speeds up when you run

payload.passage: Why do your muscles ache the day after a hard game or workout? When you push your muscles hard, you create many tiny tears in them. These small tears are not dangerous, but they cause a dull ache for a day or two. As the body repairs the tears, it builds the muscle back a little stronger. This is exactly how steady exercise makes muscles grow.
payload.title: Why muscles ache then grow stronger after exercise
decoys: Hard exercise makes tiny tears in muscles
Exercise is good for the body

payload.passage: The council had a tidy sum to spend on the village, and many loud demands for it. Some wanted the road repaired, some wanted a wall around the school, and some wanted festival lights. Rather than letting the loudest voice win, the members totalled the costs and compared them with the small budget. They chose the road and the school wall first, since broken roads and an unsafe school harmed everyone daily. Mira saw that good governing meant matching limited money to the most pressing needs, not the noisiest wishes.
payload.title: Matching a small budget to the biggest needs
decoys: Leaders should listen to their people
The council had a tidy sum to spend

payload.passage: The desert kangaroo rat may go its entire life without ever drinking a single drop of water. It survives in the driest deserts by squeezing moisture out of the dry seeds it eats. Its clever body wastes almost nothing, producing only tiny amounts of extremely concentrated waste. By day it hides in a cool, sealed burrow, escaping the burning sun and the dry air that would steal its moisture. It comes out to forage only in the cool of night. Every habit of this little animal is shaped to save the precious water it cannot drink.
payload.title: How the kangaroo rat lives without drinking water
decoys: The kangaroo rat gets moisture from dry seeds
Deserts are harsh, dry places to live
It hides in a burrow during the day

payload.passage: Why does the body need vitamin-rich fruit even in small amounts? Vitamins are tiny helpers the body cannot make for itself. Each one does a special job, like keeping the eyes sharp or the gums strong. Without them, even a well-fed body slowly grows weak and falls ill. A little fruit each day gives these helpers in just the right amount.
payload.title: Why the body needs vitamins from fruit
decoys: Each vitamin does a special job
Some vitamins keep the eyes sharp

payload.passage: Why does a balanced plate matter more than a large plate? A huge plate of just one food fills your stomach but starves your body of variety. A balanced plate gives a little of each thing the body needs: energy foods, building foods and protective foods. Together they keep you strong, well and full of energy. It is the mix, not the amount, that truly matters.
payload.title: Why a balanced plate matters more than a big one
decoys: A balanced plate gives a little of each kind
Good eating keeps the body well
One food alone starves the body of variety

payload.passage: A single cloud can carry a startling weight of water, yet it drifts lightly overhead. Its water is divided into countless tiny droplets, each almost weightless. Gentle currents of rising air also push up beneath them. So long as the droplets stay small and the air keeps lifting, the cloud floats on. Only when the droplets join into larger, heavier drops does the cloud begin to rain. A floating cloud is really a vast, light crowd of tiny drops; so a floating cloud is best pictured as a vast, light crowd of almost weightless droplets.
payload.title: How a cloud holds tonnes of water yet floats
decoys: Rising air pushes up beneath the tiny droplets
The sky is full of things we overlook
The cloud rains when droplets join into heavier drops

payload.passage: Soap looks plain, but the way it cleans is rather clever. Plain water alone cannot wash away oily dirt, because oil and water do not mix. Each tiny piece of soap has two ends: one end clings to water and the other clings to grease. The greasy ends grab the oily dirt while the watery ends let the water carry it away. This is why washing with soap removes far more germs than rinsing with water alone.
payload.title: How soap lifts away oily dirt and germs
decoys: One end of soap clings to grease
Keeping clean is important for staying healthy
Oil and water do not mix together easily

payload.passage: When autumn comes, the squirrel knows that hungry winter days lie ahead with little food to find. So all through the season of plenty it works without rest, gathering nuts and acorns. Rather than eat them all at once, it buries hundreds of them in scattered hiding places across its patch of woodland. Its sharp memory and keen nose help it find many of these stores again when snow covers the ground. The few it forgets may even grow into new trees. By storing food in good times, the squirrel survives the lean ones.
payload.title: How the squirrel survives winter by storing food
decoys: A squirrel buries nuts in scattered places
Winter brings little food to the woods
Forgotten nuts may grow into trees

payload.passage: Before the screw was invented, people held things together with nails that could easily be pulled out. The screw solved this with a clever spiral ridge that winds around its body. As you turn the screw, the spiral pulls it deep into the wood and grips tightly. Unlike a nail, it does not slip out under a sideways tug. This small twisted fastener holds furniture, machines and buildings firmly together.
payload.title: How the screw grips far better than a nail
decoys: A screw has a spiral ridge around its body
Inventions help us build sturdy things
Turning a screw pulls it into the wood

payload.passage: A rainbow appears only when sunshine and rain share the sky. Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mix of many colours blended together. As light enters a falling raindrop, it bends and splits into those separate colours. Each drop sends the colours back to your eyes at slightly different angles. Millions of drops working together paint the great arc of a rainbow across the sky; this is why a rainbow always appears in the part of the sky opposite the sun, where the falling drops can catch its light.
payload.title: How a rainbow forms from sunlight and rain
decoys: Light bends and splits inside a falling raindrop
The sky can produce beautiful displays
White sunlight is really a mix of many colours

payload.passage: Aarna saw nurses scrubbing their hands again and again between patients and thought they were being overly fussy. Her mother, a nurse herself, explained that unseen germs could ride from one patient to the next on a single unwashed hand. In a place full of the sick, such a tiny carelessness could spread serious disease. The constant washing was a quiet wall against invisible danger. Aarna learnt that the humblest habit, repeated faithfully, could protect more lives in a hospital than any expensive machine.
payload.title: Why constant handwashing protects patients
decoys: Nurses scrubbed their hands between patients
Germs can ride on an unwashed hand

payload.passage: In the children's ward, Pihu was surprised to see brightly painted walls, story books and a clown visiting on weekends. It hardly looked like the stern hospital she had imagined. A nurse explained that a frightened, tearful child heals more slowly, so calming young patients was part of the treatment itself. Laughter and colour eased their fear and even their pain. Pihu realised that caring for a sick child meant tending the mind as well as the body, and that kindness could be as healing as any medicine.
payload.title: Why a children's ward heals the mind too
decoys: A clown visited the ward on weekends
Hospitals try to make patients comfortable
Frightened children tend to heal slowly

payload.passage: Long ago, people stared at the scattered stars and began to join them with imaginary lines. They saw the shapes of animals, heroes and tools in the sky. These star pictures, called constellations, helped them remember the heavens and tell stories. Sailors and farmers used them to find directions and mark the seasons. The stars in a pattern are not truly close together, and we merely link them as they appear from Earth; these star patterns are still used today to find one's way around the night sky and to point out where to look.
payload.title: Why we group stars into patterns called constellations
decoys: Sailors used star patterns to find their way
People have always looked up at the sky
Stars in a pattern are not truly close together

payload.passage: The weekly market near Saanvi's home was not only a place to buy vegetables; it was the heartbeat of the whole village. Neighbours met between the stalls to swap news, fix wedding dates and settle small quarrels. Children begged for roasted snacks while elders argued cheerfully over the price of onions. By evening, people went home with full bags and fuller hearts. Saanvi understood that the market fed more than stomachs; it stitched the scattered families of the village into one talking, laughing community.
payload.title: A village market that binds people together
decoys: Neighbours met to swap news between the stalls
Villages have many old and lovely traditions
The market sold vegetables and roasted snacks

payload.passage: A walk to the local market beats a long drive to a far-off mall in more ways than one. The short trip burns little or no fuel and keeps the air clean. Buying from nearby shops and farmers means the goods travelled only a short way. Fresh local food needs no long, smoky journey across the country. Shopping close to home is a quiet kindness to the earth.
payload.title: Why shopping close to home is kinder to the earth
decoys: A short trip burns little fuel
Local food travels only a short way

payload.passage: Why does a doctor tell you to wash your hands before eating? Your hands touch many surfaces and pick up unseen germs all day. If these germs ride into your mouth on your food, they can make you ill. Soap and water wash the germs from your skin and rinse them away. A quick, careful wash is one of the easiest ways to stay healthy.
payload.title: Why washing hands before eating keeps us well
decoys: Hands pick up unseen germs all day
Soap and water rinse germs away

payload.passage: Diya saw a shiny gadget that everyone in her class was buying and begged her parents for one too. Her father asked a simple question: did she want it because it was useful, or only because others had it? Honestly, it was the second. He explained that buying just to match others often led to wasted money on things soon forgotten. Diya thought again and saved her money instead. She learnt that spending to copy the crowd is a poor reason, and that a wise buyer asks whether a thing serves them, not the fashion.
payload.title: Why copying the crowd wastes money
decoys: Everyone in her class was buying it
She wanted it only to match others

payload.passage: When Sana asked why banks have thick walls and heavy steel doors, her mother spoke about more than burglars. A bank must keep both the cash and the records of thousands of customers perfectly safe, so it guards them with vaults, cameras and strict rules. Even the staff cannot open the main vault alone; two trusted people must act together. If a single clerk could touch the money freely, no one would dare deposit their savings. Sana understood that all this heavy security exists to protect one fragile thing: the public's trust in the bank.
payload.title: Why heavy bank security protects public trust
decoys: Two staff together must open the main vault
Keeping things safe is important everywhere
Banks use vaults and cameras against burglars

payload.passage: A single ant could never carry a whole leaf, yet a colony strips a tree bare with ease. Leafcutter ants slice off pieces of leaf far larger than themselves and march them home in long green lines. Strangely, they do not eat the leaves at all. Deep in the nest they chew the leaves into a paste and grow a special fungus upon it, and that fungus is their real food. Different ants tend the garden, guard it, and clear away mould. By farming their food together, these tiny insects feed an enormous underground city.
payload.title: How leafcutter ants farm fungus for food
decoys: Leafcutter ants grow fungus on chewed leaves
Ants work together in large colonies
They carry leaf pieces in long lines

payload.passage: Why does a deep breath of fresh air feel so good after a stuffy room? In a closed, crowded room, the air slowly fills with the waste gas everyone breathes out. With less oxygen about, you feel dull, heavy and sleepy. Stepping outside fills your lungs with clean, oxygen-rich air. The fresh oxygen quickly reaches your brain and leaves you feeling alert again.
payload.title: Why fresh air feels good after a stuffy room
decoys: Closed rooms fill with waste gas

payload.passage: Why does your mouth fill with saliva before you even start to eat? The smell or sight of tasty food gets your body ready in advance. Your mouth begins to make saliva so the food will be easy to chew and swallow. The saliva also starts to break down the food at once. So your body prepares for a meal before the first bite even arrives.
payload.title: Why the mouth waters before a meal
decoys: Saliva makes food easy to chew
The body prepares for what is coming
Saliva starts to break down food

payload.passage: Reusing things before throwing them away is a habit worth building. An empty glass jar can store grains or hold pencils. An old shirt can become a cleaning cloth, and a box can become a toy shelf. Every item we reuse is one less that must be made afresh or dumped as waste. A little imagination turns rubbish into something useful again.
payload.title: Why reusing old things helps the environment
decoys: An empty jar can hold pencils
Reused items need not be made afresh

payload.passage: The walking-stick caterpillar of certain moths has a defence that depends entirely on stillness. Stretched out and rigid on a twig, it looks exactly like a small broken branch. To complete the trick, it grips the real twig with its hind legs and holds its body out stiff and straight at an angle, sometimes for hours on end. A passing bird scanning the bush sees only ordinary deadwood. The caterpillar does not flinch, even as danger draws near. By becoming a lifeless-looking stick, this soft creature hides from the sharpest eyes.
payload.title: How a caterpillar hides by freezing like a twig
decoys: The caterpillar holds its body out stiffly
It grips the twig with its hind legs

payload.passage: On the morning of the count, the whole town gathered around the results board as if watching a cricket match. Officials opened the sealed machines under the eyes of agents from every candidate, so no one could cheat in secret. Each batch of votes was tallied, checked and read aloud. The careful, witnessed counting took hours but left no room for doubt. Aarush saw that the slow openness was the whole point; a result everyone watched being counted was a result everyone could trust.
payload.title: Why an open vote count earns trust
decoys: Agents from every candidate watched the count
The sealed machines were opened carefully

payload.passage: A single plant can give rise to a whole new generation through its seeds. After its flowers are pollinated, the plant forms seeds packed with tiny new life. These seeds are spread by wind, water or animals to fresh ground. Where the soil is warm and moist, a seed sprouts into a young plant. In time that plant grows, flowers and makes seeds of its own. So through seeds, plants quietly pass life onward from one generation to the next; in this quiet way, a single plant can give rise to a whole field of new ones over the years.
payload.title: How a plant makes more plants from its seeds
decoys: Seeds are spread by wind, water or animals
Living things find ways to continue their kind
A sprouted seed grows up to make its own seeds

payload.passage: Why does cracking ice into small bits make a drink cool faster? Heat from the drink passes into the ice wherever the two touch. A single large cube touches only a little of the drink at a time. When you break the cube into many small pieces, far more surface touches the liquid. With more touching, heat leaves the drink quickly, and it chills in a shorter time.
payload.title: Why crushed ice cools a drink faster
decoys: Heat passes into the ice where they touch
Cold drinks are nice on a hot day
Small ice pieces touch more of the drink

payload.passage: When a younger boy tripped and spilled paint over Veer's finished project the day before submission, the class gasped. Veer felt anger flare hot inside him. The boy stood frozen, expecting a furious scolding. Veer breathed deep, said accidents happen, and quietly set about redoing the work. The boy, ashamed, stayed late to help him. The two boys, once strangers, walked home together talking and laughing. Veer learnt that meeting an accident with calm instead of rage can turn a ruined moment into an act of friendship.
payload.title: Meeting accidents with calm beats meeting them with rage
decoys: A boy spilled paint on Veer's project
Projects are submitted by a deadline

payload.passage: The old well at the village edge belonged to no single family; it belonged to everyone, which was exactly the trouble. Since no one owned it, no one cleaned it, and slowly it grew choked with weeds. At a panchayat meeting the members made a simple plan: each household would take a turn caring for the well. Soon the water ran clear again. Ishita learnt that shared things often fall apart not from bad weather but from the idea that someone else will look after them.
payload.title: Shared property needs a clear plan of care
decoys: The well grew choked with weeds
Each household would take a turn at the well

payload.passage: Your teeth do an important first job before food ever reaches your stomach. The front teeth are sharp and flat for biting off pieces. The back teeth are wide and bumpy for grinding food to a mush. Chewing well breaks the food into tiny bits and mixes in saliva. This makes the food far easier for the rest of the body to break down.
payload.title: How chewing prepares food for the body
decoys: Back teeth grind food into a mush
The body breaks down what we eat
Front teeth are sharp for biting

payload.passage: Living things need both energy and nutrients, but the two behave very differently. Energy enters from the sun, passes up the food chain, and is finally lost as heat, so it must be renewed constantly. Nutrients, however, are used again and again. When plants and animals die, decomposers free their nutrients back into the soil. So energy streams one way, while nutrients keep turning in a steady loop; understanding this difference helps explain why the sun must keep shining while the same nutrients are used again and again.
payload.title: Why energy flows but nutrients go in circles
decoys: Decomposers free nutrients back into the soil
Nature follows a few deep and simple rules
Energy is finally lost from the food chain as heat

payload.passage: A single old tree in a village can hold a whole world within it. Birds build their nests among its high branches. Squirrels race along its bark, and insects burrow into its folds. Bats and owls may roost in its hollows by day and night. Cutting one such tree does not only lose the tree but empties many small homes at once.
payload.title: Why a single old tree shelters so much life
decoys: Birds build nests in the high branches
Trees grow old over many years
Cutting a tree empties many homes

payload.passage: The trapdoor spider is a hunter that never leaves home to catch a meal. It digs a burrow in the ground and lines it with silk, then builds a hidden, hinged lid of soil and silk over the entrance. The lid blends so perfectly with the earth that nothing notices it. Holding the trapdoor almost shut, the spider waits just beneath, feeling for the footsteps of passing insects. The instant prey wanders close, the spider flings the door open and snatches it inside in a flash. By ambushing from a secret door, it dines without ever giving chase.
payload.title: How the trapdoor spider ambushes prey from a hidden door
decoys: The trapdoor spider builds a hinged lid
It waits just beneath the door

payload.passage: A bee buzzing among flowers is doing more than collecting food. As it sips sweet nectar, yellow pollen sticks to its fuzzy body. Flying to the next flower, it brushes some of that pollen onto it. This dusting lets the flower begin forming seeds, which it could not do alone. So bees and flowers help each other: the bee gets food, and the plant gets help making its seeds; this is why so many fruits and vegetables we eat depend, in the end, on the busy work of visiting bees and other insects.
payload.title: Why bees help plants make new seeds
decoys: Pollen sticks to a bee's fuzzy body
Living things often depend on one another
A flower cannot easily form seeds on its own

payload.passage: Years ago, if you wanted to send word to a relative in a far city, you wrote a letter and waited weeks for a reply. The telephone changed all of this in a remarkable way. It turned the sound of your voice into a signal that raced along a wire. At the other end, the signal became sound again in another person's ear. For the first time, people far apart could talk to each other at the very same moment.
payload.title: How the telephone let distant people talk at once
decoys: The telephone turns your voice into a signal
New machines have brought people closer together
A letter to a far city once took weeks

payload.passage: Krish proudly told everyone he had saved a thousand rupees, until his sister asked what he was saving it for. He had no answer; the money just sat there, and bit by bit he kept dipping into it for trifles. His sister suggested giving each saving a clear purpose, like a holiday or a gift, and keeping such savings in separate envelopes. With a name on each pile, Krish stopped raiding them for nothing. He learnt that savings with a clear goal are far harder to fritter away than a vague, purposeless heap.
payload.title: Why savings need a clear purpose to survive
decoys: Krish kept dipping into his savings
He kept savings in separate envelopes

payload.passage: The moon circles the Earth each month, so you might expect an eclipse just as often. Yet they are rare, and the reason is the moon's tilted path. Its orbit is slightly slanted compared with the Earth's path around the sun. Most months the moon passes a little above or below the sun in our sky, missing it. Only when everything lines up just right does its shadow fall and an eclipse occur; so an eclipse is a special event, possible only on the few occasions when the sun, moon and Earth fall into a near-perfect line.
payload.title: Why solar eclipses do not happen every month
decoys: The moon usually passes above or below the sun
Many events in space follow strict rules
The moon's orbit is slightly slanted from Earth's path

payload.passage: Pihu's neighbourhood started a tiny lending library where families pooled their books and shared them in turn. Instead of every home buying the same costly storybooks, one shared copy travelled from one house to the next. A small yearly fee kept the shelves growing, and a patient volunteer kept careful records. Children read far more books than any single family could ever have afforded on its own. Pihu realised that sharing, rather than each person owning everything, let a whole community enjoy much more for far less money.
payload.title: How sharing books gives more for less money
decoys: One book travelled from house to house
A small yearly fee kept shelves growing

payload.passage: Have you wondered why your shadow grows long in the evening but short at noon? A shadow appears wherever your body blocks the sun's light. When the sun is high overhead at midday, it blocks only a small patch, so your shadow is tiny. As the sun sinks low near sunset, the light comes in at a slant. This slanting light stretches your shadow out long across the ground.
payload.title: Why shadows grow long in the evening
decoys: A shadow appears where the body blocks light
The sun changes the way the world looks
Shadows are short when the sun is high

payload.passage: Rohan's team was losing the inter-class quiz badly, and his last teammate suddenly wanted to whisper an answer he had overheard from another group. Winning would have meant a gleaming trophy for their own classroom shelf. Rohan thought about it for a moment and then quietly said he would much rather lose fairly than win by cheating. They came last that afternoon, to a few groans from the class. Yet the teacher later praised them for their honesty in front of the whole school assembly. Rohan saw clearly that a clean defeat can stand far taller than a stolen victory.
payload.title: An honest loss beats a dishonest win
decoys: Rohan's team finished last in the quiz
Quiz trophies look nice on a classroom shelf
Cheating in a quiz is against the rules

payload.passage: When an animal dies, its body does not lie around for long. Scavengers such as crows, vultures and certain beetles soon arrive to feed on it. By eating the remains, they clear the land of waste and disease. They also pass the stored energy along to the next part of the food web. These often-unloved creatures keep a habitat clean and its energy moving; so although we may find them unpleasant, scavengers do essential work that keeps a habitat clean and its energy flowing.
payload.title: Why scavengers are nature's clean-up crew
decoys: Vultures and crows feed on dead animals
Every creature plays a part in nature
Scavengers clear the land of waste and disease

payload.passage: When a baby wildebeest is born on the open plains, it has only minutes before a hunter might notice it. Astonishingly, the wobbly calf is up on its feet within five minutes and running with the herd within the hour. It cannot afford the slow, sheltered childhood of safer animals. The herd never stops moving across the grasslands in search of fresh rain and grass, so the calf must keep pace at once. Staying close to its mother in the moving crowd is its best shield. For the wildebeest, survival begins almost the moment it is born.
payload.title: How a newborn wildebeest must run to survive
decoys: A wildebeest calf stands within five minutes
Many animals are hunted on the open plains
The herd moves to find fresh grass

payload.passage: Simran was nervous about her first public speech and forgot her lines halfway through. Laughter rippled through the hall, and she felt her face burn with shame. She could have fled the stage in tears. Instead she took a slow breath, smiled, and started that part again from the top. By the end the same hall clapped warmly for her calm. Her teacher later said her calm under pressure was the best part of the day. Simran learnt that recovering bravely from a stumble leaves a finer impression than never stumbling at all.
payload.title: Recovering bravely beats never stumbling at all
decoys: Simran forgot her lines during the speech
Public speaking can make people nervous
The hall laughed when she paused

payload.passage: When a seed sprouts underground, it cannot see, yet it still grows the right way. Its root always heads downward, while its shoot always climbs upward. The young plant senses the pull of gravity to tell down from up. The root follows that pull into the soil to find water and a firm hold. The shoot grows against it, reaching up toward the light it needs. Even in the dark, a seed grows each part in just the right direction; so even buried in the dark, a sprouting seed never sends its root and shoot the wrong way.
payload.title: How a seed knows which way to grow
decoys: The root follows gravity down into the soil
Living things sense the world around them
The shoot reaches up toward the light it needs

payload.passage: A simple paper clip holds sheets together with a single clever bend of wire. The wire is looped so that two of its arms press gently against each other. Slide papers between the arms and the springiness of the wire grips them. Nothing is pierced or torn, yet the pages stay neatly together. This tiny, cheap object is found on desks all over the world.
payload.title: How a paper clip grips sheets without piercing them
decoys: The wire's arms press gently against each other
Small inventions can be very useful
A paper clip holds papers together

payload.passage: A thunderstorm grows from a single, swelling cloud reaching high into the sky. Warm, damp air rises fast and cools, building the cloud taller and darker. Inside, water droplets and ice are flung up and down by strong currents. These movements rub tiny particles together and build up a great charge of electricity. When the charge grows strong enough, it leaps out as a flash of lightning. So the drama of a storm is really the work of rising air inside one mighty cloud.
payload.title: How a thunderstorm builds inside a towering cloud
decoys: Strong currents fling droplets up and down inside
Storms are powerful events in nature
A great charge leaps out as a flash of lightning

payload.passage: When the dry season grips the wetland and the water shrinks to scattered pools, the painted stork uses a clever fishing trick. It wades into the shallows and opens its long beak a little under the water, holding very still. With one foot it stirs the muddy bottom, frightening hidden fish into darting forward. The moment a fish touches the waiting beak, the stork snaps it shut in a flash, far faster than the eye. It need not even see its prey. By feeling rather than looking, the stork catches fish in the cloudiest water.
payload.title: How the painted stork fishes by feel in muddy water
decoys: The stork stirs the mud with its foot
Wetlands shrink in the dry season
It snaps its beak shut on a fish

payload.passage: A drinking straw seems to suck up a drink, but the truth is different. When you sip, you pull the air out of the top of the straw. This leaves less air pushing down inside the straw than outside it. The heavier air pressing on the drink in the glass then pushes the liquid up the straw. So it is really the air around us, not your mouth alone, that lifts the drink.
payload.title: How air pressure lifts a drink up a straw
decoys: Sipping pulls the air out of a straw
Drinking things is something we do daily
Air pushes down on the drink in the glass

payload.passage: Karthik was learning chess and lost twenty games in a row to his uncle. Each loss stung, and he wanted to abandon the game for good. But after every defeat he asked his uncle to show him the one move where he went wrong. Slowly his play sharpened. On the twenty-first game he finally won, fair and square, and his uncle shook his hand. Karthik learnt that each loss, studied honestly and without sulking, was really a hidden lesson carrying him steadily toward that single, hard-won victory.
payload.title: Each studied loss is a step toward winning
decoys: Karthik lost twenty chess games in a row
Chess is a hard game to learn
His uncle showed him his wrong moves

payload.passage: Meher found a hundred-rupee note on the staircase of her flats. She thought of the toys it could buy and slipped it into her pocket. But all afternoon she pictured the watchman, who often dropped coins from his small wages. She went down and asked him, and his face lit up; it was indeed his lost note. Meher handed it over and walked away light-hearted. That night she slept easily, free of the small weight a secret would have brought. She learnt that returning what is not yours feels far richer than keeping it ever could.
payload.title: Returning what is not yours feels richer
decoys: Meher returned a note to the watchman
Notes can fall on staircases unnoticed
Watchmen sometimes drop coins from their wages

payload.passage: Saanvi loved the festival market most of all, with its extra stalls and twinkling lights, but she noticed prices crept higher then too. Her uncle explained that during festivals everyone wanted to buy at once, and the sudden rush of eager buyers let sellers ask for more. The same lamp that was cheap in a quiet week grew dear in the crowded days. The demand, not the lamp, had changed. Saanvi learnt that when many people chase the same goods at the same time, prices naturally float upward.
payload.title: Why a buying rush pushes prices up
decoys: The festival market had extra stalls
Everyone wanted to buy at once

payload.passage: Sneha proudly told her father she had saved enough to buy a costly toy she had wanted for months. He asked her to wait one more day before buying, just to be sure. Overnight, she remembered a school trip she also wanted and realised the toy would leave nothing for it. With a clear head she chose the trip instead. Sneha learnt that a saver faces choices even after the money is gathered, and that a moment's pause can reveal which goal truly matters most before the money is spent.
payload.title: Why a pause reveals what you truly want
decoys: She had saved enough for the toy
Her father asked her to wait a day

payload.passage: Why do your fingernails keep growing all your life? At the base of each nail lies a small zone of busy living cells. These cells make tough new nail and push it slowly forward. As fresh nail is added underneath, the older part inches out past your fingertip. The part you trim is already hard and dead, which is why cutting it does not hurt.
payload.title: Why fingernails grow throughout our lives
decoys: Busy cells at the nail's base make new nail
The body is always renewing itself
Cutting a nail does not hurt

payload.passage: A tall tree faces a hard task: lifting water many metres up to its highest leaves. It has no pump, so it uses a gentle, steady pull instead. As water evaporates from the leaves, it tugs on the long chain of water inside the narrow tubes below. Like sipping through a very long straw, this draws fresh water up from the roots. Bit by bit, the whole tree stays watered without spending any muscle at all; remarkably, a tall tree manages this enormous lifting silently and without any moving parts, day after day.
payload.title: How a tree pulls water up to its top leaves
decoys: Water evaporates from the leaves at the top
Tall trees are some of nature's greatest wonders
The tree's tubes work like a very long straw

payload.passage: Saira's family ran a tea stall, and during a slow month her father did something she found strange: he lowered prices and added a free biscuit with each cup. She feared he would lose money. Instead, word spread, more people came, and his total earnings rose above the quiet weeks before. Drawing a bigger crowd, he made up in numbers what he gave up on each cup. Saira learnt that in a slow stretch, a small, clever sacrifice can sometimes bring back more business than stubbornly holding the old price.
payload.title: How a small offer revives slow business
decoys: He added a free biscuit per cup
More people came after the change

payload.passage: At the panchayat office, Veer watched a clerk patiently record every birth and death in a thick register. He thought it dull until his father explained how much depended on those entries. A birth record let a child join school and later claim an identity; a death record settled land and savings fairly among a family. Without these quiet papers, people could be cheated of what was rightfully theirs. Veer understood that the humble register was a backbone of civic life, guarding rights long after the ink had dried.
payload.title: Why civic records quietly protect people's rights
decoys: A clerk recorded births and deaths
Paperwork can seem boring at first
A birth record lets a child join school

payload.passage: When a stranger collapsed at the bus stand, people stood around unsure what to do, and Reyansh feared the man would not be helped. Then someone called the free emergency number, and an ambulance arrived within minutes to rush him to the hospital. No payment was asked before he was treated; his life came first. Reyansh learnt that a caring society builds quick, free emergency help that does not pause to check a person's purse. In a true crisis, he saw, saving the life must come before counting the cost.
payload.title: Why emergency help comes before counting cost
decoys: No payment was asked before treatment

payload.passage: Each year the Arctic tern makes the longest journey of any animal on Earth. It breeds in the far cold north, then flies all the way to the far cold south and back again, chasing endless summer. Over its lifetime this small bird flies a distance equal to several trips to the moon. It rests and feeds on the open ocean along the way, snatching fish from the waves. By following the sun from pole to pole, the tern always lives where food is plentiful and days are long. Its incredible voyage is the secret of its survival.
payload.title: How the Arctic tern chases summer across the world
decoys: The Arctic tern feeds on fish at sea
Many birds fly long distances each year
It breeds in the far cold north

payload.passage: A coat of pale paint on a rooftop can quietly cool a whole house. Dark roofs soak up the sun's heat and pass it down into the rooms below. A white or light roof bounces much of that sunlight straight back to the sky. The home then stays cooler without any extra fans or coolers. Less cooling means less power drawn and a smaller load on the earth.
payload.title: How a white roof keeps a house cool naturally
decoys: A dark roof soaks up the sun's heat
A light roof bounces sunlight away

payload.passage: Cooking food evenly over a flame can be tricky and slow. The microwave oven heats food in a surprising new way. It fills the box with invisible waves that make the water inside the food wobble very fast. This rapid wobbling rubs the tiny bits together and makes heat right inside the food. Because the heat starts within, a meal can warm through in just a minute or two.
payload.title: How a microwave oven heats food from within
decoys: Invisible waves make the water in food wobble
Inventions changed how we cook meals
Microwaved food warms in a minute or two

payload.passage: A pencil seems too simple to be called an invention, yet it was once a clever breakthrough. Inside its wooden case lies a thin rod made of soft grey graphite mixed with clay. As the tip drags across paper, tiny flakes of graphite rub off and leave a mark. Unlike ink, a pencil mark can be rubbed away and the writing fixed. This cheap, easy tool put writing within reach of almost everyone.
payload.title: How the humble pencil made writing easy for all
decoys: A pencil's rod is graphite mixed with clay
Even small inventions can matter greatly
A pencil mark can be rubbed away

payload.passage: Owls glide silently through the night and frighten some people, but they are great friends to farmers. A single owl can catch many rats and mice in one night. These rodents would otherwise nibble away at stored grain and growing crops. By eating the pests for free, the owl saves the farmer from poison and loss. Protecting owls and the old trees they nest in helps the harvest.
payload.title: Why owls are valuable friends to farmers
decoys: An owl can catch many mice in one night

payload.passage: On polling day Saanvi's elderly neighbour could not climb the stairs to the voting room, and the family feared she would miss her chance. But the officers had planned for exactly this. A wheelchair waited at the gate, a ground-floor room was kept ready, and a helper guided her gently to the machine. She cast her vote with a proud smile. Saanvi saw that a fair election does not stop at allowing people to vote; it works hard to remove the obstacles that might keep anyone from voting at all.
payload.title: Removing obstacles so everyone can vote
decoys: A wheelchair waited at the polling gate
The neighbour could not climb the stairs

payload.passage: A simple wooden boat let early people cross rivers and lakes. By hollowing out a log or joining planks, they made a vessel that floated. Because the boat is shaped to push aside plenty of water, the water holds it up. People could now carry goods and themselves over water that once blocked their path. The boat opened trade and travel along every coast and river.
payload.title: How the boat let people cross water
decoys: The boat pushes aside plenty of water
A hollowed log can float on water

payload.passage: A bar of metal feels cold to the touch, yet a wooden bench beside it feels warm, even in the same room. Both are really the same temperature, but they do not feel the same. Metal carries heat away from your hand very quickly, so your skin feels a sudden chill. Wood carries heat away slowly, so your hand stays warm against it. The feeling tells you how fast each object pulls heat, not how cold it really is.
payload.title: Why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature
decoys: Metal carries heat away from your hand quickly
Our senses can sometimes fool us
Wood feels warm when you touch it

payload.passage: Why do you sweat so much on a hot day or while playing a game? Hard work and heat can warm your body too much, which is risky. To cool down, your skin lets out tiny drops of salty sweat. As the sweat dries off your skin, it carries away heat with it. This is the body's clever cooling system that keeps you from overheating.
payload.title: Why sweating helps cool the body down
decoys: Skin lets out tiny drops of salty sweat
Sweat dries off and carries away heat

payload.passage: The grasshopper mouse of the desert is a tiny hunter that fears almost nothing, even a stinging scorpion. When a scorpion strikes it with venom that would hurt most animals badly, the little mouse barely flinches. Its body turns the painful venom into a harmless signal, so the sting hardly bothers it at all. The mouse then kills and eats the scorpion without trouble. This rare gift lets it feast on prey other desert animals dare not touch. By shrugging off venom, the small mouse claims a meal almost no one else can.
payload.title: How the grasshopper mouse eats stinging scorpions
decoys: The grasshopper mouse shrugs off scorpion venom

payload.passage: The Earth spins quickly and races around the sun, yet we feel perfectly still. The reason is that everything moves along with us. The ground, the air, the buildings and our own bodies all travel together at the same smooth, steady speed. With nothing left behind to compare against, there is no jolt or rush to sense. It is much like riding in a car so smooth that you seem not to move at all; so the absence of any rushing or jolting is not proof that the Earth is still, but only a sign that we move smoothly along with it.
payload.title: Why we cannot feel the Earth moving
decoys: The air and ground travel along with us
Motion can be hard to notice from inside it
A very smooth car ride can feel like standing still

payload.passage: While buying groceries, Dev realised that his shopkeeper uncle had handed back far too much change by mistake. The extra coins jingling in his pocket would have bought sweets for a whole week. Nobody at all had seen the small error happen. Dev hesitated only a moment, then turned around and walked back through the crowded market to place the extra money quietly on the counter. His uncle, busy and tired, had not even noticed it was gone, but he hugged Dev warmly all the same. Dev learnt that being honest when absolutely no one is watching is the truest test of character there is.
payload.title: Honesty matters most when nobody is watching
decoys: Dev returned the extra change to his uncle
Shopkeepers sometimes give the wrong change
Extra coins could buy a week of sweets

payload.passage: We feel perfectly still, yet we are riding a spinning planet through light and dark. The Earth turns steadily on its axis once a day. As it spins, our side swings to face the sun, and we have daytime. Then it swings away, and night falls over us. All the while we move smoothly along, sensing no motion at all. The daily change of day and night is the great turn of the Earth beneath our feet; so the gentle change from day to night is really the great turn of the Earth beneath our feet.
payload.title: How the spinning Earth carries us through day and night
decoys: Our side swings to face the sun for daytime
The Earth's motion governs our lives
We move smoothly and sense no motion at all

payload.passage: A small pond dug in a school yard can become a busy nature spot. Within weeks, frogs, dragonflies and water beetles arrive on their own. Birds come to drink and bathe along its muddy edge. Children can watch tadpoles grow and learn how a tiny world works. With a little water and care, a school pond teaches more than any book.
payload.title: How a school pond becomes a living classroom
decoys: Frogs and dragonflies arrive at the pond

payload.passage: A pinch of care for the soil rewards a gardener for years. Soil that is fed with compost and old leaves grows dark and crumbly. Worms and tiny living things thrive within it and keep it loose. Such living soil holds water well and feeds the plants steadily. Looking after the soil first is the surest way to a thriving garden.
payload.title: Why caring for the soil makes a garden thrive
decoys: Compost makes the soil dark and crumbly

payload.passage: Even after the sun has dipped below the horizon, the sky does not go dark at once. For a while a soft glow called twilight lingers. This happens because the air high above is still catching sunlight from below the horizon. That high air scatters the light gently down to us, keeping the sky pale. As the Earth turns further, the lit air sinks out of view and darkness deepens. So twilight is the slow fading of sunlight still reaching the upper sky.
payload.title: Why twilight lingers after the sun sets
decoys: High air still catches sunlight from below the horizon
The sky passes through many changes each day
Twilight fades as the Earth keeps turning

payload.passage: Mangrove trees grow with their roots standing in salty seawater along the coast. Their tangled roots act like a strong wall against the waves. When a great storm rushes in from the sea, the mangroves soften the crashing water. This shields the villages and fields just behind them. The roots also shelter young fish and crabs, making mangroves true guardians of the coast.
payload.title: How mangroves protect the coast and its life
decoys: Mangrove roots stand in salty water
The coast is a special place
Mangroves shelter young fish and crabs

payload.passage: Deepa's team won the cooking contest, but she knew the judges had not tasted the rival team's dish, which had been served cold by accident. The win felt hollow to her. She told the judges the other dish deserved a fair taste, warm. They agreed, tasted it, and declared a tie. Deepa's clear win became shared, yet she only smiled, content. The other team thanked her, surprised that a winner would ask for such a thing. Deepa learnt that a victory only feels truly hers when she knows the contest was fair to all.
payload.title: A win feels yours only when the contest was fair
decoys: Deepa asked the judges to taste the rival dish
The rival dish was served cold

payload.passage: Watch a sunrise and the sun appears to climb the sky, but this is a gentle trick. You are standing on a planet that is turning steadily beneath your feet. As the Earth rolls eastward, the sun comes into view over the horizon in the morning. Through the day your side keeps turning until the sun slips out of sight at evening. The sun stays put, and it is we who are moving past it; once you picture the Earth turning, the daily path of the sun across the sky suddenly makes perfect sense.
payload.title: How the spinning Earth makes the sun seem to move
decoys: The sun comes into view in the eastern sky
Things are not always the way they first seem
The Earth turns toward the east as it spins

payload.passage: A rainbow appears only when sunshine and rain are in the sky together. The sunlight provides the light, and the raindrops do the splitting. As light enters each falling drop, it bends and separates into its hidden colours. The drops then send those colours back toward your eyes. Without the sun there would be no light to split, and without rain no drops to split it. A rainbow is the lovely meeting of sunshine and falling rain; so a rainbow is, quite simply, the beautiful meeting of sunshine and falling rain.
payload.title: Why a rainbow needs both sun and rain
decoys: Light bends and separates inside each raindrop
The sky can make beautiful displays
Without rain there are no drops to split the light

payload.passage: Among all the bodies near us in space, the sun stands out as a true giant. It is so large that more than a million Earths could fit inside it. Its powerful gravity holds every planet, moon and comet in its grip. All of them circle the sun, while it sits almost still at the centre. Without its great size and pull, the solar system would simply scatter. So the sun is both the heart and the anchor of our whole cosmic neighbourhood.
payload.title: Why the sun is by far the largest thing nearby
decoys: More than a million Earths could fit inside the sun
Space holds objects of every possible size
The sun sits almost still at the centre

payload.passage: Bharat had failed to qualify for the football team three years running. His friends had long stopped trying out, settling for the stands. Bharat alone kept practising drills in the empty field each dawn, season after season. In his fourth year the coach finally saw his improved skill and picked him. He wept with joy on the field. His teammates, who had given up long ago, clapped the loudest of all. Bharat learnt that perseverance is simply refusing to let yesterday's failures decide what you try today.
payload.title: Perseverance refuses to let past failures decide
decoys: Bharat made the team in his fourth year

payload.passage: Why does your body have a sense of balance you rarely notice? Tiny tubes of fluid in your inner ear sense every tilt and turn of your head. Your eyes report what is level and upright around you. Your feet and muscles feel the ground beneath you. The brain blends all these messages to keep you steady whether you stand, walk or ride.
payload.title: How the body keeps its sense of balance
decoys: Tubes of fluid in the ear sense head movements
The eyes report what is level

payload.passage: When a beehive grows too hot under the summer sun, the precious young grubs could be harmed, so the bees cool it as a team. Many workers gather at the entrance and beat their wings hard, fanning streams of fresh air through the hive. Others fetch droplets of water and spread them over the comb, so that the moving air cools the hive as the water dries, much like sweat on skin. They keep this up for hours in the heat. By fanning and watering together, the bees hold the hive at just the right warmth.
payload.title: How bees cool an overheated hive together
decoys: Bees fan air through the hot hive
They spread water droplets on the comb

payload.passage: Through the year the length of daylight slowly stretches and shrinks. In summer the days are long, in winter they are short. This change comes from the Earth's tilt as it circles the sun. Plants and animals notice it as a reliable signal of the turning seasons. Longer days call plants to flower and birds to nest, while shorter ones bring rest and migration. The slow shift in daylight quietly tells living things what time of year it is; so the slow stretching and shrinking of daylight acts as a natural calendar for living things.
payload.title: How the changing day length signals the seasons
decoys: Longer days call plants to flower and birds to nest
Nature reads many signals from the world
The Earth's tilt makes the day length change

payload.passage: Honeyguide birds love to eat beeswax but cannot break open a tough wild beehive on their own. Over time they formed a remarkable partnership with people who gather honey. The bird flies up to a honey hunter, calls loudly, and leads the way from tree to tree toward a hidden hive. The hunter follows, opens the nest, and takes the honey, leaving the waxy comb behind. The honeyguide then feeds on the wax it could never have reached alone. By guiding humans, the little bird wins a meal that teamwork alone makes possible.
payload.title: How the honeyguide bird teams up with people
decoys: The honeyguide leads hunters to a beehive
The bird cannot open a hive alone

payload.passage: The thorny devil is a small spiky lizard that lives in one of the driest deserts on Earth, where rain almost never falls. Yet it drinks without a pond or stream. Its skin is covered with tiny grooves that run between the scales all the way to its mouth. When the lizard touches damp sand or a drop of dew, the water is drawn along these grooves by themselves, travelling across its body to its mouth. It can even soak up moisture standing in a puddle with its feet. By drinking through its skin, the thorny devil survives the thirsty desert.
payload.title: How the thorny devil drinks water through its skin
decoys: The thorny devil's skin has tiny grooves
Some deserts get almost no rain
Water travels along grooves to its mouth

payload.passage: Without the sun, the water cycle would freeze in place. It is sunlight that warms the oceans and lifts their water into the sky as vapour. The same heat stirs the winds that push clouds across the land. Even the rivers that race downhill were first filled by sun-lifted rain. So although we rarely think of it, every cloud, every shower and every flowing stream is really the sun's energy at work; without the sun's steady warmth, the rain would stop, the rivers would still, and the great water cycle would grind to a halt.
payload.title: How the sun powers the whole water cycle
decoys: Sunlight lifts ocean water into the sky as vapour
The sun is the source of energy for life
Winds push the rain clouds over towns and fields

payload.passage: Karthik had trained hard for the chess final and was sure of victory. Halfway through, he realised he had touched a piece by accident, a move that, by the rules, he should declare and play. No one had noticed. He could have ignored it and kept his strong position. Instead he told the judge and made the forced move, weakening himself. He lost narrowly, but with a clear conscience. Karthik learnt that following a rule even when no one would catch you is the heart of honest play.
payload.title: Following rules uncaught is the heart of honest play
decoys: Karthik declared his accidental chess move

payload.passage: A loudspeaker lets one voice fill a whole stadium. It works by turning an electric signal back into sound we can hear. The signal flows through a coil fixed to a thin cone, with a magnet close by. As the signal changes, the coil and cone are pushed in and out very fast. This rapid pushing shoves the air and creates sound loud enough for thousands to hear.
payload.title: How a loudspeaker turns a signal into loud sound
decoys: A coil and cone are pushed in and out
Inventions help people share their voice
A loudspeaker can fill a whole stadium

payload.passage: Touch a healthy, well-watered leaf on a sunny day and it often feels surprisingly cool. The leaf is cooling itself as it works. Through tiny pores, it lets water escape into the air as vapour. As that water leaves, it carries away some of the leaf's heat. This is much like the way sweat cools our skin on a hot day. Even under a strong sun, a leaf can keep itself from growing too warm; so a well-watered plant can keep its cool through the hottest hours, much as we do by sweating.
payload.title: Why a leaf feels cool even in bright sun
decoys: The leaf lets water escape through tiny pores
Living things cope with heat in clever ways
Escaping water carries away some of the leaf's heat

payload.passage: Eshan could not understand why his eighteen-year-old sister was so excited to vote for the very first time. She explained that for years she had to live by rules made by others, with no say at all. Now her single vote, however small, joined millions of others to choose the leaders who would make those rules. It was her turn to be counted rather than merely ruled. Eshan saw that the thrill was not about one button press; it was about finally holding a real, equal share in deciding the country's path.
payload.title: Why a first vote feels so powerful
decoys: His sister had just turned eighteen
Her single vote joined millions of others

payload.passage: A whistling kettle tells you the water is ready in a clever way. As the water boils, it turns into steam that rises quickly. The steam rushes out through a small hole in the spout. As it shoots through the narrow gap, it makes a high, sharp sound. The whistle is really the fast-moving steam singing as it escapes.
payload.title: Why a boiling kettle begins to whistle
decoys: Steam rushes out through a small hole
Many machines tell us when they are ready
Water turns into steam when it boils

payload.passage: A digital clock keeps near-perfect time without any swinging parts. Hidden inside it is a tiny chip of a mineral called quartz. When a small current flows through this quartz, it shakes back and forth at a steady, exact rate. The clock counts these rapid shakes very carefully. By counting a set number of shakes, it knows that exactly one second has passed.
payload.title: How a quartz clock keeps accurate time
decoys: A clock holds a tiny chip of quartz
People have always wanted to measure time
Quartz shakes when a current flows through it

payload.passage: Switching off a fan or light when you leave a room may seem like a small act. Yet most of our electricity is made by burning coal deep in distant power plants. Burning coal dirties the air and uses up the earth's buried treasure. Every unit of power we save means a little less coal is burned. So a flick of a switch adds up to a real gift for the planet.
payload.title: Why saving electricity helps protect the earth
decoys: We should be careful in all we do
Most electricity is made by burning coal

payload.passage: Sailors and fishers have long watched the tides rise and fall. The pattern they follow is set mainly by the moon. As the moon circles the Earth, its pull on the seas creates two high tides and two low tides each day. Because the moon keeps moving, the tides arrive a little later each day to match it. This steady, shifting rhythm has guided people to the sea for thousands of years; because the moon never stops moving, the tides quietly shift their timing each day to keep pace with it.
payload.title: How the moon controls the rhythm of the tides
decoys: There are two high tides and two low tides each day
The sea is full of patterns to observe
Tides arrive a little later each day to follow the moon

payload.passage: A coat of plaster and a clever design can keep a mud house cool without a cooler. Thick mud walls block the harsh heat of the day and slowly release warmth at night. Small high windows let hot air drift out while cooler air stays low. A shady veranda keeps the strong sun off the walls. Built with care, such a house stays pleasant while using almost no power.
payload.title: How a well-built mud house stays cool without power
decoys: Thick mud walls block the day's heat
Houses are built in many ways
High windows let hot air drift out

payload.passage: Vampire bats feed only on blood and will starve if they go just a few nights without a meal, yet the colony rarely loses a member to hunger. The reason is a remarkable habit of sharing. A bat that has fed well will bring up some of its blood meal and give it to a hungry roost-mate that found nothing. The bats remember who has helped them and return the favour another night. Through this give-and-take, no bat starves while others have plenty. By sharing food, the colony keeps every member alive.
payload.title: How vampire bats share food to keep each other alive
decoys: A well-fed bat shares blood with a hungry one
Vampire bats feed only on blood
Bats remember who has helped them

payload.passage: A simple radio aerial catches signals you cannot see. The signals from a station travel through the air as invisible waves. As these waves wash over the metal aerial, they stir a tiny current in it. The radio sorts out the station you want from this faint current. It then turns the chosen signal back into the music or news you hear.
payload.title: How a radio aerial catches unseen signals
decoys: Waves stir a tiny current in the aerial
Devices catch what we cannot see
The radio sorts out the station you want

payload.passage: Drop a ball and it always heads for the ground, never the ceiling. This pull is gravity, a force that every object with mass quietly has. The Earth is so huge that its gravity reaches out and tugs everything toward its centre. That is why we stay on the ground and why rain falls and rivers run downhill. Gravity is invisible, yet it shapes nearly everything that moves on our planet; though we never see or feel it directly, gravity quietly shapes nearly every movement in the world around us.
payload.title: Why everything falls down toward the Earth
decoys: The Earth's gravity pulls things toward its centre
Many forces act on us all the time
Gravity makes rivers run downhill toward the sea

payload.passage: Saying no to a single-use plastic spoon or cup is a small but meaningful choice. These items are used for just one snack and then thrown away forever. Yet they pile up in dumps and never truly break down. A spoon you carry from home can be washed and used again and again. Choosing reusable things keeps mountains of plastic out of the earth.
payload.title: Why we should avoid single-use plastic items
decoys: A plastic spoon is used just once
We should think before we act
Reusable spoons can be washed and reused

payload.passage: When the cricket ball rolled into the busy road, the boys dared Arjun to dash out and grab it before a car came. They called him scared when he hesitated. Arjun looked at the speeding traffic and refused, waiting until the road was clear instead. The others mocked him, but a moment later a fast car roared past the very spot. The other boys fell silent, suddenly glad that Arjun had refused their dare. Arjun learnt that true courage sometimes means resisting a dare and choosing the safe, sensible path against the crowd's jeers.
payload.title: Courage can mean resisting a reckless dare
decoys: Arjun waited for the road to clear
Cricket balls roll into busy roads

payload.passage: Stand in sunlight and your shadow always falls on the side away from the sun. A shadow forms because your body blocks the sun's light. The light cannot pass through you, so a dark patch is left on the ground behind. As the sun shifts across the sky, this dark patch swings to the opposite side. That is why your shadow stretches east when the sun is low in the west; so by glancing at which way a shadow falls, you can roughly tell where the sun sits in the sky at that moment.
payload.title: How the sun makes our shadows point away from it
decoys: Your body blocks the sun's light to make a shadow
Light and shadow follow simple rules
A shadow stretches east when the sun is in the west

payload.passage: Why does the body keep its inside temperature nearly the same all the time? Your organs work best at one steady, warm level. If you grow too hot, your body sweats and widens its blood vessels to lose heat. If you grow too cold, you shiver and the vessels narrow to save heat. By balancing these actions, the body holds its temperature just right.
payload.title: How the body keeps its temperature steady
decoys: Sweating helps the body lose heat
The body cares for itself well
Organs work best at one steady level

payload.passage: Look at the moon through binoculars and its face is pocked with round pits. These craters were carved by space rocks crashing down over billions of years. Each strike blasted out a bowl-shaped hollow in the moon's surface. With no wind or rain to wear them away, the craters have stayed sharp ever since. The moon's scarred face is a record of countless ancient impacts; so the pitted face of the moon is, in a way, a frozen photograph of violent events from billions of years ago.
payload.title: How the moon's craters were made long ago
decoys: Space rocks blasted out bowl-shaped hollows
Other worlds carry signs of their long past
No wind or rain wears the moon's craters away

payload.passage: The football coach made a wrong call, ruling that Veer's team had scored when the ball had clearly missed. Veer's team-mates cheered the lucky goal. Veer, the captain, knew the truth and felt uneasy. He walked up to the coach and admitted the ball had not gone in. The goal was cancelled, and his team's lead was lost. But the other side clapped him for his honesty. Veer learnt that owning the truth even when it costs your team is what real sportsmanship means.
payload.title: Sportsmanship owns the truth even when it costs
decoys: Veer admitted his team had not scored
The goal was cancelled after his words

payload.passage: Doing long sums by hand was once slow and full of mistakes. The electronic computer changed this by working with tiny switches that flip on and off. By flipping millions of these switches in clever patterns, it follows step-by-step instructions very fast. It can add, sort and store far more than any person could. Computers now help in schools, hospitals, banks and almost every part of daily life.
payload.title: How the computer follows instructions so fast
decoys: A computer works with switches that flip on and off
Machines have made hard tasks much easier
Computers help in hospitals and banks

payload.passage: Most leaves are spread out wide and thin, and this shape is no accident. A broad, flat leaf catches as much sunlight as possible across its surface. The more light it gathers, the more food the plant can make. Being thin also lets light reach the green parts inside without much waste. The wide shape gives plenty of room for the tiny pores that take in air, too. So the simple form of a leaf is really a clever design for catching the sun.
payload.title: Why leaves are usually broad and flat
decoys: Thin leaves let light reach the green parts inside
Plants are full of clever natural designs
A broad leaf gives room for the air pores

payload.passage: A spinning wheel turned a heap of loose cotton into useful thread. Raw cotton is just a soft, tangled cloud of fibres. As the wheel spins, it twists these fibres tightly around one another. The twisting locks the short fibres into one long, strong strand. From that strand, weavers could make cloth, so the spinning wheel was the first step in clothing whole villages.
payload.title: How a spinning wheel turns cotton into thread
decoys: The wheel twists loose fibres together
Inventions help us make our clothes
Raw cotton is a soft, tangled cloud

payload.passage: Why is it bad to skip meals to feel thinner? When you miss a meal, your body soon runs short of the fuel it needs. Your energy drops, and it becomes hard to think, study or play. Worse, when you finally eat, you may overeat because you are so hungry. Eating regular, balanced meals keeps your energy steady and your body well.
payload.title: Why skipping meals harms the body
decoys: Missing a meal leaves the body short of fuel
Skipping meals can lead to overeating later

payload.passage: Why does a balanced breakfast help you do well at school? After a long night without food, your brain is short of fuel. A good breakfast tops up that fuel for the morning's lessons. Foods that give steady energy keep your mind sharp until lunch. Children who eat a balanced breakfast often pay attention better and remember more in class.
payload.title: Why a balanced breakfast helps you learn
decoys: Breakfast tops up the brain's fuel
Steady-energy food keeps the mind sharp

payload.passage: Long ago, people had to drag heavy loads across rough ground, which took many hands and much time. Then someone shaped a round disc of wood and fixed it to turn on a fixed bar. This simple wheel let a heavy cart roll along instead of being dragged. One person could now move a load that once needed ten. The wheel changed travel, trade and building forever, which is why many call it the most useful invention of all.
payload.title: How the wheel changed the way we move loads
decoys: The first wheels were shaped from discs of wood
Clever ideas have shaped the world we live in
A cart can roll along instead of being dragged

payload.passage: On certain nights the sky seems to rain streaks of light, many in a single hour. These meteor showers happen when the Earth crosses a trail of dust left by a comet. The tiny dust grains slam into our air and burn up in bright flashes. Because the dust comes from one direction, the streaks all seem to spread from a single patch of sky. Such showers return at the same time each year; because the Earth crosses the same comet trails each year, keen skywatchers know just which nights to look for these showers.
payload.title: How meteor showers light up the night sky
decoys: Tiny dust grains burn up brightly in the air
The night sky offers many rare displays
The Earth crosses a comet's trail of dust

payload.passage: Every bite of food can be traced back to sunlight. Green plants catch the sun's energy and store it in grains, fruits and leaves. When we eat plants, we take that stored energy into our bodies. When we eat animals, we get energy those animals first gained from plants. Whether your meal is a fruit or a fish, the energy in it began as sunshine; so every meal we eat is, in the end, a way of borrowing a little of the sun's energy to power our own bodies.
payload.title: How the sun's energy ends up in our food
decoys: Green plants store the sun's energy in grains
The sun supports life all over the Earth
Eating animals gives energy they first got from plants

payload.passage: Why does the body shut down slowly into sleep rather than at once? Sleep comes in gentle stages, not like a switch turning off. First you drift into a light, easily broken sleep. Then your body sinks into a deep, restful sleep where it repairs itself. Passing smoothly through these stages each night is what leaves you truly rested by morning.
payload.title: Why sleep comes in gentle stages
decoys: First you drift into a light sleep
Rest is important for the body
Deep sleep is when the body repairs

payload.passage: Plants cannot move about, yet they are far from helpless in finding light. When light falls more on one side, the shaded side of the stem grows longer. This uneven growth tips the plant gently toward the brighter direction. Reaching the light is vital, since the plant needs it to make food. Over days, a windowsill plant may lean right over as it follows the brightest glow; so a plant on a windowsill is not standing still at all, but slowly and steadily reaching for the light it needs.
payload.title: Why plants stretch and bend toward sunlight
decoys: The shaded side of the stem grows longer
Plants respond to the world in many ways
A windowsill plant may lean over toward the light

payload.passage: Mohit promised his grandmother he would read to her each night, as her eyes had grown too weak for print. The first weeks he read eagerly, but soon friends and games tugged at his evenings. One night he nearly skipped it, then saw her waiting with the book ready in her lap. He sat down and read as always. Over the months it became the part of the day she loved most. Mohit learnt that faithfulness to a small promise can become a gift greater than he ever imagined.
payload.title: Faithful small promises can become great gifts
decoys: Mohit read to his grandmother each night
Weak eyes find printed words hard
Friends and games tugged at his evenings

payload.passage: A simple needle for the gramophone once turned grooves into music. A record carries sound stored as tiny wavy grooves on its surface. As the disc spins, a fine needle rides along inside the groove. The wiggles of the groove make the needle shake exactly as the sound once did. That shaking is turned back into the music we hear from the horn.
payload.title: How a record player turns grooves into music
decoys: A needle rides along inside the groove
Inventions changed how we enjoy music
A record stores sound as wavy grooves

payload.passage: A modern bridge over a wide river is a triumph of careful design. Engineers learned to spread the weight of the bridge so no single part is overloaded. Strong cables, arches or beams pass the load down to firm supports planted deep in the ground. Because the weight is shared, the bridge can carry heavy lorries day after day. Such bridges joined towns that rivers had kept apart for ages.
payload.title: How clever design lets a bridge carry great weight
decoys: Strong cables pass the load to firm supports
Building works have shaped the modern world
A bridge can carry heavy lorries

payload.passage: Tina's grandmother forgot things easily now and often repeated the very same story three times in a single afternoon. Tina's cousins soon grew bored and drifted away one by one to their phones. Tina, though, listened each time as if the tale were brand new, asking the same wide-eyed questions to make her grandmother smile. The old lady's tired face lit up at the warm attention, and she patted Tina's cheek. Telling the story yet again seemed to make her years younger. Tina found that patience offered to those we love is a quiet but powerful form of respect.
payload.title: Patience with elders is a gift of respect
decoys: Tina listened to her grandmother's repeated story
Older people sometimes forget and repeat themselves
Cousins often get distracted by their phones

payload.passage: In fields and meadows, humble grass is the quiet starting point of life. Unlike animals, grass can make its own food from sunlight, water and air. Grazing animals like cattle, deer and grasshoppers feed on it. These plant-eaters are then hunted by foxes, snakes and birds of prey. A great tower of living things rests, in the end, upon the ordinary grass beneath their feet; so the next time you see a hawk circling overhead, remember that its hunt began, far below, with humble blades of grass.
payload.title: Why grass is at the bottom of many food chains
decoys: Cattle and deer graze upon the grass
Every living thing has its place in nature
Grass makes its own food from sunlight

payload.passage: Asha was timekeeper for the relay and saw, on the stopwatch, that her own house team had actually come second, not first as the crowd cheered. Announcing the truth would dash her own friends' joy. She felt the weight of every hopeful face. Yet she read out the true times, and the result was corrected. Her friends sulked briefly, then thanked her for being fair. Asha learnt that an honest result, even one that disappoints your own side, is worth more than a false cheer.
payload.title: An honest result beats a false cheer
decoys: Asha read out the true relay times
Her own team had come second

payload.passage: Rohit found a wristwatch glittering on the cricket ground, dropped by some unknown player. It was finer than any he owned, and no one had seen him pick it up. He carried it for a day, the temptation growing. Then he handed it to the ground keeper and pinned up a small notice so the owner might find it. A week later a grateful older boy claimed it. Rohit learnt that doing right quietly, without any reward or praise, is honesty in its purest form.
payload.title: Quiet honesty needs no reward or praise
decoys: Rohit handed a found watch to the keeper
Watches can be dropped on a playground
He pinned a notice for the owner

payload.passage: Animals everywhere are quietly losing the wild places they call home. As cities and farms spread, forests and grasslands shrink year by year. With nowhere left to feed or raise their young, many animals grow fewer and fewer. Some kinds may vanish from the earth forever. Setting aside protected forests and parks gives wildlife a safe place to live on.
payload.title: Why wild animals need their homes protected
decoys: Animals are an important part of life
