payload.passage: Why do your eyes need to blink so many times each minute? Each blink spreads a thin layer of tears across the front of your eye. This wash keeps the surface clean, moist and clear. Blinking also sweeps away tiny specks of dust before they can scratch. Without this constant gentle cleaning, your eyes would soon turn dry and sore.
payload.title: Why blinking keeps our eyes clean and moist
decoys: A blink spreads a thin layer of tears
The body cares for its own organs
Blinking sweeps away tiny specks of dust

payload.passage: Old Mr Banerjee had no children and lived alone at the end of the lane. The neighbourhood boys thought him grumpy and avoided his gate. Ritu, however, began leaving a flower on his step each morning without a word. Day by day the old man's frown softened, and soon he was waiting to tell her stories of his youth. The lonely house filled with quiet laughter again. Ritu learnt that a small, steady kindness can melt a loneliness that harsh words could never reach.
payload.title: Small steady kindness melts deep loneliness
decoys: Ritu left a flower on Mr Banerjee's step
Lonely old people sometimes seem grumpy
An old man told stories of his youth

payload.passage: Many children on the street sold the very same plain pencils, and sales were slow for all of them. Then Diya began wrapping hers in bright paper and adding a tiny free eraser to each one. Buyers happily chose her pencils even at a slightly higher price, because hers felt special. The other sellers wondered at her success. Diya learnt that when everyone offers the same thing, the way to stand out is to give the customer a little something extra that no one else bothers to.
payload.title: Standing out by offering a little extra
decoys: Diya added a free eraser to each pencil
Many sellers offered the same plain pencils

payload.passage: Your blood is not just a plain red liquid; it is a busy delivery service. Floating in it are countless tiny red cells that carry oxygen to every corner of the body. Other cells in the blood hunt down germs and keep you safe. The blood also carries food from your meals and takes away waste. All day, this red river keeps every part of you supplied.
payload.title: The many jobs that blood does for the body
decoys: Red cells in blood carry oxygen
The body works as one system
Some blood cells hunt down germs

payload.passage: Why does your body need iron from foods like greens and beans? Iron is a metal your blood uses to carry oxygen. The red cells in your blood are packed with a substance built around iron. Without enough iron, the blood cannot carry oxygen well, and you feel tired and pale. Eating iron-rich food keeps your blood strong and your body full of energy.
payload.title: Why the body needs iron to carry oxygen
decoys: Red cells use a substance built around iron
Good food keeps the body strong
Too little iron leaves you tired and pale

payload.passage: Saira's bakery sold the same cakes as three others on her street, and she could not see why hers sold less. She finally asked her customers what they wished she offered, and many said they wanted smaller, cheaper slices for a quick treat. She added single slices to her menu, and a fresh crowd appeared. The answer had been in the customers' own mouths all along. Saira learnt that asking buyers what they actually want, rather than guessing, can reveal a simple change that lifts a struggling business.
payload.title: Why asking customers reveals what to sell
decoys: Her bakery sold the same cakes as others

payload.passage: While the other stars wheel slowly across the night, one star hardly moves at all. The Pole Star sits almost directly above the Earth's northern point of spin. As the Earth turns, the rest of the sky appears to circle around this fixed point. The Pole Star, being so near it, seems to hang steady. For ages travellers have used it to find north on dark, trackless nights; because it holds its place so faithfully, the Pole Star has been a trusted guide for explorers and sailors for ages.
payload.title: Why the Pole Star seems to stay still all night
decoys: Travellers used the Pole Star to find north
The sky is full of useful guides
Other stars appear to circle around a fixed point

payload.passage: A pair of butterflies fluttering in a garden hints at a bigger story. Butterflies are fussy creatures that need clean air and the right plants. Where they appear in plenty, the place is usually healthy and free of poison. When they vanish, it may warn that something has gone wrong with the land. So watching the butterflies can quietly reveal the health of a garden or field.
payload.title: How butterflies reveal the health of a place
decoys: Butterflies need clean air to live
Vanishing butterflies can warn of trouble

payload.passage: Why does the body need to move waste out every day? As your body uses food and fuel, it makes leftovers it cannot use. If these wastes stayed inside, they would slowly build up and make you unwell. Your gut, kidneys and skin all help clear the different wastes away. Drinking water and eating fibre keep this daily cleaning working smoothly.
payload.title: Why the body must clear out its waste daily
decoys: Using food makes leftovers the body cannot use
The body keeps itself clean inside
Water and fibre keep the cleaning smooth

payload.passage: The orb-weaver spider rebuilds its great round web almost every single day, and there is good reason for the effort. By night the web catches insects, but it also collects dust and tears in the wind, slowly losing its stickiness. A worn web traps far less food. So at dawn the spider often eats its own old silk, recycling the precious material, and spins a fresh, sticky web in its place. The new web glistens and snares prey far better. By renewing its trap each day, the spider keeps its hunting sharp.
payload.title: Why the orb-weaver rebuilds its web each day
decoys: The spider eats its own old silk
Webs catch insects for the spider
A worn web loses its stickiness

payload.passage: Rahul had collected stickers for a year and finally completed his prized album. His little cousin visited and longed for just one shiny sticker, but Rahul did not want to spoil his perfect set. Seeing the child's hopeful eyes, something softened in him. He peeled off his rarest sticker and pressed it into the small hand. The cousin's delight filled the room. His album now had one empty space, but he found he did not mind it at all. Rahul learnt that the happiness of giving something you treasure can be sweeter than keeping it whole.
payload.title: Giving something treasured can beat keeping it
decoys: Rahul gave his cousin a rare sticker
Sticker albums take a year to fill
His cousin longed for a shiny sticker

payload.passage: A simple bandage and antiseptic together help a small wound heal safely. Germs in the air can slip into a cut and cause an infection. An antiseptic kills many of these germs on the skin around the wound. A clean bandage then covers the cut and keeps fresh dirt out. Protected this way, the body can mend the wound without trouble.
payload.title: How a bandage and antiseptic protect a wound
decoys: An antiseptic kills germs on the skin
A bandage keeps fresh dirt out of a cut

payload.passage: Why does standing up too fast sometimes make you feel dizzy? When you lie down, blood spreads easily through your body. Stand up quickly, and gravity pulls some of that blood down towards your feet. For a moment, a little less reaches your head, and you feel faint. Your body soon adjusts the flow, and the dizzy feeling passes.
payload.title: Why standing up too fast makes us dizzy
decoys: Gravity pulls blood down towards the feet
Less blood reaches the head for a moment

payload.passage: The whole street admired old Mr Rao's mango tree, said to bear the sweetest fruit for miles around. One night a group of boys climbed it and stripped away half the ripening mangoes. The next morning a guilty Deepak, who had been among them, knew in his heart that he ought to confess. He feared the scolding more than almost anything, but he walked slowly up to Mr Rao's gate and told the plain truth. To his great surprise, Mr Rao thanked him warmly for his honesty and asked only that he help pick the rest of the fruit. Deepak learnt that telling the truth is hardest, and bravest, when you yourself have done wrong.
payload.title: Confessing a wrong takes the greatest courage
decoys: Deepak confessed to taking Mr Rao's mangoes
Mango trees can give very sweet summer fruit
Boys sometimes climb trees to steal ripe fruit

payload.passage: A simple smoke alarm can save a sleeping family from fire. The small box on the ceiling keeps a careful watch on the air. When smoke from a fire drifts up and slips inside, it disturbs a beam or sensor within. The alarm at once lets out a loud, piercing screech. That warning wakes everyone in time to escape the danger.
payload.title: How a smoke alarm warns a family of fire
decoys: Smoke disturbs a sensor inside the box
The alarm lets out a loud screech

payload.passage: A simple solar cooker lets the sun itself prepare a meal. A shiny curved sheet gathers sunshine from a wide area. It bounces all that light onto one small spot where a pot sits. The gathered sunlight heats the pot strongly enough to cook the food inside. With no fuel and no smoke, a family can cook using only the free sun.
payload.title: How a solar cooker uses sunshine to cook
decoys: A shiny sheet bounces light onto one spot
A solar cooker needs no fuel at all

payload.passage: The first time Aryan stood on the crowded platform, the railway station felt like pure chaos. Then he watched more closely and saw a hidden order beneath the rush. A glowing board told each traveller exactly which train stopped at which platform and when. Coloured signals far down the track told drivers when to halt and when to roll. Loud announcements stitched the whole scene together. Aryan realised that the swarming station was not chaos at all; it was thousands of people quietly trusting one shared system of signs and signals.
payload.title: How a busy station runs on shared signals
decoys: A glowing board lists trains and their platforms
Big stations are exciting and crowded places
Coloured signals tell drivers when to stop

payload.passage: In the cold months it grows dark soon after school, but in summer the light lingers late. The Earth's tilt explains this change. In winter your half of the world leans away from the sun, so it spends fewer hours in the light and more in the dark. In summer it leans toward the sun and bathes in light for longer. The longer the time in shadow, the longer and darker the night; so the dark, early evenings of winter and the bright, late ones of summer both come from the very same gentle tilt.
payload.title: Why nights are longer in winter than in summer
decoys: Winter half of the world leans away from the sun
Day and night are not always the same length
Summer light lingers late into the evening

payload.passage: Meena had practised the violin for months and dreamt of shining at the school concert. On the night itself, her younger friend Tara froze with stage fear and could not coax a single note from her own piece. Meena could easily have played alone and gathered all the praise for herself. Instead she walked across the stage, stood shoulder to shoulder with Tara, and played softly along until the frightened girl's hands stopped shaking. The whole hall clapped warmly for both of them, but Meena knew the real applause was for kindness. She understood that lifting another person up is braver than standing out on your own.
payload.title: True courage means helping others find theirs
decoys: Meena practised the violin for many months
Stage fear can strike even talented performers
Sharing a stage is a generous thing to do

payload.passage: The fire ant cannot swim, and a flood should drown its whole colony, but these insects have a startling survival trick. As water rises into the nest, thousands of ants grip one another with their jaws and legs, weaving their bodies into a living raft. The raft floats because the linked ants trap tiny bubbles of air against their water-repelling bodies. The queen and the young ride safe and dry on top, while the ants below take turns near the water. The raft drifts until it reaches land. By linking together, the colony floats through a flood.
payload.title: How fire ants float through a flood as one raft
decoys: Fire ants link bodies into a floating raft
The queen rides on top of the raft

payload.passage: Long before animals existed, the early Earth had little oxygen to breathe. Then tiny green living things in the sea began to make food from sunlight. As they did, they released oxygen as a by-product, day after day. Over countless ages this oxygen built up in the air and sea. That slow gift made it possible, much later, for air-breathing animals like us to live; so the air we breathe so freely today is, in a real sense, a gift left to us by the tiniest plants of the distant past.
payload.title: How the first green plants made Earth's oxygen
decoys: Tiny green life in the sea made food from sunlight
Earth has changed enormously over time
Built-up oxygen later let air-breathing animals live

payload.passage: Bats fly silently through the dark, and many people fear them without reason. In truth, bats are quiet friends of farmers and fruit growers. In a single night one bat can eat thousands of biting insects and pests. Other kinds of bats spread the seeds of fruit and help new trees to grow. Protecting bats and their roosts helps both our farms and our forests.
payload.title: Why bats are helpful friends, not pests
decoys: A bat can eat thousands of insects nightly
Some bats spread the seeds of fruit

payload.passage: A towering tree can sway in a gale yet rarely crashes down, and several hidden features keep it standing through the worst weather. Its roots spread wide and deep, gripping the soil like many strong anchors that hold it fast. Its trunk is built of tough, woody fibres that bend a little without snapping. The branches give in the wind, letting the gusts pass harmlessly through. Together these allow the tree to flex and recover instead of breaking. So a healthy tree is shaped to stand firm against the strongest storms.
payload.title: Why a tall tree does not topple in the wind
decoys: Wide, deep roots grip the soil like anchors
Plants are well suited to their surroundings
The branches give a little to let gusts pass

payload.passage: When you switch off the room light at night, the darkness is not really a thing of its own. Darkness is simply what is left when there is no light. We see objects only when light bounces off them and enters our eyes. A bright lamp sends out light that spreads across the room and reflects off the walls and furniture. Once the light is gone, nothing reflects, and so we see only darkness.
payload.title: Why we cannot see anything in the dark
decoys: Light bounces off objects into our eyes
Our eyes are wonderful and complex organs
A lamp sends light across the whole room

payload.passage: Diya was surprised that the hospital treated a poor labourer's broken arm without asking for money first, while a private clinic down the road would not. Her mother explained that the public hospital was paid for by everyone's taxes precisely so that no one would be left untreated for want of cash. Health, the town had decided, should not depend on the size of a purse. Diya felt proud of the idea. She learnt that a fair society uses shared money to make sure even the poorest can be healed when they are hurt.
payload.title: Why shared money keeps healing within reach
decoys: The hospital treated the labourer for free
Taxes pay for the public hospital

payload.passage: A simple traffic horn warns others on a busy road. When the driver presses the button, electricity flows to a small part inside the horn. This part shakes very fast against the air around it. The rapid shaking sends out a loud, sharp sound in every direction. Other drivers and walkers hear the warning and stay clear of danger.
payload.title: How a vehicle horn makes its warning sound
decoys: A part inside the horn shakes very fast
Drivers hear the warning and stay clear

payload.passage: Why does the body need a little fat in the diet, not none at all? Some people think all fat is bad, but the body truly needs a small amount. Healthy fats help the body soak up certain vitamins from food. They also give a store of energy and help build parts of your cells. The trick is to choose good fats and to eat them only in small amounts.
payload.title: Why the body needs a little healthy fat
decoys: Healthy fats help soak up some vitamins
Fats give the body a store of energy

payload.passage: Why does laughter seem to make you feel better? A good laugh sets off pleasant changes inside the body. It eases tense muscles and lets you breathe more deeply. It also helps the brain make feel-good signals that lift your mood. Doctors say a hearty laugh can leave both the body and the mind feeling lighter and calmer.
payload.title: Why laughter is good for body and mind
decoys: Laughter helps the brain make feel-good signals

payload.passage: A simple loom turns loose thread into solid cloth. It holds many lengthwise threads stretched tight and parallel. A shuttle then carries a crosswise thread over and under them, row by row. Each new row is pressed firmly against the last. Slowly the woven sheet grows, and what were once loose strands becomes strong, useful fabric.
payload.title: How a loom weaves thread into cloth
decoys: A shuttle carries a thread over and under

payload.passage: Why do you feel a lump in your throat and find it hard to swallow when upset? A strong feeling like sadness sets off changes in the body. One change tightens the muscles around your throat. This tightness gives the odd feeling of a lump that will not go away. As the feeling passes, the muscles relax and swallowing grows easy again.
payload.title: Why strong feelings give a lump in the throat
decoys: A feeling tightens the muscles in the throat
Swallowing grows easy as the feeling passes

payload.passage: Have you noticed your heart thumps faster when you are scared or excited? Your body senses the strong feeling and gets ready to act. It sends out a signal that speeds the heart and quickens the breath. More blood rushes to the muscles in case you must run or fight. This burst is your body's ancient way of preparing for sudden danger.
payload.title: Why the heart races when we are afraid
decoys: More blood rushes to the muscles
The body reacts to our feelings
A signal speeds up the heart

payload.passage: From every place on Earth, we always see the same face of the moon. The far side never turns toward us, no matter how long we watch. This is because the moon spins on its axis in step with its orbit around us. Its rotation and its circling take exactly the same time. So one side faces us forever, while the other always points away. The hidden side was a mystery until spacecraft finally flew around and photographed it; so for almost all of human history, half of our nearest neighbour remained completely unknown.
payload.title: Why the far side of the moon stays hidden
decoys: The moon spins in step with its orbit around us
Space holds many secrets to uncover
Spacecraft finally photographed the hidden side

payload.passage: Why does the body have a sense of pain at all? Pain is unpleasant, yet it is one of the body's most useful warnings. It tells you the very moment something is hurting or harming you. A hot pan, a sharp thorn or a twisted ankle all send a sharp signal. That signal makes you stop and protect the part before the harm grows worse.
payload.title: Why pain is a useful warning for the body
decoys: Pain signals the moment something hurts
A hot pan sends a sharp signal

payload.passage: A line of trees planted along a field edge does important work. On windy days the trees act as a wall that slows the rushing wind. This shelter stops the wind from blowing the precious topsoil away. The calmer air also helps the crops grow tall and strong. Birds nest in the trees and feed on the pests in the field, helping the farmer twice over.
payload.title: How a row of trees shelters a farmer's field
decoys: Birds in the trees eat field pests

payload.passage: A bee dances inside the hive, and its sisters seem to understand. When a bee finds a patch of flowers, it returns and waggles its body in a special pattern. The direction of the dance points the way to the flowers. The length of the waggle shows how far the flowers are. By reading this dance, the other bees fly straight to the food.
payload.title: How bees tell each other where flowers are
decoys: The length of the dance shows the distance
Bees are busy and clever insects
A bee waggles its body in a pattern

payload.passage: Not every seed sprouts as soon as it lands; some wait for a special signal. A few kinds will only grow after the heat of a passing fire cracks their tough coats. Others must pass through a long, cold winter before they will wake. These tricks make sure the seeds sprout only when conditions are right for survival. By waiting for the proper signal, the young plants get a far better start. So a seed's patience can be the key to its success.
payload.title: Why some seeds need fire or cold to sprout
decoys: Some seeds grow only after the heat of a fire
Living things adapt to their surroundings
Waiting for the right signal helps the seedling

payload.passage: Why does the doctor look at your tongue when you are unwell? The tongue is a strong, flexible muscle that does several jobs. Its surface is dotted with tiny bumps that pick up the taste of food. It also pushes the food around your mouth as you chew. And it presses against your teeth and lips to help you form clear words when you speak.
payload.title: The different jobs the tongue does for us
decoys: Tiny bumps on the tongue pick up taste
The body has many useful parts
The tongue pushes food around as we chew

payload.passage: Why does your body have so many bones in the hand and fingers? Your hand can grip a pencil, throw a ball and do up a button. Such fine, varied movements need many small bones and joints. Each little joint lets one part bend on its own. Together, these many bones give the hand the freedom to do an amazing range of tasks.
payload.title: Why the hand has so many small bones
decoys: Each little joint lets one part bend
The hand can grip, throw and button

payload.passage: A simple electric bell rings the moment you press the switch. The current flows into a coil that becomes a magnet. The magnet pulls an arm with a small hammer towards a metal gong. As the hammer strikes, it breaks the current, the magnet lets go, and the arm springs back. This happens over and over, so the bell keeps ringing while you press.
payload.title: How an electric bell keeps on ringing
decoys: A coil becomes a magnet when current flows
A hammer strikes a metal gong

payload.passage: Spring, summer, autumn and winter come round in the same order every year. This reliable timing is set by the Earth's journey around the sun. As the tilted Earth travels its yearly loop, each part leans toward the sun and away again at the same points. Those points mark the changing seasons. Because the orbit repeats so faithfully, the seasons return on schedule, year after year; this reliable timing has let farmers and families plan their year around the seasons for as long as people have grown food.
payload.title: Why the seasons arrive at fixed times each year
decoys: The tilted Earth leans toward and away from the sun
The seasons return on schedule each year

payload.passage: A dry seed can rest quietly for months, looking quite lifeless. Give it warmth and water, though, and a hidden plan stirs inside. The seed swells, its coat splits, and a tiny root pushes downward to anchor it and drink. Soon a pale shoot reaches up toward the light, carrying the first leaves. Once those leaves spread open, the young plant starts making its own food and no longer needs the seed's stored supply; this whole change, from a still, dry seed to a feeding young plant, is what we call germination.
payload.title: How a seed wakes up and begins to grow
decoys: A tiny root pushes down to anchor the seedling
Living things change as they grow older
A seed needs both warmth and water to sprout

payload.passage: Heavy gates and great stones were once impossible to move by hand. The crane changed this by lifting huge weights with ease. A long arm reaches out over the load, and a strong cable hangs from its tip. A set of pulleys lets a small effort raise a very heavy weight slowly. With cranes, builders could stack enormous blocks to raise towers and bridges.
payload.title: How a crane lifts enormous weights
decoys: A set of pulleys multiplies the effort
A long arm reaches over the load

payload.passage: Arjun loved being the centre of attention and often exaggerated his small adventures into grand tales. His friends began to doubt everything he said. One day he truly did spot a snake in the playground, but when he raised the alarm, no one believed him. Only when a teacher saw it too did they take cover. Shaken, Arjun stopped stretching his stories. He learnt that a habit of small lies can rob your words of all their weight when the truth really matters.
payload.title: Small lies rob your words of all weight
decoys: No one believed Arjun's snake warning
Arjun liked being the centre of attention

payload.passage: When Sana asked why the bank gave her father a little book that recorded every deposit and withdrawal, he called it his money memory. The passbook, he said, let him check at a glance whether the bank's record matched his own. If a single entry looked wrong, he could question it at once before the error grew. Without such a record, a mistake might slip by unnoticed for years. Sana learnt that keeping a clear account is how an ordinary saver keeps even a big bank honest about their own money.
payload.title: How a passbook lets you check the bank
decoys: A wrong entry could be questioned early

payload.passage: When a green caterpillar wants to avoid being eaten, it may turn into something fearsome without changing at all. Certain caterpillars have large false eyespots near the head that look exactly like the staring eyes of a snake. When a bird approaches, the caterpillar puffs up its front and sways, and the eyespots loom large and threatening. The startled bird, fearing a real snake, flutters away in alarm. The soft, harmless caterpillar has not even moved to fight. By wearing a snake's face, it scares off enemies far larger than itself.
payload.title: How a caterpillar scares birds with fake snake eyes
decoys: Some caterpillars have large false eyespots
It puffs up its front to look bigger

payload.passage: Streetlights that blaze all night long do more harm than we think. Their glare hides the stars and confuses night animals and insects. Many moths circle the bright bulbs until they tire and die. Birds that travel by night can lose their way among the lights. Softer, downward-facing lamps would let us see the road while sparing the creatures of the dark.
payload.title: Why too much night light harms wildlife
decoys: Moths circle bright bulbs until they die

payload.passage: The moon is far away, yet its gentle pull reaches all the way to our seas. Its gravity tugs hardest on the water nearest to it, drawing it into a bulge. A matching bulge forms on the opposite side of the Earth as well. As the Earth spins, coasts pass through these bulges and the sea rises as high tide. Between the bulges, the water is lower and the tide falls. So the daily rhythm of the tides is the work of the distant moon.
payload.title: How the moon's pull tugs the whole ocean
decoys: The moon draws the nearest water into a bulge
The moon shapes the Earth in many ways
Coasts pass through the bulges as the Earth spins

payload.passage: When germs invade your body, an unseen army leaps to your defence. Special cells in your blood hunt down the invading germs. Some swallow the germs whole, while others make tiny weapons to destroy them. Your body may raise a fever, since the heat helps fight the attackers. Once the battle is won, your body remembers that germ and guards against it.
payload.title: How the body fights off invading germs
decoys: Some cells swallow the germs whole
The body protects itself in many ways
A fever's heat helps fight germs

payload.passage: In a colony of ants, the dead and the rubbish would soon spread disease if left lying about. So the ants keep a strict order. Certain workers act as undertakers, carrying dead ants to a special waste pile far from the nest's living quarters. They can tell a dead ant by a particular smell it gives off. Other ants haul out spoiled food and droppings to the same dump. By keeping their waste apart from where they live and raise young, the ants stop sickness from sweeping through the crowded colony.
payload.title: How ants stop disease by removing their dead
decoys: Some ants carry the dead to a waste pile
Ant colonies are crowded with insects
Dead ants give off a particular smell

payload.passage: Sunlight looks plain white, yet it secretly holds every colour of the rainbow. When light passes through a raindrop or a glass prism, it bends. Each colour bends by a slightly different amount as it passes. This spreads the colours apart into a band, from red through to violet. What was once white light is now a glowing strip of many hues. A rainbow simply reveals the colours that were hidden inside the sunlight all along; so a rainbow is really a glimpse of the many colours that were hidden inside plain white light.
payload.title: How sunlight splits into a rainbow of colours
decoys: Each colour bends by a slightly different amount
A rainbow reveals colours hidden in the sunlight

payload.passage: The sun rises in the early morning, yet the warmest hours come much later. This is because heating the ground and air takes time. At sunrise the slanted rays are weak and the night's chill still lingers. As the sun climbs, its light grows stronger and steadily warms the land. The ground then passes its heat to the air through the afternoon. The temperature keeps climbing well past dawn, peaking in the early afternoon; so the hottest part of the day arrives well after the sun has first climbed into the sky, once the ground has had time to warm the air.
payload.title: Why the day grows warm long after sunrise
decoys: At sunrise the slanted rays are still weak
The day changes in many ways from hour to hour
The ground passes its heat to the air

payload.passage: When a colony of bees loses its way home in fading light, it does not panic. Bees navigate using the sun, but on a cloudy day or near dusk the sun may be hidden. Remarkably, a bee can still read the pattern of light in the sky that the human eye cannot see, and work out where the sun must be. With this hidden compass it steers straight back to the hive. It also remembers landmarks like trees and rivers along the way. By reading the sky and the land, the bee always finds its way home.
payload.title: How a bee finds its way home using the sky
decoys: A bee can read hidden patterns in the sky
Bees fly out from the hive to find food
It remembers landmarks along the way

payload.passage: Aditi had practised her cartwheels for the gymnastics display but still tumbled over each time. The day before the show, she fell hard and the other girls doubted she could do it. She could have quietly dropped out to avoid embarrassment. Instead she practised late into the evening, again and again. On the day she completed a clean cartwheel before the whole school. Aditi learnt that one more try, after everyone expects you to quit, can be the try that finally succeeds.
payload.title: One more try after others expect you to quit
decoys: Aditi practised cartwheels late into the evening
Gymnastics displays need a lot of practice
She fell hard the day before

payload.passage: Pari noticed that on the day before voting, all the loud campaigning suddenly went silent by law. No speeches, no posters, no last-minute promises were allowed. Her grandfather explained that this quiet day gave voters a calm space to think for themselves, free from the noise and pressure. A choice made in haste, swayed by a final shout, might not be a true one. Pari learnt that the silent day was a gift to the voter, a pause to decide with a clear and untroubled mind.
payload.title: Why campaigning stops before voting day
decoys: All campaigning went silent by law
Voters got a calm day to decide

payload.passage: When the village's only road needed repair, the panchayat could either hire an outside company or ask the villagers themselves to work for a fair wage. The members chose the second way, so the money stayed in the village and neighbours earned from mending their own path. The road was fixed, and several families gained much-needed income at the same time. Reyansh saw that a single decision could solve a problem and help people earn together. He learnt that wise spending can do double good when it keeps money close to home.
payload.title: How local hiring keeps money in the village
decoys: Villagers worked on their own road

payload.passage: A patch of moss on a damp wall is not just a stain to scrub away. Moss is one of the oldest and simplest of plants. It soaks up rainwater like a tiny sponge and holds it for a while. Like other green plants, it breathes out a little oxygen too. Small creatures shelter within its soft green carpet. Even this humble plant plays its part in the living world.
payload.title: Why even humble moss plays a part in nature
decoys: Moss soaks up rainwater like a sponge
Small creatures shelter in the moss

payload.passage: The owl butterfly is a soft, slow flier that any bird could snatch, yet it is rarely caught. The underside of each wing bears a huge dark spot ringed in pale colour, looking exactly like the staring eye of an owl. When a small bird approaches, the butterfly flashes these spots open. The bird, suddenly fearing it has disturbed a watching owl, darts away in fright. The harmless butterfly has done nothing but show its wings. By wearing the eyes of a fierce predator, it frightens off the very birds that would eat it.
payload.title: How the owl butterfly scares birds with eye-spots
decoys: The owl butterfly has owl-like eye-spots
It flashes its wings open at danger

payload.passage: Every dawn the sleepy market square wakes with a roar of carts and calls. Farmers unload baskets of tomatoes and greens picked only hours before, while buyers hunt for the freshest pile at the lowest price. A vendor who sets too high a price watches shoppers drift to the next stall, so he quietly lowers it. By mid-morning, prices have settled into a rough agreement between many sellers and many buyers. Riya saw that no one person fixes the cost of a tomato; the busy crowd decides it together.
payload.title: How a crowd sets prices in a busy market
decoys: A vendor lowers his price when shoppers leave
Markets are lively and exciting places to visit
Farmers bring vegetables picked only hours before

payload.passage: Pour a steaming drink and leave it, and it always cools toward room temperature. Heat naturally flows from the warmer thing to the cooler one around it. The hot drink passes its warmth into the cooler air and cup. As it loses that heat, its temperature falls. It will not stop until it matches the room around it. The cooling of a drink is simply heat moving from where there is more to where there is less; so the cooling of a drink is simply heat flowing from where there is more to where there is less.
payload.title: Why a hot drink slowly cools in a cold room
decoys: The hot drink passes warmth into the cooler air
Heat shapes the world around us
Cooling stops once the drink matches the room

payload.passage: Why does sugary food give you a quick burst of energy that soon fades? Sugar is taken into the blood very fast and lifts your energy in a rush. But your body quickly deals with that sudden rise, and the energy drops just as fast. You can feel tired and cranky soon after. Slow foods like grains give steadier energy that lasts much longer.
payload.title: Why sugary food gives only a brief energy rush
decoys: Sugar is taken into the blood very fast
What we eat affects how we feel

payload.passage: Shalini had spent her saved money on a movie ticket she had looked forward to for weeks. On the way she passed a small boy crying because he had lost the bus fare to reach home far away. She hesitated only a moment, then gave him the money meant for her ticket. She walked home instead of watching the film, but her heart felt unusually full. Shalini learnt that the joy of easing someone's real trouble can outshine a pleasure we give up for it.
payload.title: Easing real trouble outshines a given-up pleasure
decoys: Shalini gave her ticket money to a lost boy
The boy had lost his bus fare

payload.passage: A simple raincloud of spray, made by a sprinkler, waters a whole field evenly. Water is pumped under pressure to a spinning nozzle. As the nozzle whirls, it flings the water out in a fine, wide shower. The spray falls like gentle rain across the crops below. One sprinkler can water a large patch without anyone carrying a single pot.
payload.title: How a sprinkler waters a whole field evenly
decoys: A spinning nozzle flings the water out
The spray falls like gentle rain

payload.passage: Places by the coast often enjoy gentler seasons than lands lying far inland, and the sea itself is the reason. Water heats up and cools down slowly, far more slowly than the land beside it. So in summer the nearby sea keeps the coast a little cooler, and in winter it keeps it a little warmer. This steadying effect softens the swing between the seasons. Far from the sea, summers and winters grow far harsher. So the great ocean acts as a gentle balancer of coastal weather.
payload.title: Why the seasons feel mild near the sea
decoys: Water heats and cools more slowly than land
The world's weather varies from place to place
Inland summers and winters grow far harsher

payload.passage: A heap of electronic waste, like old phones and chargers, is more dangerous than it looks. Inside these gadgets lie metals that can poison the soil and water if simply dumped. Yet the same gadgets also hold tiny amounts of valuable metals worth saving. Special centres can take them apart safely and reuse the precious parts. Handing old gadgets to these centres protects both people and the earth.
payload.title: Why old gadgets must be recycled with care
decoys: Dumped gadgets can poison the soil

payload.passage: A glass lens may look like a simple curve, yet it opened up hidden worlds. Ground into the right shape, a lens bends light to make things look larger. One set of lenses became the microscope, which revealed tiny germs no eye had ever seen. Another set became the telescope, which brought distant stars into view. From the smallest germ to the farthest planet, lenses changed what people could study.
payload.title: How the lens revealed the unseen worlds
decoys: A lens bends light to make things look larger
Science has uncovered many hidden secrets
The microscope let people see tiny germs

payload.passage: The dwarf mongoose is small enough to be a snack for a hawk, yet it has a surprising ally that helps it stay safe. As the mongoose group forages on the ground, certain birds called hornbills gather overhead and travel with them. The birds snap up insects the mongooses stir from the grass, while their sharp eyes watch the sky for eagles. When a hornbill calls a warning, the mongooses dive for cover at once. Both sides gain from the partnership. By teaming up with watchful birds, the little mongooses feed in greater safety.
payload.title: How mongooses and birds watch out for each other
decoys: Small animals are hunted by hawks
The birds eat insects the mongooses stir up

payload.passage: Day and night arrive in a calm, dependable order, never jumbled. This steady rhythm comes from the Earth's even spin. The planet turns at a constant pace, carrying each place from the sunlit side to the shadowed side and back. Because the spin never speeds up or slows much, the cycle stays regular. So we can trust that after every night a new day will surely dawn; this dependable cycle has shaped the daily habits of nearly every living thing, from sleeping animals to flowering plants.
payload.title: Why night follows day in a steady rhythm
decoys: Each place moves from the sunlit side to shadow
The world runs on dependable patterns
The Earth's spin never speeds up or slows much

payload.passage: Atharv noticed that his city's railway station had grown a gentle, thoughtful side. A ramp curved beside every staircase so a wheelchair could roll up smoothly. Yellow strips with raised bumps guided blind travellers along the platform edge, and the announcements were read aloud as well as shown on screens. Even the ticket counter had a lowered window for shorter people. Atharv realised these small additions cost real effort and money, yet they quietly told every traveller, whatever their need, that the station was built for them too.
payload.title: How a station welcomes travellers of every need
decoys: Yellow bumpy strips guide blind travellers
Public places should be clean and pleasant
Ramps were built beside every staircase

payload.passage: A field left bare between crops is at the mercy of wind and rain. Farmers can protect it by sowing a quick cover of leafy plants. These plants hold the soil down with their roots so it is not swept away. They also smother the weeds and feed the soil when ploughed back in. A green cover keeps the bare months from robbing the field of its richness.
payload.title: How cover plants protect a resting field
decoys: Cover plants hold the soil with their roots
Farmers work hard on the land

payload.passage: Why does the body have two eyes instead of just one? Each eye sees the world from a slightly different spot. The brain joins the two pictures into a single view. From the small difference between them, the brain works out how near or far things are. This is why two eyes let you judge distance far better than one eye alone.
payload.title: Why two eyes help us judge distance
decoys: Each eye sees from a slightly different spot
The brain joins the two pictures

payload.passage: Without the water cycle, the land would soon dry to dust. The sun lifts water from the seas into the sky as vapour. There it forms clouds that the wind carries far over the continents. The clouds release rain that soaks fields, fills rivers and refreshes the soil. Plants and animals drink, and the water later returns to the sea. This endless loop keeps even the inland places green and alive; so this endless loop is the quiet reason that rain reaches even places far from any sea.
payload.title: How the water cycle waters the whole land
decoys: Wind carries the clouds far over the continents
Nature keeps the world supplied with what it needs
The water later returns from the land to the sea

payload.passage: A rooftop garden can turn a hot, bare terrace into a cool, green oasis. Pots and beds of plants soak up the sun that would otherwise bake the roof. The rooms below stay cooler, easing the need for fans. The garden grows fresh herbs and vegetables for the kitchen too. Birds and bees visit the blooms, bringing life high above the busy street.
payload.title: How a rooftop garden cools the house and feeds the family
decoys: Plants soak up the sun on the roof
Terraces can be hot in summer

payload.passage: A simple set of brakes lets a cycle stop safely. Press the lever and two rubber pads are squeezed against the spinning wheel rim. The pads rub hard against the metal, and this rubbing is friction. Friction steals the wheel's movement and turns it into heat. As the movement drains away, the wheel slows and the cycle comes to a halt.
payload.title: How brakes use friction to stop a cycle
decoys: Rubber pads squeeze against the wheel rim

payload.passage: During some full moons the bright disc slowly darkens and glows a dim, dusky red. This is a lunar eclipse, when the Earth slips between the sun and the moon. The Earth's shadow falls across the moon, cutting off the direct sunlight. Yet a little light bends through the Earth's air and reaches the moon, tinting it red. So the eclipsed moon is not black but lit by a soft, reddish glow; unlike a solar eclipse, this reddened moon can be seen safely by everyone on the night side of the Earth at once.
payload.title: Why a lunar eclipse turns the moon red
decoys: Light bends through the Earth's air onto the moon
The night sky offers rare and special sights
The Earth slips between the sun and the moon

payload.passage: Kabir thought a bank simply held the same coins and notes he had handed over, ready to give back the very same ones. His sister laughed and explained that banks deal in numbers, not in particular notes. When he deposits a hundred rupees, the bank records that it owes him a hundred, but it may lend those exact notes to someone else within the hour. As long as the bank can pay him when he asks, the actual notes do not matter. Kabir learnt that a bank balance is a promise, not a pile of his personal coins.
payload.title: Why a bank balance is a promise, not coins
decoys: The bank may lend the notes to others
Numbers can be hard to grasp
A deposit is recorded as money owed to you

payload.passage: The opossum is a slow, gentle creature with few ways to fight off a hungry dog or fox. So when it is truly cornered, it puts on a remarkable performance. Its body goes limp, its eyes glaze, its tongue hangs out, and it even gives off a sickly smell, as if it had died days ago. Few hunters want to eat something that seems long dead and rotten, so they lose interest and wander off. The opossum cannot even choose to do this; the fright triggers it automatically. Once danger has passed, it quietly comes back to life and slips away.
payload.title: How the opossum plays dead to fool predators
decoys: The opossum's body goes limp when cornered
Slow animals are easy prey for dogs
It gives off a smell like rotting meat

payload.passage: When the class went on a hike, little Pawan twisted his ankle and could not keep up. The fastest boys raced ahead, eager to reach the top first and claim the view. Deepa, who had been leading, stopped and chose to walk slowly beside the limping boy instead. They reached the summit last, long after the others. Yet Pawan never forgot who stayed with him. Deepa learnt that being a true friend can matter far more than being first to the finish.
payload.title: Standing by a friend beats finishing first
decoys: Deepa walked beside the injured Pawan
Reaching a summit first feels exciting

payload.passage: The changing seasons are like a clock that nature reads. As days shorten and cool in autumn, some birds set off on long journeys to warmer lands. Many trees drop their leaves and rest, while some animals store food or sleep through winter. When spring's longer, warmer days return, plants sprout and creatures wake to breed. In this way the steady march of the seasons tells living things when to move, rest and grow; by reading these seasonal signs, plants and animals time their journeys, their rest and their breeding to survive the year.
payload.title: How the seasons guide animals and plants
decoys: Some birds fly to warmer lands in autumn
Nature follows patterns through the whole year
Many trees rest and drop their leaves in winter

payload.passage: Why do your bones need calcium from milk and green vegetables? Calcium is a mineral that makes bones hard and strong. While you are young, your body builds most of the bone you will ever have. Without enough calcium, bones grow weak and break more easily. Drinking milk and eating greens now lays down strong bones for the rest of your life.
payload.title: Why calcium builds strong bones in children
decoys: Calcium makes bones hard and strong
Eating well keeps the body healthy

payload.passage: Sahil's group was given one umbrella to share during the sudden downpour on the way home. The bigger boys huddled under it and left the youngest, Chintu, out in the rain. Sahil could have squeezed in with his friends and stayed dry. Instead he stepped out, gave his place to Chintu, and walked home soaked. Chintu never forgot it. His clothes dripped all the way home, but his heart felt strangely light. Sahil learnt that protecting the youngest and weakest, even at your own discomfort, is what real fairness looks like.
payload.title: Fairness protects the youngest at your own cost
decoys: Sahil gave his umbrella spot to Chintu
The bigger boys left Chintu in the rain

payload.passage: When a new family moved into the village, they did not know the local rules about sharing the common grazing field. The panchayat invited them to a meeting and patiently explained the customs everyone followed, so no quarrel would arise from simple ignorance. The newcomers, grateful, settled in smoothly. Ishita saw that the council did more than judge disputes; it welcomed strangers and taught them the shared ways of the place. She learnt that a good community gently brings new members into its fold rather than letting them stumble.
payload.title: How a council welcomes and guides newcomers
decoys: The newcomers did not know the rules
The council explained the grazing customs

payload.passage: Climb a tall mountain on a hot day and the air grows chilly near the top. It seems odd, since the peak is closer to the sun. But the thin air high up holds heat poorly and lets it slip away quickly. The ground there also catches less warmth and loses it fast. High peaks often wear caps of snow all year, even while the valleys below sweat in summer; so a climber may set out from a warm valley in the morning and reach a snowy, freezing peak by the afternoon.
payload.title: Why mountain tops stay cold even in summer
decoys: Thin mountain air holds heat very poorly
Conditions change as you move around the Earth
High peaks can wear snow caps all year round

payload.passage: Why does the body have a sense of smell as well as taste? Your nose can pick up thousands of different scents in the air. Some warn you of danger, like smoke or food that has gone bad. Others bring pleasure, like a flower or a hot meal. Smell also joins with taste to give food its full flavour, so the two senses work as a team.
payload.title: How the sense of smell warns and pleases us
decoys: The nose can pick up thousands of scents
The body has many useful senses
Smell joins with taste to make flavour

payload.passage: On a hot day, plants face the same problem we do: too much heat. A leaf has a clever answer. It lets water escape from its tiny pores as vapour, and this drifting away of water carries off heat. The cooling works much like sweat on our skin. Even as the sun beats down, a well-watered leaf can keep itself from getting too hot; so on a scorching day, a well-watered plant can quietly keep its leaves from overheating, much as we cool ourselves by sweating.
payload.title: How a leaf loses water to keep cool
decoys: Water escapes from the leaf's tiny pores
Living things have ways to cope with heat
Leaf cooling works much like sweat on our skin

payload.passage: A patch of bare ground in the schoolyard can be turned into a small forest. Children dig in many tiny saplings close together in good soil. Crowded together, the young trees race upward towards the light and grow fast. In a few years a dense little wood rises where there was only dust. Birds, insects and cool shade soon follow, all from a single planting day.
payload.title: How a tiny forest can grow in a schoolyard
decoys: Saplings are dug in close together

payload.passage: When a smaller boy accidentally tore Vikram's homework, the classroom went silent, waiting for an angry outburst. Vikram felt the heat of anger rise in his chest. The boy looked terrified and kept saying sorry. Vikram took a deep breath, said it was only paper, and quietly copied the work again. The frightened boy relaxed, and the two became friends. The whole class let out a breath, surprised by how calmly he had taken it. Vikram learnt that holding back anger over a small accident shows a strength far greater than shouting ever could.
payload.title: Holding back anger shows real strength
decoys: A boy tore Vikram's homework by accident
Torn homework must be copied again
The boy kept saying he was sorry

payload.passage: Reyaan received a crisp gift of money and at once wanted to spend it all on sweets and toys. His grandfather suggested a quiet game: list everything he wished to buy, then sleep on it before spending a single coin. By morning, half the wishes had faded, and he kept his money for things that still mattered. The eager rush of wanting had cooled overnight. Reyaan learnt that the strong pull to spend often weakens with a little time, and that delaying a purchase lets a true want separate itself from a passing whim.
payload.title: How delaying a purchase reveals real wants
decoys: He wanted to spend it all on sweets
Half his wishes faded by morning

payload.passage: Aadhya was surprised to learn that the crisp notes in her purse were worth something only because everyone agreed they were. The paper itself, her teacher said, was nearly worthless; its value came from shared trust that others would accept it tomorrow. Long ago people swapped goods directly, but carrying cows to buy cloth was clumsy. Money became a clever, shared token that stood in for value and made trading easy. Aadhya realised that money works only as long as people keep believing in the promise printed on it.
payload.title: Why money's value rests on shared trust
decoys: The paper note itself is nearly worthless

payload.passage: A child's shadow is long and thin at breakfast, almost gone by lunch, and long again by evening. This dance follows the sun across the sky. When the sun is low in the morning, light strikes from the side and casts a long shadow. As the sun climbs high at noon, the shadow shortens beneath your feet. By evening the sun sinks low again, and shadows stretch out long once more; by watching how a shadow moves, people long ago learned to read the time of day from the sun alone.
payload.title: How shadows shrink and stretch through the day
decoys: A shadow is shortest around the middle of the day
The world looks different at different times
A low morning sun casts long shadows

payload.passage: When the African plains dry out, the lone hyena would struggle to feed, but the clan thrives through cooperation. Hyenas hunt in groups, working together to wear down prey far larger than themselves over a long chase. They share the food and even take turns guarding it from lions that try to steal the kill. Back at the den, several females help mind and protect the cubs of the whole clan. The matriarch leads them all. By living and hunting as a tight group, the hyenas survive a hard land together.
payload.title: How a hyena clan survives by hunting together
decoys: Hyenas hunt prey larger than themselves
The plains dry out in some seasons
Females help mind the clan's cubs

payload.passage: Rahul wanted to win the school marathon so badly that he set off far too fast and was already tiring by the halfway mark. A steadier boy named Joy jogged calmly past him, keeping exactly the same even pace from start to finish. Rahul's legs turned to lead, and he stumbled in somewhere near the very back of the pack. Joy, meanwhile, crossed the finish line fresh and smiling. Over a cup of cool drink afterwards, Joy explained that he had simply paced himself the whole way. Rahul learnt that patience spread evenly over a long road beats a single burst of early speed.
payload.title: Steady pacing beats a burst of early speed
decoys: Rahul started the marathon far too fast
Marathons are very long and tiring races
Joy kept the same pace the whole way

payload.passage: When you tune a guitar or a sitar, you are really changing how fast a string can shake. A plucked string moves back and forth very quickly and pushes the air to make sound. A tight, thin string shakes fast and gives a high note. A loose, thick string shakes more slowly and gives a low note. By twisting the pegs, a player changes the tightness and so changes the pitch.
payload.title: How the pitch of a string is changed
decoys: A tight string gives a high note
Music brings joy to people everywhere
Twisting the pegs tunes a stringed instrument

payload.passage: Watch the stars for a few hours and they slowly shift across the sky. They are not really moving; the Earth is turning beneath them. As our planet rotates, stars rise in the east and set in the west, much like the sun. Patterns that stood low at dusk climb high by midnight. By dawn they have slipped away toward the western horizon. So the slow march of the stars through the night is one more sign of the Earth's steady spin.
payload.title: Why the night sky changes through the hours
decoys: Stars rise in the east and set in the west
The sky is always gently changing
Patterns climb high by the middle of the night

payload.passage: Why does the body need a good mix of rest and movement each day? Movement keeps the heart, lungs and muscles strong and working well. But the body also needs quiet time to repair and store energy. Too much sitting makes you weak and dull, while too little rest leaves you worn out. A balance of activity and rest keeps the body in its best shape.
payload.title: Why the body needs both movement and rest
decoys: Movement keeps the heart and lungs strong
Too much sitting makes you dull

payload.passage: The water in a hill stream, a lake and the far sea may all be the same water at different stops. Rain feeds the streams, which run into rivers and lakes. Rivers carry their water onward to the sea, mixing it all together. The sun then lifts water from the sea, and rain returns it to the hills. Every body of water is just one stage in a single, shared cycle; so the water in a glass today may once have flowed in a far-off river or rolled in the waves of a distant sea.
payload.title: How rivers, lakes and seas share the same water
decoys: Rivers carry their water onward to the sea
Water connects places all over the Earth
Rain lifted from the sea returns to the hills

payload.passage: Lata's family once kept all their important papers and a little gold in a cupboard at home, until a neighbour's house was robbed. The bank offered them a small locker, a strong steel box inside the vault that only they could open with their own key. For a modest yearly fee, their treasures stayed safe behind heavy doors and watchful guards. Lata saw that the bank's service was not only about money in accounts. She learnt that a bank can also guard the precious things a family cannot afford to lose.
payload.title: How a bank locker guards a family's treasures
decoys: A neighbour's house had been robbed
The locker sat inside the bank's vault

payload.passage: Monarch butterflies are too delicate to survive a harsh winter, so they flee it by the millions. As the cold creeps in, they set off on a journey of thousands of kilometres to warmer forests far away. The astonishing part is that no single butterfly lives to make the whole round trip; it takes several short-lived generations. Somehow the great-grandchildren still find the very same forests their ancestors used, though none have ever seen them. This inherited map, carried in their tiny bodies, guides each new generation. The miracle of migration is written into them from birth.
payload.title: How monarch butterflies inherit a map for migration
decoys: Monarch butterflies fly thousands of kilometres
Many creatures escape the cold in winter
No single monarch finishes the whole trip

payload.passage: A torch is a neat little package of useful science. Inside it sits a battery that stores energy in a chemical form. When you slide the switch, you join the parts into a closed loop called a circuit. Energy then flows from the battery to the tiny bulb, which glows brightly. Open the switch and the loop is broken, so the flow stops and the light goes out.
payload.title: How a torch turns stored energy into light
decoys: A battery stores energy in a chemical form
Inventions make our daily lives much simpler
Sliding the switch makes the torch bulb glow

payload.passage: A simple seat belt holds you safe if a car stops suddenly. When a vehicle halts hard, your body keeps moving forward on its own. Without a belt you would be thrown against the dashboard or glass. The belt holds your body firmly against the seat instead. By stopping you gently with the car, it has saved countless lives.
payload.title: How a seat belt keeps you safe in a crash
decoys: Your body keeps moving when the car stops
The belt holds you against the seat

payload.passage: Now and then the bright day suddenly dims as the sun seems to vanish. This is a solar eclipse, and the moon is the cause. As the moon passes directly between the Earth and the sun, it blocks the sunlight from reaching part of the Earth. A shadow falls, and for a short while the sun is hidden behind the moon. Once the moon moves on, the sunlight returns and the day brightens again; because the moon's shadow is small, a full solar eclipse can be seen only from a narrow strip of the Earth at a time.
payload.title: How a solar eclipse hides the sun
decoys: The moon's shadow falls on part of the Earth
The sky can change in dramatic ways
The moon passes directly between the Earth and the sun

payload.passage: When Dev opened his first savings account, the manager spoke about something called compound interest. She explained that the bank pays interest not only on the money Dev puts in, but also on the interest it has already added. Year after year, his savings would earn a little on a slightly bigger pile each time. It felt slow at first, yet over many years the growth could quietly snowball. Dev learnt that the secret weapon for a young saver is not a huge deposit but simply starting early and waiting patiently.
payload.title: Why starting to save early grows money faster
decoys: Interest is added on top of earlier interest
Patience is a useful quality in life
Dev opened his very first savings account

payload.passage: Boil water in a covered pot and the lid soon drips. Heat turns the water into steam, an invisible gas that rises and fills the pot. When this hot steam meets the cooler lid, it loses heat and turns back into liquid. Tiny drops gather on the underside of the lid and slide down. This change from gas back to liquid is the same one that forms clouds and rain; watching a pot lid drip is a simple way to see, in miniature, the very change that builds clouds high in the sky.
payload.title: How steam turns back into water on a lid
decoys: Tiny drops gather on the underside of the lid
Heat can change things in many ways
Steam loses heat when it meets the cooler lid

payload.passage: Priya found the answer to the hardest puzzle in the magazine printed upside down at the back. She could have copied it and claimed she had solved it all herself. The pull to look was strong. She covered the page and worked at the puzzle for two evenings until she cracked it on her own. The pride she felt was real and warm. Priya learnt that the satisfaction of solving something yourself is a reward that copying the answer can never give.
payload.title: Solving it yourself rewards more than copying
decoys: Priya solved the puzzle on her own
Magazines print answers at the back
The puzzle took her two evenings

payload.passage: A street traffic light keeps busy crossings safe with three simple colours. Red tells every vehicle to stop and wait its turn. Green tells drivers it is now safe to move ahead. Amber warns that the light is about to change, so be ready. By taking turns in a fixed order, the lights stop different roads from clashing at the same moment.
payload.title: How traffic lights keep crossings safe
decoys: Green tells drivers it is safe to move
Many inventions help keep us safe
Amber warns the light is about to change

payload.passage: The remora is a small fish with a strange flat disc on top of its head, and it uses this for an easy life. The disc works like a powerful sucker. The remora presses it against the body of a big shark or turtle and holds on tight, riding along wherever the giant goes. It travels great distances without swimming and stays safe from hunters that dare not approach the shark. In return it eats the scraps and pests left on its host. By hitching a free ride, the remora finds food and safety at once.
payload.title: How the remora hitches a ride on sharks
decoys: The remora has a sucker on its head
Small fish must avoid larger hunters
It eats scraps left by its host

payload.passage: A noisy street can do more harm than just being unpleasant. The blare of horns and roar of engines fills the air all day. Living with so much noise can give people headaches and steal their sleep. Birds and animals are frightened away from noisy places. Quieter horns and calmer streets would make life better for people and creatures alike.
payload.title: Why too much noise harms people and animals
decoys: Loud horns can give people headaches
Cities can be busy and tiring
Noise frightens birds and animals away

payload.passage: Most stars hold fixed patterns night after night, but a few points of light slowly drift among them. Long ago, people called these wanderers, and we now know them as planets. They appear to move because they, like the Earth, circle the sun. As both they and we travel our paths, our view of them shifts against the distant stars. The far-off stars are too remote to seem to move at all. So the wandering lights are nearby planets rather than ordinary stars.
payload.title: Why the planets seem to wander among the stars
decoys: People long ago called these lights wanderers
The night sky holds many kinds of objects
The planets move because they circle the sun

payload.passage: Why does playing a sport help your mind as well as your body? Running and games keep the heart, lungs and muscles strong. But exercise also helps the brain make signals that lift your mood. Playing in a team teaches you to share, plan and stay calm under pressure. So sport builds a healthy body and a steadier, happier mind together.
payload.title: Why sport helps both the mind and the body
decoys: Games keep the heart and muscles strong
Healthy habits help us all round
Team play teaches us to share and plan

payload.passage: When a seed sprouts, it sends parts in two opposite directions at once. A root pushes downward into the soil, drawn by gravity. There it anchors the young plant and drinks in water and minerals. At the same time, a shoot climbs upward toward the light. Reaching the light lets the first leaves open and start making food. Even as a tiny seedling, the plant knows to grow both down for water and up for sunshine; so even at the very start of its life, a plant carefully sends each part where it is needed most.
payload.title: Why a young seedling reaches up and roots down
decoys: A root pushes downward into the soil
Living things grow in clever ways
Reaching the light lets the first leaves open

payload.passage: The sun has shone steadily for billions of years, but it will not burn forever. Like any fire, it slowly uses up the fuel deep in its core. In the far future, when much of that fuel is gone, the sun will swell and change. Eventually it will cool into a small, faint remnant. This will not happen for billions of years, so there is no need to worry about it now; until that far-off time, our steady sun will keep pouring out the light and warmth that all life on Earth depends upon.
payload.title: How the sun will one day run out of fuel
decoys: The sun slowly uses up the fuel in its core
Nothing in the universe lasts forever
One day the sun will swell up and change

payload.passage: A garden grown without harsh chemicals hums with quiet life. Instead of sprays, the gardener welcomes ladybirds, frogs and birds to eat the pests. Compost and old leaves feed the soil in place of factory powders. The fruit and vegetables grow free of harmful traces. Such a natural garden is safer for the family and kinder to the small creatures that share it.
payload.title: Why a chemical-free garden is safer and full of life
decoys: Ladybirds and frogs eat the pests
Gardens can be grown in many ways

payload.passage: Plant a bean and watch a quiet drama unfold underground. The swollen seed splits, and a small root dives down to grip the soil and drink. Next a bent shoot pushes up, shielding its tip as it nudges through the earth. Once above the soil, the shoot straightens and unfolds its first pair of leaves. From then on those leaves catch sunlight, and the young bean plant feeds itself; watching a bean sprout in a jar is one of the simplest ways to see the hidden steps of germination for yourself.
payload.title: How a bean seed splits open and reaches upward
decoys: The shoot shields its tip as it pushes up
Growth is a slow but steady process
A small root dives down to grip the soil

payload.passage: A spider's web looks delicate, yet it is a brilliant trap. The spider spins fine threads from its own body and weaves them into a wide net. Some threads are dry, while others are coated with a sticky glue. The spider walks only on the dry threads so that it does not get stuck. When an insect blunders into the sticky threads, it is caught fast for the spider's meal.
payload.title: How a spider's web catches its prey
decoys: Some threads of a web are coated with glue
Insects can be found nearly everywhere
A spider spins threads from its own body

payload.passage: A cloud holds its water in droplets so small they float on the air. As more vapour joins them, the droplets bump together and slowly grow larger. When a droplet becomes too heavy for the air to hold, it begins to fall toward the ground. On the way down it may swallow other drops and grow heavier still. By the time it lands, what began as a speck of mist has become a full raindrop; scientists call the steady carrying-up of vapour and the dropping of rain two key steps in the endless water cycle.
payload.title: How heavy clouds finally let their water fall
decoys: Small droplets bump and join into bigger ones
Big things in nature usually start out small
Clouds float because their droplets are very light

payload.passage: Long ago, people guessed their weight or used clumsy balances. The weighing scale gave an exact answer in a moment. Inside many scales sits a spring that squashes down under a load. The heavier the object, the further the spring is pressed. A pointer linked to the spring shows the weight on a marked dial. Shops, kitchens and clinics all came to rely on this simple machine.
payload.title: How a weighing scale measures how heavy things are
decoys: A spring squashes down under a load
Inventions help us measure the world
A pointer shows the weight on a dial

payload.passage: A heap of grass clippings left on the lawn need not be raked away. As the cut grass dries, it slowly breaks down on the ground. It returns its goodness straight to the soil beneath. This natural feeding helps the lawn grow thick and green without extra fertiliser. Leaving the clippings is less work and better for the earth at the same time.
payload.title: Why leaving grass clippings feeds the lawn
decoys: Cut grass breaks down on the ground
The clippings return goodness to the soil

payload.passage: Choosing a wooden toy over a plastic one is a small green choice. Wood comes from trees that can be grown again, while plastic is made from fuel dug from the earth. A sturdy wooden toy lasts for years and can be passed on to others. When it is finally worn out, wood rots away harmlessly. Plastic, by contrast, lingers in dumps for ages, so wood is the gentler pick.
payload.title: Why a wooden toy is gentler on the earth than plastic
decoys: Wood comes from trees that regrow
Toys are made of many materials

payload.passage: Meerkats are too small to fight a snake or eagle, so the whole group survives by teamwork and trust. While most dig for insects and scorpions, at least one always stands sentry on a high mound, watching the sky and the bushes. The sentry calls out softly to show all is well, so the others can dig in peace. A sharp alarm bark sends everyone bolting for the burrows in a heartbeat. Even the babies are minded by group members in turns. By sharing every duty, the small meerkats keep their whole family safe.
payload.title: How meerkats keep their family safe through teamwork
decoys: A meerkat sentry watches from a mound
Meerkats dig for insects and scorpions
Babies are minded by the group

payload.passage: Touch a screen on a tablet and it answers your finger right away. Beneath the glass lies a thin grid that carries a tiny electric charge. Your finger gently changes the charge at the exact spot you touch. The device works out where the change happened and acts on it. This is how a touchscreen lets you draw, type and play without any buttons at all.
payload.title: How a touchscreen senses your finger
decoys: A thin grid under the glass carries a charge
Modern gadgets can do amazing things
A touchscreen lets you type without buttons

payload.passage: Imagine a world where the only light after dark came from candles and oil lamps. That was life before the electric bulb was invented. Inside the new bulb, a thin thread glowed brightly when an electric current passed through it. This steady, safe light did not flicker or smoke like a flame. People could now read, work and play long after sunset, and whole cities began to shine at night.
payload.title: How the electric bulb lit up the night
decoys: A thin thread glows when current passes through it
Electricity changed many things in modern life
People once used candles and oil lamps after dark

payload.passage: Even on the darkest night, our eyes catch just a sliver of all that is out there. The stars we see are only the nearest and brightest. Far more lie beyond, too distant and faint for the eye to notice. Their light may be too weak, or may not yet have reached us across the vast gulf. The sprinkle of stars overhead is but a tiny window onto a far greater universe; so even the richest starry sky reminds us how vast and mostly hidden the universe beyond truly is.
payload.title: Why we see only part of the universe at night
decoys: The stars we see are the nearest and brightest
There is always more out there to discover
Faint, distant light is too weak for the eye

payload.passage: The aardvark sleeps away the hot African day and comes out only after dark to feed, and its whole body is built for one task: raiding ant and termite nests. With powerful claws it tears open rock-hard mounds that would defeat most animals. Then it pokes in its long, sticky tongue, as long as your arm, and licks up thousands of insects. Its tough skin shrugs off the bites of angry soldiers, and it can close its nostrils against the dust. Every feature helps the aardvark feast on insects safely through the night.
payload.title: How the aardvark is built to raid insect nests
decoys: The aardvark tears open mounds with its claws
Some animals feed only at night
Its long tongue licks up insects

payload.passage: A plant cannot live on sunlight alone, nor on water alone; it needs both together. Sunlight gives the energy that powers the making of food in the leaves. Water, drawn up by the roots, is one of the raw materials joined together in that food. Without light, the leaves cannot do their work and the plant fades. Without water, there is nothing to build the food from. The two must come together for a plant to feed itself and grow; so a healthy plant is one that has the light and the water it needs in good measure.
payload.title: Why a green plant needs both sunlight and water
decoys: Water is a raw material used in making food
Living things need several things to survive
Without light the leaves cannot do their work

payload.passage: The desert fennec fox is one of the smallest foxes, yet it thrives where the sun is merciless. Its most striking feature is a pair of huge, cup-shaped ears far larger than its little head. These ears do more than hear faint prey beneath the sand; they release heat from the fox's body, helping it stay cool in the burning desert. By day the fox sleeps in a deep, cool burrow, hunting only in the chill of night. Pale fur reflects the sunlight and hides it on the sand. Every feature works to help this tiny fox beat the desert heat.
payload.title: How the fennec fox's huge ears beat desert heat
decoys: The fennec fox has very large ears
Deserts are scorchingly hot by day
It hunts in the cool of the night

payload.passage: Nidhi noticed that her friend Sara always copied her drawings and passed them off as her own. It made Nidhi quietly angry. Rather than shame Sara before the class, she invited her to draw together and patiently taught her to make her own pictures. Slowly Sara found her own style and stopped copying. Their friendship grew stronger than before. The teacher never even knew there had once been a problem between them. Nidhi learnt that helping someone outgrow a fault is kinder and wiser than exposing them for it.
payload.title: Helping someone outgrow a fault beats exposing it
decoys: Nidhi taught Sara to draw her own pictures
Sara found her own style at last

payload.passage: Sometimes a bright full moon slowly darkens and dims, even on a clear night. This is a lunar eclipse, caused by the Earth itself. When the Earth passes directly between the sun and the moon, it casts a long shadow into space. That shadow falls across the face of the moon, cutting off its sunlight. The moon dims and often glows a dusky red within the shadow. Once the moon moves out of it, the full brightness returns; so a lunar eclipse is simply the moon passing quietly through the long shadow of our planet.
payload.title: How the Earth's shadow falls upon the moon
decoys: The Earth passes between the sun and the moon
The night sky offers rare events
The moon often glows a dusky red in the shadow

payload.passage: Why does a doctor check your pulse at the wrist? With each beat, your heart pushes a wave of blood through the tubes called arteries. Near the wrist an artery runs close under the skin. There you can feel that wave as a gentle throb, the pulse. By counting these throbs, a doctor learns how fast and steadily your heart is beating.
payload.title: Why the pulse shows how the heart beats
decoys: An artery runs close under the skin at the wrist
Doctors check the body in many ways
Each heartbeat pushes a wave of blood

payload.passage: It may seem cruel that hawks hunt mice, yet this hunting keeps nature steady. Without hawks and foxes, mice would multiply far too fast. Soon there would be too many mice for the seeds and plants to feed. Many would then starve, and the plants would be stripped bare. By catching some prey, the hunters keep the numbers in check so that food lasts for all; so predators are not simply cruel, but play a quiet and vital part in keeping the whole web of life healthy and steady.
payload.title: How predators keep prey numbers in balance
decoys: Hawks and foxes hunt mice in the field
Nature keeps itself in a careful balance
Too many mice would strip the plants bare
