At full moon the Earth sits between the sun and the moon, so the two are on opposite sides of us. As the sun drops below one horizon, the fully lit moon lifts above the other. They trade places in the sky like the two ends of a seesaw; so a full moon climbing as the sun goes down is a sure sign that the Earth sits squarely between the two.
payload.title: Why the full moon rises as the sun sets
decoys: At full moon the Earth sits between sun and moon
The sky follows neat and steady patterns
Sun and moon trade places like ends of a seesaw

payload.passage: Sania promised to walk her elderly neighbour's old dog every evening while he was unwell. After a few days the dog seemed slow and dull, and walking it felt like a chore. Her friends invited her to a film on one such evening. Sania almost skipped the walk, then pictured the sick neighbour counting on her. She took the dog out as always and went to the film another day. Sania learnt that a duty you have taken on does not stop mattering just because it has become dull.
payload.title: A duty still matters even when it turns dull
decoys: Sania walked the neighbour's dog every evening
Old dogs can be slow on walks
Her friends invited her to a film

payload.passage: Why does your body have a sense of touch all over the skin? Your skin is dotted with countless tiny sensors. Some sense a light brush, while others feel pressure, heat or pain. The moment any of them is triggered, a signal races to the brain. This is how a hot stove or a sharp pin warns you to pull away before you are harmed.
payload.title: How the sense of touch protects the body
decoys: Some sensors feel heat and others feel pain
The body has many useful senses
A signal races to the brain when touched

payload.passage: Cleaning floors was once a long battle with a broom and dustpan. The vacuum cleaner made it quick and easy. A fan inside sucks air in through a nozzle at great speed. The rushing air drags dust and grit along with it into the machine. A bag or filter traps the dirt while the clean air slips back out. A whole room can be cleaned in minutes.
payload.title: How a vacuum cleaner sucks up dust
decoys: Rushing air drags dust into the machine
A bag or filter traps the dirt

payload.passage: Why does your body shiver and your skin tingle when you are very tired and cold? When tiredness and cold come together, the body struggles to keep itself warm. It shivers to make heat from trembling muscles. It also pulls warm blood inward, which can make the skin feel tingly and odd. These actions are the body fighting hard to hold its warmth.
payload.title: Why cold and tiredness make us shiver and tingle
decoys: Trembling muscles make heat when shivering
The body fights to stay warm
Pulling blood inward makes the skin tingle

payload.passage: For countless ages, lost travellers have looked to one steady star for help. The Pole Star sits almost directly above the Earth's northern axis. Because of this, it hardly seems to move as the rest of the sky wheels around it. By finding the Pole Star, a person can tell which way is north on any clear night. Sailors crossing dark seas relied on it long before the compass. A single faithful star has guided people safely for generations; so even today, knowing this one star can keep a wanderer from losing their way at night.
payload.title: How the same star can guide travellers north
decoys: The Pole Star sits above the northern axis
The night sky has many uses for people
Sailors used the star before the compass existed

payload.passage: Pari ran a tiny stall selling cold drinks and noticed that on rainy days she sold almost nothing. Rather than sit idle, she watched what people wanted when it rained and began offering hot tea instead. Her stall stayed busy in every weather. The trick was not stubbornly selling one thing but reading what customers needed that day. Pari learnt that a small business survives by bending to its customers' changing wants, and that a seller who only offers one fixed thing will struggle the moment the weather or mood shifts.
payload.title: Why a stall must match changing customer wants
decoys: She offered hot tea on rainy days
Cold drinks sold poorly in the rain

payload.passage: Why does a vaccine sometimes leave your arm a little sore? After the injection, your body gets straight to work learning to fight the germ. It sends defending cells rushing to the spot where the vaccine went in. This busy gathering causes a small swelling and tenderness for a day or two. The mild soreness is actually a sign your body is building its protection.
payload.title: Why a vaccine can leave the arm briefly sore
decoys: Defending cells rush to the injection spot
Soreness shows the body is building defence

payload.passage: Anita found her examination questions a day early, left carelessly on the staffroom table. The temptation to peek and prepare burned in her for a moment. But she imagined how hollow a top score would feel if she had not truly earned it. She handed the papers to the principal without reading a single line. She scored a little lower than she might have, yet she walked tall through the corridor afterwards. Anita learnt that a score you have honestly earned is worth far more than one you have quietly stolen.
payload.title: An earned score beats a stolen one
decoys: Anita found the exam questions a day early
Exam papers are sometimes left lying around
Peeking at questions is against the rules

payload.passage: A simple shift to a cloth handkerchief saves more than it seems. Paper tissues are used once and tossed, and making them takes trees, water and energy. A cloth handkerchief tucked in a pocket can be washed and used for years. Over a lifetime, this swap spares many trees and bins of waste. Choosing cloth over paper is an easy, daily way to tread lightly on the earth.
payload.title: Why a cloth handkerchief is kinder to nature
decoys: A cloth handkerchief can be used for years

payload.passage: A pair of spectacles can rescue blurry sight in an instant. Some eyes bend light too much or too little, so the picture lands in the wrong spot inside the eye. A carefully shaped glass lens bends the light first, before it reaches the eye. This extra bending moves the picture to exactly the right place. With spectacles, millions of people who once saw a blur can read and work clearly.
payload.title: How spectacles bring blurry sight into focus
decoys: A glass lens bends light before it enters the eye
Inventions can fix the body's small faults
Some eyes bend light too much or too little

payload.passage: A bucket placed under the cold tap while the water warms up saves more than you think. We often let clean water run away while waiting for it to turn hot. A bucket catches that first cold water instead of letting it vanish down the drain. The saved water can wash a floor or feed a plant. This tiny habit rescues litres of water every single day.
payload.title: How catching cold water while it warms saves litres
decoys: We let water run while it warms
Caught water can feed a plant

payload.passage: The stars do not switch off when the sun comes up; they shine all day long. Yet we cannot see them, because the daytime sky is far too bright. Sunlight scattering through the air fills the whole sky with a brilliant glow. This glow drowns out the faint light of the distant stars. Only when the sun sets and the sky darkens can the stars finally show through again; so the stars never truly leave us, but simply wait, hidden in the daylight, for the sky to darken once more.
payload.title: Why we never see stars during the daytime
decoys: Scattered sunlight fills the sky with a glow
The sky changes from day to night
The bright daytime sky drowns out faint starlight

payload.passage: A simple wooden cart pulled by oxen carried goods for centuries. Two strong wheels turn freely on a fixed bar beneath the cart. A pair of oxen are yoked to the front to pull it along. Because the wheels roll instead of dragging, a heavy load moves with far less effort. Villages traded grain, wood and water using these sturdy carts.
payload.title: How an ox-cart carried heavy loads for villages
decoys: Two wheels turn freely on a fixed bar
Rolling wheels move a load with less effort

payload.passage: Kabir was amazed that a single misplaced digit in a postal code could send his letter to a town hundreds of miles from its real destination. The clerk explained that sorting machines read those digits exactly and never guess; one wrong number meant one wrong city. A letter meant for the hills could end up at the coast simply because of a slipped pen. Kabir double-checked every code after that. He learnt that in a vast system handling millions of items, one tiny human error can carry a surprisingly large cost.
payload.title: How one wrong digit misdirects a letter
decoys: Sorting machines read the digits exactly
Small mistakes can have big effects
A letter could reach the wrong city

payload.passage: Why do your muscles feel weak and shaky after a very long run? Muscles use a stored fuel to keep working hard. On a long run, they slowly burn through this store of fuel. When it runs low, the muscles can no longer push as they did and begin to shake. Rest and food then refill the store and bring back their strength.
payload.title: Why muscles grow shaky after a long run
decoys: Muscles burn through a stored fuel
Rest and food refill the muscles

payload.passage: On some cool mornings the world seems wrapped in soft grey mist. This fog is really a cloud, except it has formed close to the ground instead of high in the sky. It appears when moist air cools enough for its vapour to turn into tiny floating droplets. Because the droplets hang in the air around us, they scatter the light and make things look hazy. As the sun warms the air, the droplets evaporate and the fog lifts away; understanding this shows that a cloud high in the sky and the fog at your feet are really the very same thing.
payload.title: How fog is simply a cloud at ground level
decoys: Fog droplets scatter light and make things hazy
Mornings can look very different from one day to the next
Fog forms when cool air meets the warm ground

payload.passage: Pumping water from a deep well by hand was once back-breaking work. The water pump made it far simpler. By moving a handle up and down, you create a low-pressure space inside the pump. The heavier outside air then pushes water up the pipe to fill it. With each stroke, fresh water rises and pours out of the spout. Whole villages drew their daily water this way.
payload.title: How a hand pump lifts water from a deep well
decoys: Moving the handle creates a low-pressure space
Villages drew their water from hand pumps

payload.passage: When the teacher stepped out, the class began copying answers from the textbook for the surprise test. Manish felt the pull to join in, since everyone else was doing it. He thought of how meaningless his marks would be that way. He closed the book and answered only what he truly knew. His score was lower than the cheats', but when the teacher discovered the copying, only Manish was praised. He learnt that standing alone for honesty can leave you the only one with nothing to hide.
payload.title: Standing alone for honesty leaves nothing to hide
decoys: Manish answered only what he knew
The cheats scored higher at first

payload.passage: The long queue at the bank counter shrank almost overnight when the branch installed a cash machine outside. Now people could draw money at midnight or on a holiday, without waiting for the doors to open. The machine reads a plastic card and a secret number known only to the owner, so a stranger cannot simply take cash. Yet the manager still warned customers never to share that number, not even with a friend. The convenience was real, but it leaned entirely on each person guarding one small private code.
payload.title: A cash machine trades on a guarded secret code
decoys: The new machine shortened the long counter queue
Technology keeps making everyday tasks easier
People can now withdraw cash on holidays

payload.passage: When floods struck a faraway district, Reyansh's town launched a relief collection in the market square. A simple sealed box stood by the temple, and every shopper, rich or poor, dropped in what they could spare. Coins from children mixed with notes from merchants, and together the pile grew surprisingly large. The whole sum was sent to buy food and blankets for the flood victims. Reyansh saw that no single giver could have done much alone, yet many small gifts, gathered together, became real and powerful help.
payload.title: How many small gifts become powerful relief
decoys: A sealed box stood by the temple
Children's coins mixed with merchants' notes

payload.passage: A simple solar lamp can light up a home far from any wires. By day a small panel drinks in the free sunlight and stores it in a battery. When night falls, that stored energy powers a steady, clean light. Children can study and families can sit together without a smoky kerosene flame. The sun, caught by day, brightens the home by night at no cost to the air.
payload.title: How a solar lamp brings clean light after dark
decoys: A panel drinks in the free sunlight
Light helps families in the evening
Children can study by the lamp

payload.passage: Riya was surprised that the spice seller in the corner of the market never seemed to lower his prices, even when business was slow. Her mother explained that his spices were rare and of a special quality no other stall could match. Customers who wanted exactly that fragrance had nowhere else to go, so he could hold his price firm. A common vegetable seller, surrounded by rivals, had no such freedom. Riya learnt that when a seller offers something truly hard to find, the bargaining power quietly shifts into his hands.
payload.title: Why a rare product gives a seller power
decoys: The spice seller's goods were special
Markets contain many kinds of sellers
A vegetable seller faced many rivals

payload.passage: A simple thermos for a school lunch keeps a meal warm till noon. Like a vacuum flask, it slows down the loss of heat. The food sits inside a sealed container packed in a layer that heat struggles to cross. With heat unable to escape quickly, the meal stays warm for hours. A hot lunch carried from home is a small invention that many children enjoy.
payload.title: How a lunch thermos keeps a meal warm till noon
decoys: Food sits inside a sealed container
A layer slows the loss of heat

payload.passage: Priya had promised to feed the neighbour's parrot every day while the family was away for a week. By the third afternoon she was tired of the long, dusty walk in the summer heat and almost stayed home to rest. Then she remembered the trust shining in the neighbour's eyes when they had handed her the key. She set off down the baking road anyway, refilled the seed cup, and changed the stale water for fresh. The family returned to find a healthy, chirping bird waiting for them. Priya learnt that a promise kept quietly, with no one watching, is worth far more than one made loudly in front of others.
payload.title: Keeping a promise matters most when it is hard
decoys: Priya fed the neighbour's parrot for a week
Parrots need fresh seed and clean water daily
Walking in summer heat can be very tiring

payload.passage: A seedling sheltered from all wind often grows weak and floppy. A little breeze, though, helps it grow strong. As the wind gently rocks the young stem, the plant responds by thickening and toughening it. Over time the stem lays down firm fibres that let it stand tall. The same plant grown in still air may struggle to hold itself up. A bit of wind is not a threat but a training that makes a plant sturdy; so a little wind is not a danger but a kind of training that toughens a young plant.
payload.title: How a young plant grows sturdy in the breeze
decoys: The wind gently rocks the young stem
Living things respond to their surroundings
The stem lays down firm fibres to stand tall

payload.passage: Reshma found a phone left behind on the park bench, its screen glowing with messages from a worried owner. She could have kept the shiny phone, far better than her own. Instead she answered the next call and arranged to return it to the anxious owner. The grateful man offered her a reward, which she politely refused. She walked home glad, needing nothing more than the knowledge of doing right. Reshma learnt that doing the right thing should not depend on whether you are paid for it, and that honesty asks for no reward.
payload.title: Honesty asks for no reward to do right
decoys: Reshma returned a phone left on a bench
Lost phones keep ringing with calls

payload.passage: A handful of native wildflowers sown in an empty patch can do a lot of good. The bright blooms draw in bees, butterflies and other helpful insects. These insects feed on the flowers and carry their dust from bloom to bloom. The flowers also feed birds with their seeds when autumn comes. A small wild patch becomes a lively little home for many creatures.
payload.title: How a wildflower patch supports many creatures
decoys: Wildflowers draw in bees and butterflies
Flowers add colour to a place
The seeds of flowers feed the birds

payload.passage: From sunrise to sunset, the sun seems to glide slowly overhead. Yet the sun is nearly still; it is the Earth that turns. As our planet spins eastward, the sun comes into view in the morning and climbs higher. By midday it stands highest, then sinks toward evening as your side keeps turning. The whole graceful arc is really a sign of the Earth rotating beneath the sky; once we understand this, the daily arc of the sun becomes a simple, beautiful reminder that our world is turning.
payload.title: Why the sun appears to move across the sky
decoys: The sun climbs highest around the middle of the day
Appearances can hide what is truly happening
The Earth spins eastward beneath the steady sun

payload.passage: Salmon returning to spawn must climb rivers against fierce currents, and they survive the ordeal through sheer persistence. Driven by an urge to reach their birthplace, they push upstream for days without resting much. At every waterfall they hurl themselves into the air again and again, often falling back, until at last they clear the top. Bruised and exhausted, they keep on. Most never give up until they reach the very gravel where they were born. By refusing to turn back, the salmon complete the hardest journey of their lives.
payload.title: How salmon climb rivers through sheer persistence
decoys: Salmon leap waterfalls again and again

payload.passage: Geese, ducks and swans all keep their feathers waterproof through a careful daily habit. Near the base of the tail sits a small gland that makes an oily wax. Each day the bird squeezes a little of this oil onto its beak and then carefully spreads it over every feather, a task called preening. The thin coat of oil makes the feathers shed water like a raincoat, so the bird stays dry and warm even after diving. Without this grooming the feathers would soak through and the bird could chill. Careful preening keeps water birds afloat and warm.
payload.title: How water birds keep their feathers waterproof
decoys: Birds spread oil over their feathers
Many birds live on and around water
A gland near the tail makes the oil

payload.passage: Drifting near the sea's surface are plants so small they cannot be seen one by one. Yet together these tiny plants do enormous work. They soak up sunlight and make food, forming the base of nearly every ocean food chain. They also release a large share of the oxygen we breathe. So these unseen specks feed the fish, the whales and even help keep our air fresh on land; because they are so important, scientists watch these tiny ocean plants closely as a sign of the sea's overall health.
payload.title: Why the ocean's tiny plants matter so much
decoys: Tiny sea plants form the base of ocean food chains
The ocean is vital to life on Earth
These specks release much of the oxygen we breathe

payload.passage: Why does a cut heal faster when you keep it clean and covered? An open wound is a doorway through which germs can enter the body. Cleaning the cut removes germs already on the skin around it. Covering it then keeps fresh dirt and germs from getting in. With the germs kept out, the body can quietly knit the wound back together.
payload.title: Why a clean, covered cut heals faster
decoys: An open wound lets germs enter the body
Covering a cut keeps fresh dirt out

payload.passage: It may not rain for weeks, yet many rivers keep running clear and steady. The secret lies underground, where rain that fell long ago has soaked into the soil and rock. This hidden water seeps out slowly into streams and springs, feeding the river bit by bit. High mountains add their share as snow melts gently through the warm months. So a river is fed not only by today's rain but by water stored quietly out of sight; this hidden, slow-release supply is why a healthy river can run clear for months even under a cloudless sky.
payload.title: Why rivers keep flowing long after the rain stops
decoys: Melting mountain snow adds water through warm months
Nature always finds clever ways to store things
Underground water seeps slowly into nearby streams

payload.passage: Why is too little sleep bad for how you think and feel? Sleep is the time when your brain rests and sorts the day's events. When you miss sleep, your brain cannot do this work well. You find it hard to focus, remember things or stay in a good mood. After several short nights, even simple tasks feel difficult and tiring.
payload.title: Why too little sleep dulls the mind
decoys: Sleep lets the brain sort the day's events
Rest is important for the body
Missing sleep makes it hard to focus

payload.passage: Why should you not stare too long at near things like books and screens? Looking at something close makes the muscles in your eyes work hard to keep it sharp. Holding this for hours leaves those muscles tired and your eyes aching. Looking far away every little while lets the eye muscles rest. This simple habit keeps your eyes comfortable and healthy.
payload.title: Why resting the eyes from close work matters
decoys: Eye muscles work hard to keep near things sharp
Good habits care for the body
Looking far away rests the eye muscles

payload.passage: The same sun shines all day, yet noon feels far hotter than morning. The reason lies in the angle of its light. At midday the sun is high overhead, and its rays strike the ground almost straight down, packed into a small space. In the early morning the sun is low, and its slanted rays spread thin over a wider area. Concentrated light heats the ground more, which is why midday is the warmest time; so the heat you feel at noon is less about how far away the sun is and more about the angle of its rays.
payload.title: Why the sun feels stronger at midday
decoys: Slanted morning rays spread over a wider area
The weather changes throughout a single day
At midday the sun sits high overhead

payload.passage: Why does your body shed and grow new skin all the time without you noticing? The outer layer of your skin takes a lot of wear every day. Tiny flakes of dead skin rub away constantly as you move and wash. Underneath, fresh new skin is always being made to replace them. In this quiet way, your body keeps a clean, strong covering throughout your life.
payload.title: Why the body constantly renews its skin
decoys: Dead skin flakes rub away as you move
Fresh new skin replaces the old

payload.passage: Why does the body warm up slowly when you begin to exercise? Cold, stiff muscles can pull or tear if you push them suddenly. A gentle warm-up sends more blood into them and loosens them up. Warm, loose muscles move more freely and are far less likely to get hurt. This is why a few easy movements before hard exercise protect the body.
payload.title: Why warming up protects the muscles
decoys: A warm-up sends more blood into the muscles
Exercise should be done with care
Cold muscles can pull or tear

payload.passage: The whole class was told to clean the room before the holiday, but most children rushed out the moment the bell rang. Only Gaurav noticed the dustbins overflowing and the board still unwiped. He could easily have left with the others, since no teacher was watching. Instead he stayed back alone and tidied the entire room. He left late but with a quiet, satisfied feeling. Gaurav learnt that responsibility means finishing the job even when nobody is there to praise or check you.
payload.title: Responsibility finishes the job unwatched
decoys: Gaurav cleaned the classroom by himself
Children rush out when the bell rings
Dustbins overflow when no one empties them

payload.passage: The octopus has no shell and no sharp teeth, yet it is one of the ocean's great escape artists. Its soft, boneless body can squeeze through a gap no wider than its own eye. When a predator draws near, the octopus can change its skin colour and texture in an instant to match the rocks or sand. If that fails, it shoots out a cloud of dark ink and jets away while the hunter is blinded. It may even tuck itself into an empty shell for a door. By trickery rather than force, the clever octopus stays alive.
payload.title: How the octopus escapes danger using cleverness
decoys: An octopus squirts ink to escape hunters
Sea creatures must avoid many predators
It can change its colour to match rocks

payload.passage: Bhavya was surprised that her school council held an election every single year instead of letting one good leader stay forever. Her teacher explained that regular elections gave fresh students a chance to lead and stopped any one person from growing too comfortable with power. A leader who knew they faced the voters again stayed careful and worked hard. Bhavya saw that the yearly contest kept everyone honest and gave new voices a turn. She learnt that changing leaders at fixed times is itself a guard against power going stale.
payload.title: Why regular elections refresh leadership
decoys: The council held an election each year
A leader facing voters stays careful

payload.passage: The desert tortoise lives where rain may not fall for a whole year, so it has become a master at saving water. When the rare rains come, it digs shallow basins in the soil and drinks deeply, storing a large amount of water inside its body. Its bladder works almost like a water tank, holding the supply for the dry months ahead. It spends the hottest part of the year resting in a cool burrow, doing little and using little. By drinking big when it rains and saving every drop, the tortoise outlasts the long drought.
payload.title: How the desert tortoise stores water for dry months
decoys: The tortoise stores water inside its body
Deserts can go a year without rain
It rests in a cool burrow in heat

payload.passage: Why does the body need strong muscles around the middle? The muscles around your stomach and back hold your body upright. They support your spine and keep you steady as you sit, stand and lift. Weak middle muscles let the back slump and ache. Keeping these muscles strong through play and exercise protects your back for years.
payload.title: Why strong middle muscles protect the back
decoys: Weak middle muscles let the back slump

payload.passage: A heap of vegetable peels and dry leaves can become black gold for a garden. When these scraps are piled together in a corner, tiny living things begin to break them down. Over a few weeks the pile rots into a dark, crumbly soil called compost. This compost is full of food that plants love. By composting, we turn waste into healthy soil instead of dumping it away.
payload.title: How composting turns kitchen waste into rich soil
decoys: Vegetable peels can be piled in a corner
Gardens need a lot of care
Compost is full of food that plants love

payload.passage: Old Mr Sharma's cat went missing, and he searched the lane for days with worried eyes. The local boys found the game of looking for it boring and soon stopped. Only Tina kept checking gardens and rooftops every evening after her homework. After a week she found the cat trapped on a high terrace and brought it home. Mr Sharma wept with relief. Tina learnt that sticking with a kind task long after others have given up is what truly helps someone in need.
payload.title: Kindness means sticking with it after others quit
decoys: Tina kept searching for the missing cat
Cats sometimes get trapped on terraces
Mr Sharma searched the lane for days

payload.passage: Kavya's friend confided a secret worry and begged her not to tell anyone. Later, a group of girls pressed Kavya to share some juicy news, and the secret would have made her popular for a day. She felt the pull of all those eager faces. But she kept her friend's secret locked away and changed the subject. Her friend never even knew it was tested. Kavya learnt that keeping a trust no one is watching you keep is the deepest kind of loyalty.
payload.title: Keeping a trust unwatched is the deepest loyalty
decoys: Kavya kept her friend's secret safe

payload.passage: Why does drinking water before a meal help your body? Water helps your stomach break food down and move it along smoothly. A drink before eating also takes the sharp edge off a fierce hunger. With the worst of your hunger eased, you eat at a calmer, slower pace. This simple habit aids digestion and keeps you from overeating.
payload.title: Why drinking water before a meal helps the body
decoys: Water helps the stomach break food down
A drink eases a fierce hunger

payload.passage: Krish proudly counted a thick wad of notes from his snack stall and called it all profit. His accountant aunt smiled and asked about the cost of the flour, oil and gas he had used. Once those were subtracted, the real profit was far smaller than the cash in his hand. The big pile, she explained, was income, not earnings; much of it merely replaced what he had spent. Krish learnt that true profit is what remains only after every cost has been honestly taken away.
payload.title: Why true profit is what remains after costs
decoys: Krish counted a thick wad of notes
Numbers can be confusing at first
He had spent money on flour and oil

payload.passage: A marshy wetland is one of nature's busiest dining halls. Reeds and water plants soak up sunlight and grow thick along the edges. Snails and insects feed on these plants, and small fish feed on the insects. Frogs and larger fish then hunt the smaller ones in the shallow water. Wading birds step in to catch fish and frogs alike. From the green reeds to the long-legged birds, the whole wetland is joined in one rich food chain; this is why a healthy wetland can support such a remarkable crowd of living things.
payload.title: How a wetland feeds a chain of creatures
decoys: Snails and insects feed on the water plants
Watery places are full of life
Wading birds catch fish and frogs in the shallows

payload.passage: A snake feels the warmth of a hidden mouse even in the dark. Some snakes have tiny pits between their eyes and nostrils. These pits can sense the heat that warm animals give off. By reading this heat, the snake can picture where its prey is hiding. So even on the blackest night, a hungry snake can hunt with great skill.
payload.title: How a snake senses warm prey in the dark
decoys: A snake has tiny pits between its eyes
Animals can do many incredible things
Snakes are skilful hunters at night

payload.passage: During a quiz, Nidhi knew the answer to a question her own team had missed, but it was the rival team's turn. The quizmaster looked her way, and a sly nod could have passed the answer to her team out of turn. She kept silent and let the rival team try fairly. Her team lost by one point in the end. Yet Nidhi felt clean and light inside. She learnt that following the rules even when breaking them is easy is what fairness truly means.
payload.title: Fairness follows the rules when breaking them is easy
decoys: Nidhi stayed silent during the rival team's turn
Quizmasters ask teams questions in turn
Her team lost the quiz by one point

payload.passage: Why does your heart sit safely behind a cage of curved bones? The heart is a soft, vital pump the body cannot do without. Around it the ribs form a strong, curved cage. These bones shield the heart and lungs from knocks and blows. The cage is also slightly springy, so it can move a little as you breathe in and out.
payload.title: How the rib cage shields the heart and lungs
decoys: The ribs form a strong, curved cage
The body guards its vital parts
The rib cage moves as you breathe

payload.passage: Why does your heart beat a little faster just before a race or exam? Your body senses the big moment coming and gets ready in advance. It quickens the heart so that blood and oxygen are ready to flow. This early boost prepares your muscles and brain for hard effort. A faster heartbeat before a challenge is your body helping you do your best.
payload.title: Why the heart speeds up before a challenge
decoys: The body quickens the heart in advance
The body prepares for important moments
The boost readies the muscles and brain

payload.passage: When the village clinic could not treat Saanvika's grandfather, the doctor sent him onward to the large city hospital. Her mother grumbled at first, but the doctor explained the idea of a referral. Small clinics handle everyday illnesses, while bigger hospitals keep the rare machines and specialist doctors for serious cases. Sending the hardest cases upward lets each level do what it does best. Saanvika understood that the health system was built like a ladder, with each rung passing the patient to where the right help truly waited.
payload.title: How a referral ladder guides serious cases
decoys: The clinic sent grandfather to the city hospital
Good health care is important for everyone
Big hospitals keep the specialist doctors

payload.passage: A simple mud stove can change the air inside a village home. The old open fire fills the kitchen with thick, choking smoke. Breathing this smoke harms the eyes and chest, day after day. A better mud stove guides the smoke out through a small chimney. It also burns less wood, so fewer trees are cut for fuel.
payload.title: How a better stove cleans the air and saves wood
decoys: An open fire fills the kitchen with smoke
A better stove burns less wood

payload.passage: A vaccine works by playing a clever trick on the body's defences. It carries a weak or dead piece of a germ that cannot make you ill. Your body sees this harmless piece and builds tiny soldiers ready to fight it. These soldiers stay on guard long after the vaccine is given. If the real germ ever arrives, the body knows it at once and beats it before you fall sick.
payload.title: How a vaccine teaches the body to fight germs
decoys: A vaccine carries a weak or dead germ piece
Doctors give children many useful injections
The body builds tiny soldiers against germs

payload.passage: A simple shade tree planted beside a house can lower the cooling bill. In summer its leafy branches block the harsh sun from the walls and windows. The rooms inside stay cooler, so fans and coolers work less. In winter, after the leaves drop, sunlight warms the house once more. A well-placed tree shades in summer and warms in winter, all on its own.
payload.title: How a shade tree cools a house in summer
decoys: Leafy branches block the summer sun
Cooler rooms make fans work less

payload.passage: Long ago a great cloud of gas and dust drifted in space. Its own gravity pulled it inward, and most of it gathered at the centre to form the sun. The leftover material swirled around in a flat disc. Within that disc, smaller lumps clumped together to become the planets and moons. The sun and all its circling worlds grew from one spinning cloud held by gravity; so the sun and every planet, moon and asteroid around it are all the children of one ancient, collapsing cloud.
payload.title: How the sun's gravity shaped the whole solar system
decoys: Most of the cloud gathered to form the sun
Gravity shapes the largest things in space
Leftover material swirled in a flat disc

payload.passage: Aryan always wondered why train tickets cost more for a cushioned coach than for a plain wooden one on the very same train. The ticket clerk explained that the higher class offered soft seats, more space and fewer people, comforts that cost the railway more to provide. Travellers who wanted those comforts paid for them, while others saved money in the simpler coach. The train carried everyone to the same place, but at the comfort each could afford. Aryan learnt that a price often buys not just a journey but the comfort along the way.
payload.title: Why a comfortable coach costs more to ride
decoys: The higher class had soft, spacious seats
Trains carry many kinds of travellers
Both coaches reached the same place

payload.passage: Faizan saw the class bully snatch a smaller boy's lunch and toss it in the bin while others laughed. Everyone was afraid to speak. Faizan's heart hammered, for the bully was bigger than him. Still, he stepped forward, told the bully it was wrong, and shared his own lunch with the hungry boy. The bully, caught out before all, backed down. The other children, who had only watched, looked down at their shoes in shame. Faizan learnt that one voice raised against unfairness can shame a crowd into silence and give the weak a defender.
payload.title: One voice against unfairness can shame a crowd
decoys: Faizan shared his lunch with a bullied boy
Bullies sometimes throw away others' food
The other children were afraid to speak

payload.passage: Reshma had nearly finished a tough year-long reading challenge, with one thick book left. Her friends had all quit months ago and teased her for still bothering. Tired and tempted to stop just short, she pictured how close the goal stood. She read a little every night until the last page turned. The pride she felt was quiet and deep. When the teacher read out her name as the only one to finish, she glowed quietly. Reshma learnt that finishing what you start, especially when others have given up, builds a strength that stays with you.
payload.title: Finishing what you start builds lasting strength
decoys: Reshma finished a year-long reading challenge
Reading challenges can take a year
Her friends had quit months ago

payload.passage: Sahil kept failing to fold a perfect paper crane, while his sister made them with ease and laughed at his crumpled attempts. He threw several into the bin in frustration and almost gave up the craft. But each evening he tried once more, smoothing each fold a little better. After a week he held up a neat, finished crane of his own. He set the little crane on his shelf, prouder of it than of anything else. Sahil learnt that a skill mastered through patient repetition feels far prouder than one that came to you easily.
payload.title: Skill won through patience feels the proudest
decoys: Sahil finally folded a neat paper crane
His sister laughed at his attempts

payload.passage: Have you ever wondered why a heavy ship made of steel does not sink? A solid block of steel would drop straight to the bottom, yet a ship floats easily. The trick is its hollow, bowl-like shape, which holds a lot of light air inside. Because the ship pushes aside more water than its own weight, the water pushes back and holds it up. This upward push is called buoyancy, and it keeps even huge ships afloat.
payload.title: Why heavy steel ships are able to float
decoys: A ship has a hollow shape that holds air
Steel is a strong metal used to build many things
Water can push up on objects placed in it

payload.passage: Why does a baby sleep far more hours than an older child? A baby's body and brain are growing at an astonishing speed. So much of this rapid growth happens during deep sleep. Sleeping also lets the new brain rest after taking in a flood of fresh sights and sounds. That is why a baby needs many more hours of sleep than a schoolchild does.
payload.title: Why a baby needs so many hours of sleep
decoys: Much rapid growth happens during deep sleep
A baby takes in a flood of sights and sounds

payload.passage: The electric eel of the murky river cannot see well in the cloudy water, yet it hunts with deadly ease. Hidden along its long body are thousands of special cells that work like tiny living batteries. To find a meal, it sends out weak pulses of electricity and feels how they bounce off nearby creatures. When prey is near, the eel unleashes a single powerful jolt that stuns the fish completely. Then it swallows the helpless, motionless meal at leisure. By making and sensing electricity, this strange fish both finds and catches food in the dark.
payload.title: How the electric eel hunts using living electricity
decoys: The electric eel stuns prey with a jolt
River water can be cloudy and dark
Its body holds thousands of battery cells

payload.passage: Veer asked why his town was split into small voting areas, each choosing its own representative, instead of everyone simply voting for one big leader. His teacher explained that a local representative knew the streets, the broken drains and the daily troubles of that very area. People could reach their own member easily with complaints. One distant leader could never know every corner. Veer learnt that dividing a place into wards meant each neighbourhood got a voice that truly understood its own particular needs.
payload.title: Why dividing into wards gives local voice
decoys: A local member knew the area's troubles
The town was split into voting areas

payload.passage: High in the cold mountains, the snow leopard is almost impossible to spot, and that is exactly the point. Its pale grey coat, dappled with dark rosettes, melts perfectly into the rocky, snowy slopes. A huge bushy tail helps it balance on narrow ledges and wraps around its body like a scarf in icy winds. Wide, furry paws spread its weight so it can pad silently over deep snow. Creeping unseen, it stalks wild sheep among the boulders before a sudden leap. Every feature helps this ghost of the mountains hunt and survive in a harsh, thin-aired world.
payload.title: How the snow leopard is built for mountain hunting
decoys: The snow leopard has a long, bushy tail
Some big cats live high in the mountains
Its spotted coat blends with rocky slopes

payload.passage: When the dry season parches the land, the African bullfrog faces months with no pond to live in. Rather than die, it digs down into the softening mud before the water vanishes. There it sheds layers of skin that harden into a tough cocoon around its body, sealing in moisture. Wrapped in this case and barely breathing, the frog sleeps deep underground through the long drought. When the rains return and soak the earth, the frog wakes, splits its cocoon and digs up to the new pools. By sleeping out the dry months, it survives where the water failed.
payload.title: How the bullfrog sleeps through the dry season
decoys: The bullfrog wraps itself in a skin cocoon
Ponds dry up in the dry season

payload.passage: Kabir was about to buy the cheapest pair of shoes he could find when his older sister stopped him. Those flimsy shoes, she warned, would tear within a month, forcing him to buy again and again. A sturdier pair cost more today but would last for years, working out cheaper in the end. Kabir thought about the long run and chose the better shoes. He learnt that the lowest price is not always the best deal; sometimes spending a little more saves a great deal over time.
payload.title: Why the cheapest choice is not always cheapest
decoys: The flimsy shoes would tear within a month
The sturdier pair cost more at first

payload.passage: Your stomach does a busy job every time you eat a meal. As you swallow, the chewed food slides down into the stomach below. There the stomach churns the food and mixes it with strong juices. These juices break the food into a soft, soupy mush. The mush then passes on so the body can take in the goodness and throw away the rest.
payload.title: How the stomach breaks down the food we eat
decoys: Strong juices mix with food in the stomach
Eating good food keeps the body strong
Food slides down into the stomach after we swallow

payload.passage: On a long train journey, Aarav's family had finally booked the window seat he had been dreaming about for weeks. A tired old man leaning on a cane boarded at a small station and could find no place at all to sit. Aarav glanced longingly at the green fields rushing past the glass, the very view he had so wanted to watch. Then he quietly stood up and gave the old man his seat. He stood swaying in the aisle for hours, yet the man's grateful smile stayed with him far longer than any passing scenery would have. Aarav saw that comfort given away can warm you more than comfort kept.
payload.title: Comfort given away warms more than comfort kept
decoys: Aarav gave his window seat to an old man
Train journeys can last for many hours
Elderly passengers sometimes cannot find a seat

payload.passage: On clear northern nights, a famous group of stars shaped like a ladle stands out. People call it the Big Dipper, and it is a handy signpost. The two stars at the front of its bowl point almost straight at the Pole Star. By following that imaginary line, a stargazer can find north at once. For ages this trick has guided travellers when no compass was at hand; learning this single trick lets anyone find north on a clear night without a map, a compass or any tool at all.
payload.title: How the Big Dipper helps people find the Pole Star
decoys: Two stars in the bowl point toward the Pole Star
The night sky can guide those who study it
The Big Dipper is shaped like a ladle

payload.passage: A field that is shaded by tall trees can still grow good crops below. This old way of farming mixes trees and crops in the same land. The trees give shade, drop leaves that feed the soil, and shelter the crops from harsh wind. Their roots reach deep and bring up water and goodness. Growing trees and crops together lets one piece of land give far more.
payload.title: How mixing trees with crops enriches the land
decoys: Trees drop leaves that feed the soil
Tree roots bring up water from deep

payload.passage: Rishi found the long division homework dull and wanted to copy his neighbour's answers to finish faster. His pencil hovered over the neat sums beside him. Then he remembered that copying would leave him just as lost tomorrow. He set to work alone, slowly, getting some wrong and trying again. By the end he could actually do the sums himself. The next day's surprise test felt easy because he truly knew the method. Rishi learnt that the easy shortcut of copying teaches you nothing, while honest struggle quietly builds real understanding.
payload.title: Honest effort teaches what copying never can
decoys: Rishi did his long division homework alone
Long division can be dull and slow
Copying a neighbour's answers is tempting

payload.passage: Sara was nervous when her train was delayed and she might miss her connecting one. A kind official showed her the enquiry counter, where a worker traced both trains on a screen and assured her the second would be held a few minutes. The whole railway, he said, was stitched together so that a late train need not strand its passengers. Sara reached her connection with relief. She learnt that behind every journey lay a web of careful coordination, quietly working to keep travellers from being left behind by a single delay.
payload.title: How the railway protects a missed connection
decoys: The worker traced both trains on a screen
Travel can be stressful at times
The second train was held a few minutes

payload.passage: Priyanka was the best painter in class and expected to be picked to decorate the stage alone. The teacher instead asked her to lead a team of weaker painters. She felt it would only slow her down. Yet she patiently taught each one a simple part, and together they made the grandest backdrop the school had ever seen. The whole team glowed with pride. Priyanka learnt that lifting others to share in a task can create something greater than working alone ever could.
payload.title: Lifting others creates more than working alone
decoys: Priyanka led a team of weaker painters
She was the best painter in class

payload.passage: Rain does not fall the same way everywhere on Earth. In some lands, moist winds blow off warm seas throughout the year, bringing steady rain. In others, the winds shift with the seasons, so rain pours for a few months and then stops. Mountains and oceans nearby also shape how much rain a place gets. A region's rainfall pattern depends on its winds, seas and land together; so whether a place enjoys steady rain or a single wet season depends on the particular dance of its winds, seas and land.
payload.title: Why rain falls all year in some places only
decoys: Moist sea winds can bring steady rain all year
The Earth's weather varies from place to place
Mountains and oceans shape how much rain falls

payload.passage: The cleaner shrimp lives on the reef among fish that could swallow it whole, yet it is never harmed. It sets up a little station and waves its long white antennae to advertise its service. A large fish swims up and holds completely still, even opening its mouth and gills. The tiny shrimp climbs over the fish and picks off dead skin, parasites and food scraps, cleaning even between the teeth. The fish leaves clean and healthy, and the shrimp has eaten well. Because both gain, the giant never eats its tiny helper.
payload.title: How the cleaner shrimp serves fish that could eat it
decoys: The shrimp waves its antennae to advertise
Big reef fish could swallow a shrimp
It cleans even between the fish's teeth

payload.passage: Astronauts in orbit seem to drift weightlessly, tumbling slowly through the cabin. People often think there is no gravity up there, but that is not quite right. The spacecraft and everyone in it are actually falling around the Earth together. Because they all fall at the same rate, nothing presses on anything else. This shared, endless falling is what makes the astronauts appear to float; understanding this shows that the weightless feeling of space is really an endless, gentle fall around our planet.
payload.title: Why astronauts float inside their spacecraft
decoys: The crew and the craft fall at the same rate
Space is a strange place for the human body
An orbiting spacecraft is always falling around Earth

payload.passage: A simple ballpoint pen writes smoothly without smudging or leaking. At its tip sits a tiny metal ball nestled in a socket. As you write, the ball rolls and picks up thick ink from a tube inside. The rolling ball lays a thin, even line of ink onto the paper. This cheap and reliable pen quickly replaced the messy fountain pen for everyday writing.
payload.title: How a ballpoint pen rolls ink onto paper
decoys: A tiny ball rolls in a socket at the tip
The ball picks up thick ink from a tube

payload.passage: Dragonflies darting over a pond are a welcome sight for many reasons. As young ones in the water, they eat the wriggling larvae of mosquitoes. Grown up and flying, they snatch grown mosquitoes and flies from the air. In this way they keep down the pests that spread sickness. A pond busy with dragonflies is usually a healthier place to live near.
payload.title: How dragonflies help control harmful pests
decoys: Ponds are home to many insects
Dragonflies snatch flies from the air

payload.passage: A leaky old tap is not the only place water slips away at home. Letting the tap run while you brush your teeth wastes litres every morning. Washing a car with a flowing hose pours away even more. A bucket and mug in place of a running tap can save a great deal. Watching these everyday habits is the easiest way to save water at home.
payload.title: How everyday habits at home can save water
decoys: A running tap while brushing wastes water
A bucket saves water when washing a car

payload.passage: When the school garden prize was announced, the teacher thanked only Bhuvan, who had watered the plants in front of everyone. But it was timid Reshma who had quietly weeded and dug the beds at dawn each day. Bhuvan saw her face fall and knew the truth. He stood up and told the teacher that Reshma had done the hardest work. The prize was shared between them. Bhuvan learnt that fairness means speaking up for the unseen worker, even when the praise is already yours.
payload.title: Fairness speaks up for the unseen worker
decoys: Bhuvan told the teacher about Reshma's work
School gardens need weeding and watering
Reshma worked quietly at dawn each day

payload.passage: The flying fish lives in open seas full of fast, hungry hunters, and it has found an escape route no other fish can use. When a tuna or dolphin chases it, the flying fish builds up speed and bursts clean out of the water into the air. Spreading its long, stiff side fins like wings, it glides for surprising distances above the waves. By the time it splashes down, the underwater hunter has lost its trail. It can even beat its tail on the surface to launch again. By taking to the air, the flying fish leaves its enemies behind.
payload.title: How the flying fish escapes hunters by gliding
decoys: The flying fish glides on wing-like fins
Open seas are full of hungry hunters
It bursts out of the water into the air

payload.passage: The mother wolf spider carries her family in a way few other creatures do. After laying her eggs, she wraps them in a silk ball and attaches it to her body, carrying it everywhere she goes. When the spiderlings hatch, they do not scatter at once. Instead they climb onto their mother's back and ride there in a wriggling cluster as she hunts. She carries them about for many days, keeping them safe from hungry beetles and birds. Only when they are stronger do they drop off to live alone. By carrying her young, she shields them through their weakest time.
payload.title: How the wolf spider carries her young to safety
decoys: Spiderlings ride on their mother's back
Wolf spiders lay eggs in a silk ball
She hunts while carrying her young

payload.passage: Why is sitting up straight better for you than slouching all day? Your spine is a long stack of small bones that holds you upright. When you slouch, this stack bends in awkward ways and strains the muscles around it. Over time, bad posture brings aches in the back and neck. Sitting tall keeps the spine in its natural curve, so your body stays comfortable and strong.
payload.title: Why good posture protects the back
decoys: The spine is a stack of small bones
Good habits keep the body healthy
Slouching strains the muscles in the back

payload.passage: The Earth's steady tilt does more than give us seasons; it shapes the whole climate of the globe. Near the middle of the Earth, the sun stays high and the heat is strong all year, making the tropics warm. Near the poles the sun always rides low, so those lands stay cold. In between lie the milder regions with clearer seasons. The angle of the sun's light, set by the tilt, decides each zone's climate. So one gentle tilt divides the Earth into warm and cold lands.
payload.title: How the Earth's tilt creates the tropics and poles
decoys: Near the poles the sun always rides low in the sky
The Earth varies greatly from place to place
The angle of sunlight decides each zone's climate

payload.passage: A single field can feed two different sets of animals at different hours. By day, bees, butterflies and small birds are busy among the flowers and grass. When darkness falls, these rest, and a night shift takes over. Moths, owls and small hunting animals come out to feed under the moon. By using the same place at separate times, the two groups avoid crowding each other. So a habitat can support far more life than it might first appear; by taking turns through the hours, a single field quietly serves two whole communities of animals.
payload.title: How night creatures share a habitat with day ones
decoys: Moths and owls feed in the field after dark
Nature finds clever ways to share space
Day and night animals avoid crowding each other

payload.passage: Long before clocks were invented, people read the time straight from the position of the sun in the sky. In the morning the sun sits low in the east, and as the hours pass it climbs steadily higher to reach its peak at midday. Through the long afternoon it sinks slowly toward the west. By watching where the sun stood, people could judge how far the day had gone. A simple sundial captured this by tracking the slowly moving shadow. So the sun's steady march across the sky has always served as a natural clock.
payload.title: How the sun's position marks the time of day
decoys: At midday the sun reaches its highest point
People have long told time by the sky
A sundial tracks the sun by its moving shadow

payload.passage: Pari ran a small stall selling friendship bands, and one day a customer complained that the colours had faded after a single wash. Pari could have argued, but instead she calmly replaced the band and switched to better thread for the rest. The pleased customer told her friends, and Pari's sales actually rose. She learnt that a complaint is not an attack but a gift of honest information. Handled with grace, a customer's grumble can teach a small business exactly how to improve and win even more loyalty.
payload.title: How handling complaints can grow a business
decoys: Pari replaced the faded friendship band
A customer complained about fading colours

payload.passage: Why does your face go red when you are embarrassed? A strong, sudden feeling can set off a quick reaction in your body. It widens the tiny blood vessels just under the skin of your face. More warm blood rushes close to the surface, and your cheeks glow red. This blush happens all by itself, without you choosing it at all.
payload.title: Why our faces flush when we are embarrassed
decoys: Blood vessels under the face widen
More warm blood makes the cheeks glow

payload.passage: Sneha was sure she had locked the school lab, but the next morning a beaker was found broken inside. The teacher asked who had been last to leave, and Sneha's stomach turned. She could have stayed silent, since two others had also been there. Instead she said she had been last and would help clean and replace the beaker. The teacher discovered later it had cracked on its own from heat. Sneha learnt that honestly owning your part costs little, while a lie can cost your good name.
payload.title: Owning your part costs less than a lie
decoys: The beaker had cracked from heat on its own
School labs hold glass beakers and tools
Sneha was the last to leave the lab

payload.passage: Aadi opened a tiny stall selling paper boats and toys, and on the very first day he priced everything to make the biggest possible profit per item. Hardly anyone bought. A kind older seller advised him that a fair, modest price would draw far more customers than a greedy one. Aadi lowered his prices, and suddenly children crowded his stall, and his total earnings rose well above before. He learnt the surprising lesson that charging a little less, but selling far more, can earn you more than squeezing each single sale.
payload.title: Why a fair price can earn more overall
decoys: Aadi first priced his toys very high
Children crowded his stall after the change

payload.passage: Why does the body grow used to exercise over time? When you first take up running, even a short distance leaves you breathless. With practice, your heart and lungs grow stronger and work more smoothly. Your muscles learn to use oxygen better as well. After weeks of training, the same run that once tired you now feels easy.
payload.title: Why exercise grows easier with practice
decoys: The heart and lungs grow stronger with practice
The body adapts to what we do
Muscles learn to use oxygen better

payload.passage: A chameleon can shift its colour to match a leaf or a branch. Its skin holds tiny pockets of colour that it can stretch or squeeze. By changing the size of these pockets, the chameleon shows different shades. It can blend into its surroundings to hide from hungry birds. It may also change colour to show how it is feeling or to keep warm in the sun.
payload.title: How a chameleon changes its colour
decoys: A chameleon has tiny pockets of colour
The animal world is full of wonders
Changing colour helps it hide from birds

payload.passage: A simple metal spoon may seem too plain to be an invention, yet it changed how we eat. Its shallow bowl holds a mouthful of food or liquid neatly. The long handle keeps your fingers clean and away from hot dishes. Smooth and easy to wash, the spoon let people eat soup and rice without mess. Such a simple shape has served at tables for thousands of years.
payload.title: How the simple spoon changed the way we eat
decoys: The shallow bowl holds a mouthful of food
The handle keeps fingers away from heat

payload.passage: A monsoon puddle that lingers for days can turn into a problem. Still, stagnant water is just where mosquitoes love to lay their eggs. From these eggs hatch the larvae that grow into biting pests. Some of these mosquitoes carry the germs of dangerous fevers. Tipping out old water from pots, tyres and corners stops this whole trouble before it starts.
payload.title: Why standing water lets mosquitoes breed
decoys: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water
The monsoon brings a lot of rain

payload.passage: Pour a cold drink and soon the outside of the glass turns wet, though no water leaked through. The droplets come from the air itself. Warm air around the glass holds invisible water vapour. When this air touches the chilled glass, it cools and can no longer hold all that vapour. The spare water turns back into liquid on the cold surface, beading up as drops we can see; this same change, from invisible vapour back to visible water, is what fills the sky with clouds and brings us rain.
payload.title: Why condensation forms on a cold glass
decoys: Cooled air can no longer hold all its vapour
Hot and cold mix in surprising ways
Warm air around the glass holds invisible vapour

payload.passage: A simple wristwatch keeps time on your arm wherever you go. Older watches store energy in a tightly wound spring. As the spring slowly unwinds, it drives a train of tiny toothed wheels. A small swinging wheel keeps the unwinding even and steady. Those wheels turn the hands so you always know the hour at a glance.
payload.title: How a wind-up wristwatch keeps time
decoys: A wound spring drives toothed wheels
People have always wished to track time
A wristwatch shows the hour at a glance

payload.passage: During a total solar eclipse, the bright day can suddenly dim toward dusk. The moon is the cause, sliding directly in front of the sun. For a brief time it blocks the sunlight from reaching one strip of the Earth. In that strip the sky darkens and the air may turn cool and still. The darkness lasts only a few minutes before the moon moves aside. Then the sunlight floods back and the day brightens once again; so a total solar eclipse offers a brief, startling taste of night in the middle of the day.
payload.title: Why an eclipse darkens the sky for a short while
decoys: The moon slides directly in front of the sun
The sky can change in dramatic ways
The darkness lasts only a few minutes

payload.passage: Why does a scab form over a graze on your knee? When you scrape your skin, the body quickly seals the wound to keep germs out. Blood at the surface dries into a hard, crusty cover called a scab. Under this shield, new skin quietly grows to repair the damage. Once the fresh skin is ready, the old scab falls away on its own.
payload.title: Why a scab forms and protects a graze
decoys: Blood at the surface dries into a scab
The body heals itself in clever ways
New skin grows beneath the scab

payload.passage: Why does the body need a steady supply of energy through the day? Everything you do, from thinking to walking, uses up energy. If you take in all your food at once and nothing more, your energy soars then crashes. Spreading meals and healthy snacks through the day keeps the supply even. This steady fuel keeps you alert and active from morning to night.
payload.title: Why the body needs steady energy through the day
decoys: Thinking and walking use up energy
All food at once makes energy crash

payload.passage: A simple electric heater warms a cold room on a winter night. Inside it lies a coil of special wire that resists the flow of electricity. As current pushes through, the coil grows hot and glows red. The heat spreads out into the air around it. In a few minutes, the once-chilly room turns cosy and warm.
payload.title: How an electric heater warms a cold room
decoys: A coil of wire resists the current and heats up
Inventions help us face the cold
The glowing coil spreads heat into the air

payload.passage: The sun pours out staggering amounts of light, so how does it keep shining so long? Deep in its core, tiny bits of matter join together and release tremendous energy. The sun is so vast that it holds an enormous supply of this fuel. Even burning at a furious rate, it has enough to last billions of years. That is why the sun has shone steadily since long before life began; so although the sun pours out fierce energy every second, its vast store of fuel will keep it shining for ages to come.
payload.title: Why the sun does not burn out quickly
decoys: Tiny bits of matter join in the sun's core
Stars are powerful beyond easy imagining
The sun has shone since long before life began

payload.passage: Gauri was handed the answer key entirely by accident the evening before the big spelling bee. Quietly memorising it would have all but guaranteed her the gleaming trophy. She held the folded paper for a long moment, tempted. Then she walked it straight back to the teacher and asked instead for a fresh, completely unseen list of words. She did not win the contest in the end, but she stood up on that bright stage with a clear, untroubled mind. Gauri learnt that a prize means absolutely nothing if you cannot afterwards look yourself honestly in the eye.
payload.title: A prize is worthless without a clear conscience
decoys: Gauri returned the spelling bee answer key
Spelling bees test how well you spell words
An answer key could guarantee a win

payload.passage: Govind had been saving every coin to buy a new cricket ball he had wanted for months. Then his little sister fell ill, and the family needed money for her medicine. No one asked Govind for his savings, and he could have stayed quiet about the tin under his bed. Instead he brought out every coin and pressed it into his mother's hand. The ball would wait, he said, but his sister could not. Govind learnt that those we love come before the things we want, however badly we want them.
payload.title: Loved ones come before the things we want
decoys: Govind gave his savings for his sister's medicine
Cricket balls cost a lot of saving
His little sister had fallen ill

payload.passage: A simple chalk and slate let poor children learn to write. The slate is a small dark board you can write on again and again. A stick of soft chalk leaves a pale mark as it drags across it. When the board is full, a quick wipe rubs it clean for more practice. Costing very little, this pair brought learning within reach of many.
payload.title: How chalk and slate brought learning to many
decoys: Chalk leaves a pale mark on the dark slate
A wipe cleans the board for more practice

payload.passage: Why does the body need a balance of salt, not too much or too little? A little salt helps your nerves and muscles work and keeps your body's water in balance. But too much salt makes the body hold extra water and strains the heart. Too little can leave you weak and dizzy. The body works best when salt is kept at a sensible, modest level.
payload.title: Why the body needs the right balance of salt
decoys: A little salt helps nerves and muscles work
Too much salt strains the heart

payload.passage: Glass is one of the friendliest materials we can recycle. An old bottle can be washed, crushed and melted down into a brand-new one. This can be done again and again without the glass ever wearing out. Making glass from old bottles uses far less energy than making it from scratch. Dropping bottles into the recycling bin saves both fuel and raw materials.
payload.title: Why recycling glass saves energy and materials
decoys: An old bottle can be melted into a new one
Recycled glass uses far less energy

payload.passage: Ira was amazed that one signalman in a small cabin could keep many trains from crashing on the same tracks. He worked levers and buttons that turned the line's signals red or green, letting only one train onto a stretch of rail at a time. If two trains needed the same line, he held one safely back until the other had cleared. A single careless moment could be deadly, so his attention never wandered. Ira understood that the railway's safety rested less on the trains themselves and more on the steady eyes inside that quiet cabin.
payload.title: How a signalman keeps trains from colliding
decoys: Signals turn red or green for the trains
Careful work keeps many people safe
Only one train may use a stretch at a time

payload.passage: Karthik discovered that the shopkeeper had given him a fake-looking extra ten-rupee note by mistake, mixed in with his change. He could have simply spent it somewhere and let it become someone else's problem. Instead he took it back and told the shopkeeper, who checked and found it was indeed a worthless fake. The shopkeeper thanked him for his honesty and replaced it with a good note. Karthik learnt that passing on a problem to a stranger is wrong, and that honesty means not making your mistake into another's.
payload.title: Honesty means not passing problems to others
decoys: Karthik returned a fake note to the shopkeeper
Shopkeepers sometimes hand out bad notes
Fake notes are worth nothing at all

payload.passage: A street dog with a badly hurt paw limped up near Sahil's gate, snarling and snapping at everyone who dared come close. The other children quickly threw stones to drive the frightening creature away. Sahil, though truly afraid of those snapping jaws, fetched a bowl of water and some food and waited patiently a little way off each day. Slowly, day by day, the dog grew calmer. At last it let him gently clean the wound, and in time it followed him about like a faithful shadow. Sahil learnt that patient kindness can win trust where force only ever breeds fear.
payload.title: Patient kindness wins trust that force cannot
decoys: Sahil cared for a street dog's hurt paw
Hurt animals often snarl at people
Some children throw stones at street dogs

payload.passage: Sending a long letter across the country instantly once felt like a dream. Electronic mail, or email, made it ordinary. You type a message and the computer breaks it into small packets of data. These packets race across the internet and gather again on the other person's device. Within seconds your words appear on a screen that may be a thousand miles away.
payload.title: How email delivers a message in seconds
decoys: A message is broken into small packets
The internet changed how we communicate
Your words appear on a distant screen

payload.passage: Clouds may seem to come from nowhere, but the sun builds them from below. Its warmth heats the surface of seas, lakes and damp soil. The heated water turns to vapour and rises into the sky, invisible at first. High up, where the air is cooler, the vapour gathers into tiny droplets that form clouds. The fluffy clouds overhead are really water the sun has lifted from the ground; so even the highest, softest cloud began as water resting quietly on the ground until the sun lifted it skyward.
payload.title: How the sun draws water up to make clouds
decoys: Heated water turns to vapour and rises
The sun is at work all around us
Cool air high up gathers vapour into droplets

payload.passage: Without its blanket of air, the Earth would freeze hard each night. By day the sun warms the ground, and at night the ground gives off that heat. The air above acts like a soft quilt, slowing the escape of this warmth into space. So the surface stays mild instead of plunging to a deep chill. The moon, which has no air, swings between scorching days and freezing nights instead; so the thin blanket of air around our planet is one of the quiet reasons the Earth is gentle enough for life.
payload.title: How the air keeps the Earth warm at night
decoys: The ground gives off heat after dark
The air protects life on Earth in many ways
The airless moon has scorching days and freezing nights

payload.passage: Mira was puzzled that the small grocer let some trusted old customers pay at the end of the month rather than each day. Her father explained that this credit was built on years of trust, and it kept loyal families coming to his shop. But the grocer kept a careful book and never let any debt grow too large, or he himself could be ruined. The trust ran both ways, with limits. Mira learnt that offering credit can win loyal customers, but only when it is watched carefully and never allowed to spin out of control.
payload.title: Why careful credit can win loyal customers
decoys: The grocer let trusted families pay monthly
He kept a careful book of debts

payload.passage: Snails and slugs are slow and slimy, yet they do useful work in a garden. They feed on dead leaves and rotting bits, helping them break down. As they do this, they return the goodness to the soil. Birds, frogs and beetles in turn feed upon the snails. In this quiet chain, even a humble snail keeps the garden's web of life turning.
payload.title: How humble snails play a part in nature's web
decoys: Gardens are full of little creatures
Birds and frogs feed on snails

payload.passage: A simple pedal-powered dynamo lamp lets a cyclist ride safely after dark. A small wheel presses against the spinning tyre. As the cyclist pedals, the turning tyre spins this little wheel. The spinning wheel works a tiny dynamo that makes electricity. That current lights the lamp, so the faster you ride, the brighter your path glows.
payload.title: How a cycle dynamo lamp lights the way
decoys: A small wheel is spun by the turning tyre
The dynamo makes electricity as you pedal

payload.passage: Diya's mother always shopped for vegetables late in the evening, and Diya thought it was just convenient. In fact her mother knew that sellers, eager to clear their stock before going home, dropped their prices as the day ended. The same tomatoes that were dear at dawn could be had cheaply at dusk. By choosing her hour wisely, her mother stretched the family's money further. Diya learnt that even the time you shop can change the price you pay, and that a clever buyer notices such patterns.
payload.title: How the hour you shop affects the price
decoys: Sellers dropped prices at the day's end
Her mother shopped late each evening

payload.passage: Every snowflake begins its life high inside a very cold cloud. There the water vapour is so chilled that it does not form liquid drops. Instead it freezes straight onto a tiny speck, building a delicate ice crystal. As the crystal drifts, more vapour freezes onto it and it grows six fine arms. When it becomes heavy enough, it floats gently down as a snowflake. Each flake is a tiny work of ice shaped in the freezing sky; so every flake that lands on your sleeve is a delicate crystal built high in the freezing sky.
payload.title: How a snowflake forms high in a freezing cloud
decoys: Vapour freezes straight onto a tiny speck
The crystal grows six fine arms as it drifts

payload.passage: Before the dynamo, electricity could only be drawn from weak chemical cells. The dynamo learned to make electricity from movement itself. When a coil of wire is spun near a magnet, an electric current is born in the wire. Turn the coil with water, wind or steam, and a steady supply of power flows out. This discovery is the heart of every power station today.
payload.title: How the dynamo makes electricity from movement
decoys: Spinning a coil near a magnet makes current
Power stations rely on the dynamo

payload.passage: Why do we shiver when we step into a cold room? Your body works hard to keep itself at a steady, warm temperature inside. When the cold threatens to chill you, your brain sends out an order. Your muscles begin to shake quickly, all on their own. This rapid shaking makes heat that warms the body, so shivering is the body's way of fighting the cold.
payload.title: Why we shiver when we feel cold
decoys: Shaking muscles make heat for the body
The body reacts to its surroundings
The body keeps a steady inside temperature

payload.passage: A new girl named Zoya spoke with a heavy accent, and some classmates began to imitate her cruelly for cheap laughs. Geeta had very nearly joined in herself, just to seem clever and quick. Then she stopped and imagined how lonely and small she would feel if she were standing in Zoya's place. Instead of laughing, she chose to sit beside Zoya at lunch and ask all about her old town and her old school. Within a week the two had become close friends, and the teasing slowly faded away to nothing. Geeta learnt that a single welcoming heart can quietly undo a whole crowd's cruelty.
payload.title: One welcoming friend can undo a crowd's cruelty
decoys: Geeta sat with the new girl at lunch
New students sometimes speak with an accent
Classmates can be unkind to newcomers

payload.passage: Burning dry leaves and rubbish in a corner seems an easy way to clear them. But the rising smoke fills the whole neighbourhood with a sharp, stinging haze. Breathing this smoke is hard on the chest, especially for children and the old. The fire also kills the tiny creatures that would have turned the leaves into rich soil. Heaping the leaves to rot is a far better choice than burning them.
payload.title: Why burning leaves and rubbish does more harm than good
decoys: Smoke fills the neighbourhood with haze
Cleaning up is a good thing
Burning kills the soil's tiny creatures

payload.passage: A potter shapes wet clay into a pot, but the soft pot must be baked to last. Wet clay is soft because water fills the gaps between its tiny grains. When the pot is placed in a hot oven, the heat drives the water away. The grains then grip one another tightly and lock into a hard shape. This is why a baked clay pot stays firm and no longer turns soft in water.
payload.title: Why clay pots are baked to make them hard
decoys: Heat drives the water out of the clay
Pottery is a very old craft
Water makes clay soft to shape

payload.passage: Near the very top and bottom of the Earth, the sun behaves strangely. Because of the planet's tilt, these regions can lean fully toward or away from the sun for long stretches. In their summer the sun never fully sets, and daylight lasts for weeks. In their winter the sun never properly rises, and darkness lingers for months. At the poles, a single day and night can stretch across whole seasons; so near the poles a single 'day' and 'night' can each last for months, a rhythm utterly unlike our own.
payload.title: Why polar regions have months of light and dark
decoys: In polar summer the sun never fully sets
The Earth's regions differ greatly from one another
The poles can lean fully toward or away from the sun
