payload.passage: The peacock's enormous, glittering tail seems like a foolish thing to drag around a forest full of dangers. Yet that very tail is the secret to the peacock's family line. When the dull-brown peahen watches the males, she chooses the one with the largest, most perfect fan of shimmering eye-spots. A grand tail quietly tells her that this male is strong and healthy, fit to father her chicks. So the showiest peacocks are chosen again and again across the years. What looks like a burden is really a clever message of fitness.
payload.title: Why the peacock's grand tail helps it find a mate
decoys: A peahen picks the male with the largest tail
The tail signals that a male is healthy

payload.passage: Why does the body need you to chew your food well? Chewing breaks food into small pieces and mixes in saliva. Smaller, softer pieces are far easier for the stomach to break down. They also let the body soak up more goodness from the meal. Gulping food in big lumps makes the stomach work harder and can upset it.
payload.title: Why chewing food well helps the body
decoys: Chewing mixes saliva into the food
Big lumps make the stomach work harder

payload.passage: An echo in a big empty hall can be a little spooky, but it is easy to explain. Sound travels through the air as ripples, much like ripples spreading across a pond. When these sound ripples hit a hard, flat wall, they bounce straight back. If the wall is far enough away, the bounced sound returns a moment after you shout. That returning sound, slightly late, is the echo you hear.
payload.title: How a sound bounces back to make an echo
decoys: Sound bounces off a hard, flat wall
Empty halls can feel large and lonely
Sound travels through air in spreading ripples

payload.passage: On a very dark night a pale, milky band stretches across the sky. This soft glow is not a cloud but the light of countless distant stars. Our sun belongs to a vast spinning city of stars called a galaxy. When we look along its flat disc, the crowded stars blur into that glowing band. The Milky Way we see is really a view through our own home in space; so that faint, glowing band is not a distant object at all, but a view straight through the star city we live in.
payload.title: How the Milky Way reveals our own galaxy
decoys: The pale band is the light of countless stars
There is more to the sky than we can count
Our sun belongs to a vast spinning galaxy

payload.passage: In a meerkat group, the youngest pups know nothing about the dangerous scorpions they must one day eat. So the older meerkats teach them with great care. First an adult brings a dead scorpion for the tiny pup to nibble safely. Next it brings a live scorpion with the deadly stinger already bitten off. Only when the pup is older does the adult bring a whole live scorpion and watch it learn to handle the sting. Step by patient step, the elders pass on a skill the pups need to survive in the harsh desert.
payload.title: How adult meerkats teach pups to handle danger
decoys: Meerkats bring pups a stingless scorpion first
Scorpions can deliver a deadly sting

payload.passage: The youngest boy in the lane could never keep up in races and was always left behind, panting and sad. The older boys ran on without a glance. Vikram, the fastest of them, began to hang back and run alongside the little one, cheering him to the finish each time. The boy's face lit up at last. Vikram could have won every race easily. The little boy began to look forward to races instead of dreading them. He learnt that slowing down to lift another's spirit can matter far more than always finishing first.
payload.title: Slowing to lift another beats finishing first
decoys: Vikram ran alongside the slowest boy
The youngest boy was always left behind

payload.passage: Among all the worlds we know, only Earth teems with living things. Several lucky features come together here. It orbits at a gentle distance from the sun, so water can stay liquid. A protective layer of air shields the surface and holds in warmth. There is plenty of water and the right mix of ingredients for life. No other world we have found combines all these gifts so well; so far, no other world we have studied brings together all these gifts, which makes our living planet truly remarkable.
payload.title: Why Earth is the only planet known with life
decoys: Earth holds plenty of water for living things
Earth is precious and worth caring for
A layer of air shields Earth's surface and holds warmth

payload.passage: Rohit kept all his savings in a tin under his bed, proud of the growing pile. His grandfather suggested moving it into a bank instead. In the bank, he explained, the money would not only be safer from fire and theft but would slowly earn a little extra called interest. The tin, by contrast, simply sat there gathering dust. Rohit was surprised that money could grow merely by being kept in the right place. He learnt that where you store your savings can matter almost as much as how much you save.
payload.title: Where you keep savings can make them grow
decoys: Rohit kept his money in a tin under the bed
Bank savings earn a little interest

payload.passage: Have you noticed that you can taste food much less when you have a bad cold? Taste and smell work closely together, like good friends. As you chew, tiny scent particles float up from your mouth into your nose. Your nose reads these scents and adds them to the flavours your tongue picks up. When a cold blocks your nose, those scents cannot reach it, so your favourite food tastes dull and plain.
payload.title: Why food tastes dull when your nose is blocked
decoys: Scent particles float from the mouth to the nose
Having a cold can make you feel quite unwell
The tongue picks up the flavours of food

payload.passage: Each planet travels its own steady path around the sun without ever straying, and two opposite tendencies keep it in line. The sun's gravity pulls the planet inward, while the planet's own sideways speed tries to fling it away. These two balance so neatly that the planet curves into a smooth, closed path. It neither falls into the sun nor flies off into the dark. Year after year it follows the same faithful loop. So a planet's orbit is a perfect balance of pull and motion.
payload.title: Why a planet stays in its lane around the sun
decoys: The sun's gravity pulls the planet inward
The universe is held together by balance
The planet neither falls in nor flies away

payload.passage: Why does your body have eyebrows and eyelashes? These small hairs do a quiet but useful job. Eyebrows steer sweat and rain away from your eyes so your sight stays clear. Eyelashes catch dust and grit before they can land on the eye. Together they guard your eyes from the small troubles of every day.
payload.title: How eyebrows and eyelashes guard the eyes
decoys: Eyebrows steer sweat away from the eyes
The body protects its delicate parts

payload.passage: A bat flying through the pitch-dark night can catch a tiny moth in mid-air without ever seeing it. It does this by listening rather than looking. As it flies, the bat sends out streams of high squeaks far too shrill for our ears to hear. These sounds bounce off insects and obstacles and return as faint echoes. From the timing and shape of each echo, the bat builds a sound-picture of everything around it. It can tell exactly where a moth is and snap it up. By hunting with echoes, the bat owns the darkness.
payload.title: How a bat hunts in the dark using echoes
decoys: A bat sends out squeaks that bounce back
Bats are active during the night

payload.passage: We use days and years all the time, but they measure two separate movements. A day is the time the Earth takes to spin once on its own axis. A year is the far longer time it takes to travel once around the sun. While the Earth circles the sun a single time, it spins on its axis hundreds of times. So many days fit inside one year. Two different motions of the same planet give us our two main ways of counting time.
payload.title: How a year and a day measure two different motions
decoys: The Earth spins hundreds of times in one year
People measure time by watching the sky
A year is one trip of the Earth around the sun

payload.passage: During the long rains, the vegetable market near Tanvi's house suddenly turned costly. Floods in the farming districts had spoiled many crops and blocked the lorries that brought produce to the city. With far less arriving than usual, even ordinary spinach fetched a high price. Tanvi heard her mother grumble, but her father explained it was not the seller's greed. The faraway weather, not the man at the stall, had thinned the supply and pushed the prices up. Tanvi saw how a distant flood could reach right into her dinner plate.
payload.title: How distant floods raise local market prices
decoys: Floods blocked the lorries bringing produce
Weather affects people's lives in many ways
Even ordinary spinach grew costly that week

payload.passage: A shallow strip of plants beside a pond does a quiet but vital job. As rain runs off the fields, it carries loose soil and stray chemicals towards the water. The thick band of reeds and grasses catches much of this before it reaches the pond. Their roots trap the soil and soak up the chemicals. So this green border keeps the pond clear and its life safe.
payload.title: How a plant border keeps a pond clean
decoys: Reeds catch the loose soil from fields
Ponds need to be looked after
Plant roots soak up stray chemicals

payload.passage: Reyaan saw an advertisement promising to double anyone's money in just one month if they handed it over now. It sounded wonderful, and he urged his father to try. His father laughed gently and asked how any honest business could grow money so impossibly fast. Such promises, he warned, were traps that took your cash and vanished. Real savings grow slowly and steadily, never overnight. Reyaan learnt a sharp rule of money sense: when an offer sounds too good to be true, it almost always is.
payload.title: Why money offers that seem too good are traps
decoys: The advert promised to double money in a month
We should think before believing claims
Real savings grow slowly over time

payload.passage: Most fish lay their eggs and swim away, but the seahorse father does something almost unheard of in the animal world. The mother seahorse places her eggs into a special pouch on the father's belly. There the father carries them, keeping them safe and feeding them, for weeks as they develop. His pouch swells as the young grow inside. When at last they are ready, he pumps and squeezes until dozens of tiny seahorses burst out into the water. By giving birth himself, the seahorse father shields the young through their most fragile days.
payload.title: How the seahorse father carries and births the young
decoys: The seahorse father carries eggs in a pouch
Most fish lay eggs and swim away
Dozens of tiny seahorses burst out

payload.passage: Hold a snail or watch a caterpillar, and you will see how slowly they move. Inside our own bodies, food also moves along on a slow and steady journey. After the stomach, the soft food enters a long, coiled tube. The walls of this tube squeeze gently to push the food along, little by little. As the food creeps forward, the body soaks up the goodness it needs.
payload.title: How food slowly moves through the gut
decoys: The walls of the gut squeeze to push food
Living things move in many different ways
The body soaks up goodness from food

payload.passage: The sun pours out heat in all directions, yet the space between it and the Earth stays freezing cold. This puzzles many people. Sunlight travels through space as rays that carry energy but warm nothing on the way. Only when the rays strike something solid, like the ground, do they turn into heat. Empty space has almost nothing for them to warm. The rays cross the cold void untouched and heat the Earth only when they land; so the rays cross the cold void untouched and give up their warmth only when they finally land.
payload.title: How sunlight warms the Earth but not empty space
decoys: Sunlight warms something only when its rays strike it
Space is a strange and vast place
Empty space has almost nothing for the rays to warm

payload.passage: Mihika dreamed of a brand-new bicycle exactly like her friend's, but her parents could not afford one. Instead of sulking, she found a second-hand cycle in good condition for a fraction of the price and saved the rest of her money. It rode just as well, and she felt proud of the bargain. Her friend, who had paid full price, was puzzled by Mihika's cleverness. Mihika learnt that being thrifty is not about owning less; it is about getting what you truly need while spending far less than you might have.
payload.title: How being thrifty stretches limited money
decoys: Mihika bought a good second-hand cycle
The used cycle cost a fraction of the price

payload.passage: By day the sky glows blue, but at night it falls into deep darkness. The difference is the sun. In daytime the sun lights up the air above us, scattering its light into a bright blue glow. When your side of the Earth turns away from the sun, no sunlight reaches the air overhead. With nothing to light it, the sky goes dark and the faint stars finally show through; so the deep darkness of the night sky is really just the shadow of the Earth itself, cast by our turning planet.
payload.title: Why the sky is dark at night
decoys: Sunlight scatters in the air to make the sky blue
The sky looks different at different times
The faint stars show through once the sky is dark

payload.passage: Plants and animals notice the slow stretching and shrinking of daylight through the year. As days lengthen in spring, many plants flower and birds build nests. As days shorten in autumn, trees drop their leaves and some animals prepare to sleep or migrate. This change in day length is a dependable signal, set by the Earth's tilt and orbit. Living things read it to time the rhythms of their lives; so the slow stretching and shrinking of daylight acts as a quiet calendar that plants and animals read all year long.
payload.title: How the changing length of day guides nature's clock
decoys: Lengthening spring days prompt plants to flower
Nature keeps time by many signals
Day length is set by the Earth's tilt and orbit

payload.passage: Beside the dazzling sun, the moon seems faint and pale by comparison. Both shine in our sky, but for very different reasons. The sun makes its own fierce light from the furnace within it. The moon makes no light of its own; it only reflects a portion of the sunlight that falls on it. Since reflected light is far weaker than the source, the moon can never match the blazing sun; so although both ride across our sky, the dazzling sun and the gentle moon shine for completely different reasons.
payload.title: Why the moon looks pale next to the bright sun
decoys: The moon only reflects part of the sunlight
The sky holds bodies of many kinds
The sun makes its own light from a furnace within

payload.passage: Each creature in a habitat has a quiet job in the food web. Imagine the owls all leaving a field one summer. With no owls to hunt them, the mice would breed quickly and grow in number. Crowds of mice would then eat far more seeds and young plants than before. Soon the plants would suffer, and the animals that also depend on them would struggle too. One missing link can ripple through the entire web; this is why protecting even the smallest or least noticed creature can matter for the health of an entire place.
payload.title: Why removing one animal can upset a whole habitat
decoys: Owls help keep the number of mice in check
Every living thing matters in some way
Too many mice would eat most of the seeds

payload.passage: The new postmistress, Kavya, noticed that letters to one crowded lane kept coming back marked 'address not found'. Instead of blaming the senders, she walked the lane herself and saw that the houses had no clear numbers at all. She arranged for the council to paint neat numbers on every gate, then redrew her delivery map. Within a month the returned letters had almost vanished. Kavya showed that fixing a delivery problem sometimes means leaving the counter and mending the world outside it, not just stamping papers.
payload.title: A postmistress fixes deliveries by numbering houses
decoys: The lane's houses had no clear numbers at all
Good workers care about doing their jobs well
Letters were coming back marked 'address not found'

payload.passage: Summer warmth and winter chill both trace back to how high the sun climbs. In summer your part of the Earth leans toward the sun, so it rides high and its rays strike hard. This direct sunlight heats the ground strongly through long days. In winter the sun stays low, its rays slant in weakly, and the days are short. The sun's height across the year quietly sets each season's temperature; so the warmth of each season depends not on our distance from the sun but simply on how high it climbs in our sky.
payload.title: How the changing sun height brings the seasons' warmth
decoys: In summer the sun rides high and strikes hard
The seasons shape the world in many ways
A low winter sun sends weak, slanting rays

payload.passage: Saira noticed that some people who could easily have voted simply stayed home, saying their single vote made no difference. Her mother asked her to imagine if everyone thought the same way. Then no one would vote at all, and a tiny, unrepresentative group would choose for the whole town. Each vote was small, but together they were everything. Saira learnt that the worth of a vote is not measured alone but in the multitude. She saw that democracy works only when many small voices choose to be counted.
payload.title: Why every small vote together matters
decoys: Some people stayed home on voting day
A few would otherwise choose for all

payload.passage: The thin blanket of air around our planet is more delicate than it seems. It holds the oxygen we breathe and traps just enough warmth to keep us cosy. It also shields us from the sun's harsher rays. When smoke and waste gases pour into it, this blanket grows unhealthy and the climate begins to shift. Keeping the air clean protects the very thing that lets us live.
payload.title: Why our planet's thin layer of air must be kept clean
decoys: The air holds the oxygen we breathe
The earth is a special place
Waste gases make the air unhealthy

payload.passage: Hang a wet towel in still air and it dries slowly; add a breeze and it dries fast. The wind is doing quiet work. As water evaporates, a layer of damp air clings just above the towel and slows further drying. A breeze sweeps this damp air away and brings fresh, drier air to the surface. With the moist layer gone, more water can escape, and the towel dries far more quickly; so a windy day is a good drying day, while still, heavy air can leave washing damp for hours on end.
payload.title: How the wind helps wet things dry
decoys: Damp air clings just above a drying towel
A breeze brings fresh, drier air to the surface

payload.passage: Gazing up at the stars is a little like opening a history book. Light from the stars takes a long time to cross the vast distances of space. By the time it reaches us, years or even ages have passed. So we see each star not as it is tonight, but as it was when its light set out. The farther the star, the deeper into the past we are looking; so when we admire the stars, we are really studying light that left them long before we were ever born.
payload.title: Why the night sky is a window into the past
decoys: Starlight takes a long time to cross space
The farther the star, the older its light

payload.passage: Mira's village had a small fund meant for emergencies, and one year a member quietly proposed using it for a grand festival instead. An older woman stood up and reminded everyone what the fund was for: the day a flood or fire struck without warning. Spent on a feast, it would be gone when truly needed. The members agreed to leave it untouched. Mira learnt that an emergency fund only works if people resist the temptation to dip into it for ordinary, cheerful wants.
payload.title: Why an emergency fund must stay untouched
decoys: A member wanted to fund a festival
The fund was meant for floods or fires

payload.passage: Why do your eyes slowly adjust when you walk into a dark room? In bright light, the eyes use cells suited for daylight and colour. These cannot see well in the dark, so at first you see almost nothing. After a while, the eyes switch to special cells that work in dim light. Slowly the dark room begins to take shape before you.
payload.title: Why the eyes slowly adjust to a dark room
decoys: Daylight cells cannot see well in the dark
The body adapts to its surroundings
Special cells work in dim light

payload.passage: Arjun loved a video game that was free to start, but it kept asking him to pay small amounts to unlock the next bit. Each sum seemed tiny, so he kept tapping yes. At month's end his mother showed him how all those little payments had added up to a startling total. The game had been designed to make spending feel painless and endless. Arjun learnt that many small, easy payments can quietly outgrow one big purchase, and that a wise spender keeps a careful eye even on amounts that look harmlessly small.
payload.title: Why many tiny payments outgrow one big buy
decoys: The game kept asking for small payments
The little sums added to a startling total

payload.passage: When the class fund suddenly went missing, suspicion fell at once on quiet Sunil, who happened to sit nearest the teacher's desk. Soon everyone was whispering that he simply must be the thief. Aditi alone refused to judge him without any proof and asked the class to search the room properly first. They lifted books and peered under chairs. At last they found that the money had merely slipped down behind a heavy cupboard. Sunil's name was cleared in an instant, and the whispering stopped. Aditi learnt that fairness means patiently waiting for the truth before blaming anyone at all.
payload.title: Fairness means seeking proof before placing blame
decoys: The class fund had slipped behind a cupboard
Money can easily fall behind furniture
Quiet students are sometimes wrongly suspected

payload.passage: During the school fest, two food stalls run by rival classes competed fiercely for customers. When one stall's stove suddenly failed, its class faced ruin. Anaya, from the rival stall, could have enjoyed their bad luck and won every customer. Instead she lent them her spare stove without a second thought. Both stalls did well that day, and the rivalry turned to friendship. By evening the two classes were sharing leftover snacks and swapping jokes. Anaya learnt that helping a competitor in trouble is nobler than winning by their misfortune.
payload.title: Helping a competitor beats winning by their misfortune
decoys: Anaya lent her spare stove to a rival stall
School fests have competing food stalls

payload.passage: From Earth we always gaze at the same familiar face of the moon. This is because the moon turns on its axis in exactly the time it takes to circle us once. With its spin and orbit so neatly matched, one side stays turned toward us forever. The other side, hidden from every backyard telescope, was a mystery for ages. Only when spacecraft flew around the moon did people first see it. So half the moon's story stayed hidden until modern times.
payload.title: Why we see only one side of the moon's story
decoys: The moon's spin and orbit are neatly matched
There is always more about space to learn
Spacecraft first revealed the moon's hidden side

payload.passage: Setting up a small bird feeder brings the garden alive in winter. When seeds grow scarce in the cold months, birds struggle to find food. A handful of grain on a tray gives them strength to survive. In return, they brighten the garden and eat many pests. A simple feeder helps the birds through hard days and brings joy to those who watch.
payload.title: How a bird feeder helps birds through winter
decoys: Seeds grow scarce in the cold months
Grain gives birds strength to survive

payload.passage: Geese that nest on the cold tundra must protect their eggs from prowling foxes, and they do it with bold teamwork. When a fox creeps toward the nesting ground, the geese do not simply flee and leave their eggs. Several adults rush at the intruder together, hissing, beating their strong wings and snapping their beaks. Faced with a noisy crowd of angry birds, the fox usually thinks better of it and slinks away. The geese return to their nests unharmed. By driving off danger as a group, they keep their eggs safe where one bird could not.
payload.title: How nesting geese drive off foxes as a group
decoys: Geese rush at a fox together hissing
Foxes prowl the tundra for eggs

payload.passage: Myra could not see why a small board at the platform's end mattered so much to the train driver. Her grandfather, a retired guard, explained that each such board told the driver the exact speed allowed on the stretch ahead. Near a sharp curve or a crowded station, the board warned him to slow down for safety. Ignoring it could spell disaster. Myra realised that the railway spoke to its drivers through a quiet language of signs along the track. She learnt that small markers carried instructions that kept whole trains safe.
payload.title: How trackside boards guide a train's speed
decoys: A board warned the driver near a curve
Signs help us in daily life
Each board told the allowed speed

payload.passage: A comet may blaze brightly, vanish for years, and then return as if by magic. This is because it travels a long, stretched-out orbit around the sun. For most of that path it drifts far away in the cold dark, unseen. Only when it swings close to the sun does it warm up and grow a glowing tail. After rounding the sun it heads out again, set to return on its next long loop; because of these long, regular orbits, some famous comets return to our skies only once in many human lifetimes.
payload.title: How a comet's orbit brings it back again and again
decoys: A comet grows a tail when it nears the sun
Space objects often follow long journeys
A comet drifts far away and unseen for years

payload.passage: Mira always assumed that the richest-looking family on her street must be the wisest with money. Then she learnt that they had borrowed heavily for their shiny car and big television, and owed more than they owned. A quieter neighbour, who lived simply and saved steadily, actually held far more real wealth. Mira realised that flashy spending can hide a mountain of debt, while plain living can hide quiet riches. She learnt that how much someone shows off tells you very little about how secure their money truly is.
payload.title: Why flashy spending can hide real debt
decoys: The family borrowed for a car and television

payload.passage: Light a candle and tilt it gently; the flame still leans up toward the ceiling. This happens because hot air is lighter than cool air. The flame heats the air around it, and this warm air rises. As it floats up, cooler air slides in from below to take its place. The rising warm air drags the flame upward with it, so the flame keeps pointing to the sky; this is also why a candle would behave very strangely in space, where there is no up for the warm air to rise toward.
payload.title: Why a candle flame always points upward
decoys: Cooler air slides in below to replace the warm air
Heat makes things behave in certain ways
Hot air is lighter than the cool air around it

payload.passage: Imran had nearly finished a model bridge for the fair when he spotted a weak joint that no judge would ever notice. Fixing it meant taking the bridge apart and losing precious time. He was tempted to leave the hidden flaw and present it as it was. Instead he undid the section and rebuilt the joint properly. The bridge held firm under the testing weights and won praise. Imran learnt that doing a job honestly, even in the parts no one inspects, is what makes it truly sound.
payload.title: Honest work is sound even in unseen parts
decoys: Imran rebuilt a weak joint on his bridge
Model bridges are tested with weights
The flaw was hidden from the judges

payload.passage: On the school camping trip, the boys dared one another to wander off the marked path into the dark woods. Manoj badly wanted to prove he was no coward and join them. But he remembered the guide's clear warning about getting lost after dark. He chose to stay on the path, even as the others called him scared. An hour later the wanderers stumbled back, frightened and lost, glad of the lit path Manoj had kept to. Manoj learnt that true courage can mean standing firm against a dare, not giving in to it.
payload.title: Real courage can mean refusing a foolish dare
decoys: Manoj stayed on the marked path
Camping trips can be dangerous after dark
The other boys got lost in the woods

payload.passage: Why does the body have so many nerves running through it? Nerves are like thin wires that carry messages at lightning speed. Some nerves rush news from your skin and eyes to the brain. Others carry the brain's orders out to your muscles. Without this network, the brain could neither sense the world nor move a single finger.
payload.title: How nerves carry messages around the body
decoys: Some nerves carry news from skin to brain
The body is a connected system
Nerves carry orders out to the muscles

payload.passage: Aarush ran a popular sandwich stall but kept all his earnings jumbled with his own pocket money, so he never knew if the stall was really doing well. His teacher suggested keeping the business money in a separate box, with every sale and every cost written down. Suddenly Aarush could see exactly what he earned and spent. The clear figures even showed him which sandwich made the most profit. He learnt that keeping business money apart from personal money is the first step to truly understanding how a small enterprise is doing.
payload.title: Why a business keeps its money separate
decoys: Aarush kept his earnings in a separate box
One sandwich made the most profit

payload.passage: Your nose does far more than just smell flowers. As air passes through it, tiny hairs and sticky lining catch dust and germs. The nose warms the cold air and adds moisture before it reaches your lungs. It also lets you enjoy the rich smells of the world around you. So with every breath, the nose cleans, warms and tests the air you take in.
payload.title: How the nose cleans and warms the air we breathe
decoys: Tiny hairs in the nose catch dust
The body protects itself from harm
The nose lets us enjoy smells

payload.passage: A grove of bamboo grows in a way that helps both people and the earth. Bamboo shoots up faster than almost any other plant, ready to use in just a few years. As it grows, it drinks in a harmful gas and gives back plenty of oxygen. Its roots knit the soil together and stop the banks from crumbling. People use the strong stems to build, weave and make, again and again.
payload.title: Why fast-growing bamboo is good for the earth
decoys: Bamboo grows faster than most plants
Bamboo roots hold the soil together

payload.passage: The decorator crab is soft and slow, an easy target on the busy seabed, so it builds itself a living disguise. With its claws it carefully picks up bits of seaweed, sponge and tiny creatures from around it. Then it sticks these pieces onto small hooks on its own shell, planting a garden on its back. Covered in the very same things that surround it, the crab becomes almost impossible to spot. As it moves to new ground, it redecorates to match. By wearing its surroundings, the decorator crab hides from every hungry eye.
payload.title: How the decorator crab disguises itself with its surroundings
decoys: The decorator crab sticks seaweed to its shell
The seabed is full of hungry hunters

payload.passage: Switching off a tap, a light or a fan when not in use feels like a tiny thing. But across a whole city, millions of these small savings join into a mighty one. Less power is drawn, so less coal is burned and less smoke fills the sky. Less water is wasted, so more is left for the dry days. Each careful choice is a small drop, and together the drops make an ocean.
payload.title: Why small daily savings add up to a big difference
decoys: Switching off a fan saves power
We should care for the planet
Less power burned means less smoke

payload.passage: Many people think the moon belongs only to the night, yet it often shows by day. The moon shines by reflecting sunlight, so it can be seen whenever it is above the horizon. Depending on its phase, it may rise and set during daylight hours. At those times it hangs as a pale shape in the blue sky. It looks faint because the bright daytime sky outshines it. Catching the moon by day is perfectly natural, not at all strange; so spotting a pale moon in a blue sky is a perfectly ordinary part of its monthly travels.
payload.title: Why the moon appears in the daytime sometimes
decoys: The moon can be seen whenever it is above the horizon
The sky holds many sights to notice
The bright day sky makes the moon look faint

payload.passage: Aanya and her brother both sold lemonade, but he kept changing his price every single day, while she kept hers steady. Customers grew confused and annoyed by his shifting prices, never sure what to expect. Slowly they drifted to Aanya's reliable stall. A fair, steady price, she found, built trust far better than clever daily changes. Aanya learnt that customers value knowing what to expect, and that a small business often wins more by being dependable than by chasing a slightly better price each day.
payload.title: Why a steady price builds customer trust
decoys: Her brother changed his price daily
Customers were confused by shifting prices

payload.passage: Drop a stone from a height and it falls faster and faster until it lands. Gravity is pulling it downward the whole way. With every passing moment, that steady pull adds a little more speed to the fall. The longer the stone falls, the quicker it goes by the time it reaches the ground. This is why a jump from a high wall lands harder than one from a low step. So gravity does not just pull things down; it keeps speeding them up as they go.
payload.title: Why a falling object speeds up as it drops
decoys: Gravity adds more speed with each passing moment
Forces change the way objects move
A high jump lands harder than a low one

payload.passage: Why is too much screen time hard on your eyes? Staring at a screen makes you blink far less often than usual. With fewer blinks, the thin layer of tears on your eyes dries out. Dry eyes soon feel tired, gritty and sore. Looking away often and blinking on purpose keeps the eyes moist and comfortable while you use a screen.
payload.title: Why too much screen time tires the eyes
decoys: Staring at a screen makes you blink less
Dry eyes feel gritty and sore

payload.passage: When the African dry season turns the riverbeds to dust, the lungfish faces certain death without water. But it has a remarkable escape. As the mud dries, the fish burrows down and wraps itself in a slimy cocoon, leaving only a tiny breathing hole. Inside this damp case it slows its body almost to a stop and breathes air with a special lung instead of gills. There it waits, asleep in the hard-baked earth, for months on end. When the rains finally return and soak the ground, the lungfish wakes and swims free. By sleeping out the drought, it survives where other fish perish.
payload.title: How the lungfish survives a drought buried in mud
decoys: The lungfish wraps itself in a slimy cocoon
Droughts dry up rivers and ponds
It breathes air with a special lung

payload.passage: Planting trees that belong to your own region is wiser than planting any tree at all. Native trees are used to the local soil and weather, so they grow strong with little fuss. The local birds, insects and animals already know how to use them for food and shelter. Trees brought from far away may need extra water and may not suit the wildlife. Choosing native trees brings the garden and its creatures into harmony.
payload.title: Why native trees are the best ones to plant
decoys: Native trees suit the local soil
Planting trees is a good deed
Local birds already know native trees

payload.passage: Why does washing fruit before eating it matter so much? Fruit often passes through many hands and dusty places before it reaches you. Tiny germs and bits of dirt cling unseen to its skin. Eating it without washing can carry those germs straight into your body. A quick rinse under clean water sweeps the dirt and germs safely away.
payload.title: Why washing fruit before eating keeps us safe
decoys: Germs cling unseen to the skin of fruit
A rinse sweeps the dirt away

payload.passage: The water in a field is always quietly on the move, even when nothing seems to happen. Rain soaks into the soil, where roots drink it up into plants. The plants release much of it from their leaves as invisible vapour. That vapour rises, joins the clouds and later falls again as fresh rain. Some water also sinks deep underground before slowly seeping back to streams. In all these ways, a single patch of ground takes part in the endless journey of water.
payload.title: How water moves from soil to sky and back
decoys: Roots drink rainwater up into the plants
Some water sinks deep underground before returning

payload.passage: The cuckoo is a lazy parent with a sly trick for raising its young without any work. Instead of building a nest, the female cuckoo waits until a smaller bird leaves its nest unguarded. Quickly she lays a single egg among the host's own eggs and flies off for good. The unsuspecting host bird hatches and feeds the cuckoo chick as if it were her own. The cuckoo chick, often larger, may even push the other eggs out to claim all the food. By fooling another bird, the cuckoo gets its chick raised for free.
payload.title: How the cuckoo tricks other birds into raising its chick
decoys: A cuckoo lays its egg in another bird's nest
Birds build nests to raise their young
The cuckoo chick may push out other eggs

payload.passage: Aadhya was amazed that a single small coin could be saved, spent, lent and spent again, passing through many hands in one day. Her teacher explained that money keeps working as it moves: the baker pays the miller, who pays the farmer, who buys bread. The same coin helps many people in turn. Money sitting idle in a drawer helps no one, but money in motion keeps a whole community fed and busy. Aadhya learnt that the true usefulness of money lies not in hoarding it but in keeping it flowing.
payload.title: Why money in motion helps a community
decoys: A coin passed through many hands
The baker pays the miller in turn

payload.passage: Plastic that ends up in the sea does not stay in big pieces forever. The waves and sun slowly break it into tiny bits smaller than a grain of rice. Fish and other sea creatures swallow these tiny bits, mistaking them for food. The bits then move up the food chain, even into the fish that people eat. So plastic dropped on land can one day return to our own plates.
payload.title: How tiny plastic bits travel back to our food
decoys: Waves break plastic into tiny bits
The sea is affected by what we do
Fish swallow the tiny plastic bits

payload.passage: When Aarav drops a letter into the red box outside his post office, he rarely thinks about the long chain that carries it onward. A postal worker empties the box, and the letters are sorted by the names of distant towns and cities. They travel by train, van and sometimes plane to a sorting office near the address. There a local postman walks the streets and slips each letter into the right door. So a single stamp does not buy speed; it buys a careful, many-handed journey that ends at one exact home.
payload.title: How a posted letter reaches the right home
decoys: Letters are first sorted by the towns they must reach
Many useful services quietly run in the background
A postman walks the streets to deliver each letter
